洛夫莱斯临终前呼求女神，即已然蜕变的克拉丽莎·哈洛。这很难称得上是基督教式的死亡。克拉丽莎的死符合新教的教义，但她的意志力却彻底改变了她的命运。

Lovelace dies invoking a goddess, the transfigured Clarissa Harlowe. It is hardly a Christian death. Clarissa dies a Protestant death but one very much transmembered by the force of her will:

“我的好朋友们，”她继续说道，“请不要为一个不为自己悲伤，也没有理由为自己悲伤的人悲伤。相反，请与我一同欢喜，因为我所有的世俗苦难都即将结束。请相信我，先生们，即使可以重温我生命中最美好的时光，我也不愿苟活。然而，我十九年的生命中，已有十八年无比幸福。我曾如此饱受诱惑，如此容易在考验中失败，谁不为所有危险的结束而欢欣鼓舞呢？——我只求得到我亲爱的父母的原谅和祝福。我的离世看似轻松，但如果我能得到他们的祝福，那就更好了。然而，全能的上帝不让我依靠祂以外的任何人来获得安慰。”

I beseech ye, my good friends, proceeded she, mourn not for one who mourns not, nor has cause to mourn, for herself. On the contrary, rejoice with me that all my worldly troubles are so near their end. Believe me, sirs, that I would not, if I might, choose to live, although the pleasantest part of my life were to come over again: and yet eighteen years of it, out of nineteen, have been very pleasant. To be so much exposed to temptation, and to be so liable to fail in the trial, who would not rejoice that all her dangers are over!—All I wished was pardon and blessing from my dear parents. Easy as my departure seems to promise to be, it would have been still easier had I had that pleasure. BUT GOD ALMIGHTY WOULD NOT LET ME DEPEND FOR COMFORT UPON ANY BUT HIMSELF.

理查森希望我们记住，这位高贵的克拉丽莎只有十九岁。说上帝除了祂自己之外收回一切安慰，这并非谦卑之言。她按照自己的意愿死去，并在彼此强烈的意志交融中接受了上帝的敬重。可怜的洛夫莱斯在结尾处的评价相当准确。他对克拉丽莎的最终看法与她自己的评价并无太大差别。

Richardson wishes us to remember that the sublime Clarissa is only nineteen. To say that God withdraws all comfort except Himself is not exactly a humble sentiment. She dies on her own terms and accepts God’s esteem in a mutual exchange of overwhelming wills. Poor Lovelace is quite accurate at the close. His final view of Clarissa is not so very different from her own self-estimate.

我一直对那些给克拉丽莎·哈洛贴标签的评论家感到不耐烦。与理查德·洛夫莱斯相比，克拉丽莎远胜于后者——后者无法像约翰·德莱顿戏剧中的角色那样，完美地融合复辟时期放荡不羁的浪荡子和赫拉克勒斯式的英雄形象——她拥有莎士比亚笔下伟大人物的完整人格。理查森借鉴了莎士比亚对人物内心世界的刻画，克拉丽莎的形象与罗莎琳德或波西亚一样令人信服，尽管她并非出自喜剧，而是源于莎士比亚的悲剧。

I have always been impatient with critics who ascribe flaws to Clarissa Harlowe. Far more than Richard Lovelace, who cannot quite bridge the gap between Restoration libertine and Herculean hero in the mode of John Dryden’s dramas, Clarissa has the wholeness of the great Shakespearean personalities. Richardson appropriates from Shakespeare the representation of inwardness, and Clarissa is as persuasive as Rosalind or Portia, though she stems from Shakespearean tragedy and not from comedy.

1987年，我编辑了一本关于塞缪尔·理查森的评论文集，收录了伊恩·瓦特、马丁·普莱斯和马克·金凯德-威克斯等人的作品。如今，在2018年重读此书，我被最后一篇文章——罗斯玛丽·贝克勒的《解读<克拉丽莎>中的火灾场景》——深深吸引。在我看来，这是我读过的关于这部基督教杰作——探讨内心挣扎以求达到灵魂赤裸裸面对神性——的论述中最具启发性的篇章。

In 1987, I edited a volume of critical essays on Samuel Richardson, including work by Ian Watt, Martin Price, and Mark Kinkead-Weekes. Rereading it now, in 2018, I am captivated by the final essay, “Reading the Fire Scene in Clarissa,” by Rosemary Bechler. It seems to me the most enlightening discussion I have encountered on this Protestant masterpiece of internal struggle to achieve the original bareness of the soul confronting the divine.

贝克勒让我重新认识了威廉·劳（1686-1761），自早期研究威廉·布莱克以来，他一直是我的精神导师。那时我写了一部长篇著作《布莱克的启示录》（1963），还为我的朋友大卫·V·厄德曼编辑的《威廉·布莱克诗歌与散文全集》（1965）撰写了篇幅浩大的评注。威廉·劳是围绕塞缪尔·理查森（一位印刷商、出版商和小说家）的圈子的核心人物。这个圈子包括两位医生乔治·切恩和约翰·弗雷克，以及诗人约翰·拜伦——威廉·劳的门徒，也是诗歌《热情》（1752）的作者。威廉·劳最著名的作品仍然是《虔诚圣洁生活的严肃呼吁》（1729），这部作品激发了伟大的塞缪尔·约翰逊博士的精彩回应：

Bechler returns me to William Law (1686–1761), who has always been a spiritual preceptor to me since my early years as a scholar of William Blake, when I wrote a long study, Blake’s Apocalypse (1963), and also composed an immense commentary for my friend David V. Erdman’s edition of The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (1965). William Law was the center of a circle around Samuel Richardson, who was a printer and publisher as well as a novelist. The group included two physicians, George Cheyne and John Freke, as well as the poet John Byrom, disciple of William Law and author of the poem Enthusiasm (1752). William Law’s most famous work remains A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1729), which inspired a marvelous response from the magnificent Dr. Samuel Johnson:

在牛津的时候，我拿起劳的《严肃的圣洁生活召唤》这本书，原本以为它会很枯燥……甚至可能会嘲笑它。但我发现劳的思想远超我的理解范围；这是我具备理性思考能力之后，第一次认真思考宗教问题。

When at Oxford, I took up Law’s Serious Call to a Holy Life, expecting to find it a dull book…and perhaps to laugh at it. But I found Law quite an overmatch for me; and this was the first occasion of my thinking in earnest of religion, after I became capable of rational inquiry.

劳的后期作品属于雅各布·伯麦（1575-1624）复兴的赫尔墨斯传统。伯麦是一位鞋匠，他曾有过神秘的幻象，将圣父视为火，圣子视为光。为了得救，我们必须在今生经历炼狱般的磨难，并学会解读万物的本质。威廉·布莱克起初对伯麦抱有同情，就像他最初对斯威登堡一样，但他后来认为，像约翰·弥尔顿这样的诗人蕴含着更宏大的真理，而神秘主义者只能触及这些真理的​​皮毛。

Law’s later work was in the hermetic tradition that had been revived by Jacob Boehme (1575–1624). Boehme, a shoemaker, had mystical visions that identified God the Father as fire, and the Son as light. To be saved, we have to go through hell in this life, and learn to read The Signature of All Things. William Blake read Boehme with some sympathy, as he initially did with Swedenborg, but then decided that a poet like John Milton contained the larger truths that the mystics could only touch.

塞缪尔·理查森和他的同伴们意识到要复兴十七世纪英国“内在之光”清教徒的传统：洛夫莱斯曾说过，《圣经》的光芒“太过刺眼，令人难以忍受”。为了对抗这种光芒，他放火烧毁了囚禁克拉丽莎的幽会之所。

Samuel Richardson and his group were conscious of reviving the seventeenth-century tradition of the English Inner Light Puritans: at one point Lovelace remarks that the light of the Bible “is too glaring to be borne.” Against it, he sets on fire the house of assignation in which he has confined Clarissa:

与此同时，多卡斯领我上楼后，并不知道最糟糕的时刻已经过去，她每时每刻都担心房子会燃起熊熊大火。出于对她夫人的怜悯（我永远都会为此爱上这个姑娘），她跑到房门前，用力敲门，声音恢复了些，尖声喊道：“着火了！着火了！房子着火了！夫人，快起来！立刻起来——否则您就会被烧死在床上！”

她刚发出这可怕的叫喊声，我就听到她家的门被猛地猛地打开、打开、解锁，而我那迷人的情人的声音听起来就像是要发疯了一样。

你或许无法想象我当时有多么担心她。我紧张得浑身发抖，为了让她放心，我赶紧跑下楼，速度比听到火警警报时跑上楼的速度还要快，就为了让她知道危险已经过去。

当我飞奔到她房门前时，只见世上最迷人的女子，倚靠在喘息不止的朵卡斯的胳膊上，叹息着，颤抖着，几乎要晕倒。她身上只穿着一件衬裙，美丽的胸脯半开着，脚上也只套着鞋子。她一见到我，便气喘吁吁，努力想说话，却只说了句：“哦，洛夫莱斯先生！”然后便昏了过去。

我紧紧地抱着她，怀里充满了她从未感受过的热情：我亲爱的生命！不要害怕：我已经起来了——危险已经过去——火势已经控制住了——而你（愚蠢的魔鬼！对多卡斯说）怎么能用你那可怕的叫喊声惊吓我的天使呢！

哦，杰克！当我紧紧地抱着她时，她那甜美的胸脯剧烈地起伏着，喘息着！我甚至能感觉到她那颗亲爱的心脏在我胸前怦怦跳动；有那么几分钟，我真怕她会突然发作。

为了防止这位半死不活的美人衣衫不整着着着着着着，我把她抱到床上，坐在床边，用尽全力，无论是行动还是言语，都试图消除她的恐惧。

但我如此慷慨地照顾她，并成功地让她恢复理智，又得到了什么呢？——什么也没有，她如此忘恩负义！除了最激动人心的惊呼之外：因为我们俩都已经忘记了让她投入我怀抱的那个可怕的契机；我，是因为拥抱着她那几乎赤裸的身体而欣喜若狂；她，是因为发现自己在我怀里而感到更大的恐惧，我们俩都坐在那张她不久前还被吓得魂飞魄散的床上。

Meantime Dorcas, after she had directed me upstairs, not knowing the worst was over, and expecting every minute the house would be in a blaze, out of tender regard for her lady (I shall for ever love the wench for it) ran to her door, and rapping loudly at it, in a recovered voice, cried out with a shrillness equal to her love, Fire! Fire!—The house is on fire!—Rise, madam!—This instant rise—if you would not be burnt in your bed!

No sooner had she made this dreadful outcry, but I heard her lady’s door with hasty violence unbar, unbolt, unlock, and open, and my charmer’s voice sounding like that of one going into a fit.

You may believe how much I was affected. I trembled with concern for her, and hastened down faster than the alarm of fire had made me run up, in order to satisfy her that all the danger was over.

When I had flown down to her chamber door, there I beheld the charmingest creature in the world, supporting herself on the arm of the gasping Dorcas, sighing, trembling, and ready to faint, with nothing on but an under-petticoat, her lovely bosom half-open, and her feet just slipped into her shoes. As soon as she saw me, she panted, and struggled to speak; but could only say, oh, Mr Lovelace! and down was ready to sink.

I clasped her in my arms with an ardour she never felt before: My dearest life! fear nothing: I have been up—the danger is over—the fire is got under—And how (foolish devil! to Dorcas) could you thus, by your hideous yell, alarm and frighten my angel!

Oh Jack! how her sweet bosom, as I clasped her to mine, heaved and panted! I could even distinguish her dear heart flutter, flutter, flutter, against mine; and for a few minutes, I feared she would go into fits.

Lest the half-lifeless charmer should catch cold in this undress, I lifted her to her bed, and sat down by her upon the side of it, endeavouring with the utmost tenderness, as well of action as expression, to dissipate her terrors.

But what did I get by this my generous care of her, and by my successful endeavour to bring her to herself?—Nothing, ungrateful as she was! but the most passionate exclamations: for we had both already forgot the occasion, dreadful as it was, which had thrown her into my arms; I, from the joy of encircling the almost disrobed body of the loveliest of her sex; she, from the greater terrors that arose from finding herself in my arms, and both seated on the bed from which she had been so lately frighted.

洛夫莱斯对克拉丽莎的欲望中蕴含着虐待狂的成分，这一点怎么强调都不为过。他时而化身为浪荡子，时而又化身为德莱顿笔下赫拉克勒斯式的英雄，这种转变带有精神分裂的痕迹，更接近马洛而非莎士比亚。作为虐待狂，他当着老鸨和妓女的面，在掺有迷药的酒精的帮助下，强奸了克拉丽莎·哈洛。这场强奸将摧毁他们两人。克拉丽莎的意志和尊严遭到践踏，她对他可能存在的爱也永远消失了。由于她卓越的精神境界，这场悲剧对她而言更加沉重，但对洛夫莱斯来说，这也是一场悲剧，因为他内心深处的英雄情结让他真切地爱着她。

The sadistic element in Lovelace’s lust for Clarissa cannot be overstated. There is a schizophrenic trace in his alternations as rake and as Dryden’s Herculean hero, more in the mode of Marlowe than of Shakespeare. As sadistic rake he rapes Clarissa Harlowe, in the actual presence of procuress and whores, and with the aid of drugged alcohol. The rape will destroy them both. With her will and integrity violated, Clarissa’s possible love for him vanishes forever. The tragedy, because of her spiritual eminence, is greater for her, yet for Lovelace it is tragic also, because the heroic strain in him authentically loves her.

我当时丝毫没有怀疑这些女人并非她们所扮演的贵妇人；我责怪自己胆怯——我想，这样的贵妇人怎么可能唆使别人背叛她们如此疼爱的可怜人呢？她们肯定就是她们所表现的那个人——怀疑这一点真是愚蠢！贵妇人的气质、衣着、风度——我心想，这种卑劣的怀疑是多么不配她们，也多么不配我的仁慈啊！

于是，我努力恢复着昏沉的情绪（因为我越来越沉重，便问多卡斯我到底怎么了；我揉着眼睛，一小撮一小撮地吸着她的鼻烟，却几乎毫无作用），继续我的工作：但当工作结束，所有我打算收拾的东西都打包完毕后，我除了思考别无他事；他们迟迟不来，我心想自己恐怕都要疯了。我把自己关进那间曾经属于我的房间；我跪下，我祈祷；却不知自己祈求什么：然后我又跑了出去。天色已近黄昏，我问道：洛夫莱斯先生在哪里？在哪里？

他走到我面前，起初丝毫没有注意到我的惊恐和疯狂（他们给我的东西让我语无伦次、神志不清）：他说，亲爱的，一切都好！——出自《汤姆林森船长》！

一切进展得确实很顺利，这对于最残忍、最邪恶的人来说，都是一个邪恶计划！

我要求见他的姑妈！——我要求见他的表哥！——我说，夜幕降临了！——我记得，我说，我的头非常非常难受——而且越来越难受。

然而，恐惧仍然鼓舞着我；我坚持让他亲自去，以加快他们的步伐。

他叫来仆人，对着那两个女人破口大骂，责怪她们迟到：“幸好，重要的事很少取决于这些爱出风头、不守时的琐碎之人！”

他的仆人来了。

他命令他飞去他表兄利森家；并告诉他的姑妈和表兄妹，他们迟迟不来，我们俩都非常不安；他还自作主张地补充道：“让他们如果不能马上来，就派马车来，我们自己去。告诉他们，我真不知道他们会怎么为我效力！”

我觉得这话说得体贴周到，也算公平。但现在，尽管我心不在焉，却还是有时间仔细想想这个人以及他的举止。他那眼神，以及他注视我时流露出的强烈情绪，都让我感到恐惧。后来我才想起，他显然压抑着喜悦。他说话简短有力，仿佛呼吸都有些急促。我从未见过他那双令人作呕的眼睛，当时那双眼睛里充满了胜利的意味！凶狠而狂野；比我第一次见到那间肮脏房子里的女人们的眼睛还要令人厌恶：有时，他那眼神里透着一股猥琐的邪气！——我宁愿离他一百英里远。然而，他的行为举止却还算体面——尽管这种体面似乎是费尽心思才得来的——因为他两三次用力地抓住我的手，力道之大让我感到疼痛；他咬牙切齿地说着一些温柔的话；他用乞丐般卑微的嗓音说道，就像刚才那个卑鄙的女人一样；语气半是内敛的；然而他的言辞和举止却流露出强烈而近乎疯狂的激情！——哦，我的天哪！他当时究竟在盘算着什么恶作剧呢！

我抱怨了一两次口渴，感觉嘴巴干裂。当时，我以为是恐惧（我经常喘不过气来）导致上颚干裂。我叫人给我水喝，结果端来的是些桌上啤酒。我想，如果我之前喝的药不够多，啤酒或许是他们那些药水的更好载体。我告诉女仆，她知道我很少喝麦芽酒，但她对此毫无戒心，又渴得厉害，于是我喝了下去，接下来发生的事也与此无关：结果，我立刻感觉比之前更糟，就像喝醉了一样，我也不知道为什么。

他的仆人离开的时间比他需要的时间长了一倍：就在他回来之前，一个假扮成贝蒂夫人的人带着一封给洛夫莱斯先生的信来了。

他把信寄给了我。我读了之后，顿觉自己彻底完了。信里说，蒙塔古小姐当晚要去汉普斯特德，但蒙塔古小姐假装突发重病，所以推迟了行程。这时，我脑海里立刻浮现出他在这所房子里对我卑鄙的企图；想到我逃跑很可能激起他的报复，想到我之前难以原谅他、难以与他和解；想到他那凶神恶煞的眼神，我就害怕不已；想到这房子里的女人们，就连假扮贝蒂夫人的那些暗示，都让我更加恐惧。所有这些念头在我焦虑不安的脑海中翻腾，我几乎陷入了疯狂。

我不记得在那段时间里我是什么状态了；但我知道，在最初的激动中，我扯下头饰，撕碎了褶边，跑去找他。

稍稍缓过神来后，我坚持要他之前暗示的关于他们马车的事。但他告诉我，信使告诉他，马车是去请医生的，以免他的马车被收起来或还没准备好。

于是我坚持直接前往贝蒂夫人的住处。

他说，利森太太家现在人满为患；而我的急切恐怕只是出于毫无根据的担忧（哦，他当时发了多少誓言，做了多少维护自己名誉的保证啊！），所以他希望我不会给他们增添麻烦。他还说，夏洛特确实习惯了因任何突如其来的变故而发作，无论是喜悦还是悲伤；如果几个小时都无法缓解，她就会发作一个星期。

“亲爱的，你真是个观察眼睛的人，”恶棍说道；或许是在暗中侮辱你：“你难道没在汉普斯特德的蒙塔古小姐家偶尔看到她有些放荡不羁的样子吗？——我当时真为她担心——沉默和安静对她只有好处：如果你走了，你对她的关心，以及她对你的爱，只会加重这个可怜女孩的不安。”

尽管悲痛和忧虑让我焦躁不安，我仍然下定决心，绝不在那所房子里待到天亮。我倾尽所有，戒指、手表、微薄的积蓄，只为换一辆马车！如果实在找不到马车，我就当晚步行去汉普斯特德，哪怕是独自一人。

于是，有人派人去叫马车，或者假装去叫。他说，为了感谢我，无论多晚，他都愿意付出任何代价；他会全心全意地服侍我——但马车始终没能叫到。

剩下的我就不多说了。我的精神状态越来越差，时而愚钝，时而胡言乱语，时而神志不清。一个极其邪恶的女人被带过来吓唬我。我从未见过像她那样可怕的生物。

我记得，我曾苦苦哀求——我记得我说过我愿效忠于他——真的，我愿效忠于他——只为博得他的怜悯——但我却未得怜悯！——我的力量，我的理智，都已耗尽！——然后便是那般景象——哦，亲爱的，那般可怕的景象！——一次又一次的惊恐（的确，记忆模糊，断断续续）未能换来任何怜悯——但死神却从我身边留了下来。那对我来说未免太过仁慈了！

I had no suspicion yet that these women were not indeed the ladies they personated; and I blamed myself for my weak fears—It cannot be, thought I, that such ladies will abet treachery against a poor creature they are so fond of. They must undoubtedly be the persons they appear to be—what folly to doubt it! The air, the dress, the dignity, of women of quality—How unworthy of them, and of my charity, concluded I, is this ungenerous shadow of suspicion!

So, recovering my stupefied spirits as well as they could be recovered (for I was heavier and heavier; and wondered to Dorcas what ailed me; rubbing my eyes, and taking some of her snuff, pinch after pinch, to very little purpose), I pursued my employment: but when that was over, all packed up that I designed to be packed up; and I had nothing to do but to think; and found them tarry so long; I thought I should have gone distracted. I shut myself into the chamber that had been mine; I kneeled, I prayed; yet knew not what I prayed for: then ran out again. It was almost dark night, I said: where, where, was Mr Lovelace?

He came to me, taking no notice at first of my consternation and wildness (what they had given me made me incoherent and wild): All goes well, said he, my dear!—A line from Captain Tomlinson!

All indeed did go well for the villainous project of the most cruel and most villainous of men!

I demanded his aunt!—I demanded his cousin!—The evening, I said, was closing!—My head was very, very bad, I remember, I said—And it grew worse and worse.

Terror, however, as yet kept up my spirits; and I insisted upon his going himself to hasten them.

He called his servant. He raved at the sex for their delay: ’twas well that business of consequence seldom depended upon such parading, unpunctual triflers!

His servant came.

He ordered him to fly to his cousin Leeson’s; and to let his aunt and cousins know how uneasy we both were at their delay: adding, of his own accord, Desire them, if they don’t come instantly, to send their coach and we will go without them. Tell them I wonder they’ll serve me so!

I thought this was considerately and fairly put. But now, indifferent as my head was, I had a little time to consider the man and his behaviour. He terrified me with his looks, and with his violent emotions as he gazed upon me. Evident joy-suppressed emotions, as I have since recollected. His sentences short, and pronounced as if his breath were touched. Never saw I his abominable eyes look, as then they looked—triumph in them!—fierce and wild; and more disagreeable than the women’s at the vile house appeared to me when I first saw them: and at times, such a leering, mischief-boding cast!—I would have given the world to have been an hundred miles from him. Yet his behaviour was decent—a decency, however, that I might have seen to be struggled for—for he snatched my hand two or three times with a vehemence in his grasp that hurt me; speaking words of tenderness through his shut teeth, as it seemed; and let it go with a beggar-voiced humble accent, like the vile woman’s just before; half-inward; yet his words and manner carrying the appearance of strong and almost convulsed passion!—Oh my dear! What mischief was he not then meditating!

I complained once or twice of thirst. My mouth seemed parched. At the time, I supposed that it was my terror (gasping often as I did for breath) that parched up the roof of my mouth. I called for water: some table-beer was brought me. Beer, I suppose, was a better vehicle (if I were not dosed enough before) for their potions. I told the maid that she knew I seldom tasted malt-liquor: yet, suspecting nothing of this nature, being extremely thirsty I drank it, as what came next: and instantly, as it were, found myself much worse than before; as if inebriated, I should fancy: I know not how.

His servant was gone twice as long as he needed: and, just before his return, came one of the pretended Lady Betty’s, with a letter for Mr Lovelace.

He sent it up to me. I read it: and then it was that I thought myself a lost creature; it being to put off her going to Hampstead that night, on account of violent fits which Miss Montague was pretended to be seized with: for then immediately came into my head his vile attempt upon me in this house; the revenge that my flight might too probably inspire him with on that occasion, and because of the difficulty I made to forgive him and to be reconciled to him; his very looks wild and dreadful to me; and the women of the house such as I had more reason than ever, even from the pretended Lady Betty’s hints, to be afraid of: all these crowding together in my apprehensive mind, I fell into a kind of frenzy.

I have not remembrance how I was for the time it lasted: but I know that in my first agitations I pulled off my head-dress, and tore my ruffles in twenty tatters; and ran to find him out.

When a little recovered, I insisted upon the hint he had given of their coach. But the messenger, he said, had told him that it was sent to fetch a physician, lest his chariot should be put up, or not ready.

I then insisted upon going directly to Lady Betty’s lodgings.

Mrs Leeson’s was now a crowded house, he said: and as my earnestness could be owing to nothing but groundless apprehension (and oh what vows, what protestations of his honour did he then make!), he hoped I would not add to their present concern. Charlotte, indeed, was used to fits, he said, upon any great surprises, whether of joy or grief; and they would hold her for a week together if not got off in a few hours.

You are an observer of eyes, my dear, said the villain; perhaps in secret insult: saw you not in Miss Montague’s now and then, at Hampstead, something wildish?—I was afraid for her then—Silence and quiet only do her good: your concern for her, and her love for you, will but augment the poor girl’s disorder, if you should go.

All impatient with grief and apprehension, I still declared myself resolved not to stay in that house till morning. All I had in the world, my rings, my watch, my little money, for a coach! or, if one were not to be got, I would go on foot to Hampstead that night, though I walked it by myself.

A coach was hereupon sent for, or pretended to be sent for. Any price, he said, he would give to oblige me, late as it was; and he would attend me with all his soul—But no coach was to be got.

Let me cut short the rest. I grew worse and worse in my head; now stupid, now raving, now senseless. The vilest of vile women was brought to frighten me. Never was there so horrible a creature as she appeared to me at the time.

I remember, I pleaded for mercy—I remember that I said I would be his—indeed I would be his—to obtain his mercy—But no mercy found I!—My strength, my intellects, failed me!—And then such scenes followed—Oh my dear, such dreadful scenes!—fits upon fits (faintly indeed, and imperfectly remembered) procuring me no compassion—but death was withheld from me. That would have been too great a mercy!

洛夫莱斯终将明白，他对克拉丽莎的强奸对他来说是一场毁灭性的失败。

Lovelace will come to understand that his rape of Clarissa was an apocalyptic defeat for him.

他的觉悟来得很慢：直到洛夫莱斯突然意识到克拉丽莎对他来说是一个辩证的陷阱时，他才恍然大悟：

His realization is slow: it comes when Lovelace suddenly apprehends the dialectical entrapment Clarissa has been for him:

真是个可怕的宝贝！——我的天哪，她让我不寒而栗！她居然还想诉说自己的不幸，落入了世上唯一一个能像我这样对待她的男人手中！而她，也是世上唯一一个能像她这样让我震惊和不安的女人——在这方面，我们算是势均力敌。而且我觉得我比她惨得多。因为我几乎没得到什么快乐，却饱受折磨；而她所谓的惩罚，已经结束了；至于我的惩罚何时结束，或者会是什么样，谁又能说得准呢？

在这里，我只是在重复之前的话（想想我当时的心情），我不得不停下来，自言自语地唱起歌来。我本想唱一首欢快的曲子，结果却唱得嘶哑难听，最后还是落入了1月30日那阴郁沉闷的旋律中。我努力想唱出一个更轻快的音符，但还是不行，最后，我像个罪犯一样，唱出了一首死气沉沉的赞美诗。

嗨哟！——我像一只刚长出羽毛的风筝在巢里张着嘴，想吞下被它那横冲直撞的水坝在嘴边晃来晃去的小鸡！——

我这是怎么了！——我既不能思考也不能写作！——

笔啊，躺下一会儿吧！

（第226封信）

A horrid dear creature!—By my soul, she made me shudder! She had need, indeed, to talk of her unhappiness, in falling into the hands of the only man in the world who could have used her as I have used her! She is the only woman in the world who could have shocked and disturbed me as she has done—So we are upon a foot in that respect. And I think I have the worst of it by much. Since very little has been my joy; very much my trouble: and her punishment, as she calls it, is over: but when mine will, or what it may be, who can tell?

Here, only recapitulating (think, then, how I must be affected at the time), I was forced to leave off, and sing a song to myself. I aimed at a lively air; but I croaked rather than sung: and fell into the old dismal thirtieth of January strain. I hemmed up for a sprightlier note; but it would not do: and at last I ended, like a malefactor, in a dead psalm melody.

High-ho!—I gape like an unfledged kite in its nest, wanting to swallow a chicken, bobbed at its mouth by its marauding dam!—

What a devil ails me!—I can neither think nor write!—

Lie down, pen, for a moment!—

(Letter 226)

折磨他的魔鬼正是他走向毁灭的开端，他从残存的自由主义思想中彻底堕落，坠入被克拉丽莎击败的可怕深渊，被迫承认自我意志和自我主张对他而言已彻底终结。克拉丽莎，这位严苛的清教徒，不屑于接受他自认为的评价，他开始明白，从现实角度来看，他们已经互相毁灭。他的真正死亡，是对克拉丽莎死后他所遭受的“生不如死”之苦的一种解脱。

The devil that ails him is the beginning of his own end, his falling outward and downward from his last shreds of a libertine ideology into the dreadful inner space of his defeat by Clarissa, his enforced realization that self-willing and self-assertion are permanently over for him. Clarissa, a great Puritan withholder of esteem, will not accept him at his own evaluation, and he begins to know that pragmatically they have destroyed one another. His actual death is a release from the death-in-life he has suffered since Clarissa’s death.

克拉丽莎·哈洛的形象比所有受她影响的新教女性形象都要宏大：简·奥斯汀笔下的伊丽莎白·班纳特、艾玛·伍德豪斯、安妮·艾略特；霍桑笔下的海丝特·白兰；乔治·艾略特笔下的多萝西娅·布鲁克；托马斯·哈代笔下的苏·布莱德海德；亨利·詹姆斯笔下的伊莎贝尔·阿切尔、米莉·西尔；D·H·劳伦斯笔下的厄休拉·布兰温；E·M·福斯特笔下的玛格丽特·施莱格尔；以及弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫笔下的莉莉·布里斯科。这种宏大的形象是塞缪尔·理查森对莎士比亚式人物的致敬。克拉丽莎内心的光芒缓和了神圣愤怒的烈焰。如果说存在一位新教版的但丁笔下的贝阿特丽切，那非克拉丽莎·哈洛莫属。

Clarissa Harlowe is a larger form than all the heroines of the Protestant will descended from her: Jane Austen’s Elizabeth Bennet, Emma Woodhouse, Anne Elliot; Hawthorne’s Hester Prynne; George Eliot’s Dorothea Brooke; Thomas Hardy’s Sue Bridehead; Henry James’s Isabel Archer, Milly Theale; D. H. Lawrence’s Ursula Brangwen; E. M. Forster’s Margaret Schlegel; and Virginia Woolf’s Lily Briscoe. The largeness is Samuel Richardson’s Shakespearean triumph. The fire of divine wrath is mitigated by Clarissa’s inward light. If there could be a Protestant version of Dante’s Beatrice, it would be Clarissa Harlowe.

第三章

CHAPTER 3

汤姆·琼斯（1749）

Tom Jones (1749)

亨利·菲尔丁​

HENRY FIELDING

在我看来，威廉·埃姆普森越来越像是二十世纪最有用的文学批评家。但我更应该感谢伟大的加拿大哲学家诺思罗普·弗莱，他的著作塑造了我二十年，从1947年到1967年。直到有一天晚上，我做了一个噩梦，梦中出现了以西结和威廉·布莱克所说的“遮蔽天使”，之后我对他的著作产生了抵触情绪。

WILLIAM EMPSON increasingly seems to me the most useful literary critic of the twentieth century. I owe a lot more to the great Canadian magus Northrop Frye, whose writings formed me for twenty years, from 1947 to 1967, when I reacted against them after a night of bad dreams concerning the figure that Ezekiel and William Blake called the Covering Cherub:

你是那受膏遮盖神的基路伯，我已立你如此。你曾在神的圣山上，在火石中间行走。

你从受造之日起，行事完全，直到你里面发现了罪恶。

因你货物众多，他们使你中间充满了强暴，你犯了罪；因此，我必将你从神的山上赶出去，遮蔽基路伯的啊，我必将你从火石中除灭。

（以西结书 28:14-16，英王钦定本）

Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire.

Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.

By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God: and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.

(Ezekiel 28:14–16, KJV)

我杰出的学生利奥波德·达姆罗什二世在其著作《上帝的阴谋与人类的故事》（1985）中，开篇便断言菲尔丁的《汤姆·琼斯》是十八世纪最杰出的文学作品。我个人更偏爱塞缪尔·理查森的《克拉丽莎》而非《汤姆·琼斯》，因此不禁疑惑，达姆罗什为何更青睐菲尔丁而非乔纳森·斯威夫特、亚历山大·蒲柏、塞缪尔·约翰逊和威廉·布莱克。不过，达姆罗什的论证也颇具说服力。在他看来，《汤姆·琼斯》虽然告别了天命论式的虚构作品，却依然肯定了仁慈上帝的存在。

My distinguished former student Leopold Damrosch, Jr., in his book God’s Plot and Man’s Stories (1985), begins with the judgment that the most eminent literary work of the eighteenth century is Fielding’s Tom Jones. I am more attached to Samuel Richardson’s Clarissa than to Tom Jones, and wonder why Damrosch prefers Fielding to Jonathan Swift, Alexander Pope, Samuel Johnson, and William Blake. Still, Damrosch argues a considerable case. For him Tom Jones, though a farewell to providential fiction, nevertheless affirms the presence of a benign God:

《汤姆·琼斯》的奇妙之处在于它完美地平衡了情节的决定论和人物的自由意志。在上帝预定的宏大因果模式中，人类依然可以自由地即兴发挥和改变。菲尔丁和班扬、理查森一样都是基督徒，因此他也像他们一样宣扬天意安排的宇宙，但他笔下的堕落人生却截然不同，他的小说创作模式也与他们截然不同。

The marvel of Tom Jones is that it balances so perfectly between determinism of plot and freedom of character. Within the large patterns of causality that God ordains, human beings remain free to improvise and change. Like Bunyan and Richardson, Fielding is a Christian, and like them he therefore asserts a providential universe, but fallen life looks altogether different to him, and his mode of fiction stands in permanent opposition to theirs.

我不确定埃姆森会如何看待这件事。他不太喜欢T·S·艾略特及其批判追随者的新基督教思想。菲尔丁笔下的堕落人生，确实与班扬和理查森的设想截然不同。从实际角度来看，它充其量也只是伊甸园般的景象。书中结尾处索菲娅·韦斯特恩和汤姆·琼斯的婚姻，象征着未堕落的夏娃和重生的亚当。

I am not sure what Empson would make of that. He did not much care for the neo-Christianity of T. S. Eliot and his critical disciples. Fallen life to Fielding, indeed, is very different from the visions of Bunyan and Richardson. Pragmatically, it seems at its best Edenic. The marriage of Sophia Western and Tom Jones at the close of the book is that of an unfallen Eve and a regenerate Adam.

我已故的朋友兼同事马丁·普莱斯曾说过：“菲尔丁笔下的英雄之所以能获得奖赏，是因为他们不求回报。”另一位朋友兼恩师，已故的弗雷德里克·W·希尔斯，喜欢将《汤姆·琼斯》与乔伊斯的《尤利西斯》相提并论，尽管他也承认菲尔丁作为叙述者既非冷漠无情，也非隐形人。《汤姆·琼斯》是一部喜剧版的奥德赛，因此也是查尔斯·狄更斯和詹姆斯·乔伊斯作品的先驱。

My late friend and colleague Martin Price observed, “Fielding can reward his heroes because they do not seek a reward.” Another friend and former teacher, the late Frederick W. Hilles, enjoyed comparing Tom Jones to Joyce’s Ulysses, though he acknowledged that Fielding as narrator was neither indifferent nor invisible. Tom Jones is a comic Odyssey, and so the ancestor of both Charles Dickens and James Joyce.

我一生都崇拜塞缪尔·约翰逊博士，但他强烈厌恶菲尔丁的所有作品，这让我有些困惑。我本人也和约翰逊一样，更喜欢塞缪尔·理查森而非菲尔丁，尽管我很喜欢《汤姆·琼斯》，但《克拉丽莎》在我看来始终是英语文学中最杰出的小说，甚至超越了简·奥斯汀、乔治·艾略特、亨利·詹姆斯以及他们所有后继者的作品。当然，还有以狄更斯和乔伊斯为代表的另一种文学传统，其伟大先驱便是《汤姆·琼斯》，但即便如此，他们也无疑超越了菲尔丁的最佳作品。

I have idolized Dr. Samuel Johnson all my life but am somewhat baffled that he strongly disliked all of Fielding’s work. I myself share Johnson’s preference for Samuel Richardson over Fielding, though I love Tom Jones, but, then, Clarissa always seems to me much the strongest novel in the English language, surpassing even the works of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James, and all their descendants. There is the alternative tradition that includes Dickens and Joyce, and it finds its great precursor in Tom Jones, and yet certainly they surpass Fielding even at his best.

在约翰逊看来，菲尔丁的风格过于简单，但我们最伟大的评论家却误判了菲尔丁这位喜剧演员身上蕴藏的精明道德家的一面。我记得我曾大胆地指出，菲尔丁和理查森实际上瓜分了莎士比亚的艺术。理查森部分吸收了莎士比亚刻画内心世界的独特天赋，而菲尔丁则选择强调莎士比亚作品中那种能够如此巧妙地描绘浪漫世界的力量，以至于浪漫世界仿佛比现实本身更加真实。

For Johnson, Fielding was simplistic, but the greatest of our critics misread how shrewd a moralist the comic Fielding could be. I recall venturing that Fielding and Richardson in effect split up Shakespeare between them. Shakespeare’s unique gift for representing inwardness was partly absorbed by Richardson, whereas Fielding chose to emphasize the Shakespearean power that could depict the world of romance so deftly that it seemed to become more real than reality.

《汤姆·琼斯》的读者有时会与这位桀骜不驯的主人公产生共鸣，他精力充沛，总是随时准备行动，无论是打架、寻欢作乐、狩猎，还是在任何时刻展现他的善良。他真心实意地爱上了索菲娅·韦斯特恩，但两人却经历了一段曲折坎坷的旅程，直到故事的结尾，他们才最终团聚。

Readers of Tom Jones sometimes identify with the rambunctious hero, whose exuberance renders him always ready for rapid activity, whether it be fighting, whoring, hunting, or exercising his good-heartedness at every moment that comes along. He falls truly and permanently in love with Sophia Western, yet follows a labyrinthine path until, at last, they are united, at the very close of the book.

你不会去读菲尔丁的作品来探寻灵魂的历程。他的写作风格排斥内省，甚至对他自己创造的“菲尔丁”——这个始终与我们同在的叙述者——都抱持怀疑态度，这使他摆脱了自我意识的重负。约翰逊不顾博斯韦尔的反对，坚持认为：“理查森的一封信中所蕴含的关于人心的知识，比整部《汤姆·琼斯》加起来还要多。  ”这种过分的论断源于约翰逊的信念：理查森为我们展现的是“自然的性格”，而菲尔丁只能展现“风俗的性格”。理查森是一位杰出的心理学家，他曾坚称自己不会读《汤姆·琼斯》。但我怀疑他其实读过，因为他评论说菲尔丁忽略了概率论。《汤姆·琼斯》的出版距离七卷本《克拉丽莎》出版仅几周之隔，而《克拉丽莎》的出版历时一年。显然，两部作品都卖得相当不错。菲尔丁比性格阴郁的理查森要和蔼得多，他读完了《克拉丽莎》，然后给理查森写了一封热情洋溢的赞扬信。这两位小说家就像亨利·詹姆斯和詹姆斯·乔伊斯，或者福楼拜和维克多·雨果一样，截然相反。

You do not go to Fielding to trace the progress of the soul. His mode excludes inwardness, and his skepticism even toward his own created self, the “Fielding” who as narrator is always with us, absolves him from the burden of self-consciousness. Johnson, pushing away Boswell’s protests, insisted, “There is more knowledge of the heart in one letter of Richardson’s, than in all ‘Tom Jones.’ ” This excessive judgment depends upon Johnson’s conviction that Richardson gave us “characters of nature” whereas Fielding could only give us “characters of manners.” Richardson, an extraordinary psychologist, insisted that he would not read Tom Jones. I suspect that he did read it, since he comments that Fielding neglected Probability. Tom Jones was published only some weeks after the yearlong appearance of the seven volumes of Clarissa. Both evidently sold quite well, and Fielding, a much more genial person than the dour Richardson, consumed all of Clarissa and then wrote a generous letter of praise to Richardson. The two novelists were as antithetical as Henry James and James Joyce, or as Flaubert and Victor Hugo.

对我而言，我相信对大多数读者来说也是如此，《汤姆·琼斯》的亮点无疑是颇具莎士比亚风格的韦斯特恩乡绅，索菲娅那不太靠谱的父亲，休·格里菲斯在1963年托尼·理查森执导、约翰·奥斯本编剧的电影版中将这个角色演绎得淋漓尽致。尽管阿尔伯特·芬尼饰演的私生子汤姆·琼斯魅力十足，但格里菲斯凭借其近乎疯狂的活力、暴力和魔性的力量，彻底抢走了整部电影的风头。他仿佛是弗洛伊德笔下失控的肉体自我。韦斯特恩乡绅绝非莎士比亚笔下的福斯塔夫或乔叟笔下的巴斯妇。后者拥有危险的智慧和无可争议的英雄气概，他们赋予我们生命。韦斯特恩讽刺了这种生命力，但他触及了再现的极限，能够游离于小说之外，存在于莎士比亚、塞万提斯、乔叟和但丁才能带给我们的超越模仿的世界。以下便是韦斯特恩乡绅失控的一个例子：

For me, and I would believe for most readers, the glory of Tom Jones has to be the quite Shakespearean Squire Western, Sophia’s improbable father, magnificently played by Hugh Griffith in the 1963 film version directed by Tony Richardson from the screenplay of John Osborne. Charming as Albert Finney was as the bastard Tom Jones, Griffith steals the movie with his absolutely mindless energy, violence, and daemonic force. He seems to be the Freudian bodily ego run rampant. Squire Western is hardly Shakespeare’s Falstaff or Chaucer’s Wife of Bath. They have dangerous wit and indisputably heroic vitalism. They give us life. Western parodies vitalism, and yet he touches the limits of representation and can live outside the novel in that world beyond mimesis that only Shakespeare, Cervantes, Chaucer, and Dante can give us. Here is an instance of the Squire run wild:

韦斯特恩早就盼着这次会议，此刻他刚到门口准备听，听到女儿最后的心声，顿时怒火中烧，猛地推开门，大声喊道：“全是谎言！全是弥天大谎！都是那个该死的琼斯害的！要是她能找到我，她随时都想把我揍一顿！”这时，奥尔沃西插话进来，怒气冲冲地对乡绅说：“韦斯特恩先生，你没有信守诺言。你答应过要克制自己，不诉诸暴力。”韦斯特恩喊道：“我的确做到了，只要有可能就做到了；可是听到一个丫头说出如此荒谬的谎言——真是岂有此理！”她以为，既然她能把其他人变成奴隶，也能把我变成奴隶吗？——不，不，我比你更了解她。’——‘很遗憾地告诉你，先生，’奥尔沃西回答说，‘从你对待这位年轻女士的态度来看，你似乎根本不了解她。请原谅我这么说；但我认为，我们之间的亲密关系、你的欲望以及当时的场合都足以让我这么说。她是你的女儿，韦斯特恩先生，我认为她会给你的名声增光。如果我会嫉妒，我宁愿为此嫉妒你，而不是嫉妒其他任何人。’——‘真可恶！’乡绅喊道，‘我真希望她是你的——我很快就会摆脱她这个麻烦。’——‘的确，我的好朋友，’奥尔沃西回答说，‘你抱怨的所有麻烦都是你自己造成的。’ “把这份信任托付给这位小姐，她完全值得，我相信你一定会成为世上最幸福的父亲。”——“信任她？”侍从喊道，“该死！她不肯按我的意愿行事，我怎么能信任她？只要她同意按我的意愿嫁给我，我就会像信任我一样信任她。”——“邻居，你无权，”奥尔沃西回答道，“强求她同意。你女儿允许你发出反对的声音，上帝和自然都不允许你再多说一句。”——“反对的声音！”侍从喊道，“是啊！是啊！我这就让你见识见识我的反对声音有多大。——走吧，回你的房间去，走吧，你这个固执的——” “韦斯特恩先生，”奥尔沃西说道，“你对她太残忍了——我实在看不下去——你必须，也应该对她好一点。她值得最好的对待。”——“是是是，”乡绅说道，“我知道她该受什么：现在她走了，我这就让你看看她该受什么。先生，你看，这是我表妹贝拉斯顿夫人的来信，她好心地告诉我，那家伙又出狱了；她还嘱咐我好好照顾这个丫头。哎呀！奥尔沃西先生，你根本不知道管教女儿是什么滋味。”

Western had been long impatient for the event of this conference, and was just now arrived at the door to listen; when, having heard the last sentiments of his daughter’s heart, he lost all temper, and, bursting open the door in a rage, cried out—‘It is a lie! It is a d—n’d lie! It is all owing to that d—n’d rascal Jones; and if she could get at un, she’d ha’ un any hour of the day.’ Here Allworthy interposed, and addressing himself to the squire with some anger in his look, he said, ‘Mr Western, you have not kept your word with me. You promised to abstain from all violence.’—‘Why, so I did,’ cries Western, ‘as long as it was possible; but to hear a wench telling such confounded lies—Zounds! doth she think, if she can make vools of other volk, she can make one of me?—No, no, I know her better than thee dost.’—‘I am sorry to tell you, sir,’ answered Allworthy, ‘it doth not appear, by your behaviour to this young lady, that you know her at all. I ask pardon for what I say; but I think our intimacy, your own desires, and the occasion justify me. She is your daughter, Mr Western, and I think she doth honour to your name. If I was capable of envy, I should sooner envy you on this account than any other man whatever.’—‘Odrabbit it!’ cries the squire, ‘I wish she was thine, with all my heart—wouldst soon be glad to be rid of the trouble o’ her.’—‘Indeed, my good friend,’ answered Allworthy, ‘you yourself are the cause of all the trouble you complain of. Place that confidence in the young lady which she so well deserves, and I am certain you will be the happiest father on earth.’—‘I confidence in her?’ cries the squire. ‘ ’Sblood! what confidence can I place in her, when she won’t do as I would ha’ her? Let her gi’ but her consent to marry as I would ha’ her, and I’ll place as much confidence in her as wouldst ha’ me.’—‘You have no right, neighbour,’ answered Allworthy, ‘to insist on any such consent. A negative voice your daughter allows you, and God and nature have thought proper to allow you no more.’—‘A negative voice!’ cries the squire—‘Ay! ay! I’ll show you what a negative voice I ha.—Go along, go into your chamber, go, you stubborn—.’ ‘Indeed, Mr Western,’ said Allworthy, ‘indeed you use her cruelly—I cannot bear to see this—you shall, you must behave to her in a kinder manner. She deserves the best of treatment.’—‘Yes, yes,’ said the squire, ‘I know what she deserves: now she’s gone, I’ll show you what she deserves. See here, sir, here is a letter from my cousin, my Lady Bellaston, in which she is so kind to gi’ me to understand that the fellow is got out of prison again; and here she advises me to take all the care I can o’ the wench. Odzookers! neighbour Allworthy, you don’t know what it is to govern a daughter.’

贝拉斯顿夫人，一个淫欲熏心的女人，将汤姆·琼斯纳为情人，并试图除掉索菲娅·韦斯特恩，让她被亲戚强奸，从而被迫嫁给一个不幸的人。汤姆因杀人而被判处死刑，但死里逃生，活得还挺热闹。他的获释令韦斯特恩乡绅十分恼火，因为他自己也想把索菲娅嫁给可怕的布利菲尔，指望布利菲尔能成为奥尔沃西乡绅的继承人。当这一切逆转之后，韦斯特恩乡绅欣喜若狂，走向了另一个极端。他偷听到索菲娅坚决拒绝汤姆和可怕的布利菲尔。他像暴风雨般冲了进去：

Lady Bellaston, a bower of lust, had taken Tom Jones for her lover and attempted to dispose of Sophia Western by having her raped by a kinsman and thus forced into an unhappy marriage. Tom, condemned to death for having slain a man who survives quite boisterously, is released, to the discomfort of Squire Western, who himself seeks to marry Sophia to the dreadful pill Blifil, in the expectation that Blifil will be Squire Allworthy’s heir. When all this is reversed, Squire Western jubilantly swings to the other extreme. Eavesdropping, he hears Sophia resolutely rejecting both Tom and the horrible Blifil. He bursts in like a tempest:

就在这时，一直站在那里听了一会儿的韦斯特恩突然冲进房间，用他那猎猎般的嗓音和语气喊道：“去她那儿，小子，去她那儿，去她那儿！——就是这样，小宝贝们，哦，就是这样！好吧！怎么，都结束了？她定好日子了吗，小子？什么，是明天还是后天？我下定决心，一分钟也不能再拖了，就是后天。”“先生，我求求您，”琼斯说，“别让我成为你们的借口——”“求求您——”韦斯特恩喊道，“我以为你是个更有胆识的小伙子，不会轻易被少女的伎俩蒙蔽。——我告诉你，这全是骗人的把戏。我的天哪！她今晚就想结婚，不是吗，索菲？来，坦白吧，做个诚实的女孩。怎么，你哑口无言吗？” “你为什么不说话？”“先生，我为什么要坦白呢？”索菲娅说，“既然您似乎很了解我的想法？”——“好样的，”他喊道，“那你同意了吗？”“不，先生，”索菲娅说，“我没有同意。”——“那你明天，后天，也不想这样吗？”韦斯特恩问。“的确，先生，”她说，“我没有这样的打算。”“但我可以告诉你，”他回答说，“你为什么不说话；只是因为你喜欢不听话，喜欢惹你父亲生气。”“先生，”琼斯插嘴道——“我告诉你，你就像条小狗，”他喊道。 “我劝她的时候，她只会叹息、哀嚎、痛苦挣扎；现在我劝你，她却反对你。全是些反对的念头，仅此而已。她根本不听她父亲的，这就是全部真相。她就是想跟我作对，跟我唱反调。”“我爸爸要我做什么？”索菲娅喊道。“我要你做什么？”他说道，“你现在就把手给我。”“好的，先生，”索菲娅说，“我会听您的。我的手在这里，琼斯先生。”“那么，你同意明天早上给我吗？”韦斯特恩问道。“我会听您的，先生，”她喊道。“那明天早上就是时候了，”他喊道。 “那既然您这么希望，那就明天早上吧，爸爸。”索菲娅说道。琼斯随即跪倒在地，欣喜若狂地亲吻着她的手。与此同时，韦斯特恩在房间里又蹦又跳，不时喊道：“奥尔沃西在哪儿？他现在在外面，跟那个该死的律师道林聊天，他应该忙别的事才对！”说完，他便出门去找奥尔沃西，恰好留下这对恋人享受片刻的甜蜜二人世界。

At this instant Western, who had stood some time listening, burst into the room, and, with his hunting voice and phrase, cried out, ‘To her, boy, to her, go to her.—That’s it, little honeys, O that’s it! Well! what, is it all over? Hath she appointed the day, boy? What, shall it be to-morrow or next day? It shan’t be put off a minute longer than next day, I am resolved.’ ‘Let me beseech you, sir,” says Jones, “don’t let me be the occasion’—‘Beseech mine a—,’ cries Western. ‘I thought thou hadst been a lad of higher mettle than to give way to a parcel of maidenish tricks.—I tell thee ’tis all flimflam. Zoodikers! she’d have the wedding to-night with all her heart. Would’st not, Sophy? Come, confess, and be an honest girl for once. What, art dumb? Why dost not speak?’ ‘Why should I confess, sir,’ says Sophia, ‘since it seems you are so well acquainted with my thoughts?’—‘That’s a good girl,’ cries he, ‘and dost consent then?’ ‘No, indeed, sir,’ says Sophia, ‘I have given no such consent.’—‘And wunt not ha un then to-morrow, nor next day?’ says Western.—‘Indeed, sir,’ says she, ‘I have no such intention.’ ‘But I can tell thee,’ replied he, ‘why hast nut; only because thou dost love to be disobedient, and to plague and vex thy father.’ ‘Pray, sir,’ said Jones, interfering—‘I tell thee thou art a puppy,’ cries he. ‘When I vorbid her, then it was all nothing but sighing and whining, and languishing and writhing; now I am vor thee, she is against thee. All the spirit of contrary, that’s all. She is above being guided and governed by her father, that is the whole truth on’t. It is only to disoblige and contradict me.’ ‘What would my papa have me do?’ cries Sophia. ‘What would I ha thee do?’ says he, ‘why, gi’ un thy hand this moment.’—‘Well, sir,’ says Sophia, ‘I will obey you.—There is my hand, Mr Jones.’ ‘Well, and will you consent to ha un to-morrow morning?’ says Western.—‘I will be obedient to you, sir,’ cries she.—‘Why then to-morrow morning be the day,’ cries he. ‘Why then to-morrow morning shall be the day, papa, since you will have it so,’ says Sophia. Jones then fell upon his knees, and kissed her hand in an agony of joy, while Western began to caper and dance about the room, presently crying out—‘Where the devil is Allworthy? He is without now, a talking with that d—d lawyer Dowling, when he should be minding other matters.’ He then sallied out in quest of him, and very opportunely left the lovers to enjoy a few tender minutes alone.

我纳闷，约翰逊既然愿意称《汤姆·琼斯》为“浪漫喜剧”，为何对《西部乡绅》这部滑稽剧却只字未提。约翰逊曾盛赞约翰·福斯塔夫爵士，并巧妙地掩盖了自己的道德顾虑。约翰逊饱受忧郁症的折磨，只能依靠良友相伴来支撑自己。他在福斯塔夫身上找到了真正存在的东西：生命的乐趣。《西部乡绅》的滑稽之处在于，它前后矛盾，却丝毫没有意识到这一点。或许正是这种漫不经心的性格，让约翰逊对这位疯癫的乡绅失去了兴趣。约翰逊在福斯塔夫身上发现了真正的智慧，并从中汲取了养分。作为一位后来才接触到这位“大查姆”的读者，在过去的七十年里，我一直深受福斯塔夫的启发，而《西部乡绅》却远不及福斯塔夫。不过，我只能接受现状，《西部乡绅》也足以让我感到满足。

I wonder why Johnson, who was willing to call Tom Jones “the Comedy of Romance,” made no comment upon the whirligig of Squire Western. Johnson memorably extolled Sir John Falstaff, brushing away his own moral qualms. Afflicted by a vile melancholy, Johnson depended upon good company to keep him going. He found in Falstaff what is truly there: the joy of existence. Squire Western is deliciously funny as he reverses himself without the slightest realization of inconsistency. Perhaps it was the absence of mind that caused Johnson to turn from the mad Squire. Johnson found true wit in Falstaff and was nourished by it. A latecomer disciple of the Grand Cham, I have been vitalized by Falstaff for the last seven decades, and Squire Western, alas, is no Falstaff. But I take what I can get, and Squire Western gratifies me.

第四章

CHAPTER 4

《傲慢与偏见》（1813）

Pride and Prejudice (1813)

简· A·乌斯滕

JANE AUSTEN

在我人生的不同阶段，我曾更喜欢《劝导》和《爱玛》而不是《傲慢与偏见》，但如今我已步入晚年，这三部作品在我看来同样伟大。《曼斯菲尔德庄园》也是如此，不过本书暂且略过它。

AT DIFFERENT TIMES in my life I have preferred Persuasion and Emma to Pride and Prejudice, but in my advanced old age the three seem equally grand. The same holds for Mansfield Park, but I will neglect it in this book.

《傲慢与偏见》或许是简·奥斯汀最受欢迎的作品。它常常令人捧腹大笑，始终充满温情，并且蕴含着一种难以捉摸的深刻内涵。班纳特先生为何要娶荒诞不经的班纳特太太？这个问题无解，因为这对夫妇实在是不般配。

Probably Pride and Prejudice is the most popular Austen. It is frequently hilarious, always amiable, and with a curious profundity that is difficult to assess. Why did Mr. Bennet marry the absurd Mrs. Bennet? The question is unanswerable since the mismatch is preposterous:

班纳特先生性格古怪，既有轻快的一面，又有讽刺的幽默，既沉默寡言，又反复无常，即便与他相伴二十三年，他的妻子也始终无法真正了解他的为人。而她自己的心思则更容易理解。她理解力浅薄，见识有限，性情也不稳定。一旦心生不满，她便觉得自己神经兮兮的。她毕生的追求就是为女儿们筹备婚事；而她唯一的慰藉便是探望亲友，打听消息。

Mr. Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three-and-twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character. Her mind was less difficult to develop. She was a woman of mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper. When she was discontented, she fancied herself nervous. The business of her life was to get her daughters married; its solace was visiting and news.

班纳特先生最宠爱的女儿必然是伊丽莎白，她思维敏捷、精神矍铄、情感细腻，而且性格温和矜持，甚至超出了她父亲的预料。简·奥斯汀本人在1813年1月29日写给妹妹卡桑德拉的信中，对伊丽莎白给予了极高的评价：

Mr. Bennet’s favorite necessarily is Elizabeth, whose quickness of mind, spirit, and sensibility, and an amiable reserve are beyond even her father’s apprehension. Jane Austen herself, in a letter to her sister Cassandra, January 29, 1813, gives Elizabeth the ultimate guerdon:

我必须承认，我认为她是印刷品上出现过的最讨人喜欢的角色之一，至于那些至少不喜欢她的人，我该如何忍受，我不得而知。

I must confess that I think her as delightful a character as ever appeared in print, and how I shall be able to tolerate those who do not like her at least, I do not know.

我或许会把唐吉诃德和桑丘·潘萨列为竞争对手，但还有谁呢？答案必然是约翰·福斯塔夫爵士、罗莎琳德、克莉奥佩特拉、费斯特，以及莎士比亚笔下其他你心目中的角色。当然，克莉奥佩特拉绝非仅仅是令人愉悦，潘萨在某种程度上也是如此。“愉悦”一词源于拉丁语“ delicere”，意为“诱惑”。伊丽莎白·班纳特以其轻盈的气质和令人心动的力量，最终凭借其智慧和性感魅力，诱惑着菲茨威廉·达西，也诱惑着读者。

I might vote for Don Quixote and Sancho Panza as rivals, but who else is there? The answer has to be Sir John Falstaff, and Rosalind, and Cleopatra, and Feste, and who you will in Shakespeare. Of course, Cleopatra is something other than delightful, and in another way so is Panurge. Delight goes back to the Latin delicere, “to allure.” Elizabeth Bennet allures Fitzwilliam Darcy, and the reader, by her lightness and quickening power, ultimately the power both of her mind and of her sexuality.

如果衡量一部伟大小说的真正标准是反复阅读，以及不断重读带来的乐趣，那么《傲慢与偏见》足以媲美任何一部小说。尽管简·奥斯汀不像莎士比亚那样运用严格的排除法，但在我看来，她最终却是英语世界中最像莎士比亚的小说家。莎士比亚只要愿意，就能让笔下所有人物，无论主角还是配角，都拥有完全独立、前后一致且截然不同的声音。奥斯汀也同样能轻松做到这一点。由于两位作家笔下的声音既是个性的象征，也是性格的体现，因此，奥斯汀的读者在她那相对封闭的社会世界中，会遇到形形色色的自我。尽管这个世界本质上是一个世俗化的文化，但主导其中的道德观念仍然是新教的。奥斯汀笔下的女主人公们在各种判断上摇摆不定，但她们始终坚守着个人判断的权利，将其视为自我的堡垒。他们所谓的“喜爱”，我们称之为“爱”，是那种持久而非浪漫的爱。当他们评价一个人“和蔼可亲”时，这与我们每个人用来形容一位令人钦佩、有人情味的人的任何赞美之词都如出一辙。他们与我们的不同之处，更多在于程度而非本质，在于他们深刻地依赖于灵魂之间相互尊重的交流。尤其是在《傲慢与偏见》和《爱玛》中，你对另一个灵魂的本质和价值的准确评估，与你自尊的合理性，你那正当的骄傲，息息相关。

If the authentic test for a great novel is rereading, and the joys of yet further rereadings, then Pride and Prejudice can rival any novel ever written. Though Jane Austen, unlike Shakespeare, practices an art of rigorous exclusion, she seems to me finally the most Shakespearean novelist in the language. When Shakespeare wishes to, he can make all his personages, major and minor, speak in voices entirely their own, self-consistent and utterly different from one another. Austen, with the similar illusion of ease, does the same. Since voice in both writers is an image of personality and also of character, the reader of Austen encounters an astonishing variety of selves in her socially confined world. Though that world is essentially a secularized culture, the moral vision dominating it remains that of the Protestant sensibility. Austen’s heroines waver in one judgment or another, but they hold fast to the right of private judgment as the self’s fortress. What they call “affection” we term “love,” of the enduring rather than the Romantic variety, and when they judge a man to be “amiable,” it is akin to whatever superlative each of us may favor for an admirable, humane person. Where they may differ from us, but more in degree than in kind, is in their profound reliance upon the soul’s exchanges of mutual esteem with other souls. In Pride and Prejudice and Emma in particular, your accuracy in estimating the nature and value of another soul is intimately allied to the legitimacy of your self-esteem, your valid pride.

伊丽莎白·班纳特和达西之间误会的道德喜剧，曾被一些评论家比作莎士比亚《无事生非》中比阿特丽斯和本尼迪克之间的机智交锋。然而，这种比较意义有限：伊丽莎白并非以机智或讽刺著称。她真正的莎士比亚式先驱是《皆大欢喜》中的罗莎琳德。罗莎琳德的确凭借犀利的机智巧妙地驳斥了雅克和试金石，但她最根​​本的力量在于她坚定的自我认知，以及唯有精准的自我评估才能带来的智慧。这种智慧超越了冷漠，并乐于关怀他人。它造就了一种既骄傲又略带玩世不恭的气质，这与达西那不可动摇的骄傲形成了鲜明的对比。达西的自我认知建立在他对自己个人和社会地位的强烈信念之上。我们无法否认他的这种信念；他社交能力强，道德公正，而且比伊丽莎白有时更善于识人。但他咄咄逼人，尽管伊丽莎白最终的评价——“他常常很和蔼可亲”——也显得过分。伊丽莎白身上带着一丝堂吉诃德式的不切实际，而达西则游离于所谓的游戏规则之外。缺乏玩乐精神的圆滑很容易沦为道德狂热；而堂吉诃德式的不切实际不仅可能显得笨拙，还可能演变成盲目的狂热。

The moral comedy of the misunderstandings between Elizabeth Bennet and Darcy has been compared, by several critics, to the combat of wit between Beatrice and Benedick in Shakespeare’s Much Ado About Nothing. As a comparison, this has limited usefulness: Elizabeth is not primarily a wit or a social ironist. Her true Shakespearean precursor is Rosalind in As You Like It. Rosalind resorts to furious wit in properly squelching Jaques and Touchstone, but her fundamental strength is a sure sense of self, with the wisdom that only an accurate self-estimate can bring. Such wisdom transcends detachment and welcomes a generous concern with other selves. It leads to a pride that is also playful, which is an intense contrast to Darcy’s implacable pride. His sense of self relies upon an immense conviction of personal as well as societal eminence. We cannot dispute his conviction; he is socially formidable, morally fair-minded, and a better judge of character than Elizabeth sometimes proves to be. But his aggressiveness is excessive, despite Elizabeth’s final, justified verdict: “He is frequently amiable.” There is a touch of the quixotic in Elizabeth, whereas Darcy stands outside what could be termed the order of play. Tact without playfulness can yield too readily to moral zeal; but the quixotic not only can be tactless, it can decay into misguided exuberance.

这些思考虽然与《傲慢与偏见》本身相关，但若应用于这部小说生动活泼的喜剧，则显得过于抽象。惊喜不断，书中一切都出乎意料。我们仿佛置身于莎士比亚式的世界，如同罗莎琳德的阿登森林一般，充满了随机性。唯有奥斯汀叙述中那沉稳而坚定的笔触，才将这个近乎怪诞的社会世界维系在一起，因为其中的每个人都比表面看起来更加古怪。《傲慢与偏见》中，柯林斯先生堪称一个真正的“怪物”，威克姆是个装腔作势的伪君子，凯瑟琳夫人是个傲慢的暴君，而班纳特先生则是一位讽刺大师，擅长辛辣的挖苦。奥斯汀看似平常的叙述语调与那些古怪的人物之间，形成了一种奇妙的喜剧张力，正是这些人物让故事更加生动、更加奇特。

Such reflections, though germane to Pride and Prejudice, are sadly abstract when applied to the lively comedy of the novel. Surprise keeps breaking in, and nothing turns out as anyone in the book expects. We are indeed in a Shakespearean world, as random in its way as Rosalind’s Forest of Arden. Only the level firmness of Austen’s narrative voice holds together a social world that borders oddly upon the bizarre, for everyone in it is rather more idiosyncratic than at first they appear to be. Pride and Prejudice has an authentic monster in Mr. Collins, a poseur in Wickham, a tyrant of pride in the odious Lady Catherine, and a master of destructive satire in Mr. Bennet. There is a marvelous comic tension between Austen’s seemingly normative tone and the eccentric personages who perpetually render the story more vivid and more strange.

反讽，本质上就是言不由衷，是简·奥斯汀的标志性手法。奥斯汀的反讽虽然妙趣横生，却也动摇了她所有作品的既定含义。当我们似乎确信她笔下的女主人公们最终会获得幸福或完美时，我们却不得不仔细观察，揣摩其中蕴含的反讽意味。奥斯汀不仅是隐喻大师，也是未言之谜的天才：她期待敏锐的读者替她解读。但这并不意味着奥斯汀像她笔下的达西那样，是圆滑世故的典范；她更像是伊丽莎白·班纳特，是玩世不恭的化身。在某些方面，奥斯汀更像莎士比亚笔下的罗莎琳德，而非伊丽莎白。因此，奥斯汀最大的成就，在于她卓越的智慧和创造力所蕴含的纯粹的精神力量。

Irony, which essentially is saying one thing while meaning another, is Austen’s characteristic mode. Austen’s irony, though endlessly genial, unsettles all her meanings. Where we seem most assured of the happiness or perfection attained by her heroines, we learn to look more closely and to surmise the implied reservations of this ironic vision. A great master of metaphor, Austen is also a genius of the unsaid: she expects the astute reader to say it for her. Not that Austen, in the manner of her Darcy, is a triumph of tact; she is more in the mode of her Elizabeth Bennet, and is a triumph of playfulness. In some ways, Austen is more like Shakespeare’s Rosalind than Elizabeth ever could be, and so Austen’s largest triumph is in the sheer psychic and spiritual health of her magnificent wit and invention.

《傲慢与偏见》中最精彩的喜剧桥段莫过于柯林斯先生向伊丽莎白·班纳特提出的荒唐求婚。人们不禁会想起梅尔维尔·库珀，他在1940年根据这部小说改编的电影中完美地诠释了柯林斯先生这一角色：

The grandest comic moment in Pride and Prejudice is the outrageous proposal made by Mr. Collins to Elizabeth Bennet. One remembers Melville Cooper, perfect in the role of Mr. Collins in the 1940 motion picture of the novel:

我结婚的理由有三：第一，我认为对于像我这样家境优渥的牧师来说，在自己的教区树立婚姻的榜样是理所应当的；第二，我深信这会大大增进我的幸福；第三，或许我应该早点提到，这是那位尊贵的女士的特别建议和推荐，我有幸称她为我的赞助人。她曾两次纡尊降贵地就此事向我提出意见（而且还是未经我征求！）。就在我离开汉斯福德的前一个星期六晚上，在我们两家水池边跳四对舞的时候，詹金森太太正在摆放德·伯格小姐的脚凳，她对我说：“柯林斯先生，你必须结婚。像你这样的牧师必须结婚。好好挑选，为了我，选一位淑女；为了你自己，让她成为一位勤劳能干、对生活有益的人，不要出身名门，但要能把有限的收入过得很好。这就是我的建议。”你尽快找到这样一位女子，带她来汉斯福德，我会去拜访她。顺便一提，我美丽的表妹，我认为凯瑟琳·德·伯格夫人的赏识和善意，是我能提供的诸多优势中不容忽视的。她的举止优雅绝非我能言喻；而你的机智和活力，我想，她一定会喜欢，尤其是在你兼具她身份所带来的那种沉稳和尊重之后。以上便是我关于婚事的总体想法；至于我为何将目光投向朗伯恩而非我的家乡，我还要解释一下，我向你保证，我的家乡也有许多和蔼可亲的年轻女子。但事实是，既然我将在您尊敬的父亲（尽管他可能还会活很多年）去世后继承这笔遗产，我便下定决心从他的女儿中挑选一位妻子，这样，当这件令人悲伤的事情发生时，她们的损失就能降到最低——当然，正如我之前所说，这可能还要过几年才会发生。这就是我的动机，我亲爱的表妹，我自认为这不会影响您在我心中的印象。现在，我唯一要做的就是用最真挚的语言向您表达我浓烈的爱意。我对财富毫不在意，也不会向您的父亲提出任何此类要求，因为我很清楚他无法满足；而且，您唯一能得到的，就是那1000英镑的4%的收益，这笔钱要等到您母亲去世后才能归您所有。因此，关于这一点，我将始终保持沉默。你可以放心，我们结婚后，我绝不会对你出言不逊。

My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish; secondly, that I am convinced that it will add very greatly to my happiness; and thirdly—which perhaps I ought to have mentioned earlier, that it is the particular advice and recommendation of the very noble lady whom I have the honour of calling patroness. Twice has she condescended to give me her opinion (unasked too!) on this subject; and it was but the very Saturday night before I left Hunsford—between our pools at quadrille, while Mrs. Jenkinson was arranging Miss de Bourgh’s footstool, that she said, ‘Mr. Collins, you must marry. A clergyman like you must marry. Choose properly, choose a gentlewoman for my sake; and for your own, let her be an active, useful sort of person, not brought up high, but able to make a small income go a good way. This is my advice. Find such a woman as soon as you can, bring her to Hunsford, and I will visit her.’ Allow me, by the way, to observe, my fair cousin, that I do not reckon the notice and kindness of Lady Catherine de Bourgh as among the least of the advantages in my power to offer. You will find her manners beyond anything I can describe; and your wit and vivacity, I think, must be acceptable to her, especially when tempered with the silence and respect which her rank will inevitably excite. Thus much for my general intention in favour of matrimony; it remains to be told why my views were directed to Longbourn instead of my own neighbourhood, where I assure you there are many amiable young women. But the fact is, that being, as I am, to inherit this estate after the death of your honoured father (who, however, may live many years longer), I could not satisfy myself without resolving to choose a wife from among his daughters, that the loss to them might be as little as possible, when the melancholy event takes place—which, however, as I have already said, may not be for several years. This has been my motive, my fair cousin, and I flatter myself it will not sink me in your esteem. And now nothing remains for me but to assure you in the most animated language of the violence of my affection. To fortune I am perfectly indifferent, and shall make no demand of that nature on your father, since I am well aware that it could not be complied with; and that one thousand pounds in the 4 per cents, which will not be yours till after your mother’s decease, is all that you may ever be entitled to. On that head, therefore, I shall be uniformly silent; and you may assure yourself that no ungenerous reproach shall ever pass my lips when we are married.

这绝对是西方文学史上最滑稽的求婚故事。它的高潮部分简直令人瞠目结舌：

This has to be the funniest marriage proposal in Western literature. Its apex is the ultimate outrage:

现在我唯一能做的，就是用最激动人心的语言向你表达我炽烈的爱意。

And now nothing remains for me but to assure you in the most animated language of the violence of my affection.

简·奥斯汀是一位如此杰出的小说家，如果希望她也创作舞台剧，那就太可惜了。我从未因为笑得停不下来而被抬出正规剧院，但有两次，我却因为笑得太厉害而不得不离开电影院。第一次是在梅尔维尔·库珀完成他的求婚之后，第二次是在看完W·C·菲尔兹的短小精悍的杰作《致命的一杯啤酒》（1933）之后。

Jane Austen is so accomplished a novelist that one does her wrong to wish she had also written stage dramas. I have never been carried out of the legitimate theater because I became helpless with laughter, but on two occasions I became so borne away by frightening hilarity that I had to leave two cinemas, the first when Melville Cooper concluded his proposal, and the second after viewing The Fatal Glass of Beer, the brief masterpiece of W. C. Fields (1933).

撇开劳伦斯·奥利弗饰演的菲茨威廉·达西那无可置疑的俊朗外表不谈，我们是否应该认同伊丽莎白·班纳特对他的最终评价？我只见过已故的托尼·坦纳一次，那是在罗马，由他的妻子，评论家兼翻译家娜迪亚·富西尼介绍认识的。我们探讨了文学中的认同感，并就我朋友安格斯·弗莱彻的推测展开了辩论：所有富有想象力的文学作品都依赖于部分认同，因为完全认同无异于一种死亡。坦纳在简·奥斯汀的作品中找到了一种完全认同，这种认同提升了生活品质，并有助于驱散忧郁。后来我意识到，坦纳所经历的忧郁比我通常感受到的要严重得多，除了1965年我经历的中年危机之外。

Setting aside the undoubted good looks of Laurence Olivier as Fitzwilliam Darcy, are we to share Elizabeth Bennet’s final estimate of him? I met the late Tony Tanner only once, in Rome, introduced to him by his wife, Nadia Fusini, a critic and translator. We talked about recognition in literature and argued my friend Angus Fletcher’s surmise that all imaginative literature depends upon partial recognition, since total recognition is a kind of death. Tanner found in Jane Austen a kind of total recognition that enhanced life and could help banish melancholy. I realized later that Tanner had to struggle with a more dangerous melancholy than I tended to experience, except in my own midlife crisis in 1965.

问题是：我们是否应该认同简·奥斯汀的观点，认为达西是伊丽莎白·班纳特近乎完美的丈夫？坦纳赞同马文·穆德里克的观点，认为简·奥斯汀不屑于任何纯粹的性吸引力。但我对此并不完全信服。她四十一岁就去世了，生前饱受病痛折磨，我们也没有理由相信她去世时并非处女。然而，尽管她对此轻描淡写，但她似乎确实在1796年，也就是她与二十岁的爱尔兰青年汤姆·勒弗罗伊之间，经历了一段真挚而相互的爱恋。那一年，她开始创作后来成为《傲慢与偏见》的作品。在传记研究《成为简·奥斯汀》（2003）中，乔恩·斯宾塞敏锐地指出，勒弗罗伊是达西的原型，但奥斯汀将自己的特质赋予了达西，而将勒弗罗伊的特质赋予了伊丽莎白·班纳特。简·奥斯汀对自身审美自主性的自豪感，使她缺乏讽刺意识，并转化为菲茨威廉·达西对社会和个人品格的自豪。而魅力四射的汤姆·勒弗罗伊则赋予伊丽莎白·班纳特一种超越讽刺的机智和活力。

The question is: are we to agree with Jane Austen that Darcy is the all-but-perfect husband for Elizabeth Bennet? Tanner followed Marvin Mudrick in observing Jane Austen’s deprecation of any merely sexual attraction. I am not certain that I find that altogether convincing. She died at forty-one, in considerable pain, and we have no reason to believe that she did not die a virgin. And yet, though she made light of it, she does seem to have experienced an authentic and mutual falling in love with Tom Lefroy, a young Irishman, when both of them were twenty in 1796. That was the year she began what was to become Pride and Prejudice. In his biographical study, Becoming Jane Austen (2003), Jon Spence shrewdly suggested that Lefroy was a model for Darcy, but that Austen transposed her qualities to Darcy, and Lefroy’s to Elizabeth Bennet. Jane Austen’s pride in her aesthetic autonomy evades her ironical sense, and is transmuted into Fitzwilliam Darcy’s pride of social and personal integrity. The evidently charming Tom Lefroy bestows upon Elizabeth Bennet a quickness of wit and spirit that also reaches beyond irony.

尽管对《傲慢与偏见》的评论质量异常高，但往往不够深入。奥斯汀本人对这部作品略带讽刺意味的评论，温和地哀叹了我们今天所说的它对深渊的拒绝。一种带有黑格尔式意味的负面反思，使伊丽莎白·班纳特得以对菲茨威廉·达西和她自己都有了一种部分但坚定的认识。他们之间的爱慕并非缺乏性欲，而是建立在两种正当的自尊之上，彼此相互尊重。自尊由此得到救赎，偏见也变得明智，因为它在认知中赋予了“他者”应有的地位。

Though the quality of criticism devoted to Pride and Prejudice is unusually high, it does not often go deep enough. Austen’s own somewhat ironic critique of the book gently laments what we would call its refusal of the abyss. Negative reflection, in a somewhat Hegelian mode, yields knowledge of a kind that allows Elizabeth Bennet a partial but firm recognition both of Fitzwilliam Darcy and of herself. Their mutual affection does not lack sexual passion yet nevertheless is compounded of two legitimate prides that exchange esteems. Pride is thus redeemed, and prejudice becomes judicious in that it grants otherness its place in knowledge.

或许我们太容易爱上简·奥斯汀的《傲慢与偏见》。这部作品出自一位才华横溢的年轻女性之手，她心中燃起希望，又将其搁置，但希望并未完全熄灭。汤姆·勒弗罗伊和简·奥斯汀因为身无分文而被迫分手。距离《傲慢与偏见》首次出版已过去两个多世纪，当时的社会背景早已变迁。我们现在或许会说，勒弗罗伊和奥斯汀本该结婚，即便经济拮据，也能携手走过二十载。但这种说法又怎能成立呢？奥斯汀显然拒绝了后来的两位追求者，或许是因为她仍然对勒弗罗伊念念不忘。我们无从得知真相。在《傲慢与偏见》出版四年后，简·奥斯汀去世，年仅四十一岁。她留下了六部伟大的小说和一些珍贵的片段。在我八十八岁生日的第二天，我比以往任何时候都更加感伤。在感激她留下的作品的同时，人们也希望她能拥有更长久、更充实的人生。不过，她仍然敬仰塞缪尔·约翰逊博士，他在《闲人》一书中写道：

It may be too easy to love Austen’s Pride and Prejudice. It is the work of a very young woman of astonishing genius whose hopes have been kindled, set aside, but not yet extinguished. Tom Lefroy and Jane Austen gave each other up because neither had any money. It is more than two centuries since Pride and Prejudice was first published, and all social contexts have evaporated. We now might say that Lefroy and Austen ought to have married and enjoyed, despite financial vicissitudes, two decades together. But how can that be said? Austen evidently turned down two later suitors, perhaps because she still longed for Lefroy. We cannot know completely. Four years after Pride and Prejudice was published, Jane Austen died at forty-one. Six great novels and some remarkable fragments survive her. A day after my eighty-eighth birthday, I am more sentimental than ever. Grateful for the books, one wishes she could have had a more prolonged and fulfilled life. Still, she revered Dr. Samuel Johnson, who in his Idler remarked:

哲学或许会让人变得固执，但宗教只能让人变得耐心。

Philosophy may infuse stubbornness, but Religion only can give patience.

没人会把简·奥斯汀和宗教作家联系起来，但她的精神中确实有一种倔强的气质，就像伊丽莎白和达西一样。她教导人们如何在智慧和生活乐趣中保持耐心。

No one would think of Jane Austen as a religious writer, but there is something stubborn in her spirit, as there is in Elizabeth and Darcy. She teaches patience inflected by wit and the joy of being.

第五章

CHAPTER 5

爱玛（1815）

Emma (1815)

简· A·乌斯滕

JANE AUSTEN

简·奥斯汀对其小说命运最不准确的预言是关于《爱玛》的，她认为，除了她自己，没人会喜欢这个女主人公。然而，爱玛之所以如此讨人喜欢，是因为她极富想象力，而这种想象力在他人眼中，最终在她自己眼中，往往显得危险而又误入歧途。在存在的尺度上，爱玛对崇高这一亘古不变的问题给出了答案：更高？等于？还是低于？如同之前的克拉丽莎·哈洛，以及之后乔治·艾略特和亨利·詹姆斯笔下那些最强大的女主人公一样，爱玛·伍德豪斯拥有英雄般的意志，并且，也像她们一样，她冒着将自己的意志与想象力等同起来的风险。从社会角度来看，这种等同是灾难性的，因为新教的意志倾向于给其他自我赋予等级，而这种等级最终可能只是一种个人的幻想。 G·阿莫尔·克雷格曾精辟地指出：“在《爱玛》中，社会并非阶梯，而是一张由各种归因交织而成的网，将情感与行为紧密相连。”然而，爱玛本人性情奔放而非简化，她所进行的归因远比这张网所能承载的更为激烈和自由。在她获得启蒙之前，她始终威胁着要瓦解那些可能维系情感与行为之间某种稳定性的社会联系，无论是对他人而言还是对她而言。

JANE AUSTEN’S least accurate prophecy as to the fate of her fictions concerned Emma, whose heroine, she thought, “no one but myself will much like.” Aside from much else, Emma is immensely likable, because she is so extraordinarily imaginative, dangerous and misguided as her imagination frequently must appear to others and finally to herself. On the scale of being, Emma constitutes an answer to the immemorial questions of the sublime: More? Equal to? Or less than? Like Clarissa Harlowe before her and the strongest heroines of George Eliot and Henry James after her, Emma Woodhouse has a heroic will and, like them, she risks identifying her will with her imagination. Socially considered, such identification is catastrophic, since the Protestant will has a tendency to bestow a ranking on other selves, and such ranking may turn out to be a personal phantasmagoria. G. Armour Craig rather finely remarked: “Society in Emma is not a ladder. It is a web of imputations that link feelings and conduct.” Yet Emma herself, expansionist rather than reductionist in temperament, imputes more fiercely and freely than the web can sustain, and she threatens always, until she is enlightened, to dissolve the societal links, in and for others, that might allow some stability between feelings and conduct.

阿莫尔·克雷格补充道：“ 《爱玛》既不为女主人公辩解，也不嘲讽她。”相反，它以一种讽刺的爱（而非充满爱意的讽刺）对待她。简·奥斯汀对爱玛·伍德豪斯十分珍视，因为​​她的错误极富想象力，源于意志对自主视野的渴望。杰出的简·费尔法克斯更容易令人钦佩，但我不能同意韦恩·布斯将荣誉授予她而非爱玛，尽管我欣赏他措辞中微妙的平衡：

Armour Craig usefully added, “Emma does not justify its heroine nor does it deride her.” Rather, it treats her with ironic love (not loving irony). Emma Woodhouse is dear to Jane Austen, because her errors are profoundly imaginative and rise from the will’s passion for autonomy of vision. The splendid Jane Fairfax is easier to admire, but I cannot agree with Wayne Booth’s awarding the honors to her over Emma, though I admire the subtle balance of his formulation:

除了艾玛因幸运而成为书中女主角之外，简在大多数方面都胜过艾玛。无论在品味、能力、智慧还是情感方面，简都比艾玛更胜一筹……

（韦恩·C·布斯，《爱玛》中的视角与距离控制》，《十九世纪小说》，第16卷，第2期[1961年9月]）

Jane is superior to Emma in most respects except the stroke of good fortune that made Emma the heroine of the book. In matters of taste and ability, of head and of heart, she is Emma’s superior….

(Wayne C. Booth, “Point of View and the Control of Distance in Emma,” Nineteenth-Century Fiction, vol. 16, no. 2 [Sept. 1961])

品味、能力、头脑和心灵这四者固然强大；想象力和意志力若能相辅相成，则更是威力无穷，但显然它们的能量也可能被误用，用于作恶。简·费尔法克斯当然比艾玛·伍德豪斯更讨人喜欢，但她却远不如艾玛有趣。真正吸引我们的是艾玛，而她也确实做到了。奥斯汀并非在创作像《失乐园》那样的意志悲剧，而是在创作一部伟大的意志喜剧，她的女主人公必须充分展现意志力的潜能，即便这种潜能曾一度被滥用。艾玛的本性之一便是过于随心所欲，而且她也确实有点自负。当奥斯汀说这些才是“艾玛处境的真正弊端”时，我们对“弊端”一词的理解尽可能轻描淡写，而作者的理解也确实足够轻描淡写了。

Taste, ability, head, and heart are a formidable fourfold; the imagination and the will, working together, are an even more formidable twofold and clearly may have their energies diverted to error and to mischief. Jane Fairfax is certainly more amiable even than Emma Woodhouse, but she is considerably less interesting. It is Emma who is meant to charm us and who does charm us. Austen is not writing a tragedy of the will, like Paradise Lost, but a great comedy of the will, and her heroine must incarnate the full potential of the will, however misused for a time. Having rather too much her own way is certainly one of Emma’s powers, and she does have a disposition to think a little too well of herself. When Austen says that these were “the real evils indeed of Emma’s situation,” we read “evils” as lightly as the author will let us, which is lightly enough.

我们能否解释艾玛·伍德豪斯身上那些足以与乔治·艾略特的格温多琳·哈莱斯和亨利·詹姆斯的伊莎贝尔·阿切尔相提并论的特质？她所处的纯粹喜剧环境似乎已足够让她游刃有余；她显然并非世间名媛。奥斯汀精湛的写作技巧让我们相信，嫁给奈特利先生足以让这位如今完美可爱的艾玛获得圆满的人生。真的是这样吗？詹姆斯的天才之处在于，他暗示，尽管奥斯蒙德的“美好心灵”对伊莎贝尔而言如同精神牢笼，但无论如何，她都不可能找到真正合适的丈夫，因为无论是图切特还是古德伍德，都并非与她真正匹配的人。我们难道不觉得，奈特利先生即便和蔼睿智，也对她而言是一种束缚吗？这或许违背了奥斯汀的本意。

Can we account for the qualities in Emma Woodhouse that make her worthy of comparison to George Eliot’s Gwendolen Harleth and Henry James’s Isabel Archer? The pure comedy of her context seems world enough for her; she evidently is not the heiress of all the ages. We are persuaded, by Austen’s superb craft, that marriage to Mr. Knightley will more than suffice to fulfill totally the now perfectly amiable Emma. Or are we? It is James’s genius to suggest that, although Osmond’s “beautiful mind” was a prison of the spirit for Isabel, no proper husband could exist anyway, since neither Touchett nor Goodwood is exactly a true match for her. Do we, presumably against Austen’s promptings, not find Mr. Knightley something of a confinement also, benign and wise though he be?

我怀疑，从理查森笔下的克拉丽莎·哈洛到弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫笔下的克拉丽莎·达洛维，所有受新教意志约束的女主人公都找不到合适的伴侣，因为意志本身并不结婚。这种困境的寓意或悲剧性讽刺在《克拉丽莎》中体现得淋漓尽致，因为洛夫莱斯意志坚定、才华横溢，如果不是道德败坏，他本该是克拉丽莎的真命天子（他自己也心知肚明）。他临终前的呐喊（“愿此赎罪！”）毫无意义，反而巩固了英美小说中由来已久的传统：受新教意志约束的女主人公要么注定遭遇显而易见的灾难，要么与像奈特利先生或《米德尔马契》中的威尔·拉迪斯劳那样虽平庸却善良的男人幸福地结合。当乔治·艾略特笔下迷人的格温多琳·哈莱斯无可救药地爱上自命不凡的丹尼尔·德龙达时，我们只能叹息，无奈地接受虚构故事过度安排带来的悲哀。洛夫莱斯还是丹尼尔·德龙达？我认识的所有性格开朗的女性，没有一个会不喜欢前者，当然，前提是她不会嫁给这样的男人！

I suspect that the heroine of the Protestant will, from Richardson’s Clarissa Harlowe through to Virginia Woolf’s Clarissa Dalloway, can never find a fit match, because wills do not marry. The allegory or tragic irony of this dilemma is written large in Clarissa, since Lovelace, in strength of will and splendor of being, actually would have been the true husband for Clarissa (as he well knows) had he not been a moral squalor. His death cry (“Let this expiate!”) expiates nothing and helps establish the long tradition of the Anglo-American novel in which the heroines of the will are fated to suffer either overt calamities or else happy unions with such good if unexciting men as Mr. Knightley or Will Ladislaw in Middlemarch. When George Eliot is reduced to having the fascinating Gwendolen Harleth fall hopelessly in love with the prince of prigs, Daniel Deronda, we sigh and resign ourselves to the sorrows of fictive overdetermination. Lovelace or Daniel Deronda? I myself do not know a high-spirited woman who would not prefer the first, though not for a husband!

《爱玛》中充满了精彩的喜剧顿悟，我最喜欢的是第三卷第十一章，当时哈丽特透露奈特利先生是她心仪的对象，这让爱玛受到了极大的震惊：

Emma is replete with grand comic epiphanies, of which my favorite comes in Volume 3, Chapter XI, when Emma receives the grave shock of Harriet’s disclosure that Mr. Knightley is the object of Harriet’s hopeful affections:

哈丽特作完证后，向她亲爱的伍德豪斯小姐求助，问她是否有充分的理由抱有希望。

“起初我根本不会想到这一点，”她说，“要不是你。你告诉我仔细观察他，以他的行为为准则——我一直都是这么做的。但现在我似乎觉得我配得上他；而且，如果他真的选择了我，那也不会是什么天大的好事。”

这篇演讲所引起的种种痛苦感受，使得艾玛不得不竭尽全力才能开口回应：

“哈丽特，我只能大胆断言，奈特利先生是世上最不可能故意让任何女人误以为他对她的感情远超实际感情的男人。”

哈丽特似乎恨不得把朋友捧在手心，感谢她如此令人满意的判决；而艾玛则被父亲的脚步声惊醒，才免于陷入狂喜和爱慕之中——在那一刻，这简直是一种可怕的惩罚。他正穿过大厅。哈丽特激动得不敢与他对峙。“她无法控制自己——伍德豪斯先生会担心的——她最好还是离开；”于是，在朋友的鼓励下，她从另一扇门走了出去——就在她离开的那一刻，艾玛的内心涌起一阵强烈的情感：“哦，天哪！我真希望从未见过她！”

剩下的时间，包括接下来的夜晚，都不足以让她静下心来思考。——过去几个小时里，各种事情纷至沓来，让她感到困惑不已。每一刻都带来了新的惊喜；而每一个惊喜都让她感到羞愧。——这一切该如何理解！她该如何理解自己一直以来都在欺骗自己、生活在欺骗之中的种种谎言！——她犯下的错误，她头脑和心灵的盲目！——她静静地坐着，四处走动，试探着自己的房间，试探着灌木丛——无论在哪里，无论采取什么姿势，她都意识到自己表现得多么软弱；她被别人欺骗得多么屈辱；而她欺骗自己的程度更是令人羞愧；她感到自己多么可悲，而这或许只是她悲惨命运的开始。

When Harriet had closed her evidence, she appealed to her dear Miss Woodhouse, to say whether she had not good ground for hope.

“I never should have presumed to think of it at first,” said she, “but for you. You told me to observe him carefully, and let his behaviour be the rule of mine—and so I have. But now I seem to feel that I may deserve him; and that if he does choose me, it will not be any thing so very wonderful.”

The bitter feelings occasioned by this speech, the many bitter feelings, made the utmost exertion necessary on Emma’s side to enable her to say in reply,

“Harriet, I will only venture to declare, that Mr. Knightley is the last man in the world, who would intentionally give any woman the idea of his feeling for her more than he really does.”

Harriet seemed ready to worship her friend for a sentence so satisfactory; and Emma was only saved from raptures and fondness, which at that moment would have been dreadful penance, by the sound of her father’s footsteps. He was coming through the hall. Harriet was too much agitated to encounter him. “She could not compose herself—Mr. Woodhouse would be alarmed—she had better go;”—with most ready encouragement from her friend, therefore, she passed off through another door—and the moment she was gone, this was the spontaneous burst of Emma’s feelings: “Oh God! that I had never seen her!”

The rest of the day, the following night, were hardly enough for her thoughts.—She was bewildered amidst the confusion of all that had rushed on her within the last few hours. Every moment had brought a fresh surprise; and every surprise must be matter of humiliation to her.—How to understand it all! How to understand the deceptions she had been thus practising on herself, and living under!—The blunders, the blindness of her own head and heart!—she sat still, she walked about, she tried her own room, she tried the shrubbery—in every place, every posture, she perceived that she had acted most weakly; that she had been imposed on by others in a most mortifying degree; that she had been imposing on herself in a degree yet more mortifying; that she was wretched, and should probably find this day but the beginning of wretchedness.

这种强烈的审美愉悦感源于艾玛脱口而出的惊呼：“哦，天哪！我怎么从来没见过她！”与接下来这段精妙的喜剧描写之间的对比：“她静静地坐着，四处走动，试探着自己的房间，试探着灌木丛——无论在哪里，无论摆出什么姿势，她都觉得自己表现得极其软弱。” “她试探着灌木丛”和“摆出各种姿势”这两个词，将意志的极度羞辱展现得淋漓尽致。想象力无穷的艾玛如今却不得不忍受这种屈辱，她必须像那些被幻象击碎、逼入绝境的人一样，摆出同样的姿势，置身于同样的境地。简·奥斯汀似乎将自己与艾玛融为一体，她明智地选择将这一讽刺性的逆转时刻描绘成一段暂时的炼狱，而非一场炼狱般的羞辱。

The acute aesthetic pleasure of this turns on the counterpoint between Emma’s spontaneous cry, “Oh God! that I had never seen her!” and the exquisite comic touch of “she sat still, she walked about, she tried her own room, she tried the shrubbery—in every place, every posture, she perceived that she had acted most weakly.” The acute humiliation of the will could not be better conveyed than by “she tried the shrubbery” and “every posture.” Endlessly imaginative, Emma must now be compelled to endure the mortification of reducing herself to the postures and places of those driven into corners by the collapse of visions that have been exposed as delusions. Jane Austen, who seems to have identified herself with Emma, wisely chose to make this moment of ironic reversal a temporary purgatory, rather than an infernal discomfiture.

保罗·H·弗莱（Paul H. Fry）和已故的杰弗里·哈特曼（Geoffrey Hartman）一样，都是博学多识的学者，研究从感伤主义时代（始于亚历山大·蒲柏之死）到浪漫主义盛期（终于约翰·济慈、珀西·比希·雪莱和拜伦勋爵的英年早逝）的过渡时期。他曾就浪漫主义对简·奥斯汀笔下最桀骜不驯的人物的影响，撰写了一篇关于《爱玛》的精彩文章：

Paul H. Fry, like the late Geoffrey Hartman, an astonishingly erudite scholar of the transition from the Age of Sensibility, commencing with the death of Alexander Pope, on to the High Romanticism that ended with the early deaths of John Keats, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Lord Byron, wrote a brilliant essay on Emma in regard to the influence of Romance on Jane Austen’s most rugged personage:

因此，艾玛并非阅读能力欠佳的受害者。相反，她不爱读书的倾向恰恰体现了她更为微妙的堂吉诃德式特质。如同堂吉诃德，也如同夏洛特·伦诺克斯的《女堂吉诃德》（1752）一样，她过着与世隔绝的生活，部分是迫于无奈，部分是出于个人选择，她与合适的社交圈格格不入。这正是她与埃尔顿夫人无意间共有的诸多特征之一：“她所有的观念都源自于同一群人，同一种生活方式”（第四卷：272页）。如同伦诺克斯笔下的阿拉贝拉一样，艾玛的母亲已经去世，父亲也无力管教她。她在哈特菲尔德庄园展现出的王者风范，以及她对那些胆怯女孩的关爱，暗示着王室成员那种诱人的自我隔离；而她对埃尔顿夫人篡夺了她在王室“晚间女王”（第四卷：329页）地位的不满，也显得过于强烈。

（保罗·H·弗莱，《田园喜剧：简·奥斯汀的<爱玛>的虚构领域》，《小说研究》，第11卷，第2期[1979年夏季]）

Emma is not, then, a victim of bad reading. Rather her tendency not to read is a facet of her more subtle sort of quixotism. Like Quixote, and in this regard like Charlotte Lennox’s Female Quixote (1752), she lives in isolation, estranged partly by circumstance and partly by preference from suitable company. This is one of the many conditions she shares unwittingly with Mrs. Elton: “all her notions were drawn from one set of people, and one style of living” (IV:272). As is the case with Lennox’s Arabella, Emma’s mother is dead and her father cannot discipline her. Her regal bearing at Hartfield, where she favors frightened girls with her notice, suggests the tempting self-isolation of royalty, and her frustration at Mrs. Elton’s usurping her function as “ ‘queen of the evening’ ” (IV:329) at the Crown is much too pronounced.

(Paul H. Fry, “Georgic Comedy: The Fictive Territory of Jane Austen’s Emma,” Studies in the Novel, vol. 11, no. 2 [summer 1979])

人们可以同意博学的保罗·弗莱的观点，同时又能欣赏他对此判断的矛盾心理。和我们其他人一样，弗莱也几乎爱上了艾玛：

One can agree with the learned Paul Fry and still enjoy his own ambivalence in that judgment. Like the rest of us, Fry very nearly falls in love with Emma:

“如果你在评判男人和女人时，也能像对待这些孩子一样，更多地遵循自然规律，”奈特利先生对艾玛说，“并且在与他们交往时，少受幻想和任性的左右，那么我们或许就能始终意见一致了。”（第四卷：98-99页）艾玛的思维方式，再次展现出她聪明而又专横跋扈的一面。读者们一直对简·奥斯汀为何如此钟爱一位“除了我之外，没人会喜欢”的女主人公感到困惑。但如果我们意识到，即使是艾玛最令人不快的错误，也源于一个可以弥补的缺陷——在并非完全由自己创造的空虚空间中沉溺于想象，思想脱离了实际——那么我们就能明白，等待着艾玛的补救之道，即通过与奈特利先生这样的人建立起经验的联系而获得的清醒认知，绝非偶然或奇迹般的转变。

“If you were as much guided by nature in your estimate of men and women,” says Mr. Knightley to Emma, “and as little under the power of fancy and whim in your dealings with them, as you are where these children are concerned, we might always think alike” (IV:98–99). Emma thinks, again, like a very bright and autocratic child. Readers have puzzled over Jane Austen’s fondness for a heroine “whom no one but myself will very much like.” But if we see that even Emma’s most disagreeable blunders stem from a single remediable flaw—imaginism in an empty space not wholly self-created, mind without object—then we can see that the remedy awaiting Emma, her discovery of clear-sightedness through the embrace of Experience in the person of Mr. Knightley, is not at all an arbitrary or miraculous conversion.

这一精辟的见解让位于简·奥斯汀对迷人人物艾玛的救赎。而弗莱对奥斯汀自身矛盾心理的洞察则更为微妙：

That admirable observation yields to Jane Austen’s own redemption of the charming Emma. Still more subtle is Fry’s apprehension of Austen’s own ambivalence:

如同她的伦理观和政治立场一样，简·奥斯汀的领域是明确而固定的。她深知这种领域可能令人窒息，因此对任何令人不快的“小房间里的人群”（IV:249）式的喜剧表演都抱有矛盾的态度。如果爱玛失去了“唐威尔农场”的新鲜空气和“成年人的健康”（IV:39；关于爱玛），失去了“真诚与坦率之美”这片开阔的视野，那么，视野的缺失，甚至连神秘和流放带来的活力都无法企及，这便成了一种令人沮丧的状态，而时间的流逝，在非虚构的领域，只会加剧这种状态。田园诗般的婚姻，及其“完美的幸福”，是一种类型化的解决方案，一种人为的安排，但与浪漫主义中那些在地域和道德上都格格不入的结合不同，它在“英国文化”中找到了一个熟悉而迷人的镜像。简·奥斯汀将没有具体位置的“英格兰花园”改造成了一片封闭的农田，其范围之广足以将相邻的教区连接起来，但却牢牢地与外界隔绝开来。

Like her ethics and her politics, Jane Austen’s territory is determinate and fixed. Being quite aware that it is potentially stultifying, she is ambivalent about any comic dance that remains disagreeably “ ‘a crowd in a little room’ ” (IV:249). Without the fresh air and “grown-up health” (IV:39; re Emma) of the “home-farm of Donwell,” and without “the beauty of truth and sincerity” made available to Emma as an acceptably open vista, the absence of Prospect, of the invigorating scope even of mystery and exile, is a depressing condition which the passage of time, in the land of nonfiction, could only worsen. Georgic marriage, with its “perfect happiness,” is a generic solution, an artifice, but unlike the topographically and morally displaced unions of Romance, it finds near at hand, in “English culture,” a familiar and attractive mirror of itself. The unsituated “Garden of England” is transformed by Jane Austen to a rus conclusus, an enclosed farmland ample enough in range to unite adjoining parishes, but firmly immured against outlying fictions.

“坚守自我，不被外来的虚构所束缚”是奥斯汀的成功之处，但也令人略感不安。直到她创作了《劝导》，她才真正迎接了华兹华斯时代的挑战，以及那个时代关于记忆、解决和浪漫主义复兴的复杂辩证法。《劝导》如同华兹华斯最伟大的作品一样，几乎是对文艺复兴的一次复兴，是对莎士比亚式的包容、悲伤以及悲伤终结的回归。

To be “firmly immured against outlying fictions” is part of Austen’s triumph and yet remains a touch disquieting. It was not until she composed Persuasion that she fully met the challenge of the Age of Wordsworth, and of its intricate dialectics of memory, resolution, and a reopening to Romance. Persuasion, like the greatest Wordsworth, is almost a renaissance of the Renaissance, a return to Shakespearean capaciousness, sorrow, and the ending of sorrow.

第六章

CHAPTER 6

《劝导》（1817）

Persuasion (1817)

简· A·乌斯滕

JANE AUSTEN

“劝说”（Persuasion）一词源于拉丁语，意为“劝告”或“敦促”，指推荐采取或不采取某种特定行动。该词的词根意为“甜蜜的”或“令人愉悦的”，因此，采取或不采取某种行动的益处带有一种愉悦的意味，而非道德评判。简·奥斯汀选择它作为她最后一部完成的小说的标题。作为标题，它让人联想到《理智与情感》或《傲慢与偏见》 ，而非《爱玛》或《曼斯菲尔德庄园》。我们看到的不是某个人或房屋庄园的名字，而是一个抽象概念，在本例中是一个单一的概念。标题主要指的是女主人公安妮·艾略特在十九岁时，她的教母罗素夫人劝说她不要嫁给年轻的海军军官弗雷德里克·温特沃斯上尉。事实证明，这是一个非常糟糕的建议，八年后，安妮和温特沃斯上尉弥补了这一错误。如同奥斯汀所有充满讽刺意味的喜剧一样，女主人公的结局总是圆满的。然而，每次重读这部完美的小说，我都会感到非常难过。

“PERSUASION” IS A WORD derived from the Latin for “advising” or “urging,” for recommending that it is good to perform or not perform a particular action. The word goes back to a root meaning “sweet” or “pleasant,” so that the good of performance or nonperformance has a tang of taste rather than of moral judgment about it. Jane Austen chose it as the title for her last completed novel. As a title, it recalls Sense and Sensibility or Pride and Prejudice rather than Emma or Mansfield Park. We are given not the name of a person or house and estate, but of an abstraction, a single one in this case. The title’s primary reference is to the persuasion of its heroine, Anne Elliot, at the age of nineteen, by her godmother, Lady Russell, not to marry Captain Frederick Wentworth, a young naval officer. This was, as it turns out, very bad advice, and, after eight years, it is mended by Anne and Captain Wentworth. As with all of Austen’s ironic comedies, matters end happily for the heroine. And yet each time I finish a rereading of this perfect novel, I feel very sad.

这似乎并非我个人的主观感受；当我询问朋友和学生对这本书的感受时，他们经常提到一种淡淡的忧伤，这种忧伤在《劝导》中比在《曼斯菲尔德庄园》中更为明显。安妮·艾略特，一个安静而富有表现力的人，她独立自主，绝非孤苦伶仃，她的自我意识也从未动摇。我们在读完这本书时感受到的并非她的忧伤，而是小说本身的阴郁氛围。这种忧伤丰富了我所谓的小说经典的说服力，也正是它展现自身美学独特性的方式。

This does not appear to be my personal vagary; when I ask my friends and students about their experience of the book, they frequently mention a sadness which they also associate with Persuasion, more even than with Mansfield Park. Anne Elliot, a quietly eloquent being, is a self-reliant character, in no way forlorn, and her sense of self never falters. It is not her sadness we feel as we conclude the book: it is the novel’s somberness that impresses us. The sadness enriches what I would call the novel’s canonical persuasiveness, its way of showing us its aesthetic distinction.

《劝导》之于小说，正如安妮·艾略特之于小说人物——一位强大而内敛的先锋。这本书和安妮·艾略特这个人物都不算色彩鲜艳或活泼；《傲慢与偏见》中的伊丽莎白·班纳特和《爱玛》中的爱玛·伍德豪斯都充满活力，而安妮·艾略特起初似乎缺乏这种活力，这或许正是奥斯汀所说的安妮“对我来说几乎太完美了”的含义。安妮的内敛对我们来说确实近乎过分，但温特沃斯上校却能理解她，因为他与安妮之间似乎有一种神秘的默契。朱丽叶·麦克马斯特指出：“安妮·艾略特和温特沃斯上校之间始终存在着一种迂回的交流，尽管他们很少直接交谈，但彼此却总能比对方更透彻地理解对方话语的全部含义。”

Persuasion is among novels what Anne Elliot is among novelistic characters—a strong but subdued outrider. The book and the character are not colorful or vivacious; Elizabeth Bennet of Pride and Prejudice and Emma Woodhouse of Emma have a verve to them that initially seems lacking in Anne Elliot, which may be what Austen meant when she said that Anne was “almost too good for me.” Anne is really almost too subtle for us, though not for Wentworth, who has something of an occult wavelength to her. Juliet McMaster notes “the kind of oblique communication that constantly goes on between Anne Elliot and Captain Wentworth, where, though they seldom speak to each other, each constantly understands the full import of the other’s speech better than their interlocutors do.”

《劝导》中那种交流依赖于深沉的“爱慕”，奥斯汀认为这个词比“爱”更为重要。在奥斯汀的笔下，男女之间的“爱慕”是一种更为深刻持久的情感。我认为，安妮·艾略特虽然性格内敛，但却是奥斯汀倾注最多心血塑造的角色，这并不为过，因为奥斯汀将自己的才华倾注在了安妮身上。亨利·詹姆斯坚持认为，小说家必须拥有敏锐的感知力，能够捕捉到任何细微之处；按照这个标准（显然是有限的），在所有英语作家中，只有奥斯汀、乔治·艾略特和詹姆斯本人才能与司汤达、福楼拜和托尔斯泰一起跻身于一个相当有限的文学殿堂。安妮·艾略特或许是所有散文小说中唯一一个能够捕捉到任何细微之处的角色，尽管她不太可能成为小说家。

That kind of communication in Persuasion depends upon deep “affection,” a word that Austen values over “love.” “Affection” between woman and man, in Austen, is the more profound and lasting emotion. I think it is not too much to say that Anne Elliot, though subdued, is the creation for whom Austen herself must have felt the most affection, because she lavished her own gifts upon Anne. Henry James insisted that the novelist must possess a sensibility upon which absolutely nothing is lost; by that test (clearly a limited one), only Austen, George Eliot, and James himself, among all those writing in English, would join Stendhal, Flaubert, and Tolstoy in a rather restricted pantheon. Anne Elliot may well be the one character in all of prose fiction upon whom nothing is lost, though she is in no danger of turning into a novelist.

如此完美的人物形象所带来的审美风险显而易见：小说家如何才能塑造出令人信服的角色？乔伊斯的《尤利西斯》中的波尔迪之所以极具说服力，是因为他是一个如此完美的人，而这正是乔伊斯创作的初衷。奥斯汀的讽刺风格并不认可这种完美无缺的刻画：我们不会跟随她笔下的人物进入卧室、厨房或厕所。奥斯汀在《理智与情感》中戏仿的，在《劝导》中却被她提升到了极致：一种独特的、内在孤立的感性的崇高。安妮·艾略特并非奥斯汀笔下唯一拥有通情达理之心的角色。她与众不同之处在于她对他人以及自身的感知力近乎超乎常人，而这无疑是奥斯汀作为小说家最显著的特质。安妮·艾略特之于奥斯汀的作品，正如《皆大欢喜》中的罗莎琳德之于莎士比亚的作品：这两个角色几乎达到了小说家或剧作家所能达到的视角掌控力，否则小说或戏剧的所有戏剧性都会丧失殆尽。

The aesthetic dangers attendant upon such a paragon are palpable: how does a novelist make such a character persuasive? Poldy, in Joyce’s Ulysses, is overwhelmingly persuasive because he is so complete a person, which was the largest of Joyce’s intentions. Austen’s ironic mode does not sanction the representation of completeness: we do not accompany her characters to the bedroom, the kitchen, the privy.
