I do not know whether to call his a humorous savagery or a savage humor:

普加乔夫坐在指挥官家门廊的扶手椅上。他身穿一件饰有花边的红色哥萨克长袍，头戴一顶饰有金流苏的高耸貂皮帽，帽檐压得很低，遮住了他炯炯有神的双眼。他的脸庞让我觉得似曾相识。哥萨克首领们围在他身边。格拉西姆神父面色苍白，浑身颤抖，站在门廊旁，手中拿着十字架，似乎在默默地为即将受刑的人们祈求。广场上正在匆忙搭建绞刑架。我们走近时，巴什基尔人将人群驱散，我们被引荐给了普加乔夫。钟声停止了，一片死寂笼罩着大地。

“谁是指挥官？”冒名顶替者问道。我们的中士从人群中走出来，指着伊万·库兹米奇。普加乔夫恶狠狠地瞪着老人，对他说：

“你们竟敢违抗我，你们的君主？”

指挥官因伤势过重，身体逐渐虚弱，但他仍鼓起最后的力气，坚定地回答道：

“你不是我的君主，你是个窃贼，是​​个冒名顶替者，看好了！”

普加乔夫眉头紧锁，挥舞着一块白手帕。几个哥萨克人抬起老队长，把他拖到绞刑架旁。前一天我们审问过的那个伤痕累累的巴什基尔人出现在绞刑架横梁上，他手里拿着一根绳子，片刻之后，我眼睁睁地看着可怜的伊万·库兹米奇被吊了起来。随后，伊万·伊格纳季奇被带到普加乔夫面前。

“向君主彼得·费奥多罗维奇宣誓效忠！”普加乔夫对他说。

“你不是我们的君主，”伊万·伊格纳季奇重复着他船长的话回答道，“你，叔叔，是个窃贼，是​​个骗子！”

普加乔夫再次挥动手帕，这位好中尉便挂在他以前的上司旁边。

轮到我了。我大胆地看向普加乔夫，准备重复我那些高尚同志们的回答。然而，令我无比惊讶的是，我看到什瓦布林也在其中，他留着锅盖头，穿着哥萨克长袍。他走到普加乔夫面前，在他耳边说了几句话。

“绞死他！”普加乔夫头也不回地说道。

他们把绞索套在我的脖子上。我开始默默地祈祷，向上帝真诚地忏悔我所有的罪过，并祈求他拯救所有我亲近的人。他们把我拖到绞刑架下。

“别害怕，别害怕，”那些害我的人反复说道，或许他们是真心想鼓励我。突然，我听到一声喊叫：

“住手，你们这些恶魔，等等！……”

刽子手们停了下来。我环顾四周：萨维利奇躺在普加乔夫的脚边。

“亲爱的父亲！”我可怜的家庭教师说道，“我主人的孩子死了，与您何干？放了他吧，您会得到赎金的；为了杀鸡儆猴，震慑世人，让他们绞死我吧。”

普加乔夫打了个手势，他们立刻解开了我的束缚，放我走了。

“我们的父亲赦免你，”他们对我说。

我无法说获救的那一刻我感到高兴，但我也无法说我后悔。我的感觉太混乱了。他们又把我带到那个骗子面前，逼我跪在他面前。普加乔夫向我伸出了他那双肌肉结实的手。

“亲吻他的手，亲吻他的手！”周围的人喊道。但我宁愿遭受最残酷的惩罚，也不愿接受这种卑劣的羞辱。

“亲爱的彼得·安德烈！”萨维利奇站在我身后，用手指戳着我，低声说道，“别这么固执！关你什么事？朝它吐口水，亲吻那只……呸！……亲吻他的手。”

我没有动。普加乔夫放下手，带着一丝冷笑说道：

“看来他高兴得不知所措。快扶他起来！”

他们放我走了，然后放我自由了。我开始继续看那部荒诞喜剧。

Pugachev was sitting in an armchair on the porch of the commandant’s house. He was wearing a red Cossack kaftan trimmed with galoons. A tall sable hat with gold tassels was pulled down to his flashing eyes. His face seemed familiar to me. Cossack chiefs surrounded him. Father Gerasim, pale and trembling, stood by the porch with a cross in his hands and seemed to be silently pleading with him for the soon-to-be victims. A gallows was being hastily set up on the square. When we came closer, the Bashkirs drove the people aside, and we were introduced to Pugachev. The bells stopped ringing; a deep silence ensued.

“Which is the commandant?” asked the impostor. Our sergeant stepped out of the crowd and pointed to Ivan Kuzmich. Pugachev looked menacingly at the old man and said to him:

“How dared you oppose me, your sovereign?”

The commandant, growing faint from his wound, gathered his last strength and replied in a firm voice:

“You are not my sovereign, you are a thief and an impostor, see here!”

Pugachev frowned darkly and waved a white handkerchief. Several Cossacks picked up the old captain and dragged him to the gallows. The mutilated Bashkir whom we had questioned the day before turned up sitting astride the crossbar. He held a rope in his hand, and a moment later I saw poor Ivan Kuzmich hoisted into the air. Then Ivan Ignatyich was brought before Pugachev.

“Swear allegiance,” Pugachev said to him, “to the sovereign Pyotr Feodorovich!”

“You’re not our sovereign,” Ivan Ignatyich answered, repeating his captain’s words. “You, uncle, are a thief and an impostor!”

Pugachev waved his handkerchief again, and the good lieutenant hung beside his old superior.

It was my turn. I looked boldly at Pugachev, preparing to repeat the response of my noble-hearted comrades. Then, to my indescribable amazement, I saw Shvabrin among the rebel chiefs, his hair in a bowl cut and wearing a Cossack kaftan. He went up to Pugachev and said a few words in his ear.

“Hang him!” said Pugachev, without even glancing at me.

They threw the noose around my neck. I began to recite a prayer to myself, offering God sincere repentance for all my transgressions and asking for the salvation of all who were near to my heart. They dragged me under the gallows.

“Don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid,” repeated my undoers, perhaps truly wishing to hearten me. Suddenly I heard a shout:

“Stop, you fiends, wait!…”

The executioners stopped. I looked: Savelyich was lying at Pugachev’s feet.

“Dear father!” my poor tutor was saying. “What is the death of my master’s child to you? Let him go; you’ll get a ransom for him; and as an example and so as to put fear into people, have them hang my old self instead.”

Pugachev gave a sign, and they unbound me at once and let me go.

“Our father pardons you,” they said to me.

I cannot say that I was glad at that moment of my deliverance, though I also cannot say I regretted it. My feelings were too blurred. They brought me to the impostor again and made me go on my knees before him. Pugachev offered me his sinewy hand.

“Kiss his hand, kiss his hand!” said those around me. But I would have preferred the most cruel punishment to such base humiliation.

“Dearest Pyotr Andreich!” Savelyich whispered, standing behind me and prodding me. “Don’t be stubborn! What is it to you? Spit on it and kiss the vill—…pfui!…kiss his hand.”

I did not stir. Pugachev lowered his hand, saying with a little smirk:

“Seems his honor’s stupefied with joy. Stand him up!”

They stood me up and set me free. I started watching the continuation of the gruesome comedy.

叙述者彼得·安德烈耶维奇·格里尼奥夫非常讨人喜欢，却又出奇地冷漠或宿命论，尽管他勇敢而充满爱心。他十七岁，是军人父亲唯一活过婴儿期的孩子。他遵循家族传统参军，被派往奥伦堡。彼得在暴风雪中迷路，几乎看不清路，却在一位陌生人的指引下找到了出路。他感激不尽，将自己温暖的外套给了这位陌生人，而这位陌生人后来被证实是普加乔夫。格里尼奥夫和普加乔夫身上那些令人费解的矛盾之处，在普希金研究权威大卫·M·贝西亚的阐释下，得到了清晰的展现：

The narrator, Pyotr Andreevich Grinyov, is very likable yet strangely dispassionate or fatalistic, though he is courageous and loving. He is seventeen and the only child of his military father to survive past infancy. Following family tradition, he enters the army and is sent to Orenburg. Pyotr gets lost, hardly able to see in a blizzard, yet finds his way out with an unknown guide. Thankful, he gives his warm coat to the stranger, who will turn out to be Pugachev. The curious perplexities both of Grinyov and of Pugachev are illuminated for me by the leading Pushkin scholar David M. Bethea:

在创作《上尉的女儿》时，普希金显然试图回归一套古老的准则和价值观，这套准则和价值观是在十八世纪严酷的、时常充满战争的环境下形成的，在他看来，当时的环境不容许任何细微差别和诠释。在他生命最后几年的困境中，他渴望的正是这种老派的清晰，尤其是在捍卫家族荣誉和名誉的时候。这种清晰的本质在于，一个举动本身就具有美感，它兼具道德和美学的双重维度，能够独立存在，在品格受到最严峻考验的时刻，彰显高尚的品格。在《普加乔夫传》中，最令人印象深刻的例子是，穆斯林比克拜在即将被普加乔夫的军队处决时，划了个十字，并将自己的头伸进了绞索。通过赋予虚构人物普加乔夫辨识善行之美并展现慷慨——即以美报美——的能力，普希金在两个方面超越了现实中的起义。首先，他表明，尽管存在着由来已久的阶级不信任以及导致起义的种种因素，农民和贵族仍然可以拥有共同的荣誉感。其次，他表明这种“传递善意”的方式能够打破阶级仇恨，建立更人性化的关系，这正是尤里·洛特曼在其关于《上尉的女儿》“观念结构”的著名文章中所阐述的观点。当普加乔夫得知什瓦布林挟持了一名孤儿并可能虐待她时，他深受触动，决定出手相助。弱者不应被强者欺凌。同样，当普加乔夫得知玛莎是他的死敌的女儿，并且仍然决定继续扮演媒人/代理父亲的角色，释放这对年轻夫妇时，结果也类似：道德和美学结合在一起，形成了一种极其美丽的姿态，即作为一个人足够宽容（lichnost'），不计较得失。

（艾丽莎·迪内加·吉莱斯皮编，《禁忌的普希金》）

我突然想到一个奇怪的想法：冥冥之中，上帝让我第二次见到普加乔夫，似乎是为了给我一个实现我意图的机会。我决定抓住这个机会，来不及细想，便回答了普加乔夫的问题：

“我当时正要去别洛戈尔斯克要塞营救一个在那里受到虐待的孤儿。”

普加乔夫的眼神闪过一丝光芒。

“我的族人中谁敢虐待孤儿？”他喊道，“就算他狡猾如狐，也逃不过我的审判。说出来：谁是罪魁祸首？”

“是什瓦布林，”我回答说，“他囚禁了你在神父妻子家看到的那个生病的女孩，想强迫她嫁给他。”

“我要好好教训什瓦布林，”普加乔夫恶狠狠地说，“他要让我让他知道为所欲为、虐待他人的滋味。我要绞死他。”

“请允许我插句话，”赫洛普沙沙哑着嗓子说，“你急着任命什瓦布林为要塞指挥官，现在又急着把他绞死。你任命一个贵族担任哥萨克的指挥官，已经得罪了他们；现在别因为一点诽谤就处死贵族，吓坏他们。”

“没必要同情他们，也没必要赞同他们，”系着蓝丝带的小老头说道，“处决什瓦布林没什么错；不过，好好盘问一下这位军官先生，他为何如此热心前来，也未尝不可。如果他不承认您是君主，就不必指望您伸张正义；如果他承认，那他为何至今仍与您的敌人待在奥伦堡？何不下令将他押往卫兵营，在那里放把火烧了？我总觉得，他的荣誉是奥伦堡的指挥官派人送来的。”

我发现那个老恶棍的逻辑颇有说服力。想到自己落入了谁的手中，我不禁不寒而栗。普加乔夫察觉到了我的困惑。

“嗯，法官大人？”他朝我眨了眨眼说，“我的元帅说得好像挺有道理的。您觉得呢？”

普加乔夫的嘲讽让我重拾勇气。我平静地回答说，我任他摆布，他可以随意处置我。

In writing The Captain’s Daughter Pushkin was clearly trying to return to an older set of precepts and values, ones determined in the harsh, often wartime conditions of the eighteenth century, that (as he perceived it) didn’t allow space for nuance and interpretation. In his compromised situation in the last years of his life it was this old-fashioned clarity, especially when defending the honor of one’s family and name, for which he yearned. The essence of this clarity is the ability of a gesture to be beautiful in its own right, to possess both a moral and aesthetic dimension, to stand alone, as something proving nobility of character at a moment when that character is most severely challenged. In The History of Pugachev the most impressive example of such a gesture is when the Muslim Bikbai, preparing to be executed by Pugachev’s forces, crosses himself and puts his own head into the noose. By giving the fictional Pugachev the ability to recognize the beauty in a deed and to show generosity, that is, to repay beauty with more beauty, Pushkin was improving on the reality of the uprising in two ways. First, he was showing that, despite the ancient class distrust and the factors that led to the uprising in the first place, both peasant and nobleman could share a sense of honor. Second, he was showing that this “paying it forward” has a way of breaking through class enmity and establishing relations in more human terms, which is Iurii Lotman’s point in his celebrated piece on the “ideational structure” of The Captain’s Daughter. When Pugachev learns that Shvabrin is holding an orphan hostage and possibly abusing her, he is moved to act. The weak should not be taken advantage of by the strong. Likewise, when it becomes clear that Masha is the daughter of his sworn enemy and Pugachev still decides to continue in his role as matchmaker/surrogate father and to release the young couple, the result is similar: the moral and the aesthetic come together in an extravagantly beautiful gesture of being big enough as a person (lichnost’) not to keep score.

(Alyssa Dinega Gillespie, ed., Taboo Pushkin)

A strange thought occurred to me: it seemed to me that Providence, which had brought me to Pugachev a second time, was giving me the chance to carry out my intention. I decided to take advantage of it and, having no time to think over what I decided, I answered Pugachev’s question:

“I was going to the Belogorsk fortress to rescue an orphan who is being mistreated there.”

Pugachev’s eyes flashed.

“Who of my people dares to mistreat an orphan?” he cried. “Though he be sly as a fox, he won’t escape my justice. Speak: Who is the guilty one?”

“Shvabrin,” I replied. “He’s holding captive the girl you saw sick at the priest’s wife’s and wants to force her to marry him.”

“I’ll teach Shvabrin,” Pugachev said menacingly. “He’ll learn from me what it means to do as he likes and mistreat people. I’ll hang him.”

“Allow me to put in a word,” said Khlopusha in a hoarse voice. “You were in a hurry to appoint Shvabrin commandant of the fortress, and now you’re in a hurry to hang him. You’ve already offended the Cossacks by setting up a nobleman as their superior; don’t frighten the nobility now by executing them at the first bit of slander.”

“There’s no cause to pity them or approve of them,” said the little old man with the blue ribbon. “Nothing’s wrong with executing Shvabrin; but it wouldn’t be bad to give Mister Officer here a proper questioning as to why he was pleased to come calling. If he doesn’t recognize you as the sovereign, he needn’t look to you for your justice, and if he does, why has he sat there in Orenburg with your enemies up to now? Why don’t you order him taken to the guardhouse and have them start a little fire there: something tells me his honor’s been sent to us by the Orenburg commanders.”

I found the old villain’s logic quite persuasive. Chills came over me at the thought of whose hands I was in. Pugachev noticed my confusion.

“Eh, Your Honor?” he said, winking at me. “My field marshal seems to be talking sense. What do you think?”

Pugachev’s mockery restored my courage. I replied calmly that I was in his power and he was free to do whatever he liked with me.

格里尼奥夫和普加乔夫之间的互动是普希金最伟大的创作之一。莱蒙托夫（他从未见过普希金）和其他人认为，在杀戮和人类良知之下，某种东西将两人紧紧联系在一起，形成了一种比毁灭普希金的谋杀阴谋更为深不可测的契约。

The interplay between Grinyov and Pugachev is one of Pushkin’s grand inventions. Something that moves beneath the world of slaughter and human conscience binds the two together in a covenant more cavernous than was the murderous intrigue that destroyed Pushkin, according to Lermontov (who never met Pushkin) and others.

格里尼奥夫的言论恰到好处地维系了他与普加乔夫之间的关系：

Grinyov sounds the perfect chord to maintain his bond with Pugachev:

“啊！我差点忘了谢谢你的马和外套。没有你，我根本到不了镇上，路上肯定会被冻死。”

我的计谋奏效了。普加乔夫高兴起来。

“善有善报，”他眨了眨眼，眯起眼睛说，“告诉我，什瓦布林虐待那个女孩跟你有什么关系？她可不是什么年轻小伙子心目中的宠儿，对吧？”

“她是我未婚妻，”我回答普加乔夫，看到天气转暖，觉得没有必要隐瞒真相。

“你的未婚妻！”普加乔夫喊道，“你怎么不早说？我们这就为你办婚礼，好好庆祝一番！”然后，他转向别洛博罗多夫说：“听着，元帅！我和他可是老朋友了，咱们坐下来吃晚饭吧；早上比晚上更明智。明天我们再看看怎么处置他。”

我本乐意婉拒这份“殊荣”，但已无办法。两位年轻的哥萨克女子，小屋主人的女儿，铺上白色桌布，端来面包、鱼汤和几瓶伏特加和啤酒，就这样，我第二次与普加乔夫和他那些可怕的同伙共进晚餐。

“Ah! I almost forgot to thank you for the horse and the coat. Without you I wouldn’t have made it to the town and would have frozen on the way.”

My ruse worked. Pugachev cheered up.

“One good turn deserves another,” he said, winking and narrowing his eyes. “Tell me now, what have you got to do with the girl Shvabrin’s mistreating? Not the darling of a young lad’s heart, is she?”

“She’s my bride-to-be,” I replied to Pugachev, seeing the weather change for the better and finding no need to conceal the truth.

“Your bride-to-be!” cried Pugachev. “Why didn’t you say so before? We’ll get you married and feast at your wedding!” Then, turning to Beloborodov: “Listen, Field Marshal! His honor and I are old friends; let’s sit down and have supper; morning’s wiser than evening. Tomorrow we’ll see what we’ll do with him.”

I would have been glad to decline the proposed honor, but there was no help for it. Two young Cossack women, the daughters of the cottage’s owner, covered the table with a white tablecloth, brought some bread, fish soup, and several bottles of vodka and beer, and for the second time I found myself sharing a meal with Pugachev and his frightful comrades.

格里尼奥夫带着玛莎获释后，投奔年迈的父母，勉强栖身。然而，他们却发现自己被自己的农奴围困，而这些农奴的首领正是什瓦布林和几个普加乔夫的爪牙。什瓦布林是《上尉的女儿》中真正的反派，有人将其比作伊阿古，但与《奥赛罗》中邪恶的老人相比，什瓦布林简直微不足道。他是个可怕的家伙，对格里尼奥夫心爱的玛莎——上尉的女儿——垂涎三尺。遭到玛莎拒绝后，他与格里尼奥夫决斗，并伤到了这位高贵的主人公。之后，他加入了普加乔夫的爪牙，保全性命，并妄图强暴玛莎。最终，普希金对他进行了清算：

Released with Masha, Grinyov finds precarious refuge with his old parents, only to find them besieged by their own serfs under the leadership of Shvabrin and a few other Pugachev varlets. Shvabrin, authentic villain of The Captain’s Daughter, has been compared to Iago, but on the scale of Othello’s malignant Ancient, Shvabrin is no more than a water bug. A dreadful creature, he is moved by lust for Grinyov’s beloved Masha, the captain’s daughter. Rebuffed by her, he fights a duel with Grinyov and wounds the noble protagonist. Joining Pugachev’s thugs, he preserves himself and hopes to ravish Masha. In time, Pushkin keeps score on him:

就在这时，我们听到门外传来几个人声。我悄悄示意母亲和玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜退到角落里，拔出剑，倚靠在门边的墙上。父亲拿起两把手枪，上了膛，站在我身边。挂锁咔哒一声，门开了，执达吏的脑袋露了出来。我一剑砍向他，他应声倒地，堵住了入口。与此同时，父亲朝门口开了一枪。围攻我们的人群咒骂着四散奔逃。我把受伤的人拖过门槛，从里面闩上了门。院子里挤满了武装人员。我认出了其中的什瓦布林。

“别害怕，”我对女人们说。“还有希望。父亲，你别再开枪了。我们留着最后一枪吧。”

母亲默默地向上帝祈祷；玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜站在她身旁，天使般平静地等待着命运的裁决。门外传来威胁、辱骂和诅咒。我站在原地，随时准备砍倒第一个胆敢闯进来的家伙。突然，那些恶徒都安静了下来。我听到什瓦布林在呼唤我的名字。

“我来了。你想要什么？”

“投降吧，格里尼奥夫，抵抗毫无用处。可怜可怜你的老伙计们吧。顽固不化救不了你们。我要把你们全都抓起来！”

“你试试看，叛徒！”

“我不会白白送命，也不会浪费我子民的生命。我会命令他们放火烧掉粮仓，然后我们再看看你会怎么做，别洛戈尔斯克的堂吉诃德。现在是晚餐时间。你就坐在那儿，慢慢想吧。再见，玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜，我不会向你道歉的：你和你的骑士在黑暗中大概不会感到无聊吧。”

什瓦布林走了，只留下一个守卫在粮仓旁。我们沉默不语。每个人都在独自思索，不敢与他人分享自己的想法。我想象着心怀怨恨的什瓦布林会对我们做出什么事。我几乎不在乎自己。我该承认吗？就连我父母的遭遇都比不上玛丽亚·伊万诺芙娜的命运让我感到恐惧。我知道我的母亲深受农民和农奴的爱戴；我的父亲虽然严厉，但也受人爱戴，因为他为人公正，了解他所统治的人民的真正需求。他们的反抗不过是一时的妄想，一时冲动，并非出于真正的愤慨。他们或许还能得到宽恕。可是玛丽亚·伊万诺芙娜呢？那个堕落无耻的男人究竟为她准备了怎样的命运？我不敢去想那个可怕的想法，我做好了准备，上帝原谅我，我宁愿亲手杀了她，也不愿再看到她落入残暴的敌人手中。

又过了一个小时左右。村子里传来醉醺醺的歌声。我们的守卫们嫉妒不已，恼羞成怒，咒骂着要折磨我们，甚至扬言要处死我们。我们等着什瓦布林的威胁再次出现。终于，院子里传来一阵骚动，我们又听到了什瓦布林的声音：

“那么，你下定决心了吗？你愿意自愿向我投降吗？”

没有人回答他。什瓦布林等了一会儿，吩咐人拿来稻草。几分钟后，黑暗的粮仓突然燃起熊熊大火，浓烟从门缝下渗了出来。这时，玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜走到我面前，握住我的手，轻声说道：

“够了，彼得·安德烈！别为了我毁了自己和你的父母。放了我。什瓦布林会听我的。”

“不是为了任何事！”我激动地喊道，“你知道等待你的是什么吗？”

“我无法承受耻辱，”她平静地回答，“但我或许能救下我的救命恩人，以及慷慨收留我这个孤儿的家人。再见了，安德烈·彼得罗维奇。再见了，阿芙多佳·瓦西里耶夫娜。你们对我的恩惠远不止于此。请赐予我祝福。再见了，请原谅我，彼得·安德烈耶维奇。请相信……相信……”说到这里，她突然嚎啕大哭，双手捂住了脸……我当时就像个疯子。我的母亲也哭了。

“够了，玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜，”父亲说，“谁会让你一个人去跟这些强盗碰面？坐在这儿，别说话。如果我们注定要死，那就一起死。听听，他们现在在说什么？”

“你投降吗？”什瓦布林吼道，“看到了吗？五分钟后你就要被烤了。”

“我们绝不投降，恶棍！”我父亲坚定地回答道。

他满是皱纹的脸上，却洋溢着惊人的勇气，灰白的眉毛下，双眼闪烁着危险的光芒。然后，他转向我，说道：

“就是现在！”

他打开了门。火焰瞬间窜入，沿着布满干苔藓的横梁向上窜去。父亲鸣枪示警，跨过燃烧的门槛，高喊道：“所有人，跟我来！”我抓住母亲和玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜的手，迅速把她们领了出去。门槛边躺着什瓦布林，他被父亲那只衰老的手击倒了；一群在我们突然出击前逃窜的强盗，立刻鼓起勇气，开始包围我们。我设法还击了几拳，但一块扔得正中的砖头正中我的胸口。我倒在地上，短暂地失去了知觉。醒来后，我看到什瓦布林坐在血迹斑斑的草地上，我们全家都坐在他面前。有人搀扶着我。一群农民、哥萨克和巴什基尔人围在我们周围。什瓦布林脸色惨白，一只手捂着受伤的肋部。他的脸上既有痛苦，又有怨恨。他缓缓抬起头，看着我，用虚弱而含糊的声音说道：

“绞死他……绞死他们所有人……除了她……”

一群恶徒立刻将我们团团围住，一边叫喊一边把我们拖到城门前。但突然间，他们抛弃了我们，四散奔逃；祖林骑马冲进了城门，身后跟着他整个精锐的骑兵队，剑都已出鞘。

Just then we heard several voices outside the door. I silently made a sign to my mother and Marya Ivanovna to retreat into a corner, drew my sword, and leaned against the wall right next to the door. My father took the pistols, cocked them both, and stood beside me. The padlock clacked, the door opened, and the bailiff’s head appeared. I struck it with my sword and he fell, blocking the entrance. At the same moment my father fired a pistol through the doorway. The crowd besieging us ran off cursing. I dragged the wounded man across the threshold and bolted the door from inside. The yard was full of armed men. Among them I recognized Shvabrin.

“Don’t be afraid,” I said to the women. “There’s hope. And you, father, don’t shoot again. Let’s save the last shot.”

Mother silently prayed to God; Marya Ivanovna stood beside her, waiting with angelic calm for our fate to be decided. Outside the door we heard threats, abuse, and curses. I stood in my place, ready to cut down the first daredevil to come in. Suddenly the villains fell silent. I heard the voice of Shvabrin calling me by name.

“I’m here. What do you want?”

“Surrender, Grinyov, it’s useless to resist. Have pity on your old ones. Obstinacy won’t save you. I’m going to get you all!”

“Just try it, traitor!”

“I won’t risk my neck for nothing, or waste my people’s lives. I’ll order them to set the granary on fire, and then we’ll see what you do, Don Quixote of Belogorsk. It’s dinnertime now. Sit there for a while and think things over at your leisure. Good-bye, Marya Ivanovna, I won’t apologize to you: you’re probably not bored there in the dark with your knight.”

Shvabrin went away and left a guard by the granary. We were silent. Each of us was thinking to himself, not daring to share his thoughts with the others. I imagined all that the resentful Shvabrin was capable of inflicting on us. I cared little about myself. Shall I confess it? Even my parents’ lot did not horrify me so much as the fate of Marya Ivanovna. I knew that my mother was adored by the peasants and the house serfs; that my father, for all his strictness, was also loved, for he was a fair man and knew the true needs of the people subject to him. Their rebellion was a delusion, a momentary drunkenness, not the expression of their indignation. Here mercy was likely. But Marya Ivanovna? What lot had the depraved and shameless man prepared for her? I did not dare to dwell on that horrible thought, and prepared myself, God forgive me, sooner to kill her than to see her a second time in the hands of the cruel enemy.

About another hour went by. There was drunken singing in the village. Our guards were envious and, vexed with us, swore and taunted us with torture and death. We awaited the sequel to Shvabrin’s threats. Finally there came a big commotion in the yard, and again we heard Shvabrin’s voice:

“So, have you made up your mind? Do you voluntarily surrender to me?”

No one answered him. Having waited a little, Shvabrin ordered straw brought. After a few minutes, a burst of fire lit up the dark granary, and smoke began to make its way through the chink under the door. Then Marya Ivanovna came to me and, taking me by the hand, said softly:

“Enough, Pyotr Andreich! Don’t destroy yourself and your parents on account of me. Let me out. Shvabrin will listen to me.”

“Not for anything,” I cried hotly. “Do you know what awaits you?”

“I won’t survive dishonor,” she replied calmly. “But maybe I’ll save my deliverer and the family that so magnanimously sheltered a poor orphan. Farewell, Andrei Petrovich. Farewell, Avdotya Vasilyevna. You were more than benefactors to me. Give me your blessing. Farewell and forgive me, Pyotr Andreevich. Be assured that…that…” Here she burst into tears and buried her face in her hands…I was like a madman. My mother wept.

“Enough nonsense, Marya Ivanovna,” said my father. “Who is going to let you go to these brigands alone? Sit here and be quiet. If we’re going to die, we’ll die together. Listen, what are they saying now?”

“Do you surrender?” Shvabrin shouted. “See? In five minutes you’ll be roasted.”

“We don’t surrender, villain!” my father answered him in a firm voice.

His face, covered with wrinkles, was animated by astonishing courage, his eyes flashed menacingly under his gray eyebrows. And, turning to me, he said:

“Now’s the time!”

He opened the door. Flames burst in and shot up the beams caulked with dry moss. My father fired his pistol and stepped across the blazing threshold, shouting: “Everyone, follow me!” I seized my mother and Marya Ivanovna by the hands and quickly led them outside. By the threshold lay Shvabrin, shot down by my father’s decrepit hand; the crowd of brigands, who fled before our unexpected sortie, at once took courage and began to surround us. I still managed to deal several blows, but a well-thrown brick struck me full in the chest. I fell down and lost consciousness for a moment. On coming to, I saw Shvabrin sitting on the bloody grass, and before him our whole family. I was supported under the arms. The crowd of peasants, Cossacks, and Bashkirs stood around us. Shvabrin was terribly pale. He pressed one hand to his wounded side. His face expressed suffering and spite. He slowly raised his head, looked at me, and pronounced in a weak and indistinct voice:

“Hang him…hang all of them…except her…”

The crowd of villains surrounded us at once and, shouting, dragged us to the gates. But suddenly they abandoned us and scattered; through the gates rode Zurin and behind him his entire squadron with drawn swords.

一切看似圆满，只是康复后的什瓦布林指证格里尼奥夫与普加乔夫有勾结。为了保护玛莎免受牵连，异想天开的格里尼奥夫拒绝为自己辩护。然而，一切最终还是圆满结束，因为普希金巧妙地借鉴了沃尔特·斯科特爵士的《米德洛锡安之心》（1818）。在《米德洛锡安之心》中，珍妮·迪恩斯经常步行，从爱丁堡前往伦敦，试图说服阿盖尔公爵去劝说卡罗琳王后赦免她的妹妹艾菲。艾菲被诬告杀婴，本应被处决，但珍妮·迪恩斯成功了。

All’s well that ends well except that the recuperated Shvabrin testifies to Grinyov’s apparent collaboration with Pugachev. To protect Masha from any recrimination, quixotic Grinyov refuses to defend himself. All’s well then ends well, because Pushkin shrewdly borrows from Sir Walter Scott’s The Heart of Midlothian (1818), where Jeanie Deans travels, frequently by foot, from Edinburgh to London, in order to prevail upon the Duke of Argyle to persuade Queen Caroline to pardon her sister Effie. Falsely accused of infanticide, Effie would have been executed, but Jeanie Deans is successful.

按照这个模式，普希金突然让玛莎的个性得以充分展现。她主动请求觐见叶卡捷琳娜大帝，以拯救格里尼奥夫。这位性格复杂的女皇，伪装成一位衣着朴素的宫廷侍女，被玛莎说服，赦免了格里尼奥夫。玛莎的所作所为远不止于此。她的父母被普加乔夫的暴徒杀害，叶卡捷琳娜女皇慷慨地给予了她经济补偿。

On that model, Pushkin suddenly allows Masha’s personality to flower. On her own initiative, she moves to save Grinyov by requesting an audience with Catherine the Great. That complex monarch, pretending to be only a court lady, rather plainly dressed, is persuaded by Masha and reprieves Grinyov. She does much more. Masha has lost her father and mother to Pugachev’s ruffians, and the Empress Catherine is lavish in financial compensation.

普希金必须留下最后的发言权：

Pushkin has to have the final words:

彼得·安德烈耶维奇·格里尼奥夫的笔记到此结束。据家族传说，他于1774年底奉皇室之命获释；他亲眼目睹了普加乔夫的处决，普加乔夫在人群中认出了他，并向他点头致意。片刻之后，普加乔夫的头颅血淋淋地、已经死去，被展示给众人。不久之后，彼得·安德烈耶维奇与玛丽亚·伊万诺夫娜结婚。他们的后代至今仍在辛比尔斯克省繁衍生息。距离***二十英里处有一个村庄，属于十位地主。在庄园的一翼，一封叶卡捷琳娜二世亲笔书写的信件被装裱在玻璃框内展出。这封信是写给彼得·安德烈耶维奇的父亲的，信中为他的儿子辩护，并赞扬了米罗诺夫上尉女儿的才智和品格。彼得·安德烈耶维奇·格里尼奥夫的一位孙子将他的手稿提供给了我们。这位孙子得知我们正在研究一部与他祖父所描述的时代相关的作品。经格里尼奥夫家族同意，我们决定单独出版这部手稿，并为每一章都找到了合适的题词，同时修改了一些人名。

（出版商，1836年10月19日）

The notes of Pyotr Andreevich Grinyov end here. From family tradition it is known that he was released from prison at the end of 1774, by imperial order; that he was present at the execution of Pugachev, who recognized him in the crowd and nodded to him with his head, which a moment later was shown, dead and bloodied, to the people. Soon afterwards Pyotr Andreevich married Marya Ivanovna. Their descendants still prosper in Simbirsk province. Twenty miles from *** there is a village belonging to ten landowners. In one wing of the manor house a letter in the hand of Catherine II is displayed under glass and in a frame. It was written to Pyotr Andreevich’s father and contains the vindication of his son and praise of the mind and heart of Captain Mironov’s daughter. Pyotr Andreevich Grinyov’s manuscript was furnished us by one of his grandsons, who learned that we were occupied with a work related to the time described by his grandfather. We have decided, with the family’s permission, to publish it separately, having found a suitable epigraph for each chapter and allowed ourselves to change some proper names.

(The Publisher, 19 Oct. 1836)

最后的话出自普希金的圣骑士之口：

The last words are those of Pushkin’s paladin:

俄罗斯家庭浪漫的平衡（暂时）是通过小说而非历史得以恢复的。归根结底，普希金的小说向读者传达的关于普加乔夫及其起义的禁忌知识，并非仅仅是它们曾经存在过（如果叶卡捷琳娜的愿望得以实现，所有关于这段悲剧的痕迹都将被从历史记忆中抹去），而是它们在某种程度上，尽管造成了骇人的屠杀，却依然是可以理解的。它们是被压抑的群体性回归，是俄罗斯历史中挥之不去的记忆。

The equilibrium in Russia’s family romance has been restored (momentarily) through fiction, if not through history. In the final analysis, the forbidden knowledge about Pugachev and his uprising that Pushkin’s novel imparts to the reader is not simply that they existed (if Catherine had had her way, all evidence of this tragic episode would have been expunged from historical memory) but that their existence at some level, despite the horrific carnage, is understandable. They were the return of the repressed on a mass level, the haunting of Russian history by memories impossible to forget.

第十二章

CHAPTER 12

《呼啸山庄》（1847）

Wuthering Heights (1847)

艾米莉·布朗特​

EMILY BRONTË

如果说《呼啸山庄》有一部小说 ，那么它的核心人物是凯瑟琳·恩肖，她夹在埃德加·林顿的现实生活和希斯克利夫的拜伦式魔性之间。凯瑟琳·恩肖和林顿一家去世后，整部小说就完全变成了爱情故事。《呼啸山庄》几乎是唯一一部讲述早婚早逝的小说。凯瑟琳·恩肖十八岁去世，希斯克利夫的儿子林顿十七岁，辛德利二十七岁，埃德加三十九岁，可怜的伊莎贝拉三十一岁，希斯克利夫大约三十八岁（如果我没算错的话）。埃德加·林顿结婚时二十一岁，凯瑟琳·恩肖十七岁。辛德利二十岁娶了弗朗西丝，而希斯克利夫和伊莎贝拉那段如同地狱般的婚姻始于他十九岁，她十八岁。幸存者哈雷顿·恩肖和凯瑟琳·林顿分别在二十四岁和十八岁时缔结了唯一幸福的婚姻。每个人都很早就结婚，因为他们预感到自己不会长寿。除非哈雷顿和第二任凯瑟琳能够打破家族的宿命，否则艾米莉·勃朗特笔下的世界里没有一个主人公能活到四十岁，这不幸地预言，即使是坚强的夏洛蒂也活不到三十九岁。艾米莉本人三十岁就因家族遗传病——肺结核去世。

IF THERE IS A NOVEL IN Wuthering Heights, it centers upon Catherine Earnshaw, caught between the social reality of Edgar Linton and the daemonic Byronism of Heathcliff. Once Catherine Earnshaw and the Lintons are dead, the book is entirely romance. Wuthering Heights is almost uniquely the story of early marriage and early death. Catherine Earnshaw dies at eighteen, Heathcliff’s son, Linton, at seventeen, Hindley at twenty-seven, Edgar at thirty-nine, poor Isabella at thirty-one, and Heathcliff at about thirty-eight (if my arithmetic is right). Edgar Linton is twenty-one and Catherine Earnshaw seventeen when they marry. Hindley marries Frances at twenty, and the marriage made in hell between Heathcliff and Isabella starts when he is nineteen and she is eighteen. The survivors, Hareton Earnshaw and Catherine Linton, make the only happy marriage, at twenty-four and eighteen, respectively. Everyone marries very young because they intuit they will not live long. Unless Hareton and the second Catherine can defy their lineage, no protagonist in Emily Brontë’s cosmos reaches forty, unhappily prophesying that even the stalwart Charlotte did not attain thirty-nine. Emily died at thirty of the family malady, tuberculosis.

我第一次写《呼啸山庄》是在1947年，当时我还在康奈尔大学读本科。那时的感受如何，我已无从知晓，因为岁月的洗礼早已将它抹去。此后，我又写了三篇关于艾米莉·勃朗特这部爱情小说的文章，除了她那些风格迥异却又常常精彩绝伦的诗作之外，我们所知的她的作品仅限于此。如今我已八十八岁高龄，重读她的作品，比以往任何时候都更加强烈地感受到，最令我着迷的是书中那深渊般的意境。希斯克利夫的几乎所有经历都发生在这片虚空中，或许凯瑟琳的一半以上也深陷其中。我这里所说的“深渊”，指的是《创世记》1:2中希伯来语“ tehom ”所指的波涛汹涌、深不见底的大海。在诺斯替教的异端邪说中，“普勒罗玛”（Pleroma）或“神圣圆满”被等同于这深渊，它先于“埃洛希姆”（Elohim，即规范的神性）而存在。

I first wrote about Wuthering Heights as a Cornell undergraduate in 1947. Whatever that was like, I cannot know, since time’s siftings have stilled it. Since then I have written three essays on Emily Brontë’s one romance, all we have of her except for her mixed yet frequently magnificent body of poems. Rereading her at eighty-eight, I find, more strongly than before, that what fascinates me most is the abyss at the center of the book. Nearly all Heathcliff is in that void and perhaps more than half of the first Catherine. I mean “abyss” in the sense of Genesis 1:2, the Hebrew tehom, for a turbulent bottomless sea. In the Gnostic heresy the Pleroma or Divine Fullness is equated with that abyss, which precedes Elohim, the normative godhead.

虽然艾米莉·勃朗特的父亲是一位虔诚的爱尔兰人，后来成为了一名英国圣公会牧师，但基督教对《呼啸山庄》的作者艾米莉·勃朗特的影响甚微。她的诗歌颂扬的是“我胸中的上帝”：

Though Emily Brontë’s father, an Irishman who became an Anglican priest, was devout, Christianity had little effect upon the visionary of Wuthering Heights. Her poetry celebrates the “God within my breast”:

我没有懦弱的灵魂

在饱受风暴侵袭的世界里，没有丝毫震颤。

我看见天堂的光辉闪耀。

信仰之光同样照亮我，使我免受恐惧的侵袭。

No coward soul is mine

No trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere

I see Heaven’s glories shine

And Faith shines equal arming me from Fear

哦，我胸中的神啊

O God within my breast

全能无所不在的神

生命，在我里面安息，

作为不朽的生命，我拥有你的力量

Almighty ever-present Deity

Life, that in me hast rest,

As I Undying Life, have power in Thee

千百种信条都是徒劳。

Vain are the thousand creeds

那能打动人心的，无比虚荣，

毫无价值，如同枯萎的杂草

或无垠大海中最无意义的泡沫

That move men’s hearts, unutterably vain,

Worthless as withered weeds

Or idlest froth amid the boundless main

唤醒一个人的怀疑

To waken doubt in one

紧紧抓住你的无限，

所以肯定锚定在

永恒的磐石。

Holding so fast by thy infinity,

So surely anchored on

The steadfast rock of Immortality.

满怀爱意

With wide-embracing love

你的灵魂赋予永恒岁月以生命

弥漫并盘旋于上方，

变化、维持、消解、创造和孕育

Thy spirit animates eternal years

Pervades and broods above,

Changes, sustains, dissolves, creates and rears

虽然地球和月亮都已消失

Though earth and moon were gone

于是，太阳和宇宙不复存在了。

而你，却孤身一人。

一切存在都将存在于你之中。

And suns and universes ceased to be

And Thou wert left alone

Every Existence would exist in thee

死亡没有容身之地

There is not room for Death

即使是原子，他的力量也无法将其化为虚空

因为你是存在和呼吸

而你所拥有的，将永不消逝。

Nor atom that his might could render void

Since thou art Being and Breath

And what thou art may never be destroyed.

在《论自助》一书中，神圣的爱默生给了我指路明灯：“正如人的祈祷是意志的疾病，他们的信条也是理智的疾病。”这与艾米莉·勃朗特的观点又有多么不同呢？

In “Self-Reliance,” the sacred Emerson gave me my guiding spur: “As men’s prayers are a disease of the will, so are their creeds a disease of the intellect.” How far is that from Emily Brontë?

千百种信条都是徒劳。

那能打动人心的，无比虚荣，

毫无价值，如同枯萎的杂草

或无垠大海中最无意义的泡沫

Vain are the thousand creeds

That move men’s hearts, unutterably vain,

Worthless as withered weeds

Or idlest froth amid the boundless main

虽然有些学者认为这首惊世之作是夏洛蒂·勃朗特所作，但对于任何有鉴赏力的人来说，这一定是艾米莉·勃朗特最伟大的作品：

Though some scholars believe that Charlotte wrote this astonishing poem, to anyone with an inner ear this must be Emily Brontë at her greatest:

屡遭责备，却总能回归

致我最初与生俱来的那些感觉，

抛开忙碌的财富追逐和学习

为那些无法实现的虚幻梦想：

Often rebuked, yet always back returning

To those first feelings that were born with me,

And leaving busy chase of wealth and learning

For idle dreams of things which cannot be:

今天，我不会去探寻那幽暗的领域；

To-day, I will seek not the shadowy region;

它那令人难以承受的广袤无垠变得凄凉；

异象升起，一波又一波，

将虚幻的世界诡异地拉近。

Its unsustaining vastness waxes drear;

And visions rising, legion after legion,

Bring the unreal world too strangely near.

我会走，但不会再沿着昔日英雄的足迹走。

I’ll walk, but not in old heroic traces,

而且并非走在道德高尚的道路上，

而且，他并不在那些略显逊色的面孔之中。

遥远历史的朦胧轮廓。

And not in paths of high morality,

And not among the half-distinguished faces,

The clouded forms of long-past history.

我会顺着我的本性而行：

I’ll walk where my own nature would be leading:

换个向导让我很烦恼：

灰雁群在蕨类植物丛生的山谷中觅食；

山坡上狂风呼啸的地方。

It vexes me to choose another guide:

Where the gray flocks in ferny glens are feeding;

Where the wild wind blows on the mountain side.

这些孤寂的山脉究竟有什么值得揭示的秘密？

What have those lonely mountains worth revealing?

荣耀与悲伤，远超我的言语所能表达：

唤醒人类心灵的土地

可以同时连接天堂和地狱两个世界。

More glory and more grief than I can tell:

The earth that wakes one human heart to feeling

Can centre both the worlds of Heaven and Hell.

我觉得这既晦涩难懂又发人深省。约翰·济慈——而不是拜伦、华兹华斯、雪莱——或许会更欣赏这最后一节沉思冥想的诗句。

I find this difficult and revelatory. John Keats—rather than Byron, Wordsworth, Shelley—might have admired the final, contemplative stanza.

威廉·布莱克是我童年时代最喜欢的诗人之一，他会把这斥为自然宗教。但我认为这种说法并不准确；这超越了自然，摒弃了宗教。

William Blake, one of the poets I loved most in my childhood, would have dismissed this as Natural Religion. I do not think that would have been accurate; this transcends nature and tosses away religion.

在艾米莉·勃朗特的这部小说中，无论是她那个时代还是我们这个时代的道德评判，都迅速变得无关紧要。尽管书中描绘了社会和自然的力量，但这些力量在希斯克利夫超自然的力量以及第一任凯瑟琳截然相反的一面面前，都显得黯然失色。当魔性的力量远远超越我们自身时，魔性的痛苦也必然存在，或许也远超我们自身的痛苦。但这种痛苦对我们来说是陌生的；艾米莉·勃朗特承担了美学上的风险，赋予希斯克利夫几乎无法被我们感知到的悲悯之情。我们惊叹于他因睡眠不足和食物匮乏而缓慢死去的可怕痛苦，但我们感受不到他的煎熬，因为他与我们之间的距离越来越远。我们一方面为第一任凯瑟琳的死而动容，因为社会和自然都参与了她的衰落；另一方面，我们又置身事外，因为凯瑟琳也深深地融入了她与希斯克利夫共享的那个世界。在他生命的最后半年里，她就像幽灵一样存在着，但这与她以前对他而言并没有什么不同。

Moral judgments, whether of her own day or of ours, become rapidly irrelevant in the world of Emily Brontë’s one novel. Though the book portrays both social and natural energies, these are dwarfed by the preternatural energies of Heathcliff and of the antithetical side of the first Catherine. Where daemonic energy so far exceeds ours, then daemonic suffering will also be present, perhaps also in excess of our own. But such suffering is foreign to us; Emily Brontë accepts the aesthetic risk of endowing Heathcliff with very little pathos recognizable by us. We wonder at his terrible sufferings, as he slowly dies from lack of sleep and lack of food, but we do not feel his agony, because he has become even more distant from us. We are partly moved by the first Catherine’s death, since both society and nature are involved in her decline, but partly we stand away from participation, because Catherine is also very much of the realm she shares with Heathcliff. For the last half-year of his life, she is a ghostly presence, but one not much different from what she has been for him before.

在所有浪漫小说中，我实在想不出比希斯克利夫和凯瑟琳·恩肖的关系更极端的了。想到希斯克利夫和凯瑟琳的第一次结合，简直令人作呕。他们或许会化为灰烬。本质上，他们本就是一体。

I cannot think of a relationship in prose romance more extreme than that of Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw. It is grotesque to think of Heathcliff and the first Catherine coupling. They might go up in smoke. In essence they are one.

艾米莉·勃朗特是一位独树一帜的作家，某种程度上来说，她没有先例。她熟知古典文学、钦定版圣经、莎士比亚的全部作品，或许最直接的当属沃尔特·斯科特爵士。然而，她的语言、立场、视野，乃至浪漫主义的模式，都独树一帜。在她这种北方浪漫主义风格中，托马斯·哈代、D·H·劳伦斯以及如今被人们遗忘的约翰·考珀·波伊斯都算是她的后继者。

Emily Brontë is so much an original that in a sense she had no precursors. She knew the classics, the King James Bible, all of Shakespeare, and perhaps most immediately Sir Walter Scott. And yet her language, stance, vision, even mode of romance are her own. Her descendants in her kind of Northern romance include Thomas Hardy, D. H. Lawrence, and the now neglected John Cowper Powys.

我可以在一位在世的诗人——加拿大诗人安妮·卡森身上找到艾米莉·勃朗特的精神，尤其是在她那首激烈而又令人心碎的诗作《玻璃散文》（1994年）中：

I can locate the spirit of Emily Brontë in one living poet, the Canadian Anne Carson, particularly in her fierce and rending poem “The Glass Essay” (1994):

我当时在楼下读《呼啸山庄》的剧本。

暴风雨中，希斯克利夫紧紧抓住屋檐，呜咽哭泣

进来吧！进来吧！来见见他心中挚爱的亡灵。

and I was downstairs reading the part in Wuthering Heights

where Heathcliff clings at the lattice in the storm sobbing

Come in! Come in! to the ghost of his heart’s darling,

呼啸山庄也同样冷酷无情，艾米莉称之为《呼啸山庄》。

Pitiless too are the Heights, which Emily called Wuthering

因为它们具有“令人振奋的通风”

“边缘刮起了北风。”

because of their “bracing ventilation”

and “a north wind over the edge.”

北风吹拂着荒原

Whaching a north wind grind the moor

她父亲的房子被四周包围着，

由一种叫做磨石砂岩的岩石构成，

that surrounded her father’s house on every side,

formed of a kind of rock called millstone grit,

她将自己所知道的关于爱及其必需品的一切都教给了艾米丽——

taught Emily all she knew about love and its necessities—

一段充满愤怒的教育塑造了她性格的形成。

互相利用。“我对希斯克利夫的爱，”凯瑟琳说。

an angry education that shapes the way her characters

use one another. “My love for Heathcliff,” says Catherine,

“如同下方永恒的岩石”

“resembles the eternal rocks beneath

虽然不能带来显而易见的愉悦，但却是必需的。

有必要吗？我注意到太阳已经暗了下来。

a source of little visible delight, but necessary.”

Necessary? I notice the sun has dimmed

以及下午的空气磨刀。

and the afternoon air sharpening.

我转身开始穿过荒原，朝家的方向走去。

有哪些必要条件？

I turn and start to recross the moor towards home.

What are the imperatives

那些关押着像凯瑟琳和希斯克利夫这样的人的人

that hold people like Catherine and Heathcliff

既相连又分离，就像吹入炽热岩石的毛孔。

然后被困在无法触及的地方

together and apart, like pores blown into hot rock

and then stranded out of reach

当它变硬时，它们会彼此相依为命吗？这究竟是什么样的必然性？

of one another when it hardens? What kind of necessity is that?

“Whaching”是艾米莉·勃朗特对“watching”的拼写，卡森也采用了这种拼写。“Necessity”指的应该是古希腊语ananke，意为强迫力，因为安妮·卡森是一位古典文学学者。“像凯瑟琳和希斯克利夫那样的人”：除了安妮·卡森本人，我从未见过这样的人。我只见过她一次，但多年前我们曾有过大量的通信往来。

“Whaching” was Emily Brontë’s spelling for “watching” and is adopted by Carson. “Necessity” must mean the ancient Greek ananke, compulsive force, Anne Carson being a scholar of the classics. “People like Catherine and Heathcliff”: I have never met any, except Anne Carson herself, whom I met only once, but with whom many years ago I carried on an extensive correspondence.

希斯克利夫既是人，也是魔。他是个身世不明的弃儿，或许是水手或吉普赛人，被老恩肖从利物浦街头捡到，与凯瑟琳·恩肖如同兄妹般共同抚养长大。他们亲密无间，彼此融为一体，这既不可能，也不合常理。然而，第一个凯瑟琳身上的关键特质也带有魔性。她和希斯克利夫共享着一个不属于我们，也不属于呼啸山庄任何人的宇宙。我读过的对希斯克利夫最深刻的论述，出自亨利·斯泰顿的《精神化为物质》（2014）：

Heathcliff is both a person and a daemon. A foundling of uncertain origin, perhaps lascar or Gypsy, picked up on the streets of Liverpool by the elder Earnshaw, he is raised with Catherine Earnshaw as a quasi-brother. They become so close that they are one another, which is neither possible nor sane. But, then, the crucial element in the first Catherine is also daemonic. She and Heathcliff share a cosmos that is not ours, or indeed that of anyone else in Wuthering Heights. The most profound discussion I have found of Heathcliff is that of Henry Staten in his Spirit Becomes Matter (2014):

希斯克利夫对肉体死亡的终结没有丝毫绝望；对曾经的天堂没有丝毫怀念；没有用基督教道德取代基督教信仰；没有对宗教形而上学表现出任何痛苦、无奈或英雄般的反抗……就像一个真正的异教徒一样，希斯克利夫只是在凯瑟琳死后感到绝望，对超越性没有任何想法。

There is in Heathcliff no despair at the finality of the death of the body; no nostalgia for the heaven that once was; no turn to Christian morality as a replacement for Christian belief; no stance of bitter, or resigned, or heroic defiance of religious metaphysics….Like an authentic pagan, Heathcliff merely despairs in the wake of Catherine’s death, with no thought of any kind regarding transcendence.

斯塔顿将艾米莉·勃朗特笔下的哀悼比作悲恸，但并非圣经式的，而是荷马史诗《伊利亚特》中的那种。他还极力为希斯克利夫辩护，驳斥其虐待狂的指控，指出书中充斥着无休止的暴力，而希斯克利夫却不愿以牙还牙。对艾米莉·勃朗特令人震惊的叙事暴力，最初的反应来自诗人兼画家但丁·加布里埃尔·罗塞蒂，他在1854年写给爱尔兰诗人威廉·阿林厄姆的一封信中这样说道：

Staten compares mourning in Emily Brontë to lamentation, not in the Biblical mode, but in Homer’s Iliad. He also strongly defends Heathcliff from accusations of sadism, noting both the endless violence of the book, and Heathcliff’s reluctance to return physical injury. The initial reaction to Emily Brontë’s startling narrative brutality was that of the poet-painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti, in an 1854 letter to the Irish poet William Allingham:

我对《呼啸山庄》非常感兴趣，这是我好久以来读的第一部小说，也是近两年来（除了《西多尼亚》之外）读过的最佳小说（就其力量和文笔而言）。但这本书简直是个魔鬼——一个不可思议的怪物，它融合了勃朗宁夫人和布朗里格夫人所有强烈的女性特质。故事发生在炼狱之中——只是那里的人名和地名似乎都是英文的。你读过吗？

I’ve been greatly interested in Wuthering Heights, the first novel I’ve read for an age, and the best (as regards power and sound style) for two ages, except Sidonia. But it is a fiend of a book—an incredible monster, combining all the stronger female tendencies from Mrs. Browning to Mrs. Brownrigg. The action is laid in hell,—only it seems places and people have English names there. Did you ever read it?

威廉·梅因霍尔德的《女巫西多尼亚》（1848年）于次年由简·怀尔德夫人（奥斯卡·王尔德的母亲）翻译成英文。但丁·加布里埃尔·罗塞蒂对伊丽莎白·巴雷特·勃朗宁的刻薄态度是其作品的典型特征；布朗里格夫人因残酷鞭打年轻女仆，其中一人因伤口感染而死，于1767年被处以绞刑。

Sidonia the Sorceress by Wilhelm Meinhold (1848) was rendered into English by Lady Jane Wilde (the divine Oscar’s mother) the next year. The nastiness toward Elizabeth Barrett Browning is typical of Dante Gabriel Rossetti; Mrs. Brownrigg was hanged in 1767 for whipping her young female servants so viciously that one died of the infected wounds.

希拉·史密斯在 1992 年一篇关于艾米莉·勃朗特和传统民谣的有用文章《“既强烈又诡异”》中，阐明了这部北方浪漫小说中超自然的方面：

Sheila Smith, in a useful 1992 essay on Emily Brontë and traditional ballads, “ ‘At Once Strong and Eerie,’ ” illuminates aspects of the preternatural in this Northern romance:

在《呼啸山庄》中，艾米莉·勃朗特运用结构手法、主题和题材，使小说这种文学形式焕发了新的活力。这些手法、主题和题材都源自勃朗特家所有子女都熟悉的口头传统，尤其体现在约克郡女子塔比莎·艾克罗伊德的叙述中。塔比莎在勃朗特家做了三十年的女仆。伊丽莎白·盖斯凯尔在为夏洛蒂所作的传记中这样描述塔比莎：“在那个原始的年代，她就熟悉了山谷，那时仙女们会在月光皎洁的夜晚出没于小溪边，她也认识一些见过仙女的人。”

In Wuthering Heights Emily Brontë revitalizes the literary form of the novel by use of structural devices, motifs, and subjects which properly belong to the oral tradition with which all the Brontë children were familiar, particularly through the agency of Tabitha Aykroyd, the Yorkshire woman who for thirty years was a servant in the Brontë household. Elizabeth Gaskell, in her biography of Charlotte, says of Tabby that ‘she had known the “bottom”, or valley, in those primitive days when the fairies frequented the margin of the “beck” on moonlight nights, and had known folk who had seen them.’

史密斯继续她的论述，并引用了《呼啸山庄》中的一段话：

Smith continues her discussion with a passage from Wuthering Heights:

如果你问乡亲们，他们会对着圣经发誓说他还在走动。有人说在教堂附近、荒原上，甚至在这房子里都见过他——你会说是无稽之谈，我也这么认为。然而，厨房炉火旁的那位老人却信誓旦旦地说，自从他去世后，每个雨夜他都看到两个鬼魂从他房间的窗户向外张望。一天傍晚，我正要去农庄——那天晚上天色昏暗，雷声隆隆——就在山脊的拐角处，我遇到一个小男孩，前面牵着一只母羊和两只小羊羔，他哭得撕心裂肺，我想那两只小羊羔大概是受惊了，不肯被牵走。

“我的小家伙，怎么了？”我问道。

“是希斯克利夫和一个女人，就在那边，在纳布下面，”他呜咽着说，“哎呀，真讨厌，不能让他们过去。”

The country folks, if you asked them, would swear on their Bible that he walks. There are those who speak to having met him near the church, and on the moor, and even within this house—Idle tales, you’ll say, and so say I. Yet that old man by the kitchen fire affirms he has seen two on ’em, looking out of his chamber window, on every rainy night, since his death. I was going to the Grange one evening—a dark evening threatening thunder—and, just at the turn of the Heights, I encountered a little boy with a sheep and two lambs before him, he was crying terribly, and I supposed the lambs were skittish, and would not be guided.

‘What is the matter, my little man?’ I asked.

‘They’s Heathcliff and a woman, yonder, under t’ Nab,’ he blubbered, ’un’ Aw darnut pass ’em.’

希斯克利夫和凯瑟琳·恩肖是亡灵，是清晰可见的幽灵，从看似死去的人身上复活。但从某种意义上说，他们从一开始就不是亡灵吗？艾米莉·勃朗特有时在我看来就像某种亡灵，一个完全神秘莫测的存在。

Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw are revenants, quite visible ghosts returned from the apparently dead. But were they not in some sense always revenants from the very beginning? Emily Brontë sometimes seems to me a kind of revenant herself, a being totally uncanny.

第十三章

CHAPTER 13

名利场（1848 年）

Vanity Fair (1848)

威廉· M·梅克皮斯· T ·萨克雷

WILLIAM MAKEPEACE THACKERAY

我第一次读 《名利场》是在1947年，就在我即将升入康奈尔大学一年级之前。随着阅读次数的增加，我越来越喜欢贝基·夏普，却越来越困惑于威廉·梅克比斯·萨克雷。书中的叙述声音常常令我难以忍受。夏洛蒂·勃朗特崇拜萨克雷，但她对男性读者的粗暴对待却让我望而却步。我不喜欢在阅读时被人用重物敲打脑袋。可怜的罗切斯特，作为乔治·戈登·拜伦勋爵的化身，被夏洛蒂·勃朗特和她的化身简·爱逐渐摧残。我已年近八十八，不想再被小说家用棍棒敲打或冷嘲热讽来羞辱。想当年我和菲利普·罗斯相处的那段时间，他会安慰我说：“哈罗德，我们来这里就是为了被羞辱。”也许吧。

I FIRST READ Vanity Fair in 1947, just before going up to my freshman year at Cornell. With each successive reading I am more and more delighted by Becky Sharp and even more puzzled by William Makepeace Thackeray. The voice speaking the book is frequently intolerable to me. Charlotte Brontë, who venerated Thackeray, drives me away by her brutality toward her male readers. I do not like to be thumped over the head as I read. Poor Rochester, a surrogate for George Gordon Lord Byron, is progressively mutilated by Charlotte Brontë and her surrogate Jane Eyre. Approaching eighty-eight, I do not want either to be cudgeled or sneered at by a novelist. Back in the days when I spent some time in the company of Philip Roth, he would cheer me by saying: “Harold, we are here to be insulted.” Perhaps.

我读过萨克雷的大部分小说，除了《名利场》之外，我还很欣赏 他的《亨利·埃斯蒙德传》（1852）。如果想了解萨克雷，我推荐朱丽叶·麦克马斯特和约翰·萨瑟兰的作品。戈登·雷的萨克雷传记也值得一读。但我越了解萨克雷其人，就越觉得他荒诞可笑。《名利场》对我来说，主角是贝基·夏普，一个杰出的反英雄人物，在一个收入微薄、别无选择的社会里，她只能做自己不得不做的事。

I have read most of Thackeray’s fiction and admire, in addition to Vanity Fair, The History of Henry Esmond (1852). For reading about Thackeray, I recommend Juliet McMaster and John Sutherland. There are also Gordon Ray’s admirable biographical studies of Thackeray. But the more I read about Thackeray as a person, the sillier he becomes. Vanity Fair for me is Becky Sharp, a superb anti-heroine who does what she has to do in a society that gives her lack of an income no options whatsoever.

在企鹅经典版《名利场》的一篇糟糕透顶的导言中，约翰·凯里断言《名利场》完全有资格被称为英语世界最伟大的小说，甚至超越了托尔斯泰的《战争与和平》。可怜的萨克雷，他不该遭受这样的赞誉。然而，萨克雷总是忍不住要说教：

In a rather dreadful introduction to the Penguin Classics Vanity Fair, the egregious John Carey asserts that Vanity Fair has strong claims to be the greatest novel in the English language and is superior to Tolstoy’s War and Peace. Poor Thackeray; he does not deserve that. But, then, Thackeray could not stop moralizing:

只有当那些不雅的名字被喊出来时，你的矜持才会显露出惊恐或愤慨。而笔者在整部作品中，都一心想顺应当下的风尚，以轻松、愉悦的方式暗示邪恶的存在，以免冒犯任何人的美好情感。我敢说，我们这位确实有些恶习的贝基，在呈现给读者时，绝对称得上是举止优雅、无伤大雅。在描写这位歌声嘹亮、笑容可掬、哄骗诱人的妖女时，作者带着一丝谦逊的自豪，向所有读者发出质问：他是否曾忘记礼貌的准则，将这怪物的丑陋尾巴暴露在水面上？不！那些感兴趣的人可以窥视那几乎透明的波浪之下，看到它扭动翻滚，丑陋不堪、黏糊糊的，在白骨间拍打，或缠绕在尸体上；但我想问，水面之上，难道一切不都那么得体、和谐、优雅吗？就连《名利场》里那些最矫情的道德败坏者，又有什么资格大喊“呸”呢？然而，当美人鱼消失，潜入水底，沉入死者之中时，水面自然变得浑浊，再去仔细观察也无济于事。她们坐在岩石上，拨弄着竖琴，梳着头发，唱歌，招手示意你过来拿起镜子时，看起来确实很漂亮；但当她们沉入水中，回到她们的“家园”时，你最好还是不要去探究这些邪恶的海洋食人族，她们正沉浸在对着腌制尸体的狂欢和盛宴之中。所以，当贝基不在的时候，可以肯定的是，她并没有得到什么特别好的安排，而且关于她的所作所为，少说为妙。

It is only when their naughty names are called out that your modesty has any occasion to show alarm or sense of outrage, and it has been the wish of the present writer, all through this story, deferentially to submit to the fashion at present prevailing, and only to hint at the existence of wickedness in a light, easy, and agreeable manner, so that nobody’s fine feelings may be offended. I defy any one to say that our Becky, who has certainly some vices, has not been presented to the public in a perfectly genteel and inoffensive manner. In describing this siren, singing and smiling, coaxing and cajoling, the author, with modest pride, asks his readers all round, has he once forgotten the laws of politeness, and showed the monster’s hideous tail above water? No! Those who like may peep down under waves that are pretty transparent, and see it writhing and twirling, diabolically hideous and slimy, flapping amongst bones, or curling round corpses; but above the water-line, I ask, has not everything been proper, agreeable, and decorous, and has any the most squeamish immoralist in Vanity Fair a right to cry fie? When, however, the siren disappears and dives below, down among the dead men, the water of course grows turbid over her, and it is labour lost to look into it ever so curiously. They look pretty enough when they sit upon a rock, twangling their harps and combing their hair, and sing, and beckon to you to come and hold the looking-glass; but when they sink into their native element, depend on it those mermaids are about no good, and we had best not examine the fiendish marine cannibals, revelling and feasting on their wretched pickled victims. And so, when Becky is out of the way, be sure that she is not particularly well employed, and that the less that is said about her doings is in fact the better.

这段文字令人不安。萨克雷的情爱生活并不顺利。年轻时在伦敦，他经常光顾妓院，25岁时娶了一位19岁的爱尔兰女子，她才华平庸，婚姻不幸。他们育有三个女儿，但第三个女儿的出生使他患上了无法治愈的产后抑郁症。萨克雷将妻子送去疗养院，将生活重心放在女儿身上。然而，1842年，他爱上了一位已婚女子，而这位女子的丈夫是他的大学好友。尽管这段恋情毫无益处且令人痛苦，却持续了数年，期间他创作了《名利场》。这部小说大获成功，使萨克雷成为狄更斯的有力竞争对手，但这并非萨克雷能够战胜的对手。

There is a disturbing flavor to that paragraph. Thackeray was unfortunate in his own erotic life. As a young man in London, he frequently visited bordellos and made an unfortunate marriage when he was twenty-five to a nineteen-year-old Irish girl of no particular abilities. Three daughters were born to them, but the third brought on a postnatal melancholia that became incurable. Thackeray put his wife away into private care and centered his life upon his daughters. Yet, in 1842, he fell in love with a woman married to a college friend. Although the passion was useless and agonizing, it continued for several years, during which he composed Vanity Fair. The novel was enormously successful and established Thackeray as a supposed rival to Dickens, not at all an agon that Thackeray could win.

萨克雷五十二岁便去世了，除了《名利场》和《亨利·埃斯蒙德》之外，人们或许会认为他未能充分发挥其毋庸置疑的才华。狄更斯热爱莎士比亚；萨克雷却认为《李尔王》 “乏味”，并觉得《哈姆雷特》平庸无奇。或许有人会辩解说萨克雷厌恶悲剧，但这并不能为他开脱。现在，我不再对他有任何贬低之意，转而赞同贝基·夏普的观点。我不知道谁会想要赞同威廉·梅克比斯·萨克雷，但我承认，乔治·艾略特、安东尼·特罗洛普以及夏洛蒂·勃朗特都对他推崇备至。

Dead at fifty-two, Thackeray could be judged as not having fulfilled his indubitable gifts, except for Vanity Fair and Henry Esmond. Dickens loved Shakespeare; Thackeray considered King Lear to be a “bore” and regarded Hamlet as being trivial. I suppose you could defend Thackeray by saying he was averse to tragedy, but that does not give him very much. I now cease all dispraise by embracing Becky Sharp. I have no idea who would want to embrace William Makepeace Thackeray, yet I grant how greatly he was admired by George Eliot and Anthony Trollope as well as by Charlotte Brontë.

在近年的学者和评论家中，萨克雷备受沃尔夫冈·伊瑟、前文提到的朱丽叶·麦克马斯特、约翰·萨瑟兰、戈登·雷以及玛丽亚·迪巴蒂斯塔和J·希利斯·米勒等人的推崇。我略带不情愿地也加入了他们的行列，幻想萨克雷对贝基·夏普的爱远胜于他自己承认的。如果福楼拜是包法利夫人，那么萨克雷岂不就是贝基·夏普吗？

Among recent scholar-critics, Thackeray enjoys the esteem of Wolfgang Iser, the heretofore mentioned Juliet McMaster, John Sutherland, Gordon Ray and also Maria DiBattista and J. Hillis Miller. A touch reluctantly, I would join that company by fantasizing that Thackeray loved Becky Sharp more than he would acknowledge. If Flaubert was Madame Bovary, is not Thackeray Becky Sharp?

这一点在第64章“浪荡篇”中体现得最为明显。这一章以我之前引用的那段不幸的美人鱼描写开头，然后讲述了贝基在法国港口城市布洛涅过着波西米亚式的生活：

This is perhaps clearest in Chapter 64, entitled “A Vagabond Chapter.” It does begin with the unfortunate mermaid paragraph I have quoted already. It then goes on to Becky making a bohemian life for herself in the French port of Boulogne:

事实上，她不过是个游手好闲的流浪汉。她挣了钱就去赌博；输光了钱，就得靠打零工勉强糊口；谁也不知道她是怎么混过来的。据说她曾在圣彼得堡出现过，但很快就被警察赶出了首都，所以她后来在托普利茨和维也纳当过俄国间谍的说法根本不可能。我还听说，她在巴黎遇到了自己的一个亲戚，正是她的外祖母，但那人根本不是什么蒙莫朗西家族的人，而只是林荫大道上一家剧院里一个丑陋的老收银员。据说其他人也知道她们的会面，想必是一次非常感人的会面。可惜，我本人无法提供关于此事的任何确切细节。

She was, in fact, no better than a vagabond upon this earth. When she got her money, she gambled; when she had gambled it, she was put to shifts to live; who knows how or by what means she succeeded? It is said that she was once seen at St Petersburg, but was summarily dismissed from that capital by the police, so that there cannot be any possibility of truth in the report that she was a Russian spy at Töplitz and Vienna afterwards. I have even been informed, that at Paris she discovered a relation of her own, no less a person than her maternal grandmother, who was not by any means a Montmorenci, but a hideous old box-opener at a theatre on the Boulevards. The meeting between them of which other persons, as it is hinted elsewhere, seem to have been acquainted, must have been a very affecting interview. The present historian can give no certain details regarding the event.

萨克雷自得其乐，同时又与贝基保持着恰到好处的距离。然而，随着萨克雷逐渐屈服于贝基的热情，这种距离随时都有可能消失：

Thackeray is enjoying himself while keeping Becky at a judicious distance. That distance is always in danger of vanishing as Thackeray yields to her gusto:

于是，贝基从佛罗伦萨一路跋涉而来，在一家简陋的客栈里勉强栖身。她弄到了一张波兰王子招待会的请柬，女仆为她精心打扮了一番。她挽着洛德少校的胳膊，前往参加这场盛大的舞会。碰巧当时她正和洛德少校同行——（就是第二年在拿波里枪杀拉沃利王子，并因帽子里除了玩掷骰子游戏用的那几个之外还藏着四个国王头像，而被约翰·巴克斯金爵士用藤条抽打的那个人） ——两人一同走进舞厅，贝基看到了许多熟悉的面孔，那是她年轻时快乐时光的记忆，那时她并非清纯无辜，但尚未被人发现。洛德少校认识许多外国人，他们个个面容锐利，蓄着胡须，纽扣孔里别着脏兮兮的条纹丝带，身上只穿着几件亚麻布；但值得一提的是，他的同胞们却对这位少校敬而远之。贝基也认识一些零星的女士——法国寡妇，来路不明的意大利伯爵夫人，她们的丈夫都对她们不好——呸——我们这些在名利场上叱咤风云的人，该如何评价这些无赖之徒呢？如果我们要玩牌，那就用干净的牌，而不是这副肮脏的牌。但是，每一个曾加入过无数旅行者队伍的人都见过这些劫掠成性的流氓，他们像尼姆和皮斯托尔一样，依附在主力部队上；他们穿着国王的旗帜，吹嘘着国王的委任状，却为自己劫掠，有时还会被吊死在路边。

她挽着洛德少校的胳膊，两人一起穿过房间，在自助餐台上喝了很多香槟。人们，尤其是少校的非正规军，为了争抢茶点而疯狂地打闹。两人喝够了之后，继续往前走，直到来到公爵夫人位于套房尽头的粉色天鹅绒沙龙（那里摆放着维纳斯雕像和镶着银框的威尼斯大镜子）。王室成员正在那里用圆桌宴请最尊贵的客人。这正是贝基记忆中她在斯泰恩勋爵家参加过的那种小型私人宴会——她看到斯泰恩勋爵就坐在波洛尼亚的桌旁。

So Becky, who had arrived in the diligence from Florence, and was lodged at an inn in a very modest way, got a card for Prince Polonia’s entertainment, and her maid dressed her with unusual care, and she went to this fine ball leaning on the arm of Major Loder, with whom she happened to be travelling at the time—(the same man who shot Prince Ravoli at Naples the next year, and was caned by Sir John Buckskin for carrying four kings in his hat besides those which he used in playing at écarté)—and this pair went into the rooms together, and Becky saw a number of old faces which she remembered in happier days, when she was not innocent, but not found out. Major Loder knew a great number of foreigners, keen-looking whiskered men with dirty striped ribbons in their button-holes, and a very small display of linen; but his own countrymen, it might be remarked, eschewed the Major. Becky, too, knew some ladies here and there—French widows, dubious Italian countesses, whose husbands had treated them ill—faugh—what shall we say, we who have moved among some of the finest company of Vanity Fair, of this refuse and sediments of rascals? If we play, let it be with clean cards, and not with this dirty pack. But every man who has formed one of the innumerable army of travellers has seen these marauding irregulars hanging on, like Nym and Pistol, to the main force; wearing the king’s colours, and boasting of his commission, but pillaging for themselves, and occasionally gibbeted by the roadside.

Well, she was hanging on the arm of Major Loder, and they went through the rooms together, and drank a great quantity of champagne at the buffet, where the people, and especially the Major’s irregular corps, struggled furiously for refreshments, of which when the pair had had enough, they pushed on until they reached the Duchess’s own pink velvet saloon, at the end of the suite of apartments (where the statue of Venus is, and the great Venice looking-glasses, framed in silver), and where the princely family were entertaining their most distinguished guests at a round table at supper. It was just such a little select banquet as that of which Becky recollected that she had partaken at Lord Steyne’s—and there he sat at Polonia’s table, and she saw him.

显然，萨克雷更喜欢亨利五世，而不是李尔王和哈姆雷特，他对尼姆和皮斯托尔的运用可谓巧妙。贝基想接近斯泰恩勋爵，但她无法如愿，因为她结交的都是些下三滥之徒。最终，她和好色的斯泰恩发生了婚外情，而这最终导致了贝基与罗顿·克劳利婚姻的破裂。罗顿是家里的幼子，一个老千，一个优秀的士兵，他曾对贝基痴迷不已，直到最后才看清她究竟是多么狡猾、不道德、冷酷无情和危险。

Evidently, Thackeray liked King Henry V more than he cared for King Lear and Hamlet, and his employment of Nym and Pistol is adroit. Becky would like to get at Lord Steyne but she cannot, since the company she keeps is rock bottom. In time, she and the lustful Steyne will have their adulterous moment, and it will help end Becky’s marriage to Rawdon Crawley. Rawdon is a younger son, a cardsharp, a good soldier, and infatuated with Becky until, at last, he comes to understand how manipulative, immoral, cold, and dangerous she truly is.

萨克雷通过把自己塑造成名利场展位上的表演者，与他笔下的故事和人物保持距离。从书名开始，约翰·班​​扬在其巨著《天路历程：从今世到来世》（1678）中对清教徒在名利场的描绘，对这部小说至关重要。以下是班扬的关键段落：

Thackeray distances himself from his story and characters by presenting himself as the showman of a booth at Vanity Fair. Crucial to the novel from the title onward is John Bunyan’s vision of the Pilgrims at Vanity Fair in his great work The Pilgrim’s Progress: From This World to That Which Is to Come (1678). Here is the crucial passage from Bunyan:

我在梦中看见，他们出了旷野，立刻看见一座城，名叫虚空城。城里有一个集市，也叫虚空集市，常年举办。之所以叫虚空集市，是因为集市所在的城市比虚空还要虚空，而且集市上出售的、运到那里的一切都是虚空。正如智者所说：“一切皆是虚空。”

这个集市并非新近设立，而是一个历史悠久的传统；我将带你们参观它的原址。

大约五千年前，有一些朝圣者前往天城，就像这两位诚实的人一样。别西卜、亚波伦和雷吉翁，以及他们的同伴，从朝圣者所走的路上看出，他们通往天城的路要经过这座虚荣之城，于是他们便在此设立了一个集市，出售各种虚荣之物，并且要持续一整年。因此，在这个集市上，出售各种各样的商品，例如房屋、土地、行业、场所、荣誉、晋升、头衔、国家、王国、欲望、享乐和各种各样的乐趣，例如妓女、老鸨、妻子、丈夫、孩子、主人、仆人、生命、血液、肉体、灵魂、金银、珍珠、宝石等等。

此外，在这个集市上，随时都能看到杂耍、骗术、游戏、戏剧、傻瓜、猿猴、恶棍和流氓，以及各种各样的人。

这里也能看到，而且毫无意义的是，盗窃、谋杀、通奸、发假誓，以及血红色的东西。

就像其他规模较小的集市一样，这里也设有按国家和王国划分的摊位和街道，售卖各种各样的商品；同样，这里也有专门的摊位、街道（即国家和王国），方便人们快速找到集市上的商品。这里有英国摊位、法国摊位、意大利摊位、西班牙摊位、德国摊位，出售各种各样的商品。但是，就像其他集市一样，总会有一种商品占据主导地位，罗马的商品在这个集市上也得到了大力推广；只有我们英国人和其他一些人对罗马商品不太感兴趣。

正如我所说，通往天城的道路就穿过这座举办盛大集市的城镇；若有人想去天城却不经过这座城镇，那他必定“脱离尘世”。就连万王之王本人，当年也曾途经此城返回故土，而且还是在一个晴朗的日子。是的，我想，正是这场集市的主宰别西卜邀请他购买自己的珍宝，如果他在经过城镇时对他表示敬意，别西卜甚至想让他成为集市的主宰。是的，因为这位圣人如此尊贵，别西卜便带着他走遍大街小巷，在短时间内向他展示了世间万国，希望能引诱这位圣人以低价购买一些珍宝；但他对这些商品毫无兴趣，因此离开城镇时，一分钱也没花。因此，这个集市历史悠久，规模盛大。

Then I saw in my dream, that when they were got out of the wilderness, they presently saw a town before them, and the name of that town is Vanity, and at the town there is a fair kept, called Vanity Fair. It is kept all the year long; it beareth the name of Vanity Fair, because the town where it is kept is lighter than vanity, and also because all that is there sold, or that cometh thither, is vanity. As is the saying of the wise, “all that cometh is vanity.”

This fair is no new-erected business, but a thing of ancient standing; I will show you the original of it.

Almost five thousand years agone there were pilgrims walking to the Celestial City, as these two honest persons are, and Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion, with their companions, perceiving by the path that the pilgrims made that their way to the city lay through this town of Vanity, they contrived here to set up a fair; a fair wherein should be sold all sorts of vanity, and that it should last all the year long. Therefore at this fair are all such merchandise sold, as houses, lands, trades, places, honours, preferments, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures, and delights of all sorts, as whores, bawds, wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold, pearls, precious stones, and what not.

And, moreover, at this fair there is at all times to be seen jugglings, cheats, games, plays, fools, apes, knaves, and rogues, and that of every kind.

Here are to be seen, too, and that for nothing, thefts, murders, adulteries, false swearers, and that of a blood-red colour.

And as in other fairs of less moment there are the several rows and streets under their proper names, where such and such wares are vended; so here likewise you have the proper places, rows, streets, (viz. countries and kingdoms), where the wares of this fair are soonest to be found. Here is the Britain Row, the French Row, the Italian Row, the Spanish Row, the German Row, where several sorts of vanities are to be sold. But as in other fairs some one commodity is as the chief of all the fair, so the ware of Rome and her merchandise is greatly promoted in this fair; only our English nation, with some others, have taken a dislike thereat.

Now, as I said, the way to the Celestial City lies just through this town where this lusty fair is kept; and he that will go to the City, and yet not go through this town, must needs ‘go out of the world.’ The Prince of princes himself, when here, went through this town to his own country, and that upon a fair day too; yea, and as I think, it was Beelzebub, the chief lord of this fair, that invited him to buy of his vanities, yea, would have made him lord of the fair, would he but have done him reverence as he went through the town. Yea, because he was such a person of honour, Beelzebub had him from street to street, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a little time, that he might, if possible, allure that Blessed One to cheapen and buy some of his vanities; but he had no mind to the merchandise, and therefore left the town without laying out so much as one farthing upon these vanities. This fair therefore is an ancient thing, of long standing, and a very great fair.

《蝇王》中的别西卜被萨克雷取代，萨克雷在扉页上称他的故事为“一部没有英雄的小说”。小说中有两个英雄：萨克雷本人和他的影子自我——贝基·夏普。一些读者认为威廉·多宾是英雄，但在我看来，他只是个枯燥乏味的角色，虽然和蔼可亲，却很容易被遗忘。萨克雷的个性和人物设定令我难以理解。他的语气和立场反复无常，对所有人物都态度暧昧，但不知为何，他的真实存在却贯穿整部小说。他的语气阴险狡诈、居高临下、故作高傲、尖酸刻薄，仿佛他鄙视自己的道德观。他必须被赋予一种邪恶的智慧。

Beelzebub, Lord of the Flies, is replaced by Thackeray, who on the title page calls his story “A Novel without a Hero.” It has two heroes, Thackeray the Showman and his shadow self, Becky Sharp. Some readers suggest that William Dobbin is heroic, but he seems to me a dry stick, amiable enough yet easily forgettable. Thackeray as a personality and character defies my understanding. He is inconstant in tone and in stance, ambivalent in regard to all his characters, yet somehow his real presence pervades the novel. His tone is insinuating, condescending, knowingly snobbish, and edgy, as if he despises his own moralism. A wicked intelligence must be granted him.

萨克雷笔下的贝基·夏普是一个反英雄式的人物。她的缺点罄竹难书：她对自己唯一的儿子缺乏母爱，除了自己，她谁也爱不起来，而且在一无所有时，她甚至出卖自己。她很可能为了骗取保险金而谋杀了某个不幸的人。即使斯泰恩勋爵用钞票和贵重珠宝堆砌起来，她也不愿将丈夫从债务人牢狱中解救出来。她肆意妄为，只为追求享乐。她的缺点还可以继续列举下去，但如果把她从小说中移除，谁还会读这本书呢？正是她的性魅力支撑着整部作品，正如克利奥帕特拉的狂喜为莎士比亚的伟大戏剧注入了激情与活力。

Thackeray intends Becky Sharp to be an anti-heroine. You can heap up all her demerits: she is not motherly toward her only son, she is incapable of loving anyone except herself, and she sells herself when she has nothing else to sell. It seems likely that she murders one unfortunate character in order to reap his insurance. She will not bail her husband out of a debtor’s confinement, even when Lord Steyne has showered her with banknotes and valuable jewelry. She lives defiantly for all the pleasure she can gain. One could extend the catalogue, but take her out of the novel and who would ever read it? It is her sexuality that sustains the book as much as Cleopatra’s triumphant ecstasies provide Shakespeare’s great play with fire and air.

《名利场》的乐趣可以用贝基和她的经纪人之间一段巧妙的对峙文字来概括：

The joys of Vanity Fair can be encapsulated in a cunning paragraph playing point-counterpoint between Becky and her impresario:

“做个乡绅的妻子并不难，”丽贝卡心想。“如果我一年有五千块钱，我想我可以做一个好女人。我可以闲逛在苗圃里，数数墙上的杏子。我可以给温室里的植物浇水，摘掉天竺葵的枯叶。我可以问问老太太们风湿病的情况，还可以花半克朗给穷人买汤。一年五千块钱，我也不会觉得缺什么。我甚至可以开车十英里去邻居家吃饭，穿上前年的流行服饰。我可以去教堂，在大家庭长椅上保持清醒，或者如果我练习得当，也可以在窗帘后面，放下面纱，睡着。如果我有钱，我可以付清所有人的工资。这就是这里的魔术师引以为豪的事情。他们怜悯我们这些一无所有、可怜的罪人。”他们觉得给我们的孩子五英镑纸币就算慷慨，而如果我们没钱，他们就觉得我们卑鄙无耻。谁知道丽贝卡的猜测会不会是对的——也许她和诚实的女人之间的区别仅仅在于金钱和财富？如果把诱惑考虑进去，谁又能说他比邻居更好呢？一份舒适富裕的工作，即使不能让人变得诚实，至少也能让人保持诚实。一个刚从海龟盛宴回来的市议员不会下马车去偷羊腿；但让他挨饿，看看他会不会偷一块面包。贝基这样安慰自己，认为世间善恶的分配是均等的。

‘It isn’t difficult to be a country gentleman’s wife,’ Rebecca thought. ‘I think I could be a good woman if I had five thousand a year. I could dawdle about in the nursery, and count the apricots on the wall. I could water plants in a greenhouse and pick off dead leaves from the geraniums. I could ask old women about their rheumatisms, and order half-a-crown’s worth of soup for the poor. I shouldn’t miss it much out of five thousand a year. I could even drive out ten miles to dine at a neighbour’s, and dress in the fashions of the year before last. I could go to church and keep awake in the great family pew, or go to sleep behind the curtains, with my veil down, if I only had practice. I could pay everybody, if I had but the money. This is what the conjurors here pride themselves upon doing. They look down with pity upon us miserable sinners who have none. They think themselves generous if they give our children a five-pound note, and us contemptible if we are without one.’ And who knows but Rebecca was right in her speculations—and that it was only a question of money and fortune which made the difference between her and an honest woman? If you take temptations into account, who is to say that he is better than his neighbour? A comfortable career of prosperity, if it does not make people honest, at least keeps them so. An alderman coming from a turtle feast will not step out of his carriage to steal a leg of mutton; but put him to starve, and see if he will not purloin a loaf. Becky consoled herself by so balancing the chances and equalizing the distribution of good and evil in the world.

“如果我一年能挣五千块钱，我想我就能成为一个好女人。”贝基的这句格言，很适合写进吉卜林或布莱希特的诗里。它甚至可以成为萨克雷的座右铭。难道它不也是我们的座右铭吗？如果一个人饿得皮包骨头，他/她岂不也成了冉阿让？

“I think I could be a good woman if I had five thousand a year.” Becky’s motto would do very well for a refrain in a poem by Kipling or Bert Brecht. It may as well be Thackeray’s motto. Is it not ours? Who would not be Jean Valjean if he or she were starving?

萨克雷的谜团让我不禁思考，我对他矛盾的态度是否源于我自身情感的过度投入。情欲上的失望几乎成了他人生的主旋律。这或许也是乔治·奥斯本在凝视着他的未婚妻阿米莉亚时，表现出的那种施虐受虐式的自恋倾向的根源之一：

The puzzle of Thackeray makes me wonder if my own excess of affect is at fault in my ambivalence toward him. Erotic disappointment was almost the law of his life. That could be an element in the sadomasochistic narcissism of George Osborne contemplating his bride-to-be Amelia:

这匍匐在地、毫无怨言的顺从深深打动了乔治·奥斯本，令他倍感荣幸。他从眼前这个单纯顺从、忠诚的女子身上看到了一个奴隶，而他内心深处却因意识到自己的权力而暗自颤抖。他心地善良，即便身为苏丹，也要将这跪着的埃丝特扶起来，册封她为王后。此外，她的悲伤和美丽与她的顺从一样深深地触动了他，于是他安慰她，扶她起来，仿佛宽恕了她。她所有那些因失去生命之光而日渐凋零的希望和情感，都重新绽放，光芒重现。你几乎认不出那天晚上躺在阿米莉亚枕头上的那张容光焕发的小脸，与前一天晚上躺在那里的那张苍白、死气沉沉、对周围的一切都漠不关心的脸截然不同。那位诚实的爱尔兰女仆看到这番变化，欣喜不已，请求允许亲吻她那突然变得红润的脸颊。阿米莉亚搂住女孩的脖子，像个孩子一样全心全意地吻她。她自己也差不多是个孩子了。那天晚上她睡得香甜，精神焕发——当她在晨曦中醒来时，心中充满了难以言喻的幸福！

This prostration and sweet unrepining obedience exquisitely touched and flattered George Osborne. He saw a slave before him in that simple yielding faithful creature, and his soul within him thrilled secretly somehow at the knowledge of his power. He would be generous-minded, Sultan as he was, and raise up this kneeling Esther and make a queen of her: besides, her sadness and beauty touched him as much as her submission, and so he cheered her, and raised her up and forgave her, so to speak. All her hopes and feelings, which were dying and withering, this her sun having been removed from her, bloomed again and at once, its light being restored. You would scarcely have recognized the beaming little face upon Amelia’s pillow that night as the one that was laid there the night before, so wan, so lifeless, so careless of all round about. The honest Irish maid-servant, delighted with the change, asked leave to kiss her face that had grown all of a sudden so rosy. Amelia put her arms round the girl’s neck and kissed her with all her heart, like a child. She was little more. She had that night a sweet refreshing sleep, like one—and what a spring of inexpressible happiness as she woke in the morning sunshine!

令人厌恶的奥斯本竟然原谅了可怜的阿米莉亚，这简直太荒谬了。他在滑铁卢战役中英勇牺牲后，我们对他的好感也丝毫未减。我还要继续为贝基在哑剧中扮演克吕泰涅斯特拉而感到高兴吗？

It is merely outrageous that the odious young Osborne forgave poor Amelia. We do not like Osborne any better after he dies heroically at Waterloo. Do I go on being delighted by Becky as she performs Clytemnestra in a charade?

闹剧的第二部分开始了。场景依旧是东方风情。哈桑换了身衣服，摆出祖莱卡的姿势，祖莱卡对他完全和解了。基斯勒·阿加变成了一个温顺的黑奴。沙漠日出，土耳其人转向东方，向沙丘鞠躬。由于附近没有骆驼，乐队便戏谑地演奏起《骆驼来了》。一个巨大的埃及人头出现在画面中。这颗人头会唱歌——令东方旅行者们惊讶的是，它唱起了一首由瓦格先生创作的滑稽歌曲。东方的旅行者们像《魔笛》中的帕帕基诺和摩尔国王一样，载歌载舞地离开了。“最后两个音节！”人头咆哮道。

最后一幕开始了。这次的场景是一顶希腊帐篷。一位身材高大魁梧的男子正卧在帐篷里的卧榻上。他的头盔和盾牌悬挂在他上方。现在它们已不再必要。伊利昂陷落了。伊菲革涅亚被杀。卡珊德拉被囚禁在他的外厅里。人中之王（正是克劳利上校，他确实对伊利昂的陷落和卡珊德拉的征服一无所知），这位“人中之王”正在阿尔戈斯的寝宫里沉睡。一盏灯在墙上投下沉睡战士的宽阔影子，灯光闪烁——特洛伊的剑和盾在灯光下熠熠生辉。乐队奏响了凄厉的《唐璜》乐曲，随后雕像登场。

埃吉斯托斯面色苍白，踮着脚尖悄悄溜了进来。那张阴森恐怖的脸从帷幔后探出来，恶狠狠地盯着他，那是什么？他举起匕首，想要刺向睡梦中的主人，那人却在床上翻了个身，敞开宽阔的胸膛，仿佛要承受这一击。他无法刺中这位高贵的沉睡首领。克吕泰涅斯特拉像幽灵般轻盈地滑入房间——她双臂裸露，皮肤苍白——一头棕褐色的秀发披散在肩上——脸色惨白得可怕——她的眼中闪烁着令人毛骨悚然的笑容，让人不寒而栗。

房间里一阵震动。“我的天哪！”有人说，“是罗顿·克劳利太太。”

她轻蔑地从埃吉斯托斯手中夺过匕首，走向床边。你看到匕首在她头顶上方，在灯光的映照下闪闪发光，然后——灯光呻吟一声熄灭了，一切都陷入了黑暗。

The second part of the charade takes place. It is still an Eastern scene. Hassan, in another dress, is in an attitude by Zuleikah, who is perfectly reconciled to him. The Kislar Aga has become a peaceful black slave. It is sunrise on the desert, and the Turks turn their heads eastwards and bow to the sand. As there are no dromedaries at hand, the band facetiously plays “The Camels are coming.” An enormous Egyptian head figures in the scene. It is a musical one—and to the surprise of the oriental travellers, sings a comic song, composed by Mr Wagg. The Eastern voyagers go off dancing, like Papageno and the Moorish King in the “Magic Flute.” “Last two syllables,” roars the head.

The last act opens. It is a Grecian tent this time. A tall and stalwart man reposes on a couch there. Above him hang his helmet and shield. There is no need for them now. Ilium is down. Iphigenia is slain. Cassandra is a prisoner in his outer halls. The king of men (it is Colonel Crawley, who, indeed, has no notion about the sack of Ilium or the conquest of Cassandra), the anax andrôn is asleep in his chamber at Argos. A lamp casts the broad shadow of the sleeping warrior flickering on the wall—the sword and shield of Troy glitter in its light. The band plays the awful music of ‘Don Juan’, before the statue enters.

Ægisthus steals in pale and on tiptoe. What is that ghastly face looking out balefully after him from behind the arras? He raises his dagger to strike the sleeper, who turns in his bed, and opens his broad chest as if for the blow. He cannot strike the noble slumbering chieftain. Clytemnestra glides swiftly into the room like an apparition—her arms are bare and white—her tawny hair floats down her shoulder—her face is deadly pale—and her eyes are lighted up with a smile so ghastly, that people quake as they look at her.

A tremor ran through the room. ‘Good God!’ somebody said, ‘it’s Mrs Rawdon Crawley.’

Scornfully she snatches the dagger out of Ægisthus’s hand and advances to the bed. You see it shining over her head in the glimmer of the lamp, and—and the lamp goes out, with a groan, and all is dark.

从某种意义上说，克吕泰涅斯特拉这个角色并不适合贝基，因为她根本不在乎自己是否生下了伊菲革涅亚，也不在乎这位美丽的年轻女子是否为了让希腊船只航行而被牺牲。但从另一个角度来看，这个角色对贝基来说却非常精彩，因为她要对男性主导的权力、权威、财富世界以及对一位伟大女性性欲的否定进行复仇。贝基·夏普虽然缺乏克吕泰涅斯特拉的那种恢弘气势，但她将维多利亚时代的女性形象演绎得淋漓尽致。

In one sense the role of Clytemnestra scarcely suits Becky, because she could not have cared less had she borne Iphigenia and had that splendid young lady been sacrificed so the Greek ships could sail. Otherwise it is a splendid part for Becky, as she has much to revenge against the male world of power, authority, wealth, and the denial of a grand woman’s sexuality. Becky Sharp lacks Clytemnestra’s grandeur but does very well as a Victorian reduction.

可以说，贝基·夏普每天早上醒来，当然既决心享受生活，又决心对抗男性主导的财富、权力与虚伪的世界。她也接受了自己虚伪行为所付出的代价：

One could say of Becky Sharp that of course she gets up each morning determined both to enjoy her existence and to fight off the male world of wealth, power, hypocrisy. She accepts the price of her own duplicity:

她从未成为克劳利夫人，尽管她一直自称如此。尊敬的罗顿·克劳利上校阁下在考文垂岛死于黄热病，他生前备受爱戴和哀悼，去世时间比他的兄弟皮特爵士早六周。因此，庄园传给了现任罗顿·克劳利爵士（男爵）。

他也拒绝见他的母亲，尽管他慷慨地给予她生活费，而且她似乎非常富有。男爵完全住在女王克劳利庄园，与简夫人和她的女儿同住；而克劳利夫人丽贝卡则主要在巴斯和切尔滕纳姆一带活动，那里有一群德高望重的人认为她是一位极其受委屈的女人。她也有敌人。谁没有呢？她的生活就是对他们的回应。她致力于虔诚的善行。她去教堂，而且总是有男仆随行。她的名字出现在所有慈善名册上。贫困的卖橘子女工、被冷落的洗衣妇、生活困苦的松饼小贩都能在她那里找到一位热情慷慨的朋友。她总是在集市上摆摊，为这些不幸的人们提供帮助。

She never was Lady Crawley, though she continued so to call herself. His Excellency Colonel Rawdon Crawley died of yellow fever at Coventry Island, most deeply beloved and deplored, and six weeks before the demise of his brother, Sir Pitt. The estate consequently devolved upon the present Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.

He, too, has declined to see his mother, to whom he makes a liberal allowance, and who, besides, appears to be very wealthy. The Baronet lives entirely at Queen’s Crawley, with Lady Jane and her daughter; whilst Rebecca, Lady Crawley, chiefly hangs about Bath and Cheltenham, where a very strong party of excellent people consider her to be a most injured woman. She has her enemies. Who has not? Her life is her answer to them. She busies herself in works of piety. She goes to church, and never without a footman. Her name is in all the Charity Lists. The Destitute Orange-girl, the Neglected Washerwoman, the Distressed Muffin-man find in her a fast and generous friend. She is always having stalls at Fancy Fairs for the benefit of these hapless beings.

萨克雷的语气依然令人难以捉摸。如果可以，我会尽量缓和语气，但这并非读者应有的反应。我同意萨克雷的最后一段评论，其中深深回响着《传道书》或《圣经》，希伯来语中的“vanitas”是“hevel”，意为“空虚”。

Again Thackeray’s tone is virtually indecipherable. I would soften it if I could, but that is not a legitimate reaction for a reader. I yield to Thackeray for his final comment, with its deep echoes of Qoheleth or Ecclesiastes, where vanitas in the Hebrew is hevel, “emptiness”:

啊！虚空虚空！我们之中谁在这世上快乐？我们之中谁能如愿以偿？或者，即便拥有了，又能感到满足？——孩子们，来吧，让我们关上盒子，放下木偶，因为我们的游戏已经结束了。

Ah! Vanitas Vanitatum! Which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied?—Come children, let us shut up the box and the puppets, for our play is played out.

第十四章

CHAPTER 14

《白鲸记》（1851年）

Moby-Dick (1851)

H·埃尔曼· M·埃尔维尔

HERMAN MELVILLE

除了《堂吉诃德》、《克拉丽莎》和《追忆似水年华》之外，我 个人最喜欢的散文史诗或鸿篇巨制是《白鲸》。我从小就喜欢它，而且始终坚信亚哈船长与其说是亦正亦邪的英雄，不如说是真正的英雄。

EXCEPT FOR Don Quixote, Clarissa, and In Search of Lost Time, my personal favorite among all prose epics or vast novels is Moby-Dick. I have loved it since I was a child and have never given up my passionate conviction that Ahab is more a hero than a hero-villain.

我已经记不清教过多少次《白鲸》了。虽然我反复阅读，但大部分内容我都已背诵下来，而这种对它的掌握改变了我对许多其他书籍的看法。对我而言，沃尔特·惠特曼的《草叶集》就像是美国的圣经。我们不能失去正确的视角。惠特曼和梅尔维尔是美国文学的两大巨匠。他们并非耶路撒冷的以赛亚或但丁。荷马和雅典的悲剧作家，柏拉图和品达，卢克莱修和维吉尔，在崇高境界方面也更胜一筹。即使是对审美和认知价值的传承充满热情的人，也会被岁月磨砺。我读惠特曼，他仿佛将手放在我身上，说他想让我成为他的诗篇。我回到《白鲸》的第一章“预兆”，化身为以实玛利：

I cannot recall how many times I have taught Moby-Dick. Though I keep rereading it, I have most of it by heart, and that possession alters my perception of many other books. With Walt Whitman’s Leaves of Grass, it is for me a kind of American Scripture. One does not want to lose perspective. Whitman and Melville are the two titans of American literature. Neither of them is Isaiah of Jerusalem or Dante. Homer and the Athenian tragic dramatists, Plato and Pindar, Lucretius and Virgil, are also larger on the scale of the Sublime. Very old age plays its tricks upon even a mind passionate for the survival of aesthetic and cognitive values. I read Walt Whitman and he places his hand upon me and says he wants me to be his poem. I go back to the first chapter of Moby-Dick, “Loomings,” and become Ishmael:

叫我以实玛利吧。几年前——具体多久我记不清了——我囊中羞涩，岸上也没什么特别吸引我的事情，于是我想出海游玩一番，看看这水世界。这是我驱散忧愁、调节心绪的办法。每当我发现自己愁眉苦脸；每当我的灵魂如同十一月阴雨绵绵般阴冷潮湿；每当我不由自主地在棺材堆前驻足，跟在每一支送葬队伍的队伍后面；尤其当我的抑郁症发作，让我不得不依靠强大的道德准则才能阻止自己故意走到街上，有条不紊地打掉别人的帽子——那时，我就觉得是时候尽快出海了。这就像我的手枪和子弹一样。就像卡托带着哲学家的姿态拔剑自刎；而我则默默地登上船。这没什么好奇怪的。如果他们知道的话，几乎所有男人，无论程度如何，在某个时候，都会和我一样对海洋怀有几乎相同的情感。

Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen, and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other, cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.

以实玛利，其名意为“全能者聆听”，是亚伯拉罕与埃及妾夏甲所生的长子。在伊斯兰教中，以实玛利是穆罕默德的祖先，并创建了麦加圣地。在撒拉与夏甲发生争执后，这位埃及女子逃往沙漠，生下了以实玛利，他是所有流浪者的原型。

Ishmael, whose name means “the Almighty listens,” was Abraham’s firstborn son by his Egyptian concubine, Hagar. In Islam, Ishmael is the ancestor of Muhammad and founded the shrine at Mecca. After a dispute between Sarah and Hagar, the Egyptian woman fled to the desert and bore Ishmael, archetype of all wanderers.

梅尔维尔笔下的以实玛利是一位朝圣者，也是一位幸存者。只有他才能在亚哈船长所乘的捕鲸船“裴廓德号”的沉没中幸存下来。我的朋友小保罗·布罗德科布（Paul Brodtkorb, Jr.）写了一本书，名为《以实玛利的白色世界》（Ishmael's White World ，1965），其创作灵感来源于J·H·范登伯格（J. H. Van Den Berg）的《人的变迁》（The Changing Nature of Man，1961）。范登伯格反对弗洛伊德的观点，认为心理学必须具有历史性，奇迹可能在一个时代发生，而在另一个时代则不会，并且自我如同奥维德和莎士比亚笔下那样，是变化莫测、千变万化的。布罗德科布笔下的亚哈船长是一位典型的浪漫主义人物，其风格与弥尔顿笔下的撒旦、雪莱笔下的普罗米修斯以及拜伦笔下的拜伦相似。亚哈船长属于十九世纪中期。他是一位美国人，一位贵格会教徒，也是一位约伯式的反叛者。但是，沃尔特·惠特曼是美国人，是希克斯派贵格会教徒，也是反抗利维坦的叛逆者，反抗自然对男女的暴政，这种暴政是由一个自称为耶和华的布莱克式无名之辈所规定的。

Melville’s Ishmael is a pilgrim and a survivor. Only he will survive the wreck of the Pequod, Ahab’s whaler. My friend Paul Brodtkorb, Jr., wrote a book called Ishmael’s White World (1965) founded on J. H. Van Den Berg’s The Changing Nature of Man (1961). Van Den Berg argued against Freud that psychology had to be historical, that miracles could happen in one age but not in another, and that the self was as mutable and metamorphic as Ovid and Shakespeare took it to be. Brodtkorb’s Ahab is a High Romantic in the mode of Milton’s Satan, Shelley’s Prometheus, Byron’s Byron. Ahab belongs to the middle of the nineteenth century. He is an American, a Quaker, and a Jobean rebel. But, then, Walt Whitman is an American, a Hicksite Quaker, and another rebel against Leviathan, the tyranny of nature over women and men as ordained by a Blakean Nobodaddy who calls himself Yahweh.

莎士比亚对《白鲸》的影响最为显著。诗人兼先知查尔斯·奥尔森（Charles Olson）在20世纪60年代曾与我有过几次交谈，他在其著作《叫我以实玛利》（Call Me Ishmael，1947）中率先对莎士比亚的影响进行了研究。奥尔森身材魁梧，身高约六英尺七英寸（约2米），但我发现他举止温和，平易近人。尽管我们对埃兹拉·庞德（Ezra Pound）的诗歌看法不一，但庞德的诗歌对奥尔森的“投射诗”的启发远胜于梅尔维尔。

Shakespeare is the dominant influence on Moby-Dick. The poet-seer Charles Olson, with whom I had several conversations during the 1960s, pioneered in studying that influence in his book Call Me Ishmael (1947). Olson was a giant of a man, six foot seven or so, but I found his manner gentle and engaging, though we could not agree on the poetry of Ezra Pound, who more than Melville sparked Olson’s own “projective verse.”

这就是奥尔森对《白鲸》的精髓所在：

This is the essence of Olson on Moby-Dick:

梅尔维尔将亚哈船长孤立于世，如同“一位大喇嘛”般高高在上。他之所以能成为“裴廓德号”的船长，是因为“他那头脑中某种苏丹般的特质”。他骄傲而阴郁，任性而又充满复仇心。他戴着一顶“空心王冠”，并非理查的王冠，而是拿破仑曾佩戴过的伦巴第铁王冠。王冠边缘的锯齿状设计，源自耶稣受难的钉子，令他感到刺痛。他崇拜火焰，并发誓要击碎太阳。

总而言之，仇恨——巨大而执着于那些难以察觉之物。美国人提蒙抨击的并非人类，而是所有令人类恐惧的隐秘力量。这种超乎人类的仇恨牵连了他的船员，《白鲸》将他们拖入死亡，正如亚哈船长也走向了死亡——一位英雄因唯我论而走向毁灭，最终也导致了一个世界的崩塌。

在书的结尾，在白鲸号毁灭的中心，船员们、皮普、布尔金顿和亚哈一起躺了下来。

全部散落在海底。

Melville isolates Ahab in “a Grand-Lama-like exclusiveness.” He is captain of the Pequod because of “that certain sultanism of his brain.” He is proud and morbid, willful, vengeful. He wears a “hollow crown,” not Richard’s. It is the Iron Crown of Lombardy which Napoleon wore. Its jagged edge, formed from a nail of the Crucifixion, galls him. He worships fire and swears to strike the sun.

OVER ALL, hate—huge and fixed upon the imperceptible. Not man but all the hidden forces that terrorize man is assailed by the American Timon. That HATE, extra-human, involves his Crew, and Moby-Dick drags them to their death as well as Ahab to his, a collapse of a hero through solipsism which brings down a world.

At the end of the book, in the heart of the White Whale’s destruction, the Crew and Pip and Bulkington and Ahab lie down together.

All scatt’red in the bottom of the sea.

以实玛利是唯一的幸存者。我很好奇梅尔维尔对《暴风雨》作何感想。他引用的莎士比亚作品大多是经典悲剧：《哈姆雷特》、 《奥赛罗》、 《李尔王》、 《麦克白》、 《安东尼与克莉奥佩特拉》。我过去不同意奥尔森关于亚哈船长“唯我论”的观点，现在依然如此。亚哈船长深谙艾米莉·狄金森所说的“邻居与太阳”之道。他像一位指挥家驾驭小型交响乐团一样操控着他的船员。小皮普因一次危险的海难而精神错乱，成了亚哈船长手中的弄臣，如同李尔王一般。英勇的大副斯塔巴克最终屈服于亚哈船长的偏执，因为他无法抗拒权威的约束。

Ishmael is the one survivor. I wonder what Melville made of The Tempest. Most of his Shakespearean allusions are to the High Tragedies: Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra. I disagreed with Olson and still do as to Ahab’s “solipsism.” Captain Ahab is well aware of what Emily Dickinson called “Neighbors and the Sun.” He plays upon his crew like a master conductor leading a small orchestra. Little Pip, crazed by a dangerous immersion in the sea, becomes the Fool to Ahab’s Lear. Starbuck, the heroic first mate, yields to Ahab’s monomania because he cannot resist authentic authority.

伊什梅尔让我们第一次领略到永恒的莫比·迪克：

Ishmael gives us the first intimation of the eternal Moby-Dick:

因此，捕鲸之旅令人欣喜；奇妙世界的大门敞开，在我心中涌动着狂野的幻想，无数鲸鱼的身影浮现在我的灵魂深处，在它们之中，一个巨大的、戴着兜帽的幽灵，像空中的雪山。
