Fedallah seems beyond affect while Ahab is insanely heroic. Rescued by Stubbs’s boat, the warlike Ahab has to suspend his quest as the night comes on, and then returns to the chase for a second day:

“伟大的上帝啊！哪怕只现身一瞬间，”斯塔巴克喊道，“你永远也抓不到他，老家伙——奉耶稣的名，别再这样了，这比魔鬼的疯狂还可怕。追了两天；两次被烧成碎片；你的腿又一次被夺走；你的邪恶影子消失了——所有善良的天使都围着你发出警告：——你还想要什么？——我们要一直追着这条杀人鱼，直到他吞噬最后一个人吗？我们要被他拖到海底吗？我们要被他拖到地狱吗？哦，哦——为了继续追捕他，你竟要亵渎神明！”

“斯塔巴克，近来我对你莫名地动了心；自从那一刻起，我们都看到了——你知道的，在彼此的眼中。但在这鲸鱼的事上，你对我而言，要像对我这只手掌一样，毫无表情，一片空白。亚哈永远是亚哈，伙计。这一切都是命中注定，无法更改。在你我排练过的亿万年前，在这片海洋翻滚之前。蠢货！我是命运的副官；我奉命行事。听着，下属！你要服从我的命令。——伙计们，都围过来。你们看到的是一个被砍成残肢的老人；倚靠着一根颤抖的长矛；用一只孤零零的脚支撑着。那是亚哈——他的身体；但亚哈的灵魂是一条蜈蚣，用百足爬行。我感到筋疲力尽，半搁浅，就像拖着断桅护卫舰的绳索一样……”在狂风中；我或许看起来如此。但在我断裂之前，你们会听到我的断裂声；在你们听到之前，要知道亚哈船长的缆绳依然牵引着他的目标。你们相信那些所谓的预兆吗，伙计们？那就放声大笑，再来一次吧！因为在沉没之前，沉没之物会两次浮出水面；然后再次浮出水面，永远沉入海底。莫比·迪克也是如此——它已经浮了两天了——明天将是第三天。是的，伙计们，它还会再次浮出水面——但那只是为了喷出它最后的毒液！你们觉得自己勇敢吗，伙计们，勇敢吗？

“像无畏的火焰一样！”斯塔布喊道。

“而且像机械一样，”亚哈嘟囔着。然后，当船员们继续前进时，他又开始低声说道：“那些所谓的预兆！昨天我和斯塔巴克也谈到了我的破船。哦！我多么努力地想要把那些在我心中根深蒂固的东西从别人心中赶走！——那个帕西人——那个帕西人！——走了，走了？他本来应该先走的：——但在我死之前，他还会再次出现——怎么回事？——现在有个谜题，恐怕连所有律师，甚至所有法官的亡灵都会束手无策：——它像鹰喙一样啄着我的脑袋。不过，我会解开它的！”

黄昏降临时，鲸鱼仍然在背风面的视线范围内。

“Great God! but for one single instant show thyself,” cried Starbuck; “never, never wilt thou capture him, old man—In Jesus’ name no more of this, that’s worse than devil’s madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; thy very leg once more snatched from under thee; thy evil shadow gone—all good angels mobbing thee with warnings:—what more wouldst thou have?—Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh,—Impiety and blasphemy to hunt him more!”

“Starbuck, of late I’ve felt strangely moved to thee; ever since that hour we both saw—thou know’st what, in one another’s eyes. But in this matter of the whale, be the front of thy face to me as the palm of this hand—a lipless, unfeatured blank. Ahab is for ever Ahab, man. This whole act’s immutably decreed. ’Twas rehearsed by thee and me a billion years before this ocean rolled. Fool! I am the Fates’ lieutenant; I act under orders. Look thou, underling! that thou obeyest mine.—Stand round me, men. Ye see an old man cut down to the stump; leaning on a shivered lance; propped up on a lonely foot. ’Tis Ahab—his body’s part; but Ahab’s soul’s a centipede, that moves upon a hundred legs. I feel strained, half stranded, as ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But ere I break, ye’ll hear me crack; and till ye hear that, know that Ahab’s hawser tows his purpose yet. Believe ye, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For ere they drown, drowning things will twice rise to the surface; then rise again, to sink for evermore. So with Moby Dick—two days he’s floated—to-morrow will be the third. Aye, men, he’ll rise once more,—but only to spout his last! D’ye feel brave, men, brave?”

“As fearless fire,” cried Stubb.

“And as mechanical,” muttered Ahab. Then as the men went forward, he muttered on:—“The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same to Starbuck there, concerning my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I seek to drive out of others’ hearts what’s clinched so fast in mine!—The Parsee—the Parsee!—gone, gone? and he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How’s that?—There’s a riddle now might baffle all the lawyers backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges:—like a hawk’s beak it pecks my brain. I’ll, I’ll solve it, though!”

When dusk descended, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

伯南森林将降临邓西纳。死去的费达拉将再次出现。命运主宰着亚哈。梅尔维尔引领我们走向第三日的灾难：

Birnam Wood will come to Dunsinane. Dead Fedallah will be seen again. The Fates govern Ahab. And Melville sails us to the catastrophe of the Third Day:

“……他说了什么？他应该继续走在我前面，我的领航员；而且还会再次出现？可是会在哪里呢？如果我沿着那无尽的阶梯下去，我能在海底看到他吗？我整夜都在航行，远离他，不管他沉到哪里去了。是啊，是啊，你像许多人一样，说了些可怕的真话，说的都是关于你自己的，帕西人啊；但是，亚哈，你的箭射偏了。再见了，桅杆顶——在我离开的这段时间里，好好看着那条鲸鱼。我们明天再谈，不，今晚就谈，等那条白鲸头尾相连地躺在那里的时候。”

他一声令下，目光仍环顾四周，缓缓地穿过湛蓝的天空，降落到甲板上。

过了一段时间，小艇被放下来了；但当亚哈站在他的小艇尾部，悬停在下沉点时，他向甲板上拿着一根滑轮绳的大副挥了挥手，示意他停下。

“星巴克！”

“先生？”

“星巴克，这是我的灵魂之船第三次启航了。”

“是的，先生，您就如愿以偿吧。”

“有些船从港口启航后就再也没有出现过，斯塔巴克！”

“先生，这是实话：最令人悲伤的实话。”

“有些人死于退潮；有些人死于低潮；有些人死于涨潮；——而我现在感觉自己就像一个长满冠毛的海浪，斯塔巴克。我老了；——跟我握个手吧，伙计。”

他们的手相触；他们的目光交汇；星巴克的眼泪将他们紧紧相连。

“哦，我的船长，我的船长！——高尚的心——不要走——不要走！——你看，一个勇敢的人竟然会哭泣；那劝说的过程该是多么痛​​苦啊！”

“放低点！”亚哈喊道，一把甩开大副的胳膊。“站在船员旁边！”

“…What’s that he said? he should still go before me, my pilot; and yet to be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I descend those endless stairs? and all night I’ve been sailing from him, wherever he did sink to. Aye, aye, like many more thou told’st direful truth as touching thyself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there thy shot fell short. Good-bye, mast-head—keep a good eye upon the whale, the while I’m gone. We’ll talk to-morrow, nay, to-night, when the white whale lies down there, tied by head and tail.”

He gave the word; and still gazing round him, was steadily lowered through the cloven blue air to the deck.

In due time the boats were lowered; but as standing in his shallop’s stern, Ahab just hovered upon the point of the descent, he waved to the mate,—who held one of the tackle-ropes on deck—and bade him pause.

“Starbuck!”

“Sir?”

“For the third time my soul’s ship starts upon this voyage, Starbuck.”

“Aye, sir, thou wilt have it so.”

“Some ships sail from their ports, and ever afterwards are missing, Starbuck!”

“Truth, sir: saddest truth.”

“Some men die at ebb tide; some at low water; some at the full of the flood;—and I feel now like a billow that’s all one crested comb, Starbuck. I am old;—shake hands with me, man.”

Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck’s tears the glue.

“Oh, my captain, my captain!—noble heart—go not—go not!—see, it’s a brave man that weeps; how great the agony of the persuasion then!”

“Lower away!”—cried Ahab, tossing the mate’s arm from him. “Stand by the crew!”

我总是反复思索，怎么会有人不敬佩亚哈船长呢？他更像约伯而非麦克白，更像哈姆雷特而非伊阿古，更像李尔王而非埃德蒙。这些是美国虚构的英雄：亚哈船长、海丝特·白兰、哈克贝利·费恩和吉姆，以及“沃尔特·惠特曼，一个美国人，一个粗犷的人，一个宇宙”这样的形象。现实中，他们还有亚伯拉罕·林肯和沃尔特·惠特曼——一位包扎伤口的医生。亚哈船长是否应该为船员的毁灭负责？除了斯塔巴克之外，所有人都热情地加入了这场冒险，包括幸存者以实玛利。或许，白鲸才是最具美国特色的英雄：

I always wonder, repeating this to myself, how anyone could not admire Ahab. He is more Job than Macbeth, more Hamlet than Iago, more King Lear than Edmund. These are the American fictive heroes: Ahab, Hester Prynne, Huckleberry Finn and Jim, and the persona: “Walt Whitman, an American, one of the roughs, a kosmos.” Add to them from reality Abraham Lincoln and Walt Whitman the Wound-Dresser. Is Ahab culpable for destroying his crew? Except for Starbuck, all of them enthusiastically joined in the quest, including Ishmael the survivor. Perhaps the White Whale is the most American of heroes:

突然间，周围的水面缓缓泛起宽阔的圆圈；随后猛然翻腾，仿佛从一座水下冰山上侧滑而出，迅速升至水面。一阵低沉的隆隆声响起，如同地底的嗡鸣；接着，所有人都屏住了呼吸；只见一个巨大的身影，拖着绳索、鱼叉和长矛，斜向从海面纵身跃出。它笼罩在一层薄薄的、下垂的薄雾之中，在彩虹般的空中盘旋片刻；然后重重地坠入深海。被抛到三十英尺高的海面上，水流瞬间如同喷泉般飞溅，随后破碎地沉入水中，如同雪花般飘落，只留下环绕着鲸鱼大理石般光滑的海面，如同新鲜的牛奶般洁白。

“让开！”亚哈向划桨手们喊道，小艇立刻向前冲去；但莫比·迪克似乎被昨天新添的铁器腐蚀得发狂，仿佛所有将他从天堂拉下来的天使都同时附身于他。他宽阔的白色额头上，透明的皮肤下，层层叠叠的肌腱交织在一起，如同编织而成；他迎面而来，在小艇间搅动着尾巴；再次将小艇撕开；两个副手的船上铁器和长矛散落一地，船头一侧也被撞得粉碎，而亚哈的船却几乎毫发无损。

当达古和塔什特戈正忙着固定绷紧的木板时，鲸鱼从他们身边游了出来，转身，再次从他们身边疾驰而过，露出了整个侧身；就在这时，一声急促的喊叫响起。帕西人的半身残破的尸体被鲸鱼紧紧地缠绕在背上，被鲸鱼一夜之间用绳索缠绕的绳索紧紧地束缚着；他那身乌黑的衣服已经破烂不堪；他那双肿胀的眼睛直直地盯着老亚哈。

鱼叉从他手中滑落。

“上当了，上当了！”——他深深吸了一口气——“是啊，帕西人！我又见到你了。——是啊，你走在前面；这就是你答应的灵车。但我可要你说到做到。第二辆灵车在哪儿？伙计们，快上船！那些小艇现在没用了；如果可以，就赶紧修好，然后回来；否则，亚哈就该死——下去，伙计们！谁要是敢从我站着的这艘船上跳下去，我就用鱼叉把它叉死。你们不是别人，而是我的胳膊和腿；所以都得听我的。——鲸鱼在哪儿？又沉下去了吗？”

Suddenly the waters around them slowly swelled in broad circles; then quickly upheaved, as if sideways sliding from a submerged berg of ice, swiftly rising to the surface. A low rumbling sound was heard; a subterraneous hum; and then all held their breaths; as bedraggled with trailing ropes, and harpoons, and lances, a vast form shot lengthwise, but obliquely from the sea. Shrouded in a thin drooping veil of mist, it hovered for a moment in the rainbowed air; and then fell swamping back into the deep. Crushed thirty feet upwards, the waters flashed for an instant like heaps of fountains, then brokenly sank in a shower of flakes, leaving the circling surface creamed like new milk round the marble trunk of the whale.

“Give way!” cried Ahab to the oarsmen, and the boats darted forward to the attack; but maddened by yesterday’s fresh irons that corroded in him, Moby Dick seemed combinedly possessed by all the angels that fell him from heaven. The wide tiers of welded tendons overspreading his broad white forehead, beneath the transparent skin, looked knitted together; as head on, he came churning his tail among the boats; and once more flailed them apart; spilling out the irons and lances from the two mates’ boats, and dashing in one side of the upper part of their bows, but leaving Ahab’s almost without a scar.

While Daggoo and Tashtego were stopping the strained planks; and as the whale swimming out from them, turned, and showed one entire flank as he shot by them again; at that moment a quick cry went up. Lashed round and round to the fish’s back; pinioned in the turns upon turns in which, during the past night, the whale had reeled the involutions of the lines around him, the half torn body of the Parsee was seen; his sable raiment frayed to shreds; his distended eyes turned full upon old Ahab.

The harpoon dropped from his hand.

“Befooled, befooled!”—drawing in a long lean breath—“Aye, Parsee! I see thee again.—Aye, and thou goest before; and this, this then is the hearse that thou didst promise. But I hold thee to the last letter of thy word. Where is the second hearse? Away, mates, to the ship! those boats are useless now; repair them if ye can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die—Down, men! the first thing that but offers to jump from this boat I stand in, that thing I harpoon. Ye are not other men, but my arms and my legs; and so obey me.—Where’s the whale? gone down again?”

如果说《白鲸》有什么缺点，那就是莎士比亚式的描写太多了。但还有什么缺点比这更高尚呢？第二辆灵车将是奎奎格的棺材，以实玛利将骑着它逃往安全之地。很难评判亚哈和白鲸这两个恶魔，他们都拥有绝望的决心，但可惜的是，力量却不相上下：

If Moby-Dick has a fault, it is too much flooded by Shakespeare. But what fault could be nobler? The second hearse shall be Queequeg’s coffin, upon which Ishmael will ride to safety. It is difficult to judge between the two daemons, Ahab and Moby-Dick, matched in desperate resolution but not, alas, in power:

最终，当小船被甩到一边，沿着白鲸的侧翼游弋时，它似乎对鲸鱼的逼近浑然不觉——就像鲸鱼有时会做的那样——亚哈已经完全置身于山间浓雾之中，那雾气是从鲸鱼喷出的，环绕着它巨大的莫纳德诺克山脊；他离鲸鱼如此之近；这时，他弓起背，双臂高举，摆出战斗姿势，将锋利的铁剑和更加恶毒的咒骂刺向那条可恨的鲸鱼。随着铁剑和咒骂沉入鲸鱼的嘴里，仿佛被吸入泥潭一般，莫比·迪克侧身扭动；它痉挛般地用近侧的船身撞击船头，船身没有被撞出一个洞，却突然倾斜，要不是亚哈紧紧抓住凸起的舷缘，他恐怕又要被抛入大海了。当时，三名划桨手——他们事先并不知道飞镖的确切落点，因此对飞镖的威力毫无准备——被抛了出去；但他们摔得如此之快，以至于其中两人瞬间又抓住了舷缘，并借助涌来的波浪回到舷缘的高度，然后猛地跳回船内；第三个人无助地向船尾坠落，但仍然漂浮在水面上并游着。

几乎与此同时，白鲸号以迅雷不及掩耳之势，瞬间冲破了波涛汹涌的大海。但当亚哈船长大声命令舵手重新调整缆绳的缠绕方向并牢牢抓住缆绳，并命令船员们转身，将船拖到标记处时，那条危险的缆绳就在感受到双重拉力的瞬间，在空中断裂了！

“我体内哪里出了问题？一些筋腱断裂了！——它又完整了；桨！桨！冲向他！”

听到船只在海浪中呼啸而过的巨大声响，鲸鱼转过身，露出它光秃秃的额头；但就在这时，它看到了靠近的黑色船体；似乎把它看作是所有迫害的根源；把它当成了——也许是——一个更大、更高贵的敌人；突然间，它猛地扑向驶来的船头，张开大嘴，在滚滚的泡沫中猛击。

At length as the craft was cast to one side, and ran ranging along with White Whale’s flank, he seemed strangely oblivious of its advance—as the whale sometimes will—and Ahab was fairly within the smoky mountain mist, which, thrown off from the whale’s spout, curled round his great, Monadnock hump; he was even thus close to him; when, with body arched back, and both arms lengthwise high-lifted to the poise, he darted his fierce iron, and his far fiercer curse into the hated whale. As both steel and curse sank into the socket, as if sucked into a morass, Moby Dick sideways writhed; spasmodically rolled his nigh flank against the bow, and, without staving a hole in it, so suddenly canted the boat over, that had it not been for the elevated part of the gunwale to which he then clung, Ahab would once more have been tossed into the sea. As it was, three of the oarsmen—who foreknew not the precise instant of the dart, and were therefore unprepared for its effects—these were flung out; but so fell, that, in an instant two of them clutched the gunwale again, and rising to its level on a combing wave, hurled themselves bodily inboard again; the third man helplessly dropping astern, but still afloat and swimming.

Almost simultaneously, with a mighty volition of ungraduated, instantaneous swiftness, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea. But when Ahab cried out to the steersman to take new turns with the line, and hold it so; and commanded the crew to turn round on their seats, and tow the boat up to the mark; the moment the treacherous line felt that double strain and tug, it snapped in the empty air!

“What breaks in me? Some sinew cracks!—’tis whole again; oars! oars! Burst in upon him!”

Hearing the tremendous rush of the sea-crashing boat, the whale wheeled round to present his blank forehead at bay; but in that evolution, catching sight of the nearing black hull of the ship; seemingly seeing in it the source of all his persecutions; bethinking it—it may be—a larger and nobler foe; of a sudden, he bore down upon its advancing prow, smiting his jaws amid fiery showers of foam.

或许，白鲸与其说是约伯的利维坦，或是耶和华的利维坦，不如说是诺斯替教造物主的化身。从莫比·迪克的视角来看，“裴廓德号”就是撒旦，是他所有迫害的根源。我真希望威廉·布莱克能活到读到《莫比·迪克》的那天。他会更加有力地告诉我们，这段历史已被双方所接受：

It may be that the White Whale is not so much Job’s Leviathan, or Yahweh’s, as it is the Gnostic Demiurge incarnate. From Moby-Dick’s perspective, the Pequod is Satan, source of all his persecutions. I wish William Blake had lived to read Moby-Dick. He would have told us even more forcefully that this history has been adopted by both parties:

船头几乎所有水手都呆立不动，手中仍机械地握着锤子、木板、长矛和鱼叉，如同刚才从各自的岗位上飞奔而来一般。他们所有人的目光都如痴如醉地盯着那头鲸鱼，它那仿佛命中注定般左右摇晃的脑袋，激起一片宽阔的半圆形泡沫。报应、迅猛的复仇、永恒的恶意充斥着它的全身，尽管凡人竭尽全力，它那坚实的白色额头还是猛烈地撞击在船的右舷船头，直到人和木头都摇摇晃晃。有些人脸朝下摔倒在地。高处鱼叉手的脑袋像脱缰的野马般在粗壮的脖子上剧烈摇晃。他们听到海水从破洞中倾泻而下，如同山洪奔腾而下。

“那艘船！那辆灵车！——第二辆灵车！”亚哈从船上喊道；“它的木头只能是美国产的！”

鲸鱼潜入正在下沉的船底，沿着船底的龙骨颤抖地游动；但在水下转身，迅速再次冲出水面，远离船头，但距离亚哈船只有几码远，亚哈船在那里静静地躺了一会儿。

“我背对太阳。嚯，塔什特戈！让我听听你的锤声。哦！我那三座不屈不挠的尖顶；你那未裂的龙骨；你那唯一受神力加固的船体；你那坚固的甲板，你那傲慢的舵，你那尖锐的船首——死而无憾的战舰！难道你们注定要沉没，而我却要独自承受？难道我连最卑微的遇难船长最后的骄傲都失去了？哦，孤独的死亡，孤独的生命！哦，如今我感到，我最伟大的地方，竟在于我最深沉的悲痛。嚯，嚯！从你们最遥远的边界，倾泻而下吧，我逝去生命中汹涌澎湃的波涛，淹没我死亡的这堆巨浪！我向你翻滚，你这毁灭一切却又不可征服的巨鲸；我与你搏斗到最后一刻；我从地狱之心刺向你；为了仇恨，我向你吐出我的最后一口气。”你！让所有的棺材和灵车都沉入同一个水池！既然它们都不属于我，那就让我一边追逐你，一边将你拖成碎片吧，你这该死的鲸鱼！即便我们被束缚在一起，我也要追随你！就这样，我放弃了长矛！

鱼叉射出，受伤的鲸鱼向前跃出，绳索以惊人的速度穿过凹槽——却卡住了。亚哈弯腰去解开绳索，他解开了，但飞速旋转的绳索缠住了他的脖子，就像土耳其哑剧演员用弓弦射杀受害者一样，他无声地被抛出船外，船员们还没反应过来他就不见了。下一刻，绳索末端沉重的环状接头从空荡荡的船舱中飞出，击倒了一名划桨手，然后猛地落入大海，消失在深渊之中。

From the ship’s bows, nearly all the seamen now hung inactive; hammers, bits of plank, lances, and harpoons, mechanically retained in their hands, just as they had darted from their various employments; all their enchanted eyes intent upon the whale, which from side to side strangely vibrating his predestinating head, sent a broad band of overspreading semicircular foam before him as he rushed. Retribution, swift vengeance, eternal malice were in his whole aspect, and spite of all that mortal man could do, the solid white buttress of his forehead smote the ship’s starboard bow, till men and timbers reeled. Some fell flat upon their faces. Like dislodged trucks, the heads of the harpooners aloft shook on their bull-like necks. Through the breach, they heard the waters pour, as mountain torrents down a flume.

“The ship! The hearse!—the second hearse!” cried Ahab from the boat; “its wood could only be American!”

Diving beneath the settling ship, the whale ran quivering along its keel; but turning under water, swiftly shot to the surface again, far off the other bow, but within a few yards of Ahab’s boat, where, for a time, he lay quiescent.

“I turn my body from the sun. What ho, Tashtego! let me hear thy hammer. Oh! ye three unsurrendered spires of mine; thou uncracked keel; and only god-bullied hull; thou firm deck, and haughty helm, and Pole-pointed prow,—death-glorious ship! must ye then perish, and without me? Am I cut off from the last fond pride of meanest shipwrecked captains? Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief. Ho, ho! from all your furthest bounds, pour ye now in, ye bold billows of my whole foregone life, and top this one piled comber of my death! Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee. Sink all coffins and all hearses to one common pool! and since neither can be mine, let me then tow to pieces, while still chasing thee, though tied to thee, thou damned whale! Thus, I give up the spear!”

The harpoon was darted; the stricken whale flew forward; with igniting velocity the line ran through the groove;—ran foul. Ahab stooped to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying turn caught him round the neck, and voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim, he was shot out of the boat, ere the crew knew he was gone. Next instant, the heavy eye-splice in the rope’s final end flew out of the stark-empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and smiting the sea, disappeared in its depths.

“裴廓德号”沉没了，但这毫无意义的沉没究竟是为了什么？

The Pequod goes down but to what purposeless purpose?

但当最后几股汹涌的波涛交织着倾泻而下，淹没了主桅上印第安人沉没的头颅，只留下几英寸的桅杆残存，以及长长的旗帜飘扬在几乎触及的毁灭性巨浪上，平静地起伏着，带着讽刺的巧合——就在那一刻，一只红色的手臂和一把锤子在空中向后悬停，正将旗帜越钉越快地钉在即将沉没的桅杆上。一只鹰隼嘲弄地从星空中的家园飞来，一路啄食着旗帜，戏弄着塔什特戈；这只鹰隼此刻恰巧挡住了它宽阔的翅膀，它扑腾的翅膀落在了锤子和木头之间；与此同时，感受到那令人心醉神迷的快感，沉没在水下的野蛮人在临死前的喘息中，将锤子僵在了那里。于是，天上的鸟儿发出天使般的尖叫，高高扬起它那威严的喙，它整个被俘虏的身躯被折叠在亚哈的旗帜中，与他的船一同沉入了海底。而这艘船，就像撒旦一样，非要拖着一部分活生生的天堂一同沉入地狱，并用它戴上头盔才肯罢休。

现在，小鸟尖叫着飞过依然深不见底的海湾；阴沉的白色浪花拍打着陡峭的海湾；然后一切都崩溃了，大海的巨大帷幕像五千年前那样继续翻滚。

But as the last whelmings intermixingly poured themselves over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast, leaving a few inches of the erect spar yet visible, together with long streaming yards of the flag, which calmly undulated, with ironical coincidings, over the destroying billows they almost touched;—at that instant, a red arm and a hammer hovered backwardly uplifted in the open air, in the act of nailing the flag faster and yet faster to the subsiding spar. A sky-hawk that tauntingly had followed the main-truck downwards from its natural home among the stars, pecking at the flag, and incommoding Tashtego there; this bird now chanced to intercept its broad fluttering wing between the hammer and the wood; and simultaneously feeling that ethereal thrill, the submerged savage beneath, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there; and so the bird of heaven, with archangelic shrieks, and his imperial beak thrust upwards, and his whole captive form folded in the flag of Ahab, went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell till she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her, and helmeted herself with it.

Now small fowls flew screaming over the yet yawning gulf; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.

塔什特戈将鹰视为自由翱翔于大海深渊的象征。弥尔顿笔下撒旦的出现令我略感不安，但我认为我们必须从布莱克和雪莱的视角来解读这里的天堂与地狱。诺斯替主义的梅尔维尔总是能直击人心。我们回到诺亚方舟的故事，但这次方舟只有奎奎格的棺材，孤身一人的以实玛利幸存下来，讲述他的故事。剩下的，便是精彩绝伦的尾声：

Tashtego takes the hawk as an emblem of the freedom of the air down into the great shroud of the sea. I am a little unnerved by the manifestation of Milton’s Satan, yet I think we must read hell and heaven here from a Blakean and Shelleyan perspective. The Gnostic Melville always strikes through the mask. We return to Noah’s flood but with an ark consisting only of Queequeg’s coffin, with an isolated Ishmael surviving to tell his story. What remains is the superb epilogue:

尾声​

“只有我一个人逃脱出来，来告诉你这件事。”

工作。

悲剧已经落幕。那么，为什么还有人站出来呢？——因为有人在那场灾难中幸存了下来。

事情就是这样，帕西人消失后，命运安排我接替亚哈船长的弓箭手，而那位弓箭手则接过了空缺的职位；也是我，在最后一天，当三人被抛出摇晃的小船时，被扔到了船尾。于是，我漂浮在即将发生的场景边缘，完全看得见，当沉船残存的吸力到达我身边时，我被缓慢地拉向正在闭合的漩涡。当我到达那里时，它已经消散成一滩乳白色的水洼。于是，我像另一个伊克西翁一样，不停地旋转，不断地向着那缓慢旋转的圆圈中心的纽扣状黑色气泡收缩。直到到达那个至关重要的中心，黑色气泡向上破裂；现在，这口棺材救生圈凭借其狡猾的弹簧挣脱束缚，又因其巨大的浮力，猛地跃出海面，纵身一跃，翻了个身，漂到我身边。靠着这口棺材，我几乎整整漂了一天一夜，漂浮在轻柔如挽歌般的海面上。那些无害的鲨鱼，如同嘴上挂着一把锁，滑行而过；凶猛的海鹰则张着紧闭的喙翱翔天际。第二天，一艘帆船渐渐靠近，最终将我救起。原来是狡猾的瑞秋，她一直在寻找失踪的孩子，却只找到了另一个孤儿。

FINIS

EPILOGUE

“And I only am escaped alone to tell thee.”

Job.

The drama’s done. Why then here does any one step forth?—Because one did survive the wreck.

It so chanced, that after the Parsee’s disappearance, I was he whom the Fates ordained to take the place of Ahab’s bowsman, when that bowsman assumed the vacant post; the same, who, when on the last day the three men were tossed from out the rocking boat, was dropped astern. So, floating on the margin of the ensuing scene, and in full sight of it, when the half-spent suction of the sunk ship reached me, I was then, but slowly, drawn towards the closing vortex. When I reached it, it had subsided to a creamy pool. Round and round, then, and ever contracting towards the button-like black bubble at the axis of that slowly wheeling circle, like another Ixion I did revolve. Till, gaining that vital centre, the black bubble upward burst; and now, liberated by reason of its cunning spring, and, owing to its greatest buoyancy, rising with great force, the coffin life-buoy shot lengthwise from the sea, fell over, and floated by my side Buoyed up by that coffin, for almost one whole day and night, I floated on a soft and dirge-like main. The unharming sharks, they glided by as if with padlocks on their mouths; the savage sea-hawks sailed with sheathed beaks. On the second day, a sail drew near, nearer, and picked me up at last. It was the devious cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.

FINIS

这部史诗的最后一段题词是《约伯记》1:19的结尾，四个人共同讲述了同样的悲惨遭遇：约伯的儿女、仆人和牲畜都惨遭毁灭。我曾想过，如今的以实玛利究竟是拉结的儿子，救赎者约瑟，还是她年幼的儿子便雅悯——那个悲痛欲绝的雅各始终陪伴在身边的孩子？以实玛利如此执着地解梦，似乎就像约瑟，精通解梦之术。然而，以实玛利虽然讨人喜欢，却不可靠，因此没有约瑟那样的威望。他其实是便雅悯，另一个失落的孩子。

The epic’s final epigraph is the culmination of Job 1:19, where four individuals express the same dreadful report, the destruction of Job’s children, servants, flocks. I once wondered whether Ishmael now would be Rachel’s son Joseph the Redeemer or her younger son, Benjamin, whom the grieving Jacob kept always by his side. Insofar as Ishmael is a persistent interpreter, he might seem to be Joseph, skilled in the art of clarifying dreams. Yet Ishmael, though very likable, is unreliable, and so has not the eminence of a Joseph. He is a Benjamin, another lost child.

第十五章

CHAPTER 15

《荒凉山庄》（1853）

Bleak House (1853)

C ·哈利斯·狄更斯

CHARLES DICKENS

四十多年前，我最喜欢的狄更斯作品是他的第一部小说《匹克威克外传》（1836-1837）。当时我十三岁，被它深深吸引。五年后，我又迷上了《荒凉山庄》，这份喜爱一直持续到我读完狄更斯的所有作品，并被他最后一部完成的小说——阴郁而恐怖的《我们共同的朋友》——所吸引。狄更斯于1870年6月9日去世，当时《艾德温·德鲁德之谜》只完成了一半多一点，这部小说更加阴暗，但我们永远无法知道它的结局。狄更斯去世时五十八岁，他因长期不间断地为众多热情洋溢的听众朗读自己的作品而精疲力竭。如果他没有成为最伟大的小说家之一，他或许也能在舞台上拥有辉煌的职业生涯。在导致他中风去世的五年前，他和他的年轻女演员得意门生艾伦·特南遭遇了一场火车事故，造成十名乘客死亡，多人受伤，其中包括狄更斯本人。狄更斯竭尽全力救助其他伤者。1858年，他与妻子凯瑟琳分居，结束了长达二十二年颇为坎坷的婚姻。在这二十二年里，凯瑟琳经历了十次怀孕。

THREE-QUARTERS OF A CENTURY AGO, my favorite Dickens was The Pickwick Papers (1836–37), his first novel. I was thirteen and enchanted by it. Five years after, I became obsessed with Bleak House, a choice that lasted until I had read all of Dickens and was drawn in by the dank and frightening Our Mutual Friend, his last completed novel. The Mystery of Edwin Drood, left a bit more than half done when he died on June 9, 1870, is even darker, but we will never know how it was to end. Dickens died at fifty-eight, worn out by his incessant and exhausting public reading of his works to large and enthusiastic audiences. Had he not become one of the greatest novelists, he could have had a remarkable career on the stage. Five years before the stroke that killed him, he and his young actress protégée Ellen Ternan had been in a train wreck that killed ten passengers and injured many, including Dickens, who did his heroic best to attend to the other victims. He had separated from his wife, Catherine, in 1858, after twenty-two years of a rather difficult marriage in which she had endured ten pregnancies.

彼得·阿克罗伊德 (Peter Ackroyd) 于 1991 年撰写的狄更斯传记最为生动。我从亚历山大·韦尔什 (Alexander Welsh) 的著作《狄更斯之城》(The City of Dickens，1971) 中获益匪浅。任何经常深入阅读狄更斯作品的人都会被他对耶稣形象的虔诚所深深打动。对狄更斯而言，基督教就是耶稣，它体现在对个人的怜悯、真诚和慈善之中。狄更斯鄙视所有自称基督徒却憎恶、剥削或漠视穷人、无家可归者、童工、被社会遗弃的妇女以及伦敦乃至全世界所有受伤害和受侮辱之人的苦难的人。

The liveliest biography of Dickens is by Peter Ackroyd (1991). I have learned a great deal from a study by Alexander Welsh, The City of Dickens (1971). Anyone who reads Dickens frequently and deeply will be impressed by the personal quality of his attachment to the figure of Jesus. For Dickens, Christianity was Jesus and consisted in compassion, sincerity, charity on an individual basis. Dickens felt contempt for all who professed to be Christian but loathed, exploited, or ignored the sufferings of the poor, the homeless, child laborers, outcast women, all the injured and insulted of London and the world.

《我们共同的朋友》 （1865）中的狄更斯与《悲惨世界》 （1862）中的维克多·雨果有着诸多相似之处。这两位文学巨匠都为世间苦难者辩护，也都深入到各自城市和河流的底层。死亡与复活都源于泰晤士河和塞纳河的污泥、尘土和人类的排泄物。金钱及其腐败，在他们笔下都与粪便相提并论。雨果最终比狄更斯更加乐观，因为维克多·雨果将自己与上帝混淆了。而狄更斯，令他悲哀的是，他更清醒地认识到了这一点。

The Dickens of Our Mutual Friend (1865) has affinities with the Victor Hugo of Les Misérables (1862). Both titans defend the wretched of the earth, and both descend into the underbelly of their cities and rivers. Death and resurrection alike come out of the muck, dust piles, and human waste of the Thames and the Seine. And money in all its corruption is identified by both with feces. Hugo is more optimistic ultimately than Dickens, because Victor Hugo confused himself with God. Dickens, to his sorrow, knew better.

《荒凉山庄》于1852年至1853年连载发表，脾气暴躁却才华横溢的怪老派作家G·K·切斯特顿认为它是狄更斯最好的小说，尽管未必是他最好的作品。从形式上看，我认为这个评价是正确的。狄更斯以精湛的技艺驾驭了众多性格迥异的人物，并通过对每个人物的恰当运用，巧妙地解决了错综复杂的情节。

Bleak House, which appeared as installments from 1852 to 1853, was judged by the irascible yet brilliant curmudgeon G. K. Chesterton to be Dickens’s best novel, though not necessarily his best book. As a formal judgment, this seems right to me. With enormous skill Dickens juggles a remarkably diverse cast of characters and resolves an intricate plot by making precisely appropriate employment of them all.

其中最重要的人物是埃丝特·萨默森，如果我没记错的话，她是狄更斯小说中唯一一位担任重要叙述者的女性。我小时候非常喜欢埃丝特，她一哭我就哭。虽然现在我已经不再这样了，但直到今天，我仍然深受她的感动。可怜的埃丝特由芭芭丽小姐（她未透露姓名的姑妈）抚养长大，这位可怕的女士让她觉得自己生来就是私生女，父母身份不明，这让她感到愧疚。因此，心地善良的埃丝特对快乐不抱任何期望，缺乏自信，任何好运或小事都会让她欣喜若狂。有时我觉得狄更斯对埃丝特的描写有些过火，比如她从自己照料的患病儿童身上感染了天花，失去了大部分美貌。

The most important is Esther Summerson, who, if I remember properly, is the only woman to narrate a substantial part of a Dickens novel. When I was very young, I so loved Esther that I wept when she wept. I have ceased from that but am very moved by her to this day. Raised by a Miss Barbary (her undisclosed aunt), poor Esther was made to feel by that dreadful lady that she was somehow guilty for her birth as the bastard of supposedly unknown parents. In consequence, the sweet-natured Esther has no expectations of joy, lacks all self-esteem, and is heartbreakingly cheered by any good fortune or incident. I sometimes feel Dickens rather piles it on when Esther catches smallpox from a stricken child she is nursing, and loses much of her beauty.

小说后文揭示，霍诺莉亚·戴德洛克夫人是埃丝特的母亲，而尼莫（拉丁语意为“无名氏”）是她的父亲，两人曾有过一段无疾而终的恋情。尼莫的真实身份是詹姆斯·霍顿上尉，他曾是一名军官，也是英勇的骑兵乔治先生的指挥官。如今，霍顿沦落为一名抄写员，为心地善良的斯纳格斯比先生誊写法律文件。斯纳格斯比先生与可怜的街头流浪儿乔成了朋友，乔是个清洁工，尼莫也曾与他交好，直到他因吸食鸦片过量而死。巴克特探长原本非常讨人喜欢，但他却做了一件坏事：他收受了心怀恶意的律师图尔金霍恩先生的贿赂，骚扰乔，企图将他赶出伦敦。图尔金霍恩是莱斯特·戴德洛克爵士的律师，他杞人忧天地担心尼莫可能已经把埃丝特的身世之谜告诉了乔。狄更斯笔下还有其他残暴的律师，但我尤其憎恨图尔金霍恩，当他被戴德洛克夫人的法国女仆霍滕斯谋杀时，我感到非常高兴。霍滕斯与《双城记》中的特蕾丝·德法奇夫人一样，是狄更斯笔下最性感的复仇者之一。

Later in the novel we learn that Lady Honoria Dedlock was Esther’s mother and that one Nemo (“nobody” in Latin) was her father in a love affair that could not endure. Nemo was actually Captain James Hawdon, once an army officer and the commander of the admirable trooper Mr. George. Hawdon has been reduced to a scrivener copying law documents for the good-natured Mr. Snagsby, who befriends the street urchin Jo, a pathetic sweeper, as does Nemo until he dies of an opium overdose. Inspector Bucket, who otherwise is very likable indeed, in his one bad act accepts payment from the malign lawyer Mr. Tulkinghorn to harry Jo so as to force him out of London. Tulkinghorn is Sir Leicester Dedlock’s attorney and fears needlessly that Nemo might have told Jo the secret of Esther’s birth. There are other savage lawyers in Dickens, but I particularly loathe Tulkinghorn and am delighted when he is murdered by Hortense, the French maid to Lady Dedlock, who vies with Madame Thérèse Defarge of The Tale of Two Cities as one of Dickens’s sexiest avengers.

埃丝特的监护人是约翰·贾恩迪斯，他慷慨和蔼，却不情愿地卷入了旷日持久的贾恩迪斯诉贾恩迪斯的衡平法院诉讼。他慈爱地爱着埃丝特，出于父爱，他想娶她为妻，但当埃丝特爱上各方面都令人敬佩的年轻外科医生艾伦·伍德考特时，他毫不犹豫地放手了。埃丝特经历了一番与自身自卑感的挣扎后，最终接受了伍德考特。

Esther’s guardian is John Jarndyce, a generous and amiable man who is an unwilling principal in the endless Chancery lawsuit of Jarndyce v. Jarndyce. He is benignly in love with Esther and in a fatherly way wishes to marry her but readily gives her up when she falls in love with Allan Woodcourt, a young surgeon in every way estimable. After her customary struggle with her sense of personal unworthiness, Esther accepts Woodcourt.

狄更斯巧妙地将两条叙事线交织在一起，创作了《荒凉山庄》：一条是埃丝特的叙述，另一条是旁白，讲述事件的发生过程。旁白占据了三十四个章节，而埃丝特的叙述则占了三十三个章节，但我感​​觉这部小说本质上是埃丝特的故事。还能是谁的故事呢？书中塑造了许多鲜活的人物，他们共同构成了《荒凉山庄》的鲜活生命：骑兵乔治先生、寄生虫哈罗德·斯金波尔（利·亨特饰）、劳伦斯·博伊索恩（沃尔特·萨维奇·兰多饰）以及埃丝特的母亲，戴德洛克夫人霍诺莉亚。利·亨特是一位名不见经传的诗人兼激进记者，如今人们记住他是因为他与济慈和雪莱都是挚友；而兰多是一位才华横溢的诗人，也是引人入胜的《虚构对话录》（1824-1829）的作者，他以脾气暴躁、官司缠身、几乎与所有人都有矛盾而闻名。狄更斯对斯金波尔-亨特夫妇进行了辛辣的讽刺，却和我们一样欣赏博伊索恩-兰多夫妇。乔治先生是一位正直的典范，但不幸的霍诺莉亚却自杀身亡，她并不知道悲痛欲绝的丈夫已经原谅了她的一切。

Dickens ingeniously fashions Bleak House by intermingling two narratives, Esther’s and a voice describing things as they occur. That narrator occupies thirty-four chapters, whereas Esther has thirty-three, but the impression I receive is that the novel is essentially Esther’s story. Whose else could it be? There are the vivid characters who carry much of the life of Bleak House: Mr. George the trooper, Harold Skimpole the sponger (Leigh Hunt), Lawrence Boythorn (Walter Savage Landor), and Honoria, Lady Dedlock, Esther’s mother. Leigh Hunt, a minor poet and radical journalist, is remembered now as the close friend of both Keats and Shelley, while Landor, a very good poet and the author also of the engaging Imaginary Conversations (1824–29), was famously irascible, endlessly involved in lawsuits, and quarreling with almost everyone. Dickens skewers Skimpole-Hunt and enjoys Boythorn-Landor as much as we do. Mr. George is a pillar of honor, but the unfortunate Honoria dies a suicidal death, unaware that her bereaved husband forgives her everything.

然而，这仍然是埃丝特的小说。福楼拜曾说他就是包法利夫人。埃丝特·萨默森既不是大卫·科波菲尔，也不是皮普。他们都是狄更斯本人。不过，我不禁怀疑，她是否也是狄更斯笔下那个被遗弃的孩子，父亲因债务入狱后，她被父母抛弃到一家鞋油厂。查尔斯·狄更斯一生都饱受十二岁时遭受的屈辱的折磨。令我震惊的是，他竟然被冷酷无情的母亲囚禁在鞋油厂里。即使摆脱了这种束缚，他仍然怨恨他的母亲。想必，他关于女性应该待在家中做妻子和母亲的信念，正是源于这段经历。

Yet it remains Esther’s book. Flaubert said that he was Madame Bovary. Esther Summerson is neither David Copperfield nor Pip. They are Dickens. Still, I wonder if she also is not the abandoned child in Dickens himself, cast off by his parents into a blacking factory when his father went to prison for debt. Charles Dickens all his life was haunted by that humiliation at the age of just twelve. I find it astonishing that he was kept at the factory by his callous mother. Long after his release from that bondage, he continued to resent his mother. Presumably, his conviction that women should stay home as wives and mothers emerged from this experience.

我最爱狄更斯的作品，莫过于他那些惊世骇俗之作，这也是为什么我现在把《我们共同的朋友》排在《荒凉山庄》之上。我在《荒凉山庄》中最喜欢的角色，同样也适合出现在《我们共同的朋友》里。他就是克鲁克，一个终日沉迷于杜松子酒的酒鬼，经营着一家堆满纸张、破布和酒瓶的店铺。他的住户包括最终死在那里的尼莫，以及疯癫的老妪弗莱特小姐——她也是大法官府的受害者，养了一群小鸟，并声称只有在末日审判时才会放生它们。克鲁克最终自燃而亡，这件奇事，狄更斯竟然真的相信它会发生。

I love Dickens most fiercely when he is totally outrageous, which is why I now set Our Mutual Friend over even Bleak House. My favorite character in Bleak House could also adorn Our Mutual Friend. This is Krook, who lives entirely on gin and runs a shop overflowing with papers, rags, and bottles. The dwellers in his house include Nemo, who dies there, and the mad Miss Flite, an aged crone who is another victim of Chancery and who keeps a horde of little birds, which she says will be released only at the Last Judgment. Krook ignites in spontaneous combustion, a splendid event in whose probability Dickens actually believed.

理查德·卡斯通，这位大法官法庭的最终受害者，秘密迎娶了另一位大法官法庭的受监护人艾达·克莱尔。案件结束后，由于所有钱都进了律师的腰包，卡斯通身无分文，最终以一种颇为高尚的方式死去，他原谅了自己的一切，并恳求妻子也这样做。

Richard Carstone, the ultimate victim of Chancery, has secretly married Ada Clare, another ward of Chancery. When the case is resolved and there is no money left, as everything has gone to the lawyers, Carstone collapses and dies rather virtuously, forgiving himself everything and urging his wife to do the same:

“我亏欠你太多，都是我自己的错。我像个可怜的流浪影子一样闯入你的生活，我让你嫁给了贫穷和苦难，我把你的财产挥霍一空。我的女儿，在我创造世界之前，你会原谅我这一切吗？”

她俯身吻他，他脸上绽放出灿烂的笑容。他缓缓将脸埋入她的胸膛，双臂紧紧环住她的脖颈，临别时一声哽咽，世界仿佛就此崩塌。不是这个世界，哦，不是这个世界！是那个能拨乱反正的世界。

夜深人静之时，可怜的疯癫的弗莱特小姐哭着来找我，告诉我她已经放飞了她的鸟儿。

‘I have done you many wrongs, my own. I have fallen like a poor stray shadow on your way, I have married you to poverty and trouble, I have scattered your means to the winds. You will forgive me all this, my Ada, before I begin the world?’

A smile irradiated his face, as she bent to kiss him. He slowly laid his face down upon her bosom, drew his arms closer round her neck, and with one parting sob began the world. Not this world, O not this! The world that sets this right.

When all was still, at a late hour, poor crazed Miss Flite came weeping to me, and told me she had given her birds their liberty.

无论人们对《荒凉山庄》的结尾作何评价，它都堪称狄更斯笔下最接近世界末日的结局，直到他创作了《我们共同的朋友》和最后的残篇《艾德温·德鲁德之谜》才有所改观。我认为最后一句话在某种程度上挽救了整个结局。

This ending of Bleak House, whatever one thinks of it, is as close to an apocalypse as Dickens gets until he writes Our Mutual Friend and the final fragment, The Mystery of Edwin Drood. I think that the last sentence partly redeems the conclusion.

第十六章

CHAPTER 16

我们共同的朋友（1865）

Our Mutual Friend (1865)

C ·哈利斯·狄更斯

CHARLES DICKENS

我所见过的对《我们共同的朋友》的最佳评论，是阿德里安·普尔在企鹅经典丛书（1997 年版）的导言中所作的：

THE BEST REMARKS I have seen on Our Mutual Friend are made by Adrian Poole in his introduction to the Penguin Classics volume (1997):

《我们共同的朋友》在最终的评判上，不如作者之前的作品那样自信。它在悬念迭起的时刻，更能体现出作者最深切的关注。仿佛作者和读者，如同医生和他的助手，守候在一个世界的躯体之上，而这个世界的灵魂似乎在新生与消亡之间徘徊闪烁。试图复活腐烂尸体的医生只是作者众多化身之一。还有另一位医生，温柔地陪伴垂死的孩子离开这个世界。此外，还有许多其他工作需要处理，比如验尸官、病理学家、宗教人士和骨骼修复师的工作。

Our Mutual Friend boasts less confidence than earlier works in its own last judgements. It finds a truer sense of its deepest attention in the moments of suspense. As if the writer and his readers were poised, like a doctor and his attendants, over the body of a world, the soul of which seems to hover and flicker, between renewal and extinction. The doctor who seeks to revive the dank corpse is only one of the writer’s possible guises. There is another doctor who gently eases the passage of a dying child out of this world. And there is plenty of other work to be done over corpses, for coroners and pathologists, for ministers of religion and articulators of bones.

在普尔看来，书名可以解读为：《死亡是我们共同的朋友》。这无疑是一个令人信服的标题。然而，正如罗伯特·勃朗宁所言，“一种普遍的灰色笼罩着一切”。普尔曾友好地反驳过我的观点，即除了麦克白和他的夫人之外，莎士比亚将悲剧中的人物都简化成了普遍的灰色。出于同样的友好，我或许可以大胆地提出，在《死亡是我们共同的朋友》中，死亡与复活在一个如此污浊又如此丰饶的宇宙中融合在一起，以至于所有界限都变得更加虚幻，即便狄更斯的语言也呈现出一种新的锐利感。

In Poole’s view, the title could be read: Death Is Our Mutual Friend. A palpable hit. And yet, to quote Robert Browning, “A common greyness silvers everything.” Poole once amiably disputed my notion that, except for Macbeth and his Lady, Shakespeare subdued the tragedy’s characters to a common grayness. With appropriate amiability, I might venture that death and resurrection fuse in Our Mutual Friend in a cosmos so fetid and so fecund that all demarcations are rendered ghostlier even as the sounds of Dickens’s diction achieve a new keenness.

《我们共同的朋友》是一部鸿篇巨制，长达八百页，是我读过的所有作品中最独特的一部。我能想到的勉强与之相似的，只有维克多·雨果的《悲惨世界》。在后记中，狄更斯回忆起1865年6月9日那场可怕的铁路事故，他本人也受了伤，但他英勇地尽力帮助和安慰那些受伤和垂死的人。他最终活了下来，完成了《我们共同的朋友》，并在后记的结尾留下了一句令人心碎的话：

Our Mutual Friend is a vast eight-hundred-page prose poem unlike anything else that I have ever read. I can think only of Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables as a rough analogue. In his postscript, Dickens concluded with a terrible memory of the railway accident of June 9, 1865, in which he was injured but heroically labored to help and comfort the maimed and the dying. He survived to finish Our Mutual Friend and ended the postscript with a poignant sentence:

我怀着虔诚的感激之情记得，我离与读者永远告别，再也没有比那时更近的距离了，直到我的生命被铭记，写下我今天结束这本书时所说的这两个字：——完。

1865年9月2日。

I remember with devout thankfulness that I can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with which I have this day closed this book:—The END.

September 2nd, 1865.

火车事故发生五年后的同一天，查尔斯·狄更斯于1870年6月9日去世，享年58岁。他的《远大前程》（1860-1861）和《我们共同的朋友》（1864-1865）之间存在一段空白期。对于狄更斯来说，近三年的创作空白期实属罕见。创伤或许是部分原因。1858年，他与妻子凯瑟琳分居，而就在一年前，他爱上了年仅18岁的女演员艾伦·特南。彼得·阿克罗伊德令人信服地论证了狄更斯与特南的这段关系——这段关系持续了狄更斯的余生——从未发生过性关系。狄更斯去世六年之后，特南结婚生子，并于1914年去世，享年75岁。大多数传记作家并不认同阿克罗伊德的这一观点。我觉得这很有道理，因为狄更斯在四十五岁时开始再次受到童年创伤的影响，并在艾伦·特南身上找到了一个理想化的对象。

Five years to the day after the train wreck, Charles Dickens died, on June 9, 1870, at the age of fifty-eight. There is a gap between Great Expectations (1860–61) and Our Mutual Friend (1864–65). It was unlike Dickens to lie fallow for almost three years. Trauma may be a part of the explanation. The separation from his wife, Catherine, in 1858 took place a year after he fell in love with the eighteen-year-old actress Ellen Ternan. Peter Ackroyd persuasively argues that the relationship with Ternan, which lasted the rest of Dickens’s life, was never sexually consummated. Six years after the novelist’s death, she married, then had two children, and died at seventy-five in 1914. Most biographers disagree with Ackroyd’s judgment. It seems sound to me, because Dickens at forty-five started to yield again to his childhood traumas and found in Ellen Ternan an idealized object.

那些本可以让我们阅读其他小说的精力——就像我们现在反复阅读《荒凉山庄》和《我们共同的朋友》一样——却被狄更斯没完没了的公开朗读会所消耗殆尽。在这些朗读会上，狄更斯为众多听众表演他笔下的人物和他们的故事。如果电影艺术在那时就已经存在，我们就能欣赏到这些无与伦比的演绎，但既然电影艺术尚未出现，而且所有观众都已离世，这只能被视为一种浪费和损失。

The energies that would have given us other novels to read, as we now read and reread Bleak House and Our Mutual Friend, were absorbed by endless public readings in which Dickens performed to huge audiences his own characters and their stories. If only the art of the film had existed that early, we would have these unrivaled enactments, but since we cannot, and all their auditors are deceased, it has to be regarded as a waste and a loss.

狄更斯的小说开头几乎总是精彩绝伦，结尾却往往显得苍白无力。《我们共同的朋友》以泰晤士河为背景，开篇便气势磅礴，令人叹为观止：

Dickens is almost always magnificent at openings and curiously weak when ending a novel. Our Mutual Friend begins on the Thames with grotesque power:

在如今这个时代，虽然具体年份无需精确考证，但在一个秋日的傍晚，一艘外观肮脏破败的船，船上有两个人影，漂浮在泰晤士河上，位于铁制的南华克桥和石制的伦敦桥之间。

船上坐着一个身强力壮的男人，他头发蓬乱，面色黝黑；还有一个十九、二十岁左右的黑皮肤女孩，长相酷似他，一眼就能认出是他的女儿。女孩划着桨，轻松地拉着两支单桨；男人手里松松地握着舵绳，双手随意地插在腰间，警惕地四处张望。他没有渔网、鱼钩或鱼线，不可能是渔夫；他的船上没有坐垫，没有油漆，没有铭文，除了一个生锈的船钩和一卷绳子之外，什么也没有，不可能是水手；他的船又小又破，根本运不了货，不可能是驳船夫或河运货人；没人知道他在寻找什么，但他确实在寻找着什么，目光专注而探寻。潮水在一个小时前就已转向，现在正缓缓退去。他目不转睛地盯着宽阔河面上每一处细小的湍流和漩涡，小船时而逆流而上，时而船尾朝前，这一切都取决于他向女儿示意的方向。女儿也像他注视着河面一样，专注地看着他的脸。然而，在她专注的目光中，却夹杂着一丝恐惧或惊骇。

由于船身被淤泥覆盖，湿漉漉的，它与其说是漂浮在水面上，不如说是沉在河底。这艘船和船上的两个人显然在做着他们经常做的事情，寻找着他们经常寻找的东西。那男人看起来半野蛮，蓬乱的头发上没有遮盖，棕色的胳膊裸露到肘部和肩膀之间，一条松松垮垮的头巾松松垮垮地系在裸露的胸前，周围是茂密的胡须。他身上的衣服似乎是用船上的泥巴做成的。然而，他那沉稳的眼神中却透着一丝公事公办的意味。那女孩的每一个轻盈的动作，每一次手腕的转动，尤其是她脸上那恐惧或惊骇的神情，都像是某种例行公事。

In these times of ours, though concerning the exact year there is no need to be precise, a boat of dirty and disreputable appearance, with two figures in it, floated on the Thames, between Southwark Bridge which is of iron, and London Bridge which is of stone, as an autumn evening was closing in.

The figures in this boat were those of a strong man with ragged grizzled hair and a sun-browned face, and a dark girl of nineteen or twenty, sufficiently like him to be recognizable as his daughter. The girl rowed, pulling a pair of sculls very easily; the man, with the rudder-lines slack in his hands, and his hands loose in his waistband, kept an eager look out. He had no net, hook, or line, and he could not be a fisherman; his boat had no cushion for a sitter, no paint, no inscription, no appliance beyond a rusty boathook and a coil of rope, and he could not be a waterman; his boat was too crazy and too small to take in cargo for delivery, and he could not be a lighterman or river-carrier; there was no clue to what he looked for, but he looked for something, with a most intent and searching gaze. The tide, which had turned an hour before, was running down, and his eyes watched every little race and eddy in its broad sweep, as the boat made slight head-way against it, or drove stern foremost before it, according as he directed his daughter by a movement of his head. She watched his face as earnestly as he watched the river. But, in the intensity of her look there was a touch of dread or horror.

Allied to the bottom of the river rather than the surface, by reason of the slime and ooze with which it was covered, and its sodden state, this boat and the two figures in it obviously were doing something that they often did, and were seeking what they often sought. Half savage as the man showed, with no covering on his matted head, with his brown arms bare to between the elbow and the shoulder, with the loose knot of a looser kerchief lying low on his bare breast in a wilderness of beard and whisker, with such dress as he wore seeming to be made out of the mud that begrimed his boat, still there was a business-like usage in his steady gaze. So with every lithe action of the girl, with every turn of her wrist, perhaps most of all with her look of dread or horror; they were things of usage.

泰晤士河本身就是《我们共同的朋友》的主角。莉齐·赫克瑟姆、莫蒂默·莱特伍德、尤金·雷伯恩、珍妮·雷恩、里亚先生、布拉德利·海德斯通、法西恩·弗莱奇比、罗格·莱德胡德，以及那个有三个名字的男人——约翰·哈蒙、约翰·罗克斯密斯、朱利叶斯·汉福德——是书中九位至关重要的人物，但如果没有泰晤士河，他们或许无法完全吸引读者的兴趣。莉齐·赫克瑟姆的父亲加弗、布拉德利·海德斯通和罗格·莱德胡德都死于溺水。约翰·哈蒙表面上是溺水身亡，但这只是他略显奇特的诡计。尤金·雷伯恩在遭到海德斯通从背后袭击后落水，被莉齐从河里救起，莉齐悉心照料他，使他慢慢恢复了健康。罗格·莱德胡德在被一心求死的海德斯通拖入水中溺亡之前，他自己也在书中早些时候经历了一次溺水后的死里逃生。令人憎恶的费辛尼·弗莱奇比遭到了应有的毒打，但不幸的是他活了下来。莫蒂默·莱特伍德、珍妮·雷恩和那位令人厌烦的好心犹太人里亚先生，是仅有的几个没有被威廉·布莱克在其诗作《伦敦》早期草稿中称为“肮脏的泰晤士河”的浑浊河水（姑且这么称呼吧）所玷污的主要人物。

The Thames itself is the protagonist of Our Mutual Friend. Lizzie Hexam, Mortimer Lightwood, Eugene Wrayburn, Jenny Wren, Mr. Riah, Bradley Headstone, Fascination Fledgeby, Rogue Riderhood, and the man with three names—John Harmon, John Rokesmith, Julius Handford—are nine vital figures in the book, but without the Thames they might not sustain our full interest. Lizzie Hexam’s father, Gaffer; Bradley Headstone; and Rogue Riderhood all suffer death by water. John Harmon supposedly does, but that is his rather peculiar subterfuge. Eugene Wrayburn, after a brutal attack from behind by Headstone, is rescued from the river by Lizzie, who helps nurse him slowly back to health. Rogue Riderhood, before being wrestled into drowning by the suicidal Headstone, himself undergoes a resurrection from near drowning earlier in the book. The abominable Fascination Fledgeby receives a much-deserved beating but unfortunately survives. Mortimer Lightwood, Jenny Wren, and the tiresomely good Jew, Mr. Riah, are the only major figures left unstained by the turgid water (to call it that) of what William Blake in an earlier draft of his poem “London” termed “the dirty Thames.”

《莉亚》是狄更斯对《雾都孤儿》中费金这个精彩人物的补偿，但这补偿注定是苍白无力的。在夏洛克之后，费金是所有反犹丑角中最具说服力的一个。

Riah was Dickens’s apology for the wonderful Fagin in Oliver Twist, an apology inevitably lame. After Shylock, Fagin is the most persuasive of all anti-Semitic caricatures.

—

《他以不同的声音扮演警察》是T·S·艾略特最初为后来成为《荒原》（1922）的作品所作的标题。埃兹拉·庞德巧妙地对艾略特的手稿进行了大幅修改，最终创作出了我们今天所读到的这首诗。艾略特在引用《我们共同的朋友》时非常精准，这首诗描绘了伦敦末日景象，为《荒原》拉开了序幕。

“He Do the Police in Different Voices” was T. S. Eliot’s original title for what became The Waste Land (1922). Ezra Pound brilliantly hacked away at Eliot’s manuscript, thus producing the poem we have all read. Eliot was precise when he invoked Our Mutual Friend, which is the London apocalypse that preluded The Waste Land.

在《我们共同的朋友》中，谁最终幸存下来？除了约翰·哈蒙和贝拉·威尔弗这对婚姻美满却略显苍白的夫妇之外，还有尤金·雷伯恩和莉齐·赫克瑟姆，他们那段拯救人生的婚姻深深打动了读者。雷伯恩逐渐觉醒，重获新生；而我们最初见到的莉齐，是她划着小船陪父亲去拾荒，之后她变得更加天使般纯洁，更加令人感到慰藉。还有莫特默·莱特伍德，他曾经漫不经心、略带讽刺，如今却因尤金和莉齐的感情而备受鼓舞。带着一丝微妙的讽刺，他在小说结尾重返上流社会，并对此感到无比厌恶。最精彩的莫过于珍妮·雷恩和斯洛皮，斯洛皮似乎爱上了她，狄更斯或许暗示他们最终会走到一起。

Who survives in Our Mutual Friend? Aside from John Harmon and Bella Wilfer, who achieve harmonious marriage but are pale figures, there are Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam, whose saving marriage charms the reader. Wrayburn matures into a resurrected consciousness, and the wonderful Lizzie, whom first we saw rowing her father on his scavenging expedition, becomes even more angelic and comforting. Then there is Mortmer Lightwood, once insouciant and ironic, who is exalted by the relationship between Eugene and Lizzie. With a finer edge of irony, he concludes the novel by returning to Society, and is rightly appalled by it. Best of all are Jenny Wren and Sloppy, who seems to fall in love with her, and Dickens perhaps intimates that they may yet make a match.

珍妮·雷恩是狄更斯笔下最被低估的人物之一。她是个跛脚的少女，饱受照顾酗酒父亲的折磨——她把父亲视作自己的孩子，而父亲最终也因醉酒而死。珍妮·雷恩本人却有着一种奇特的机智。有一次，当令人厌恶的费辛尼翁·弗莱奇比在她和里亚的小屋顶花园里呼唤她们时，她喊道：“上来死吧！上来死吧！”

Jenny Wren is one of the most underpraised figures in Dickens. A lame teenager, afflicted by her care of an alcoholic father, whom she calls her child and who finally yields to a drunken death, she has a strange wit of her own. At one moment when the abominable Fascination Fledgeby calls to her and Riah in their little roof garden, she cries out: “Come up and be dead! Come up and be dead!”

珍妮·雷恩是一位技艺精湛的玩偶制作师，以此为生。她称里亚为她的仙女教父，并告诉他以及我们所有人，她正在等待她的王子带她离开。斯洛皮是个弃儿，但他比任何王子都更温柔善良，如果他们最终真的走到了一起，那将是狄更斯赐予我们的又一份恩赐。

As a doll maker Jenny Wren is a consummate artist, and maintains herself by it. She calls Riah her fairy godfather and tells him and the rest of us that she awaits her prince to take her away. Sloppy, a foundling, is sweeter and kinder than any prince could be, and if indeed they wind up together, that would be another blessing Dickens confers upon us.

泰晤士河依旧奔流不息，狄更斯笔下那幽暗的河水依然历历在目。这条河令人难忘，却又冷酷无情，它毁灭一切，鲜少滋养万物。

There remains the riding Thames, and nothing mitigates Dickens’s vision of the dark waters. Memorable and unforgiving, the river destroys and rarely nourishes.

第十七章

CHAPTER 17

《包法利夫人》（1857）

Madame Bovary (1857)

G ·乌斯塔夫· F ·洛贝尔

GUSTAVE FLAUBERT

我第一次读 《包法利夫人》是埃莉诺·马克思·阿维林的译本，译文生硬，据说是我已故的朋友保罗·德曼稍作修订的。埃莉诺·马克思是卡尔·马克思的女儿，后来成为一名社会主义活动家。她四十三岁时自杀，因为她发现伴侣爱德华有重婚罪。

I FIRST READ Madame Bovary in the wooden translation by Eleanor Marx Aveling, with some revisions supposedly by my late friend Paul de Man. Eleanor Marx was a daughter of Karl Marx and became a socialist activist. She committed suicide at the age of forty-three, when she discovered that her partner, Edward, was a bigamist.

幸运的是，1987年我终于读到了法文版，从此便一直被它深深吸引。我最近读了莉迪亚·戴维斯的精彩译本，在我看来，这堪称文学翻译的标杆之作。她的《包法利夫人》堪称奇迹，她的《斯万之路》（2004）亦是如此。我仍在细细品读她那些令人惊艳的短篇小说，因为它们独树一帜。

Fortunately, in 1987 I finally read it in French and began the long process of being haunted by it. I have just read the marvelous version by Lydia Davis, which seems to me a touchstone for literary translation. Her Madame Bovary is a kind of miracle, as is her Swann’s Way (2004). I am still absorbing her startling short fictions, as they are sui generis.

1832年，11岁的福楼拜读了《堂吉诃德》，这部作品与歌德以及巴尔扎克（程度稍轻）一起，构成了他最重要的文学启蒙。尽管他阅读范围广泛且深入，其文学氛围足以与蒙田相媲美。福楼拜似乎患有某种癫痫，但真正危害他健康的，是他中东之旅中与男女妓女的滥交。他早年感染了梅毒，58岁去世，但很可能是死于癫痫引发的心脏病。

In 1832, at the age of eleven, Flaubert read Don Quixote, which, together with Goethe and, to a smaller extent, Balzac, constituted his prime literary influences, though he read so widely and deeply that he rivals Montaigne in his ambience. Flaubert seems to have had a form of epilepsy, but the major hazards to his health came from his promiscuity with female and male prostitutes in his Middle Eastern tours. He contracted syphilis early in his life, and died at fifty-eight, but probably from a heart attack brought on by epilepsy.

福楼拜终身未婚，也没有子女。他在写给他的情人、诗人路易丝·科莱的一封信中，谴责了生育，称他不想“传递……存在的痛苦和耻辱”。

Flaubert did not marry and had no children. In a letter to his sometime mistress, the poet Louise Colet, he denounced childbearing, saying he did not wish to “transmit…the aggravations and the disgrace of existence.”

称福楼拜为厌女者似乎并不恰当。多年来，他对已婚且比他年长十岁的伊丽莎·施莱辛格怀有深沉的爱恋，这种爱恋几乎不涉及性欲。众所周知，他与《包法利夫人》中的爱玛·包法利有着某种认同感。评论家阿尔伯特·蒂博代在其著作《古斯塔夫·福楼拜》（1922年）中，精彩地将福楼拜对爱玛的态度与弥尔顿对夏娃的态度进行了比较：“每当他以纯粹的感官视角来看待爱玛时，他都会以一种细腻的、近乎宗教般的情感来谈论她，就像弥尔顿谈论夏娃一样。”

It seems wrong to call Flaubert a misogynist. For many years he had a deep love, scarcely sexual, for Elisa Schlesinger, who was married and a decade older. He famously identifies with Emma Bovary. The critic Albert Thibaudet in his Gustave Flaubert (1922) splendidly compares Flaubert’s stance toward Emma to Milton’s in regard to Eve: “Whenever Emma is seen in purely sensuous terms, he speaks of her with a delicate, almost religious feeling, the way Milton speaks of Eve.”

和许多读者一样，我觉得弥尔顿渴望的是夏娃。福楼拜对爱玛的爱必然是自恋的。称爱玛·包法利为女版堂吉诃德可谓一针见血，因为她和堂吉诃德一样，最终被现实所扼杀。没有桑丘的爱玛，在荒诞的鲁道夫身上找到了她心目中的杜尔西内娅。福楼拜将乡野社会现实的毒药与爱玛对崇高激情的幻想交织在一起，以此惩罚她​​、惩罚自己、也惩罚我们。我觉得这很残酷，但对于波德莱尔的作品，我们不得不承认它具有无与伦比的审美尊严。福楼拜颠覆了维克多·雨果的浪漫主义，让我们相信他纯粹的风格甚至能以一种提升生命的力量来描绘倦怠。

Like so many readers, I feel that Milton desires Eve. Flaubert’s love for Emma necessarily is narcissistic. It is a useful truism to call Emma Bovary a female Quixote, since, like the Knight, she is murdered by reality. Emma, who has no Sancho, discovers her enchanted Dulcinea in the absurd Rodolphe. Flaubert punishes her, himself, and us by fusing the poison of provincial social reality with the poison of Emma’s hallucinated fantasies of a sublime passion. I find this very cruel, but with Baudelaire one has to grant its unmatched aesthetic dignity. Flaubert so inverts Victor Hugo’s Romanticism as to persuade us that his own pure style can represent even ennui with a power that enhances life.

明天我就八十八岁了，比以往任何时候都更加忧伤，也更加浪漫。这几天，我一直在反复阅读莉迪亚·戴维斯的《包法利夫人》。它让我心潮澎湃，却也让我无比悲伤。我想约翰·济慈一定会喜欢《包法利夫人》，因为他也是那种不追求奇迹，只探寻人性本质的探索者。

Tomorrow I turn eighty-eight and am, more than ever, a sorrowful Romantic. These last few days, I have been reading and rereading Lydia Davis’s Madame Bovary. It exalts me yet also makes me very sad. I think John Keats would have loved Emma Bovary, because he was one of those questers who seek no wonder but the human face.

这是福楼拜创作《艾玛·包法利》时的场景：

Here is Flaubert at work murdering Emma Bovary:

今晚六点，当我写下“歇斯底里”这个词时，我完全被情绪所裹挟，情不自禁地大声呐喊，深深地感受到我的小包法利正在经历的一切，以至于我害怕自己也会歇斯底里。我从桌前起身，打开窗户让自己冷静下来。我头晕目眩。现在我的膝盖、背部和头部都剧痛难忍。我感觉自己像个性生活过度的男人（请原谅我的用词）——一种狂喜的倦怠感。

——福楼拜致路易丝·科莱特，信，1853年12月23日

At six o’clock tonight, as I was writing the word “hysterics,” I was so swept away, was bellowing so loudly and feeling so deeply what my little Bovary was going through, that I was afraid of having hysterics myself. I got up from my table and opened the window to calm myself. My head was spinning. Now I have great pains in my knees, in my back, and in my head. I feel like a man who has been fucking too much (forgive me for the expression)—a kind of rapturous lassitude.

—Flaubert to Louise Colet, letter, December 23, 1853

1857年，夏尔·波德莱尔在评论《包法利夫人》时，将福楼拜视为同道中人，并沉溺于自己对人类生活的灾难性看法：

Charles Baudelaire, reviewing Madame Bovary in 1857, regarded Flaubert as a fellow poet and indulged his own catastrophic vision of human life:

我不会重复那个以颠覆性著称的“狼人”（彼得鲁斯·博雷尔）的话，他曾说过：“面对当今时代的一切庸俗和无能，我们难道不能躲进香烟和通奸之中吗？” 但我认为，即便用精密的秤来衡量，我们的世界也显得异常残酷，毕竟它是基督所创造的；它又怎有资格对通奸大加指责呢？几个戴绿帽的人不太可能加快宇宙的自转速度，更不可能让宇宙的最终毁灭提前一秒。

I will not echo the Lycanthrope [Petrus Borel], remembered for a subversiveness which no longer prevails, when he said: “Confronted with all that is vulgar and inept in the present time, can we not take refuge in cigarettes and adultery?” But I assert that our world, even when it is weighed on precision scales, turns out to be exceedingly harsh considering it was engendered by Christ; it could hardly be entitled to throw the first stone at adultery. A few cuckolds more or less are not likely to increase the rotating speed of the spheres and to hasten by a second the final destruction of the universe.

《包法利夫人》的社会丑闻如今已如同福楼拜和波德莱尔所奉行的精神禁欲主义一般遥远，在贝克特和品钦的时代，他们似乎显得有些自我放纵。将《包法利夫人》与《马龙之死》并置重读，会是一次令人悲伤却又发人深省的体验。在马龙和麦克曼的陪伴下，爱玛显得像霍加斯或拉伯雷一样喧闹。然而，她却是他们的祖母，即便普鲁斯特、乔伊斯和卡夫卡的人物也如同她的子女一般。随着她的出现，小说进入了一种停滞的状态，主人公们感到厌倦，但读者却并非如此。可怜的爱玛，她并非死于爱情，而是死于高利贷，但她的生命力如此旺盛，以至于她的愚蠢都无关紧要。她是一位远超常人的感性女性，她对生活和爱的热情正是我们钦佩她，甚至爱上她的原因。

The societal scandal of Madame Bovary is as remote now as the asceticism of the spirit practiced by Flaubert and Baudelaire, who seem almost self-indulgent in the era of Samuel Beckett and Thomas Pynchon. Rereading Madame Bovary side by side with, say, Malone Dies, is a sadly instructive experience. Emma seems as boisterous as Hogarth or Rabelais in the company of Malone and Macmann. And yet she is their grandmother, even as the personages of Proust, Joyce, and Kafka are among her children. With her the novel enters the realm of inactivity, where the protagonists are bored, but the reader is not. Poor Emma, destroyed by usury rather than love, is so vital that her stupidities do not matter. She is a much more than averagely sensual woman, and her capacity for life and love is what moves us to admire her, and even to love her.

为什么爱玛如此不幸？凡事皆有可能出错，而她注定要遭遇不幸。弗洛伊德和一些古代哲学家一样，认为世间没有偶然。人格特质（Ethos）是守护神，你的性格决定你的命运，发生在你身上的一切皆源于你自身。重读此书，我们目睹爱玛走向自我毁灭的种种阶段，不禁感到痛苦。尽管福楼拜以其著名的超脱笔触著称，但这种痛苦却愈发强烈，部分原因在于他敏锐地暗示了众多不同的意识如何侵入并影响着任何一个单一的意识，即便是像爱玛这样平凡的意识。爱玛的“我”已然成为他者，而当感官的焦虑最终融入爱玛自身时，情况就变得更加糟糕了。

Why is Emma so unlucky? If it can go wrong, it will go wrong for her. Freud, like some of the ancients, believed there were no accidents. Ethos is the daemon, your character is your fate, and everything that happens to you starts by being you. Rereading, we suffer the anguish of beholding the phases that lead to Emma’s self-destruction. That anguish multiplies despite Flaubert’s celebrated detachment, partly because of his uncanny skill at suggesting how many different consciousnesses invade and impinge upon any single consciousness, even one as commonplace as Emma’s. Emma’s I is an other, and so much the worse for the sensual apprehensiveness that finds it has become Emma.

“癔症患者主要受回忆困扰”是弗洛伊德一句著名而精辟的论断，但他后来超越了这一论断。如同之前的福楼拜一样，他逐渐意识到，像艾玛这样的人——实际上几乎我们所有人——都饱受压抑本能的折磨。更晚的时候，在弗洛伊德的晚期思想中，他最终形成了一套清晰的理论，并在《抑制、症状与焦虑》的最后一部分得到了淋漓尽致的阐述，在我看来，这部分是对《包法利夫人》的关键性解读。焦虑并非源于被压抑的欲望，而是源于一种原始的焦虑，而这种焦虑又导致了压抑行为。至于各种神经症，弗洛伊德推测，癔症源于对失去爱的恐惧。艾玛因一场微不足道的经济纠纷而陷入癔症并最终自杀，但在这癔症的背后，隐藏着她对未来不再有爱人的恐惧。

“Hysterics suffer mainly from reminscences” is a famous and eloquent formula that Freud outgrew. Like Flaubert before him, he came to see that the Emmas—meaning nearly all among us—were suffering from repressed drives. Still later, in his final phase, Freud arrived at a vision that achieves an ultimate clarity in the last section of Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety, which reads to me as a crucial commentary on Emma Bovary. It is not repressed desire that issues in anxiety, but a primal anxiety that issues in repression. As for the variety of neurosis involved, Freud speculated that hysteria results from fear of the loss of love. Emma kills herself in a hysteria brought on by a fairly trivial financial mess, but underlying the hysteria is the terrible fear that there will be no more lovers for her.

这听起来似乎合情合理，但重读这部小说并不会让我们渴望一个更强大、更聪慧的爱玛。在她彻底陷入歇斯底里之前，她体现了人类对感官生活、对更感官生活的普遍渴望。一个杰出的爱玛或许会发展出坚韧和机敏，使她成为法国版的贝基·夏普，甚至足以让她在十九世纪中叶的巴黎生存下去。但詹姆斯巧妙地忽略了这一点，而阿尔伯特·蒂博代却永远地抓住了这一点：

That sounds right enough, yet rereading the novel does not make us desire a larger or brighter Emma. Until she yields to total hysteria, she incarnates the universal wish for sensual life, for a more sensual life. A remarkable Emma might have developed the hardness and resourcefulness that would have made her a French Becky Sharp, and fitted her for survival even in mid-nineteenth-century Paris. But James sublimely chose to miss the point, which Albert Thibaudet got permanently right:

她热情似火，却又略显狂热。她热爱生活、享乐，热爱爱情本身，远胜于爱男人；她天生就该拥有情人，而非仅仅是一个情人。诚然，她曾以肉体的全部热情爱着鲁道夫，与他在一起时，她体验到了短暂而完美的圆满；然而，鲁道夫离她而去后，她的疾病足以治愈这份爱。她并非死于爱情，而是死于软弱和对未来的全然无知，这种天真使她在爱情和事业中都极易受骗。她活在当下，无法抗拒任何一丝冲动。

She is more ardent than passionate. She loves life, pleasure, love itself much more than she loves a man; she is made to have lovers rather than a lover. It is true that she loves Rodolphe with all the fervor of her body, and with him she experiences the moment of her complete, perfect and brief fulfillment; her illness, however, after Rodolphe’s desertion, is sufficient to cure her of this love. She does not die from love, but from weakness and a total inability to look ahead, a naivete which makes her an easy prey to deceit in love as well as in business. She lives in the present and is unable to resist the slightest impulse.

这是《包法利夫人》中艾玛·博瓦利临终前的画面：

Here is the dying moment of Emma Bovary:

神父起身拿起十字架；这时，她像渴了一般伸长脖子，将嘴唇贴在人神的身体上，用尽最后一丝力气，献上她此生最热烈的爱吻。然后，他诵读了《求主垂怜经》和《赎罪经》，用右手拇指蘸了蘸圣油，开始涂抹圣油：先涂抹在她那双曾贪恋世间一切荣华的双眼上；再涂抹在她那渴望微风和爱意的鼻孔上；接着涂抹在她那张曾张开说谎、曾因骄傲而呻吟、曾因欲望而呼喊的嘴唇上；然后涂抹在她那双曾沉醉于光滑肌肤的双手上；最后涂抹在她那双曾让她奔向欲望、如今却再也无法行走的脚底上。

The priest rose to take up the crucifix; at that, she strained her neck forward like someone who is thirsty, and, pressing her lips to the body of the Man-God, she laid upon it with all her expiring strength the most passionate kiss of love she had ever given. Then he recited the Misereatur and the Indulgentiam, dipped his right thumb in the oil, and began the unctions: first on the eyes, which had so coveted all earthly splendors; then on the nostrils, greedy for mild breezes and the smells of love; then on the mouth, which had opened to utter lies, which had moaned with pride and cried out in lust; then on the hands, which had delighted in the touch of smooth material; and lastly on the soles of the feet, once so quick when she hastened to satiate her desires and which now would never walk again.

莉迪亚·戴维斯为这篇一丝不苟的祷文找到了精准的语气。我承认，它令我感到痛苦，甚至让我对古斯塔夫·福楼拜有些忘恩负义。这是一种多角度的讽刺，几乎无一幸免。这位文风的殉道者如此深信“存在的耻辱”，以至于他可以是一位公元二世纪的苦行僧，或者像波德莱尔、内瓦尔和兰波一样，成为十九世纪的瓦伦廷式灵知的化身。

Lydia Davis has found precisely the accurate tone for this fastidious litany. I confess that it ravages me and renders me a touch ungrateful to Gustave Flaubert. This is an irony cutting so many ways that little is spared. The martyr of style is so persuaded of “the disgrace of existence” that he could be an ascetic of the second century of the Common Era, or, like Baudelaire, Nerval, and Rimbaud, a nineteenth-century version of the Valentinian Gnosis.

我本人很同情瓦伦提努斯，因为我也认为创世与堕落是同一事件。除了普鲁斯特之外，福楼拜才是真正的小说家。世上没有不劳而获的事，当生存本身似乎是一种耻辱时，就必须付出代价。

I myself am sympathetic to Valentinus, since I also believe that the Creation and the Fall were the same event. Flaubert, except for Proust, is the true artist of the novel. Nothing is got for nothing, and there is a cost when existence seems a disgrace.

第十八章

CHAPTER 18

《悲惨世界》（1862）

Les Misérables (1862)

维克多· H·乌戈

VICTOR HUGO

维克多·雨果并非唯一一位涉足小说创作的伟大诗人。人们还会想到亚历山德罗·曼佐尼、艾米莉·勃朗特、赫尔曼·梅尔维尔、托马斯·哈代和D·H·劳伦斯。乔治·艾略特、薇拉·凯瑟、詹姆斯·乔伊斯和厄休拉·勒古恩，尤其是后者，都创作过一些令人赞叹的诗歌，但我们反复阅读的却是他们的小说。

VICTOR HUGO is scarcely the only great poet to have indulged himself in the composition of novels. One thinks of Alessandro Manzoni, Emily Brontë, Herman Melville, Thomas Hardy, and D. H. Lawrence. George Eliot, Willa Cather, James Joyce, and Ursula Le Guin, particularly the latter, wrote some admirable poems, but it is their novels that we reread.

我赞同保罗·瓦雷里关于维克多·雨果是法国诗人中的泰斗的评价。虽然我痴迷于《悲惨世界》，但它无法与司汤达、巴尔扎克和福楼拜的巅峰之作相提并论。它真的算得上是一部小说吗？它是一部不知何时收尾的鸿篇巨制，堆砌了大量与故事主线无关的素材。我只完整地读过一遍原著，当时既感到震撼又困惑。诺曼·丹尼于1976年翻译的版本堪称佳作，现已由企鹅经典文库出版。该译本将雨果对修道院以及十九世纪中期巴黎俚语（尤其是犯罪阶层的俚语）的奇特论述置于附录之中，而丹尼则选择完整地呈现了第二部分“珂赛特”开篇中关于滑铁卢战役的详细描述。只有第十九章对整个故事至关重要，因为它讲述了拾荒者德纳第在战场上无意中救起蓬梅西上校的故事。蓬梅西上校是马吕斯的父亲，而马吕斯正是维克多·雨果笔下《悲惨世界》的主人公。然而，在这部鸿篇巨制中，最缺乏说服力的两个角色却是马吕斯和他心爱的珂赛特。珂赛特是不幸的芳汀的女儿，芳汀为了养活珂赛特，甘愿沦为妓女，过着悲惨的生活，最终早逝。珂赛特后来被德纳第一家从饥饿中解救出来，而英勇的主人公冉阿让——在很多方面，冉阿让就是整部作品的灵魂——救了出来。

I am content with Paul Valéry’s judgment that Victor Hugo was the titan among all French poets. Though I am obsessed with Les Misérables, it is not of the company of Stendhal, Balzac, and Flaubert at their best. Is it actually a novel? A vast extravaganza that never knows where to stop, it sprawls over a mass of materials that are irrelevant to the story that supposedly it tells. I have read it straight through only once in the original, and was both exalted and baffled. There is an admirable translation by Norman Denny (1976), now available in Penguin Classics, which performs the necessary task of relegating to appendices Victor Hugo’s extraordinary excursions into the idea of the convent and into the Parisian argot of the mid-nineteenth century, particularly in the criminal class. Denny chooses to print all of the detailed account of the Battle of Waterloo that constitutes the initial section of Part Two: Cosette. Only Chapter XIX is in any way crucial to the story, since it recounts the involuntary rescue of Colonel Pontmercy from the battlefield by the scavenger Thénardier. Colonel Pontmercy is the father of Marius, who is intended by Victor Hugo to be the hero of Les Misérables. Unfortunately, the two least persuasive characters in this vast book are Marius and his beloved Cosette, the child of the unfortunate Fantine, who has supported her by a miserable life as a prostitute and dies very early. Cosette is then rescued from the Thénardier family that starves her by the heroic protagonist Jean Valjean, who in most regards is the book.

话虽如此，我还是怀疑这是否属实。每当我回想起《悲惨世界》，首先浮现在脑海的便是那群聚集在一起的年轻革命者，他们自称为“ABC社”。他们最终都惨遭杀害，因为他们的街垒根本抵挡不住敌军的炮火和压倒性的兵力。我按照维克多·雨果的原著顺序列出他们的名字：安灼拉、孔布费尔、普鲁韦尔、弗伊、古费拉克、巴奥雷尔、莱格尔或莱格尔、若利、格朗泰尔。

Having said that, I wonder if it can be true. When I think back to Les Misérables, what first comes to mind are the remarkable band of young revolutionaries gathered together in what they call the ABC Society. They all go down to needless deaths, since their barricade cannot withstand the cannons and overwhelming numbers of the troops sent against them. I list them in Victor Hugo’s own order: Enjolras, Combeferre, Jean Prouvaire, Feuilly, Courfeyrac, Bahorel, Lesgle or Laigle, Joly, Grantaire.

这位引人入胜的人物是安灼拉：

The fascinating figure is Enjolras:

我们首先提到安灼拉，原因稍后会解释。他是富裕家庭的独子，一个魅力四射却又令人胆寒的年轻人。他俊美绝伦，宛如天使，又像个桀骜不驯的安提诺乌斯。从他沉思的眼神中，人们或许会以为，在前世，他曾亲历过革命的动荡岁月。他对那场伟大事件的每一个细节都了如指掌，仿佛亲身经历过一般，一切都已融入他的血液。他兼具学者的严谨和尚武的性格，这在青少年中实属罕见。他既是思想家，又是行动者，短期内是民主的战士，同时又是超越当下运动的理想化身。他有一双深邃的眼睛，眼睑微微泛红，下唇厚实，常常带着一丝轻蔑的微笑，额头高耸——宽阔的额头如同地平线上广袤的天空。与本世纪初和上个世纪末一些早早成名的青年一样，他浑身散发着青春的活力，肌肤如少女般白皙，却又时常泛着苍白。长大成人后，他依然保持着少年的模样，二十二岁的年纪在他眼中仿佛只有十七岁。他性格冷峻，似乎对世间存在着名为“女人”的生物浑然不觉。他唯一的追求是正义，唯一的念头是克服一切障碍。在阿文提诺山上，他会是格拉古；在国民公会中，他会是圣茹斯特。他几乎不曾注意到玫瑰，对春天浑然不觉，对鸟儿的鸣唱也充耳不闻。仙女伊瓦德涅裸露的胸膛也无法打动他，就像哈尔莫狄乌斯一样，他除了用来藏剑之外，对鲜花毫无兴趣。他举止严谨，对一切与共和国无关的事物都保持着纯洁的眼光，是一位热爱自由的伟人。他的言辞尖锐而强烈，却又带着一丝抒情的韵味，时不时会迸发出令人意想不到的雄辩。任何试图让他误入歧途的恋情都会让他碰壁。如果一个来自康布雷广场或圣让德博韦街的年轻女子，看到他那稚嫩的脸庞、少年般的身形、蓝色眼眸上长长的睫毛、微风吹拂的头发、鲜嫩的嘴唇和洁白的牙齿，被他的美貌所倾倒，想要接近他，她将会面对他冰冷而轻蔑的目光，如同深渊的入口，让她明白不要把博马舍的凯鲁比尼和以西结书中的基路伯混淆。

We have named Enjolras first, and the reason for this will be seen later. He was the only son of wealthy parents, a charming young man who was capable of being a terror. He was angelically good-looking, an untamed Antinous. From the thoughtfulness of his gaze one might have supposed that in some previous existence he had lived through all the turmoil of the Revolution. He was familiar with every detail of that great event; he had it in his blood as though he had been there. His was a nature at once scholarly and warlike, and this is rare in an adolescent. He was both thinker and man of action, a soldier of democracy in the short term and at the same time a priest of the ideal rising above the contemporary movement. He had deep eyes, their lids slightly reddened, a thick lower lip which readily curled in disdain, and a high forehead—a large expanse of forehead in a face like a wide stretch of sky on the horizon. In common with certain young men of the beginning of this century and the end of the last who achieved distinction early in life, he had the glow of over-vibrant youth, with a skin like a girl’s but with moments of pallor. Grown to manhood, he still appeared a youth, his twenty-two years seeming no more than seventeen. He was austere, seeming not to be aware of the existence on earth of a creature called woman. His sole passion was for justice, his sole thought to overcome obstacles. On the Aventine hill he would have been Gracchus, in the Convention he would have been Saint-Just. He scarcely noticed a rose, was unconscious of the springtime and paid no heed to the singing of birds. The bared bosom of the nymph Evadne would have left him unmoved, and like Harmodius he had no use for flowers except to conceal a sword. He was austere in all his pleasures, chastely averting his eyes from everything that did not concern the republic, a marble lover of Liberty. His speech was harsh and intense, with a lyrical undertone, and given to unexpected flights of eloquence. It would have gone hard with any love-affair that sought to lead him astray. Had a grisette from the Place Cambrai or the Rue Saint-Jean-de-Beauvais, seeing that schoolboy face, the pageboy figure, the long, fair lashes over blue eyes, the hair ruffled in the breeze, the fresh lips and perfect teeth, been so taken with his beauty as to seek to thrust herself upon him, she would have encountered a cold, dismissive stare, like the opening of an abyss, which would have taught her not to confuse the Cherubini of Beaumarchais with the cherubim of Ezekiel.

安灼拉是1832年6月5日在巴黎起义的一小群革命者的领袖，他们希望领导一场推翻路易·菲利普国王资产阶级政权的全国起义。然而，他们的希望落空了。他们全部战死，而《悲惨世界》中最迷人的人物——街头顽童伽弗洛什也随之死去。安灼拉在处决了杀人如麻的警察间谍勒卡布克之后，发表了一番充满理想主义自我牺牲的无尽悲怆的预言：

Enjolras is the leader of the small group of revolutionaries who rise up in Paris on June 5, 1832, and who hope to lead a national insurrection against the bourgeois regime of King Louis-Philippe. Their hope is vain. All of them die, and with them dies the most charming person in Les Misérables, the street urchin Gavroche. Enjolras, after executing a murderous police spy, Le Cabuc, delivers a prophetic oracle marked by the infinite sadness of idealistic self-sacrifice:

“公民们，”安灼拉说道，“那人所作所为令人发指，而我所作所为也同样可怕。他杀人，所以我才杀人。我不得不这样做，因为这场叛乱必须受到约束。在这里，谋杀比在其他地方更加罪恶。我们身处革命的注视之下，是共和国的祭司，是这项事业的象征，我们的行为绝不能受到诽谤。因此，我审判了那人，判处他死刑。但与此同时，我被迫这样做，却又对此深恶痛绝，所以我对自己也进行了审判，你们很快就会知道我的判决是什么。”

听众中响起一阵颤栗。

“我们将与你同归于尽！”孔布费尔喊道。

“或许如此，”安灼拉说道，“我还有话要说。处死那个人，我屈服于必然。但这必然，乃是旧世界孕育的怪兽，它的名字叫作宿命。按照进步的法则，这宿命必将让位于博爱。此时此刻谈论‘爱’这个词并不合适；然而，我还是要说，并且为此感到自豪。爱就是未来。我曾诉诸死亡，但我憎恨它。公民们，未来将不再有黑暗，不再有闪电，不再有野蛮的无知，不再有血仇。既然不再有撒旦，也就不再有米迦勒。没有人会残杀同胞，大地将充满光辉，人类将被爱所感动。公民们，那时代终将到来，和平、光明与和谐的时代，充满欢乐与生命的时代。它必将到来。而我们死亡的目的，正是为了加速它的到来。”

‘Citizens,’ said Enjolras, ‘what that man did was abominable and what I have done is horrible. He killed, and that is why I killed. I was obliged to do it, for this rebellion must be disciplined. Murder is an even greater crime here than elsewhere. We are under the eyes of the revolution, priests of the republic, the tokens of a cause, and our actions must not be subject to calumny. Therefore I judged this man and condemned him to death. But at the same time, compelled to do what I did but also abhorring it, I have passed judgement on myself, and you will learn in due course what my sentence is.’

A quiver ran through his audience.

‘We will share your fate,’ cried Combeferre.

‘It may be,’ said Enjolras. ‘I have more to say. In executing that man I bowed to necessity. But the necessity was a monster conceived in the old world, and its name is fatality. By the law of progress, this fatality must give way to fraternity. This is a bad moment for speaking the word “love”; nevertheless I do speak it, and glory in it. Love is the future. I have had resort to death, but I hate it. In the future, citizens, there will be no darkness or lightnings, no savage ignorance or blood-feuds. Since there will be no Satan there will be no Michael. No man will kill his fellow, the earth will be radiant, mankind will be moved by love. That time will come, citizens, the time of peace, light, and harmony, of joy and life. It will come. And the purpose of our death is to hasten its coming.’

这种高亢的修辞手法，既符合当时的场合，也符合说话者的性格。维克多·雨果首先是一位诗人，《悲惨世界》是一部鸿篇巨制的散文诗。安灼拉站在街垒顶端高声呐喊：

This high rhetoric is justified by its occasion and by the character of its speaker. Victor Hugo above all was a poet, and Les Misérables is a vast prose poem. Enjolras cries out from the top of the barricade:

“是的，教育！光明！——光明——万物皆源于光明，万物亦归于光明！公民们，我们的十九世纪固然伟大，但二十世纪将会更加幸福。它将与古代历史截然不同。今日的一切恐惧都将被消除——战争与征服、武装国家的冲突、文明进程依赖于王室联姻、世袭暴政的诞生、国家被国会瓜分或王朝的覆灭、宗教如同公羊在无垠的荒野中互相攻讦。人们将不再惧怕饥荒或剥削、因贫困而沦为娼妓、因失业而陷入赤贫——也不再惧怕断头台、刀剑，或任何其他命运交织的厄运。事实上，几乎可以说，将不再有任何事件发生。人们将幸福安康。人类将如同地球一般遵循自身的法则，人类的灵魂与苍穹之间也将重归和谐。”灵魂将围绕真理运转，如同行星围绕太阳运转。朋友们，我此刻正身处黑暗时刻，向你们讲话；但这正是未来必须付出的沉重代价。革命是一道收费站。但人类终将获得解放、提升和慰藉。我们在此，在这道路障前，对此作出肯定。若非来自这献祭的祭坛，爱的呼喊又将从何而来？兄弟们，这里是反思者与苦难者的交汇之地。这道路障并非由瓦砾和铺路石构成；它由两种元素构成：思想与苦难。在此，苦难与理想交融。白昼拥抱黑夜，对她说：“我将与你同死，你将与我同生。”信仰诞生于绝望的拥抱之中。苦难带来死亡，但思想带来永生。那痛苦与永生将在一次死亡中交织融合。兄弟们，我们这些死在这里的人，将死在未来的光辉之中。我们将前往一座沐浴在黎明之光中的坟墓。

‘Yes, education! Light!—light—all things are born of light and all things return to it! Citizens, our nineteenth century is great, but the twentieth century will be happy. Nothing in it will resemble ancient history. Today’s fears will all have been abolished—war and conquest, the clash of armed nations, the course of civilization dependent on royal marriages, the birth of hereditary tyrannies, nations partitioned by a congress or the collapse of a dynasty, religions beating their heads together like rams in the wilderness of the infinite. Men will no longer fear famine or exploitation, prostitution from want, destitution born of unemployment—or the scaffold, or the sword, or any other malic of chance in the tangle of events. One might almost say, indeed, that there will be no more events. Men will be happy. Mankind will fulfill its own laws as does the terrestrial globe, and harmony will be restored between the human souls and the heavens. The souls will circle about the Truth as the planets circle round the sun. I am speaking to you, friends, in a dark hour; but this is the hard price that must be paid for the future. A revolution is a toll-gate. But mankind will be liberated, uplifted and consoled. We here affirm it, on this barricade. Whence should the cry of love proceed, if not from the sacrificial altar? Brothers, this is the meeting place of those who reflect and those who suffer. This barricade is not a matter of rubble and paving-stone; it is built of two components, of ideas and of suffering. Here wretchedness and idealism come together. Day embraces night and says to her, “I shall die with you and you will be reborn with me.” It is of the embraces of despair that faith is born. Suffering brings death, but the idea brings immortality. That agony and immortality will be mingled and merged in one death. Brothers, we who die here will die in the radiance of the future. We go to a tomb flooded with the light of dawn.’

2018年3月7日，这则预言令人悲伤。自诩为神的维克多·雨果借由安灼拉之口诉说，而安灼拉深知自己不过是个即将死去的人。然而，安灼拉的狂喜却深深打动了我们。我们能否在未来的光辉中死去？我认识一些男男女女，他们在生命的尽头都这样认为。几年后，当我的生命走到尽头时，我无疑会想起我爱过的人，但这念头却丝毫不会让我感受到永生。如果没有安灼拉，《悲惨世界》或许无法打动我。冉阿让与其说是人，不如说是神话。沙威则是一个只知法律而走向自杀的人。维克多·雨果将自己投射到马吕斯身上，从而让这部杰作蒙上了感伤的阴影。我不确定这是否重要。《悲惨世界》与其说是一本书，不如说是一场席卷一切的巨浪。伟大的诗人波德莱尔无法摆脱维克多·雨果的影响，他曾戏言，大海和雨果真是天生一对。与海浪搏斗不过是徒劳的消遣。

On March 7, 2018, this prophecy is a sorrow. Victor Hugo, who thought he was a god, speaks through Enjolras, who knows he is only a man about to die. Yet Enjolras in his rapture moves us. Is it possible to die in the radiance of the future? I have known men and women who at the end thought so. When my time comes, in only a few years, doubtless I will think about those I have loved, yet the idea will bring no intimation of immortality. Without Enjolras, Les Misérables might not hold me. Jean Valjean is more myth than man. Javert is a man who goes to suicide by knowing only the law. Victor Hugo projected himself as Marius and thus marred his masterwork by sentimentality. I am not sure this matters. Les Misérables is more a tidal wave than a book. Baudelaire, a great poet unable to evade Victor Hugo’s influence, joked that the Ocean and Hugo deserved one another. Fighting the waves is an idle pastime.

然而，然而，《悲惨世界》将永垂不朽。为什么？是因为孤儿伽弗洛什在枪林弹雨中依然歌唱吗？是因为冉阿让逐渐成长为不情愿的普罗米修斯吗？一定是维克多·雨果，他本身就是一首诗。这就是他漫长的观察与期盼的终结：

And yet, and yet, Les Misérables will live forever. Why? Is it the urchin Gavroche singing even as the bullets strike him? Is it Jean Valjean growing into a reluctant Prometheus? It has to be Victor Hugo, who was his own poem. This is how he concludes his cavalcade of watching and hoping:

然而，研究社会健康状况的人，有时难免会摇头叹息。即使是意志最坚定、思维最清晰的人，也难免会有疑虑之时。未来究竟何时才会到来？当我们想到前方笼罩的阴影，想到利己主义者与被社会遗弃者之间那令人不安的对峙时，这个问题似乎就显得合情合理了。利己主义者一方，充斥着偏见——这种源于优渥教育的阴暗面——贪婪与沉溺交织，富裕带来的迷茫麻痹了我们的感知，对苦难的恐惧甚至让我们憎恨所有受苦之人，以及根深蒂固的自满，还有膨胀到窒息灵魂的自我；而被社会遗弃者一方，充斥着贪婪与嫉妒，对他人幸福的怨恨，人类在追求个人满足感时所经历的内心挣扎，被迷雾、痛苦、需求和宿命论所充斥的心灵，以及单纯的、不纯粹的无知。

我们是否应该继续仰望星空？我们如今在天空中看到的光芒，是否也即将消逝？理想令人望而生畏，它迷失在深渊之中，渺小、孤立、如同针尖般闪耀，却又被四面八方的黑暗势力所威胁；然而，它所处的危险，并不比云层深处的一颗星辰更大。

Nevertheless, those who study the health of society must now and then shake their heads. Even the strongest-minded and most clear-thinking must have their moments of misgiving. Will the future ever arrive? The question seems almost justified when one considers the shadows looming ahead, the somber confrontation of egoists and outcasts. On the side of the egoists, prejudice—that darkness of a rich education—appetite that grows with intoxication, the bemusement of prosperity which blunts the sense, the fear of suffering which in some cases goes so far as to hate all sufferers, and unshakeable complacency, the ego so inflated that it stifles the soul; and on the side of the outcasts, greed and envy, resentment at the happiness of others, the turmoil of the human animal in search of personal fulfilment, hearts filled with fog, misery, needs, and fatalism, and simple, impure ignorance.

Should we continue to look upwards? Is the light we can see in the sky one of those which will presently be extinguished? The ideal is terrifying to behold, lost as it is in the depths, small, isolated, a pin-point, brilliant but threatened on all sides by the dark forces that surround it: nevertheless, no more in danger than a star in the jaws of the clouds.

第十九章

CHAPTER 19

一位运动爱好者的笔记（1852 年）

A Sportsman’s Notebook (1852)

伊万·图尔根涅夫

IVAN TURGENEV

欧内斯特·勒南是著名作家，他创作了荒诞的《耶稣传》（1863年），该书宣称耶稣并非犹太人，而是雅利安人。有时我觉得勒南似乎只读过《约翰福音》。尽管如此，勒南口才极佳，并于1883年在巴黎的屠格涅夫葬礼上发表了讲话。亨利·詹姆斯后来引用并赞同了勒南的讲话：

ERNEST RENAN was the celebrated author of the absurd Life of Jesus (1863), a work that asserted Yeshua was not a Jew but an Aryan. Sometimes I have the impression that Renan read only the Gospel of John. Nevertheless, Renan was eloquent and spoke at Turgenev’s funeral in Paris in 1883. Henry James later quoted and approved Renan’s remarks:

“图尔根涅夫，”M·雷南说道，“蒙受了那神秘的天命，那天命决定着人类的使命，赋予了他超越一切的崇高天赋：他生来就具有超凡脱俗的特质。”这段话如此精辟，以至于必须全文引用。“他的良知并非源于自然对他或多或少的眷顾，而是某种意义上的民族良知。在他出生之前，他已活了数千年；无数的遐想在他内心深处积聚。没有人能像他那样，成为整个民族的化身：沉睡了数个世纪、无言无语的先祖，通过他重获新生，得以表达。”

（詹姆斯，《伊万·屠格涅夫》）

“Turgenev,” said M. Renan, “received by the mysterious decree which marks out human vocations the gift which is noble beyond all others: he was born essentially impersonal.” The passage is so eloquent that one must repeat the whole of it. “His conscience was not that of an individual to whom nature had been more or less generous: it was in some sort the conscience of a people. Before he was born he had lived for thousands of years; infinite successions of reveries had amassed themselves in the depths of his heart. No man has been as much as he the incarnation of a whole race: generations of ancestors, lost in the sleep of centuries, speechless, came through him to life and utterance.”

(James, “Ivan Turgenev”)

已故的兰德尔·贾雷尔，我只见过他几次，但一直很敬佩他。他于1958年出版了《锚出版社故事集》 ，我第一次读到屠格涅夫的《猎人笔记》。六十年后，我依然记得当时读屠格涅夫故事时的愉悦。它们的确“本质上是客观的”。《别任草甸》一直萦绕在我的脑海中，尤其是它的结尾：

The late Randall Jarrell, whom I met only a few times but admired, published The Anchor Book of Stories in 1958, where I first encountered Turgenev’s A Sportsman’s Notebook. After sixty years I remember my pleasure in Turgenev’s stories. They were indeed “essentially impersonal.” “Bezhin Meadow” stayed in my mind, particularly its conclusion:

“你还记得瓦西里吗？”科斯佳突然问道。

“什么事，瓦西里？”费佳问道。

“就是那个溺水的孩子，”科斯佳回答说，“就在这条河里。他真是个好孩子啊！哦，真是个好孩子！他的母亲费克莉斯塔多么爱他啊！费克莉斯塔似乎觉得，他注定要溺水而亡。瓦西里夏天常和我们一起来河里洗澡——她每次看到都会惊慌失措。其他母亲们一点也不在意，她们提着水桶走过，摇摇摆摆地走过去，但费克莉斯塔会放下水桶，开始呼唤他。“回来，回来，”她会说，“回来吧，我的宝贝！哦，回来吧，我的小雄鹰！”至于他是怎么溺水的，只有上帝知道。他当时正在河岸边玩耍，他的母亲也在那里耙干草，突然她听到水下好像有人在吹泡泡——她一看，只见瓦西里的帽子漂浮在水面上。从那以后，费克利斯塔的精神也变得不正常了。她来到他溺水的地方，躺在那里；孩子们，她就躺在那里，开始唱歌——你们还记得吗，瓦西里总是唱一首歌——她也唱着那首歌，哭个不停，向上帝痛苦地抱怨。

“帕维尔来了。”费佳说道。

帕维尔手里拿着满满一锅东西走到火边。

“好了，孩子们，”沉默片刻后他开口说道，“情况不太好。”

“什么？”科斯佳急忙问道。

“我听到了瓦西里的声音。”

所有人都打了个寒颤。

“你说什么？”科斯佳低声问道。

“上帝作证。我刚开始弯腰去够水，突然听到有人叫我的名字，是瓦西里的声音，好像是从水下传来的：‘帕维尔，帕维尔，过来！’我赶紧跑开了。不过，我还是拿到了水。”

“我的天哪！”男孩们一边说着，一边划着十字。

“那是水妖精在叫你，帕维尔，”费佳补充道，“我们刚才还在聊瓦西里呢。”

“哦，那是不祥之兆，”伊柳沙沉思着说道。

“算了，别管它了！”帕维尔斩钉截铁地说，然后又坐了下来。“你逃不掉你的命运。”男孩们安静了下来。显然，帕维尔的故事给他们留下了深刻的印象。他们开始在火堆前安顿下来，仿佛准备睡觉。

“那是什么？”科斯佳突然抬起头问道。

帕维尔认真地听着。

“那是白腰杓鹬飞过并发出哨声。”

他们要飞往哪里？

“致那个本应没有冬天的国家。”

“世上真有这样一个国家吗？”

“是的，有。”

'离这很远？'

“遥远的地方，越过温暖的海洋。”

科斯佳叹了口气，闭上了眼睛。

（译者：查尔斯和娜塔莎·赫本）

‘D’you remember Vasily?’ added Kostya suddenly.

‘What Vasily?’ asked Fedya.

‘The one who was drowned,’ answered Kostya. ‘In this very same river. What a fine chap he was! Oh, what a fine chap! His mother, Feklista, how she loved him! It was as if she felt, Feklista did, that his death would come by water. Vasily used to come with us in summer to bathe in the river—and she’d get all in a fluster. The other mothers didn’t care a bit, they’d walk past with their washpails, they’d waddle by, but Feklista would put her pail down and start calling him. “Come back, come back,” she’d say, “come back, light of my eyes! Oh, come back, my little eagle!” And how he came to drown, Lord alone knows. He was playing on the bank, and his mother was there too, raking hay, and suddenly she heard what sounded like someone blowing bubbles under water—she looked, and there was only Vasily’s cap floating in the water. Well, since then, Feklista, too, hasn’t been right in the head. She comes and lies at the place where he drowned; there she lies, boys, and starts to sing—d’you remember, Vasily always used to sing a song—well that’s the one she sings, too, and cries and cries, and complains bitterly to God.

‘Here comes Pavel’ said Fedya.

Pavel came up to the fire with a full pot in his hand.

‘Well, boys,’ he began after a silence, ‘there’s something bad.’

‘What?’ asked Kostya hurriedly.

‘I heard Vasily’s voice.’

Everyone shuddered.

‘What’s that you say?’ whispered Kostya.

‘So help me God. I’d just begun to bend down to the water, and suddenly I heard my name being called, in Vasily’s voice, like it was from under the water: “Pavel, Pavel, come here!” I went away. I got the water, though.’

‘Good Lord!’ said the boys, crossing themselves.

‘That was a water-goblin calling you, Pavel,’ added Fedya. ‘And we were just talking about Vasily.’

‘Oh, that’s an evil sign,’ said Ilyusha, with deliberation.

‘Well, never mind, forget about it!’ said Pavel resolutely, and sat down again. ‘You can’t escape your fate.’ The boys became quieter. It was clear that Pavel’s story had made a deep impression on them. They began to settle down in front of the fire, as if preparing for sleep.

‘What’s that?’ asked Kostya suddenly, lifting his head.

Pavel listened intently.

‘That’s curlews flying past and whistling.’

‘Where are they flying to?’

‘To the country where there’s supposed to be no winter.’

‘Is there really such a country?’

‘Yes, there is.’

‘Far away?’

‘Far, far away, beyond the warm seas.’

Kostya sighed and closed his eyes.
