(trans. Charles and Natasha Hepburn)

猎人兼叙述者屠格涅夫在此消失了。他和孩子们都睡着了。叙述者醒来的场景被描绘得极其细腻，几乎毫无情感流露：

Here Turgenev the hunter and narrator has vanished. He and the boys fall asleep. The narrator’s waking is rendered exquisitely, almost without affect:

一股清爽的气息涌上我的脸庞。我睁开双眼——天已破晓。黎明的曙光尚未完全显现，东方却已泛起淡淡的苍白。我隐约能辨认出周围的环境。浅灰色的天空渐渐明亮、寒冷而湛蓝；繁星闪烁微弱，有的甚至熄灭；大地湿润，树叶滴落着水珠；不知何处传来生机勃勃的声音和人声；黎明的微风已然弥漫开来，萦绕在大地之上。我的身体也随之涌起一丝淡淡的兴奋。我迅速起身，走到孩子们身边。他们都像死人一样围着即将熄灭的篝火沉睡；只有帕维尔半起身子，直直地盯着我。我向他点点头，沿着冒着热气的河水继续前行。我还没走两里，就见四周开阔的草地上，前方山峦渐绿，林木间，身后尘土飞扬的小路，闪闪发光的灌木丛，以及在薄雾笼罩下泛着淡淡蓝色的河水——先是猩红，然后是红色，最后是金色，如同青春的光芒奔涌而来……世界开始沙沙作响，苏醒过来，开始歌唱，低语，诉说。四周沉甸甸的露珠闪烁着，如同璀璨的钻石；教堂的钟声清澈明亮地迎面而来，仿佛也被清晨的凉意洗涤过一般；突然，我的朋友们——几个男孩——驱赶着一群刚睡醒的骏马，从我身边飞驰而过……

令人悲痛的是，帕维尔在年底前就去世了。他不是溺水身亡，而是从马上摔下来摔死了。真是可惜，他是个非常优秀的年轻人！

A flood of freshness coursed over my face. I opened my eyes—the day was breaking. There was still no flush of dawn, but a growing pallor in the East. I could vaguely make out my surroundings. The pale-grey sky was growing light, and cold, and blue; the stars twinkled feebly or went out; the earth had grown damp, the leaves dripped, from somewhere came sounds of life, and voices, and the damp breath of dawn was already abroad, hovering above the earth. My body answered it with a faint thrill of exhilaration. I rose quickly and went across to the boys. They were all sleeping like the dead around the dying fire; only Pavel half-raised himself and stared fixedly at me. I nodded to him and went my way along the steaming river. I had not gone two versts when, around me in the broad water-meadow and ahead on the deepening green of the hills, from wood to wood, and behind me over the long dusty track, over the flushed sparkling bushes, and along the river, which was of a timid blue below the thinning mist—flowed scarlet, then red, then golden torrents of youthful, blazing light…The world began to rustle, awoke, began to sing, to murmur, to speak. On all sides the heavy dewdrops flashed into blazing diamonds; to meet me, pure and clear, as if they too had been washed in the coolness of morning, came the sounds of a church bell, and suddenly, driven by my friends the boys, the herd of horses, fresh from sleep, galloped past me…

With sorrow I must add that Pavel died before the year was out. He was not drowned, but killed by a fall from a horse. A pity, he was a splendid lad!

鹬鸟飞向遥远的无冬之地，这便是为瓦西里和帕维尔——两位杰出的青年——举行的葬礼的序幕。仅此而已。

The flight of the curlews to a faraway land with no winter is prologue to obsequies performed for Vasily and Pavel, both of them splendid lads. And that is all.

男性往往需要被提醒，而不是被告知。

（塞缪尔·约翰逊，1750年3月22日，《漫步者》，第2期）

Men more frequently require to be reminded than informed.

(Samuel Johnson, March 22, 1750, The Rambler, Number 2)

那句著名的格言或许出自屠格涅夫之口。我怀着深深的同情阅读屠格涅夫的作品，但我却不知该如何评价他这个人。陀思妥耶夫斯基憎恨屠格涅夫，并在《群魔》中以卡尔马济诺夫的形象嘲讽他。由于陀思妥耶夫斯基是我所厌恶的几位主要作家之一，而《群魔》又荒诞不经，所以我更愿意对屠格涅夫其人抱有好感。正如他那部充满苦涩怀旧之情的中篇小说《初恋》所描绘的那样，他的家庭背景十分坎坷。他的父亲谢尔盖·尼古拉耶维奇·屠格涅夫，年仅四十一岁便英年早逝，曾是一名参加过对拿破仑战争的骑兵上校。他的母亲瓦尔瓦拉·彼得罗夫娜·图尔根涅娃于 1816 年嫁给了谢尔盖。瓦尔瓦拉比丈夫年长，丈夫娶她是为了她的财富，她对丈夫的风流韵事越来越感到愤恨，并对他们三个儿子变得严厉专横，其中一个儿子早逝。

That famous apothegm might have been Turgenev’s. I read Turgenev with deep sympathy, but I do not know what to make of Turgenev the person. Dostoevsky loathed Turgenev and ridiculed him as Karmazinov in Demons. Since Dostoevsky is one of those major writers whom I abominate, and Demons is hysterical, I would prefer to think better of Turgenev the man. As his bitterly nostalgic novella First Love traces, his parental background was difficult. His father, Sergei Nikolaevich Turgenev, who was to die at only forty-one, was a cavalry colonel who served in the war against Napoleon. His mother, Varvara Petrovna Turgeneva, married Sergei in 1816. Older than her husband, who had married her for her wealth, Varvara was increasingly embittered by his philandering, and became harsh and tyrannical toward their three sons, one of whom died early.

伊万·屠格涅夫终身未婚，除非你把他与法国著名女中音歌唱家宝琳·维亚尔朵之间那段漫长的恋情也算在内——这是一段三角关系，屠格涅夫与宝琳的丈夫路易·维亚尔朵（一位比她年长二十一岁的记者）共同拥有她。屠格涅夫和路易·维亚尔朵始终保持着朋友关系，而屠格涅夫与一位农奴女裁缝所生的私生女则被维亚尔朵家收养。

Ivan Turgenev never married, unless you can count his endless relationship with Pauline Viardot, a famous French mezzo-soprano—a ménage à trois in which he shared her with her husband Louis, a journalist twenty-one years older than Pauline. Turgenev and Louis Viardot always remained friends, and Turgenev’s illegitimate daughter, fathered upon a serf seamstress, was absorbed into the Viardot household.

屠格涅夫一生中似乎只有一件不光彩的事。1838年，这位19岁的作家前往柏林求学，途中乘坐的轮船起火，他不幸遇难。据他的译者兼传记作者伦纳德·夏皮罗所述：

There seems to have been only one discreditable incident in Turgenev’s life. In 1838, the nineteen-year-old writer, bound for Berlin to study, was on a steamer that caught fire and was incinerated. According to his translator and biographer Leonard Schapiro:

出海第三天，轮船在距离特拉沃明德约一英里处起火，并被彻底烧毁。绝大多数乘客毫发无损地逃生。屠格涅夫在火灾中的行为引起了广泛关注。据莫斯科和圣彼得堡流传的故事，他当时完全失去了理智，大声哀叹自己即将死去，试图挤进救生艇，粗暴地推开妇女儿童，最后，当着所有人的面，抓住一名水手的胳膊，以他母亲的名义提出给他一万卢布，让他救自己，并说自己是富裕寡妇的独子，无法忍受这么年轻就死去。

On the third day out the steamer, then about a mile away from Travemünde, caught fire, and was completely destroyed. The great majority of the passengers escaped without injury. Turgenev’s behaviour during the fire excited a great deal of talk. According to stories that circulated in Moscow and St Petersburg he had completely lost his head, loudly lamented his approaching end, tried to push his way into the lifeboat, brutally shoving aside women and children, and finally, in full sight of the entire company, seized a sailor by the arm and offered him ten thousand roubles in his mother’s name if he would save him, saying that he was the only son of a rich widow and could not bear to die so young.

俄罗斯历史学家伦纳德·夏皮罗是一位幽默风趣的人，他可能和我一样是马克思兄弟的粉丝，因为这段话里确实带有一丝格劳乔·马克思的风格。瓦尔瓦拉斥责她那不幸的儿子懦弱，并感叹这给她原本就十分单薄的社交生活带来了怎样的影响。

Leonard Schapiro, a jovial historian of Russia, may have been a fan of the Marx Brothers, as I am, since there is a flavor of Groucho in this paragraph. Varvara castigated her unfortunate son for cowardice, lamenting its effect upon her rather minimal social life.

屠格涅夫死得缓慢而痛苦，却也颇具英雄气概，他始终心系他人。他曾写信给托尔斯泰——两人关系一直很紧张——敦促这位俄罗斯文学巨匠重拾小说创作，而不是继续撰写道德说教。

Turgenev died a slow, painful, rather heroic death, thinking as always of others. He wrote a letter to Tolstoy, with whom he had a tempestuous relationship, urging the great writer of the Russian land to come back to composing fiction rather than moral tracts.

诚然，屠格涅夫的童年十分艰辛，父亲冷漠无情，母亲残暴虐待农奴，但他依然是人性之美和审美情趣的奇迹，只是其创作范围略显局限。他的素描、故事、片段和中篇小说比他那些更具野心的长篇小说更胜一筹。或许，除非你是古斯塔夫·福楼拜，否则客观冷静的视角难以支撑长篇小说的创作。

Granted that his childhood had been difficult, with an uncaring father and a sadistic mother who flogged her serfs, Turgenev is a miracle of human goodness and of aesthetic sensibility, somewhat limited in its range. His sketches, stories, fragments, novellas are stronger than his more ambitious novels. Perhaps an impersonal stance cannot sustain a long fiction, unless you are Gustave Flaubert.

我重读《猎人笔记》，想起来自费尔斯普林斯的矮人卡西扬那令人难忘的形象。卡西扬谴责一切杀戮：鸟兽皆不杀，人亦不杀。在他与猎人的交谈中，威廉·布莱克所说的“神圣的人形”显灵了：

I return to A Sportsman’s Notebook and the lovely vision of the dwarf Kasyan from Fair Springs. Kasyan condemns all letting of blood: bird, beast, human. In the midst of his exchange with the sportsman, there is a visitation of what William Blake called “the human form divine”:

他突然一动不动，沉默不语，目光死死地盯着林间的灌木丛。我转过身，看到一个大约八岁的小农家女孩，穿着蓝色连衣裙，头上裹着一块格子手帕，裸露的、晒得通红的胳膊上挎着一个柳条篮。她大概没想到会遇到我们；她绊倒在我们身上，一动不动地站在一片绿松石丛生的阴凉草地上，用她那双黑亮的眼睛怯生生地看着我。我还没来得及看清她的脸，她就嗖地一下窜到一棵树后去了。

“安努什卡，过来，别害怕，”老人温柔地喊道。

“我害怕，”她细小的声音传来。

“别害怕，别害怕，到我这里来。”

安努什卡缓缓离开了藏身之处，悄无声息地绕了过来，小脚丫踩在茂密的草丛里几乎没有发出任何沙沙声，然后从老人身旁的灌木丛中走了出来。起初，我以为她只有八岁，但根据她的身材判断，我以为她只有八岁，而实际上她有十三四岁。她身材娇小纤细，却又匀称优雅，她那张漂亮的小脸蛋和卡相惊人地相似，尽管卡相本人并不算俊美。她有着同样的棱角分明的五官，同样的奇特神情——既狡黠又信任人，既沉思又洞察人心，连动作都一模一样……卡相上下打量着她；她就站在他身边。

“你们有蘑菇吗？”他问道。

“是的，一些蘑菇，”她怯生生地笑着回答。

“你找到很多吗？”

“是的，很多。”她迅速看了我一眼，又笑了笑。

“也有一些白色的吗？”

“是的，白色的也有。”

“给我示范一下……”

她从胳膊上放下篮子，半掀开盖在蘑菇上的一片宽大的牛蒡叶。

“哦，”卡西扬弯腰看着篮子说，“多么漂亮的篮子啊！干得好，安努什卡！”

“她是你的女儿吗，卡西扬？”我问道。安努什卡的脸上泛起了一丝红晕。

“她算是我的亲戚吧，”卡西扬漫不经心地说道。

“好了，安努什卡，你走吧，”他立刻补充道，“你走吧，祝你好运。小心点……”

“可是她为什么要走呢？”我打断他，“我们可以送她一程……”

安努什卡脸红得像罂粟花一样，双手紧紧抓住篮子的提手，焦急地看着老人。

“不，她肯定能到那儿，”他用同样冷漠随意的语气重复道，“我们为什么要去？……她肯定能到那儿……你走吧。”

安努什卡轻盈地走进了森林。卡西扬望着她的背影，然后垂下目光，露出了微笑。在这悠长的微笑中，在他与安努什卡说的寥寥数语中，在他提起她时的语气中，都蕴含着远超语言所能表达的炽热爱意和温柔。他再次望向她消失的方向，又笑了笑，擦了擦脸，点了点头。

“你为什么那么快就把她打发走了？”我问他，“我还想买些她种的蘑菇呢……”

“这跟你没关系，你想什么时候在家买都可以，”他回答我，这是他第一次使用敬语“你”。

“嗯，你这儿有个挺漂亮的。”

“不……嗯……就是这样……”他回答道，语气似乎有些不情愿，从此又恢复了之前的沉默。见我再也无法与他搭话，便去了林间空地。这时天气稍稍凉了些，但我依然一无所获，除了新买的车轴，我只带回了一只秧鸡。我们开车来到他家院子前，卡相突然转向我，开口道：“主人，我说，主人，”他说道，“我为我之前对您做的事感到抱歉；您看，是我把所有的鸟都赶走了。”

'你是什么意思？'

“这是我的绝招。你这条狗很聪明，也很乖，但即便如此，它也无能为力……仔细想想，人算什么？它也只是一条动物，他们把它变成了什么？”

Suddenly he started and fell silent, looking fixedly into the undergrowth of the forest. I turned and saw a little peasant-girl of about eight, in a blue dress, with a check handkerchief over her head and a wicker basket over her bare sunburnt arm. She had probably never expected to meet us; she had stumbled on top of us and stood motionless in a green hazel-thicket on a shady patch of grass, looking timorously at me with her black eyes. I had hardly caught sight of her when she darted behind a tree.

‘Annushka, come here, don’t be afraid,’ called the old man tenderly.

‘I am afraid,’ came her thin little voice.

‘Don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid, come to me.’

Annushka slowly abandoned her hiding-place, walked quietly round, her little feet hardly rustling in the thick grass, and came out of the bushes beside the old man. This was no girl of eight, as I had thought at first, judging by her small size, but one of thirteen or fourteen. Her whole body was small and thin, but trim and graceful, and her pretty little face was strikingly like Kasyan’s own, although Kasyan himself was no beauty. She had the same sharp features, the same strange expression, at once cunning and trustful, reflective and penetrating, and the same movements…Kasyan looked her over; she was standing beside him.

‘Well, have you got some mushrooms?’ he asked.

‘Yes, some mushrooms,’ she answered, with a timid smile.

‘Have you found plenty of them?’

‘Yes, plenty.’ She looked quickly at me and smiled again.

‘Some white ones, too?’

‘Yes, white ones, too.’

‘Show me, do…’

She lowered the basket from her arm and half-lifted a broad burdock leaf which covered the mushrooms.

‘Oh,’ said Kasyan, stooping over the basket, ‘what fine ones! Well done, Annushka!’

‘Is she your daughter, Kasyan, eh?’ I asked. Annushka’s face showed a slight blush.

‘She’s a sort of relation,’ said Kasyan, with assumed carelessness.

‘Well, Annushka, off you go,’ he added at once; ‘off you go, and good luck to you. And be careful…’

‘But why should she walk?’ I interrupted him. ‘We could give her a lift…’

Annushka flushed the colour of a poppy, clutched with both hands at the string handle of her basket and looked anxiously at the old man.

‘No, she’ll get there all right,’ he rejoined in the same indifferent, casual voice. ‘Why should we?…She’ll get there all right…Be off with you.’

Annushka went nimbly off into the forest. Kasyan looked after her, then lowered his gaze and smiled. In this long smile, in the few words which he had said to Annushka, in the very tone of his voice when he spoke of her, there was more passionate love and tenderness than language can express. He looked again in the direction in which she had vanished, smiled again, wiped his face, and nodded his head several times.

‘Why did you send her off so quickly?’ I asked him. ‘I should like to have bought some of her mushrooms…’

‘Why, it does not matter to you, you can buy them at home whenever you like,’ he answered me, using the formal ‘you’ for the first time.

‘Well, you’ve got a pretty one there.’

‘No…well…there it is…’ he answered, as if reluctantly, and from that moment he relapsed into his earlier mood of silence. Seeing that all my efforts to engage him again in conversation were proving vain, I went off to the clearing. Meanwhile it had grown slightly less hot; but my ill-success continued, and I returned to the hamlet with only one corncrake besides my new axle. As we were driving up to his yard, Kasyan suddenly turned to me: ‘Master, I say, Master,’ he began. ‘I’m sorry for what I did to you; you see, it was I who called all the birds away from you.’

‘What do you mean?’

‘It’s my trick. That’s a clever dog you have, and a good one, but all the same there was nothing he could do…When you come to think of it, what are men? Here’s an animal, too, and what have they made of him?’

安努什卡显然是卡相的女儿，她身上散发的魅力冲淡了卡相身上那股神秘莫测的气息。屠格涅夫令人耳目一新地拒绝一切超验的论证，他只相信人性本善的可能性。对于一位十九世纪的俄罗斯作家来说，这种鲜明的无神论必然会引起一些争议，但屠格涅夫却巧妙地将东西方的感性、思想和情感模式融会贯通。亨利·詹姆斯、古斯塔夫·福楼拜、伊迪丝·华顿、欧内斯特·海明威和薇拉·凯瑟都对他推崇备至：他们发现他是一位与他们精神契合的俄罗斯小说家。凯瑟在她那部精妙绝伦的小说《迷失的女人》（1923）中重述了《初恋》，但如今在我看来，它更像是屠格涅夫的低调演绎。

Annushka clearly is Kasyan’s daughter, and the charm of her being offsets the tint of the uncanny in Kasyan. Turgenev refreshingly refused all transcendent argumentations and believed only in the possibility of human goodness. For a nineteenth-century Russian writer, that clear atheism had to cause some scandal, but Turgenev somehow reconciled in himself Western and Eastern modes of sensibility, thought, feeling. He was admired by Henry James, Gustave Flaubert, Edith Wharton, Ernest Hemingway, and Willa Cather: they found in him a Russian crafter of fictions who shared their spirit. Cather rewrote First Love in her exquisite A Lost Lady (1923), but it now reads to me as Turgenev in a minor key.

《运动家的笔记》中最令人难忘的小品是《活着的遗物》，可怜的卢克里亚已经慢慢死去很久了，或者说——如果你能这么称呼的话——活得太久了：

The most memorable sketch in A Sportsman’s Notebook is “The Live Relic,” in which poor Lukerya has been dying slowly for a long time, or living—if you can call it that—for too long:

“哦，我不能！”她突然说道，“我没有力气……见到你我太高兴了。”

她闭上了眼睛。

我把手放在她纤细冰凉的手指上……她抬起头看着我——她那浓密的眼睑，像古老雕像的眼睑一样，镶着金色的睫毛，再次闭上了。片刻之后，它们在暮色中闪闪发光……一滴泪水浸湿了它们。

我像之前一样，一动不动地坐在那里。

“看看我！”卢克莉娅突然用一种出乎意料的语气说道，她睁大眼睛，试图擦掉眼泪。“我难道不应该感到羞愧吗？我这是怎么了？我已经很久没有这样了……自从去年春天瓦西里·波利亚科夫来过之后就再也没有过。只要他坐在那里和我说话——我并不介意——但是当他走开之后——我就忍不住独自哭了起来！这一切到底是从哪里来的？……但是眼泪对我们这样的女孩来说又不是什么大事。师傅，”卢克莉娅接着说，“我想您应该有手帕吧……别客气，帮我擦擦眼泪。”

‘O, I can’t!’ she said suddenly. ‘I haven’t the strength…I’ve been so pleased to see you.’

She closed her eyes.

I put my hand on her tiny, cold fingers…She looked up at me—and her dark eyelids, trimmed with golden lashes, like those of an ancient statue, closed again. After a moment, they glittered in the twilight…A tear had moistened them.

I sat there motionless as before.

‘Just look at me!’ said Lukerya suddenly, with unexpected force, and, opening her eyes wide, tried to wipe the tears from them. ‘Oughtn’t I to be ashamed? What do I want? This hasn’t happened to me for a long time…not since the day when Vasily Polyakov was here last spring. As long as he was sitting talking to me—I didn’t mind—but when he went away—I fairly cried away to myself! Where did it all come from?…But tears cost nothing to girls like us. Master,’ added Lukerya, ‘I expect you’ve got a handkerchief…Don’t be put off, wipe my eyes.’

我几乎不知道该如何应对这种难以承受的悲痛。然而，这仅仅是更剧烈痛苦的序幕：

I hardly know how one reacts to that unbearable poignance. Yet it is only prelude to what hurts far more:

“我什么都不需要，我非常满足，感谢上帝！”她费力地、却又饱含深情地说道，“愿上帝保佑大家健康！主人，请您跟您的母亲说说——这里的农民都很穷——如果她能稍微降低一下他们的租金就好了！他们的土地不够，根本赚不到钱！……他们会为您向上帝祈祷的……但我什么都不需要，我非常满足。”

我答应了卢克莉娅的要求，正要出门时，她又叫住了我。

“主人，您还记得吗？”她说道，眼睛和嘴唇都亮了起来，“我以前的头发有多长？您还记得吗——一直到膝盖！我犹豫了很久……那头发真是太漂亮了！……可是我这副样子，怎么梳啊！所以我把它剪掉了……是的……好了，主人，再见！我不能再说别的了……”

当天出发拍摄前，我和当地的警员聊起了卢克里亚。我从他那里得知，在山谷里，她被称为“活的圣物”，而且她从不惹事生非；她从不抱怨，也从不发牢骚。“她什么都不求，相反，她对一切都心存感激；她安静得不能再安静了，我必须这么说。毫无疑问，她是因为自己的罪孽而受到了上帝的惩罚；但我们不去深究。至于谴责她，比如，不，我们当然不会谴责她。让她安息吧！”

几周后，我听说卢克莉娅去世了。死神最终还是降临在了她身上……而且是在“圣彼得教堂之后”。据说，在她去世的那天，她一直听到钟声，尽管从阿列克谢耶夫卡到教堂有五俄里多的距离，而且那天还是工作日。此外，卢克莉娅说，钟声不是从教堂里传来的，而是“从上面”传来的。或许她不敢说——是从天堂传来的。

‘I need nothing; I’m absolutely content, praise be to God,’ she pronounced, with extreme effort, but also with emotion ‘May God grant health to everyone! And you, master, please speak to your mother—the peasants here are poor—if she would only bring down their rent, just a little! They haven’t enough land, they make nothing out of it!…They would pray to God for you…but I need nothing, I’m absolutely content.’

I gave Lukerya my word to carry out her request, and was already making for the door when she called me back.

‘D’you remember, master,’ she said, with a wonderful brightening of her eyes and lips, ‘what hair I had? D’you remember—right down to my knees! For a long time I couldn’t make up my mind…Such hair it was!…But how could I comb it! In my condition! So I cut it off…yes…Well, good-bye, master! I can’t say more…’

The same day, before setting out to shoot, I had a talk about Lukerya with the local constable. I learnt from him that in the valley she was called ‘the Live Relic’, also that she caused no trouble; there was not a grumble to be heard from her, not a complaint. ‘She asks nothing for herself, on the contrary she’s grateful for everything; she’s as quiet as quiet can be, that I must say. She’s been smitten by God,’ so the constable concluded, ‘for her sins, no doubt; but we don’t go into that. As for condemning her, for example, no, we certainly don’t condemn her. Let her be!’

A few weeks later I heard that Lukerya was dead. Death had come for her after all…and ‘after St. Peter’s’. The story went that on the day of her death she kept hearing the sound of bells, although it is more than five versts from Alexeyevka to the church, and it was on a weekday. Besides, Lukerya said that the sound came, not from church, but ‘from above’. Probably she did not venture to say—from heaven.

屠格涅夫不相信奇迹，但这又是什么呢：疯狂和匮乏的钟声，还是庆祝卢克里亚这位悲伤的圣人获得一个并不存在的“上天”的禧年？

Turgenev could not believe in miracles, yet what else is this: the bells of madness and of deprivation, or of a jubilee celebrating Lukerya as a sad saint meriting an “above” that is not there.

第二十章

CHAPTER 20

初恋（1860）

First Love (1860)

伊万·图尔根涅夫

IVAN TURGENEV

可以说，中篇小说《初恋》是屠格涅夫最具自传色彩的作品，除非是那部充满奇思妙想的《春洪》（1872）。在《初恋》中，叙述者弗拉基米尔重温了他十六岁时的初恋之痛。当时二十一岁的齐娜伊达公主是一位任性而又爱嘲弄人的美人，她擅长戏弄那些求爱失败的追求者。弗拉基米尔的父亲彼得是一位技艺精湛的骑手，也是一位风流成性的花花公子，他比他那歇斯底里、野蛮的妻子年轻，娶她只是为了她的钱。彼得为人冷漠矜持，很少对儿子流露感情。随着故事的展开，我们逐渐了解到彼得和齐娜伊达之间存在着一段隐秘而又充满虐待意味的恋情，而齐娜伊达，一个道德上的受虐狂，爱上了彼得。

IT IS REASONABLE TO SAY that the novella First Love is Turgenev’s most autobiographical work, unless that be the charmingly crazy Spring Torrents (1872). In First Love, the narrator, Vladimir, returns to his experience of an initial sorrow when he was sixteen. The princess Zinaida, then twenty-one, is a capricious and mocking beauty who is ingenious at tormenting her phalanx of frustrated suitors. Vladimir’s father, Pyotr, a skilled horseman and philanderer, is younger than his hysterical and savage wife, whom he married for her money. Pyotr is cold and reserved in manner, and only rarely shows affection for his son. It is revealed to us slowly that Pyotr and Zinaida are immersed in a covert and sadistic erotic affair, and that Zinaida, a kind of moral masochist, is in love with Pyotr.

弗拉基米尔的叙述是屠格涅夫的最佳作品：表面上冷漠疏离，情感内敛，但总是暗示着爱情和生命本身是脆弱的，濒临消失：

Vladimir’s narrative is Turgenev at his best: apparently impersonal, withdrawn in affect, yet always intimating that love and life itself are tenuous and on the verge of vanishing:

齐娜伊达一眼就看出我爱上了她，不过我本来也没打算掩饰。我的热情让她觉得很有趣。她取笑我，戏弄我，折磨我。能成为别人最大的快乐和最深沉的痛苦的唯一来源，那种感觉真是妙不可言，而且这种来源还很随意，完全不负责任。在齐娜伊达手中，我就像一块柔软的蜡；当然，爱上她的人并非只有我一个。所有来她家的男人都无可救药地迷恋上了她，她把他们都玩弄于股掌之间。她觉得在他们心中激起交替的希望和恐惧很有趣，可以随心所欲地摆布他们。她把这叫做“把人推来推去”；他们甚至没有想过反抗，而是心甘情愿地臣服于她。她整个人，充满活力，美丽动人，身上有一种奇特的魅力，狡黠与漫不经心、矫揉造作与朴实无华、温柔与欢快交织在一起。她的一言一行，她的每一个动作，都笼罩着一种微妙而精致的魅力。一切都展现着她体内那独特而奇特的生命力。她的脸庞也总是变幻莫测，仿佛永远处于一种状态。几乎在同一瞬间，它既显得嘲讽，又显得沉思，还带着一丝热情。无数轻盈而迅疾的情感，如同夏日微风中变幻的云影，在她眼中和唇间交替出现。每一个爱慕者对她来说都不可或缺。别洛夫佐罗夫，她有时称他为“我的野兽”，有时则简单地称他为“我的”，他甚至愿意为她赴汤蹈火。他对自己才智和其他方面都缺乏自信，却不断地向她求婚，暗示其他人只是说说而已。迈达诺夫对她灵魂深处的诗意情怀有所感触；他天性有些冷漠，就像几乎所有作家一样，但他热情地向她保证，或许也是在向自己保证，他爱慕她。他为她谱写了无数赞美诗，并以既矫揉造作又真挚热情地吟诵。她同情他，却又暗暗嘲讽他。她并不真正信任他，听他滔滔不绝地倾诉了一段时间后，便让他读普希金，正如她常说的，是为了“解惑”。

Zinaida guessed at once that I had fallen in love with her, but then I wouldn’t have thought of concealing it. My passion amused her. She made fun of me, played with me, and tormented me. It is sweet to be the sole source, the arbitrary and irresponsible source of the greatest joys and profoundest miseries to someone else. I was like soft wax in the hands of Zinaida; not that I alone had fallen in love with her. All the men who visited the house were hopelessly infatuated, and she kept them all on leading-strings at her feet. She found it amusing to excite alternate hopes and fears in them; to twist them according to her whim. She called this ‘knocking people against each other’; they did not even think of resistance, but gladly submitted to her. In her whole being, vital and beautiful, there was a peculiarly fascinating mixture of cunning and insouciance, artifice and simplicity, gentleness and gaiety. Over everything she did and said, over every movement there hovered a subtle, exquisite enchantment. Everything expressed the unique, peculiar force of the life which played within her. Her face, too, was constantly changing. It, too, was always in play. It seemed at almost the same instant mocking, pensive and passionate. An infinite variety of feelings, light and swift, succeeded each other like shadows of clouds on a windy summer day, in her eyes and on her lips. Every one of her admirers was necessary to her. Byelovzorov, whom she sometimes called ‘my wild beast’, or sometimes simply ‘mine’, would gladly have leapt into the fire for her. With no confidence in his own brains or other qualities, he was constantly proposing marriage to her, implying that the others only talked. Maidanov was responsive to the poetic strain in her soul; somewhat cold by nature, like nearly all writers, he assured her fervently, and perhaps himself too, that he adored her. He composed endless verses in her honour, and recited them with an ardour at once affected and sincere. She sympathized with him and, at the same time, faintly mocked him. She did not really trust him, and after listening to his effusions for a while, used to make him read Pushkin, in order, as she used to say, to clear the air.

字里行间，你能感受到屠格涅夫式的对迷人齐娜伊达的某种保留。难道只有调情的乐趣才需要“把人推来推去”吗？齐娜伊达不信任任何人，包括她自己。

Between the lines you can read a certain Turgenevian reserve in regard to the delightful Zinaida. Is it only the joy of flirtation that requires “knocking people against each other”? Zinaida trusts no one, herself included.

“是啊！”她看着我，像之前那样说道，“就是这样。还是那双眼睛——”她补充道；然后陷入沉思，双手捂住了脸。“一切都变得如此糟糕，”她低声说道，“我为什么不去世界的另一端呢！我受不了了，我无法改变这一切……而我面前又是什么呢？……天哪，我真是太痛苦了！”

“为什么？”我怯生生地问。

齐娜伊达没有回答，只是耸了耸肩。我继续跪着，无比悲痛地看着她。她说的每一句话都像刀子一样刺痛着我的心。那一刻，我想，如果能以悲伤告终，我宁愿放弃生命。我看着她，仍然不明白她为何如此悲伤，脑海中浮现出一幅清晰的画面：她突然间，在无法控制的悲痛中，走进花园，像被割草机割倒在地。我们周围的一切都明亮而翠绿。风吹拂着树叶，不时地将覆盆子枝条吹弯，掠过齐娜伊达的头顶。远处，鸽子咕咕叫着，蜜蜂嗡嗡地飞舞，在稀疏的草地上低低地穿梭。头顶上，天空湛蓝而温柔，但我却感到无比悲伤。

“给我读首诗吧，”齐娜伊达低声说道，并用一只胳膊肘撑起身子。“我喜欢你读诗。你读起来像唱歌一样，但我并不介意，这就是年轻人的风格。给我读《在乔治亚的山丘上》，不过先坐下。”

我坐下来，背诵了《在乔治亚的山丘上》。

“‘它情不自禁地爱上它’，”齐娜伊达跟着我重复道。“这就是诗歌的力量。它向我们诉说着不存在的事物，这不仅比存在的事物更好，而且更接近真理。‘它情不自禁地爱上它’——它本不想爱，却又无法自拔！”她再次沉默下来，突然起身。“我们走吧。迈达诺夫和妈妈在一起。他把诗带给我了，但我离开了。他现在也很伤心，可是又能怎么办呢？总有一天你会明白的……只是别太生我的气。”

她急忙握住我的手，迅速向前走去。我们回到了旅馆。

‘Yes!’ she said, looking at me as before, ‘it is so. The same eyes—’ she added; then became thoughtful and covered her face with her hands. ‘Everything has become horrible to me,’ she whispered, ‘why don’t I go to the other end of the world! I can’t bear it, I can’t make it come right…and what is there before me?…God, I am so wretched!’

‘Why?’ I asked timidly.

Zinaida did not reply, but only shrugged her shoulders. I went on kneeling and looking at her with infinite distress. Every one of her words pierced my heart like a knife. At that moment I would, I think, gladly have given up my life if only that could end in grief. I looked at her, and still not understanding why she was so unhappy, conjured a vivid image of how, suddenly, in a paroxysm of ungovernable grief, she had walked into the garden and fallen to the ground as though mown down. All round us it was bright and green. The wind murmured in the leaves of the trees, now and then bending the raspberry canes above Zinaida’s head. Somewhere doves were cooing and bees were buzzing, flying low from blade to blade over the sparse grass. Overhead, the sky was blue and tender, but I felt terribly sad.

‘Read me some poetry,’ said Zinaida in a low voice, and raised herself on one elbow. ‘I like your reading poetry. You speak it in a sing-song, but I do not mind it, that’s youth. Read me On Georgia’s Hills, only first sit down.’

I sat down, and recited On Georgia’s Hills.

‘ “Which it cannot help but love”,’ Zinaida repeated after me. ‘That is what poetry can do. It speaks to us of what does not exist, which is not only better than what exists, but even more like the truth. “Which it cannot help but love”—it would like not to, but cannot help itself!’ She was silent again and suddenly started and stood up. ‘Let’s go. Maidanov is with Mama. He has brought me his poem, but I left him. He is hurt too, now, but what can one do? One day you will discover…only don’t be too angry with me.’

She pressed my hand hastily and moved quickly forward. We went back to the lodge.

屠格涅夫是一位敏锐的心理学家。弗拉基米尔压抑了他新领悟的一个关键方面：他既知道又不知道，她的情人就是他的父亲。

Turgenev was a sharp psychologist. Vladimir represses a crucial aspect of his new realization: he both knows and does not know that her lover is his father.

我回到家，发现家里一片狼藉。母亲正试图和父亲“解决问题”。她责备他某件事，而他像往常一样，礼貌而冷淡地回应了几句，很快就离开了。我听不清母亲在说什么，也没心情听。我只记得，事情结束后，她叫我去书房，非常不赞同我频繁拜访那位老公主，用她的话说，那位老公主是个“无所不能的女人”。我鞠躬吻了吻她的手（我总是这样结束谈话），然后上楼回了自己的房间。

齐娜伊达的眼泪让我难以承受。我完全不知所措，自己也几乎要哭了。毕竟，尽管我已经十六岁了，但我内心深处仍然是个孩子。

I returned home to find a disagreeable state of affairs. My mother was trying to ‘have things out’ with my father. She was reproaching him for something, and he, as was his habit, answered with polite and frigid sentences, and soon went away. I could not hear what my mother was saying, nor was I in a mood to listen. I remember only that when the scene was over, she sent for me to the study, and spoke with great disapproval about my frequent visits to the old princess, who, in her words, was une femme capable de tout. I bowed to kiss her hand (I always did this when I wanted to end a conversation) and went up to my room.

Zinaida’s tears were altogether too much for me. I simply didn’t know what to think, and was on the point of tears myself. I was after all still a child, in spite of my sixteen years.

作为叙述者的屠格涅夫更喜欢浅滩而不是深渊，但在这里，他似乎在四十二岁时就明白，他存在的中心永远不会超过十六岁。

Turgenev as a narrator prefers the shallows to the depths, but here he seems to know, at the age of forty-two, that a center of his being will never be older than sixteen.

但我现在隐约觉得，我在齐娜伊达身上看到了某种东西，某种我无法接受的东西……我母亲曾称她为“女冒险家”。女冒险家——她，我的偶像，我的女神！这个词像火焰般灼烧着我，我试图躲进枕头里逃避。我怒火中烧，但同时，为了成为那个幸运儿，那个喷泉边的男人，我愿意付出一切，付出一切！

But there was something which I now fancied I dimly perceived in Zinaida, something to which I could not reconcile myself…An adventuress my mother had once called her. An adventuress—she, my idol, my goddess! The word seared me like a flame, I tried to escape from it into my pillow. I burned with indignation, yet at the same time what would I not have done, what would I not have given, to be that darling of fortune, the man by the fountain!

屠格涅夫在 1843 年对宝琳·维亚尔朵一见钟情，并于 1845 年追随她来到巴黎。在巴黎生活了 15 年后，他创作了《初恋》，并回忆起他的母亲称宝琳为吉普赛女郎和冒险家。

Turgenev had fallen in love at first sight with Pauline Viardot in 1843 and followed her to Paris in 1845. Fifteen years after his Parisian bondage commenced, he composes First Love and recalls his mother terming Pauline a Gypsy and an adventuress.

我不敢质问他们，但我跟厨房里一个名叫菲利普的男孩是特别要好的朋友，他酷爱诗歌，吉他弹得也很好，于是我向他求助。从他那里我才知道，父母之间发生了一场可怕的争吵。（女佣们在房间里都能听到争吵的每一个字；大部分都是法语，但贴身女佣玛莎曾和一位来自巴黎的裁缝一起生活了五年，所以她听得一清二楚。）显然，母亲指责父亲对她不忠，还和隔壁的年轻小姐有染；父亲起初为自己辩解，但后来却勃然大怒，说了些粗鲁的话——“好像是跟夫人的年龄有关”——把母亲弄哭了；母亲还暗示有人借钱给老公主，然后又对她和她的女儿说了些难听的话，于是父亲开始威胁她……

我把菲利普打发走，然后把自己扔到床上。我没有哭泣；我没有让自己陷入绝望；我没有问自己这一切究竟是从哪里、怎么发生的；我没有纳闷为什么我之前没有猜到——其实我早就猜到了。我甚至没有对父亲心怀怨恨……我所知道的一切，对我来说太过沉重。这突如其来的真相彻底击垮了我；一切都结束了。一瞬间，我所有的花朵都被连根拔起，散落在我周围——破碎、凋零、被践踏。

I did not dare to question them, but one of the pantry boys, called Philip, who was passionately fond of poetry and a beautiful guitar player, was a particular friend of mine, and to him I turned. From him I discovered that a terrible scene had taken place between my parents. (Every word of it could be heard in the maids’ room; much of it was in French, but Masha, the lady’s maid, had lived for five years with a seamstress from Paris and understood every word.) Apparently my mother had accused my father of being unfaithful to her and of having relations with the young lady next door; my father had at first defended himself but then flared up and said something brutal—‘something to do with Madame’s age’—which had made my mother cry; my mother also alluded to a loan supposed to have been made to the old princess, and then made disagreeable remarks about her and about her daughter too, whereupon my father began to threaten her….

I sent Philip away and flung myself on the bed. I did not sob; I did not give myself up to despair; I did not ask myself where and how all this had happened; I did not wonder how it was that I had not guessed it earlier—guessed it long ago. I did not even harbour bitter thoughts about my father…what I had learned was too much for me to manage. The sudden revelation crushed me; all was ended. In one swoop all my flowers were torn up by the roots and lay about me—scattered, broken, trampled underfoot.

屠格涅夫和弗拉基米尔一样，无法不崇拜自己的父亲。他那歇斯底里、占有欲极强的母亲，显然是个严厉的管教者，一个“夜魔”（俄语为koshmar），从一开始就让他对女性心生恐惧。

Turgenev, like Vladimir, was incapable of not revering his father. His hysterical and possessive mother, clearly a martinet, a koshmar (Russian for “night hag”), gave him a fear of women from the start.

“我？”我痛苦地重复道，我的心开始颤抖，就像往常一样，被她那无法抗拒、难以言喻的魅力所迷惑。“我？相信我，齐娜伊达·亚历山德罗芙娜，无论你做了什么，无论你让我多么痛苦，我都会爱你、崇拜你，直到我生命的尽头。”

她猛地转身面向我，张开双臂，环住我的头，给了我一个热情而温暖的吻。只有上帝才知道，这漫长的告别之吻究竟是给谁的，但我却贪婪地品尝着它的甜蜜。我知道，这样的吻再也不会有了。

‘I?’ I repeated painfully, and my heart began to quiver, as it always did under the spell of her irresistible, inexpressible fascination. ‘I? Believe me, Zinaida Alexandrovna, that whatever you did, however much you make me suffer, I shall love you and adore you to the end of my days.’

She quickly turned towards me, and opening her arms wide, put them round my head, and gave me a strong, warm kiss. God only knows for whom that long farewell kiss was seeking, but I tasted its sweetness avidly. I knew that it would never come again.

萨福的一首残篇诗作广为人知：

Sappho famously has a fragment:

爱神再次让我四肢舒展；

我是一个无助的爬行生物，苦乐参半。

（译者：彼得·圣安德烈）

在离我大约四十步远的街上，一栋小木屋敞开的窗户前，我父亲背对着我站着。他倚在窗台上，胸膛贴着窗台；屋里，窗帘半遮着一个穿着深色连衣裙的女人正和我父亲说话；她是齐奈达。

我彻底懵了。说实话，我完全没想到会这样。我的第一反应是逃跑。“爸爸会四处查看的，”我想，“我会迷路的。”但一种奇怪的感觉，比好奇更强烈，甚至比嫉妒和恐惧更强烈，攫住了我。我站在那里，看着。我竖起耳朵仔细听。爸爸似乎在坚持什么。齐娜伊达不肯答应。她的脸现在就在我眼前，悲伤、严肃而美丽，脸上印着难以言喻的悲伤、奉献、爱，以及一种绝望——我找不到其他词来形容。她说话时只说几个音节，眼睛始终没有抬起，只是微微一笑，既顺从又固执。仅仅凭着这个笑容，我就认出了我的齐娜伊达，她曾经的样子。父亲耸了耸肩，把帽子戴正，这在他身上总是表示不耐烦……然后我听到他说：“Vous devez vous séparer de cette…”（你得离开这里……）齐娜伊达直起身子，伸出手。接下来，一件难以置信的事情发生在我眼前。父亲突然举起马鞭，他之前一直用马鞭拂去外套上的灰尘，我听到一声清脆的鞭笞声，落在她裸露到手肘的手臂上。我竭力克制住自己，才没叫出声来。齐娜伊达颤抖着，默默地看着父亲，缓缓抬起手臂，吻了吻那道鲜红的伤疤。

Again limb-loosening Eros shakes me;

A helpless crawling thing I am, sweet-bitter.

(trans. Peter Saint-Andre)

In the street, about forty paces from me, before the open window of a small wooden house, with his back to me, stood my father. He was leaning with his chest over the window sill; inside the house, half concealed by a curtain, sat a woman in a dark dress, talking with my father; it was Zinaida.

I was utterly stunned. This, I admit, I did not expect. My first impulse was to run away. ‘My father will look round,’ I thought—‘I shall be lost.’ But an odd feeling, a feeling stronger than curiosity, stronger even than jealousy, stronger than fear, gripped me. I stood still and looked. I strained my ears to hear. My father seemed to be insisting on something. Zinaida would not consent. Her face is before my eyes now, sad and serious and beautiful, and upon it the imprint—impossible to convey—of grief, devotion, love, and a kind of despair—I can find no other word for it. She spoke in monosyllables, without lifting her eyes, and only smiled, submissively and stubbornly. By this smile alone I recognized my Zinaida, as she once was. My father gave a shrug of his shoulders, and set his hat straight on his head, which with him was always a sign of impatience…then I could hear the words ‘Vous devez vous séparer de cette…’ Zinaida straightened herself and held out her hand. Then something unbelievable took place before my eyes. My father suddenly lifted his riding-crop, with which he had been flicking the dust off the folds of his coat, and I heard the sound of a sharp blow struck across her arm which was bared to the elbow. It was all I could do to prevent myself from crying out. Zinaida quivered—looked silently to my father—and raising her arm slowly to her lips, kissed the scar which glowed crimson upon it.

屠格涅夫的母亲以残酷鞭打女农奴（也包括男农奴）而臭名昭著。人们只能猜测屠格涅夫与女农奴（其中一位为他生下了一个女儿）的性关系中，他的行为究竟如何。然而，屠格涅夫的性格中显然存在着性虐待倾向。弗洛伊德或许会对小弗拉基米尔将母亲的性情转移到父亲身上感到疑惑。

Turgenev’s mother was notorious for severely whipping female serfs, and males also. One can only speculate how Turgenev behaved in his own erotic encounters with his female serfs, one of whom bore him a daughter. Yet there is clearly sexual sadism in Turgenev’s makeup. Freud would have wondered at the boy Vladimir’s transposition of his mother’s nature to his father.

我茫然地盯着河面，浑然不觉泪水正从眼眶涌出。他们在打她，我想，打，打……

那天晚上我做了一个奇怪又可怕的梦。我梦见自己走进一间低矮昏暗的房间。父亲站在那里，手里拿着一根马鞭，跺着脚。齐娜伊达蜷缩在角落里，她的额头上，而不是手臂上，有一块鲜红的印记……

Unseeingly I stared at the river, unconscious of the tears which were streaming from my eyes. They are beating her, I thought, beating, beating….

That night I dreamt a strange and frightening dream. I fancied that I entered a low, dark room. My father was standing there, holding a riding-crop in his hand, and stamping with his feet. Zinaida was cowering in the corner, and there was a crimson mark, not upon her arm, but upon her forehead…

额头上那道传统的印记似乎让可怜的齐娜伊达变成了女版的该隐。年轻的弗拉基米尔是她不知何故杀死的弟弟吗？而真正的受害者，很快，却是她的父亲：

The traditional mark upon the forehead seems to make poor Zinaida into a female Cain. Is young Vladimir the brother she has somehow murdered? The actual victim, soon enough, is the father:

两个月后，我考入了大学。六个月后，父亲在圣彼得堡去世（死于中风）。他刚带着我和母亲搬到那里不久。去世前几天，他收到了一封来自莫斯科的信，信中他非常难过。他去向母亲求助，据说，他竟然崩溃大哭——他，我的父亲！就在他中风的那天早上，他用法语给我写了一封信。“我的儿子，”他写道，“要警惕女人的爱；要警惕那种狂喜——那种慢性毒药。”

他去世后，我母亲寄了一大笔钱到莫斯科。

Two months later, I entered the University, and six months after that my father died (as the result of a stroke) in St Petersburg, where he had only just moved with my mother and me. Several days before his death he had received a letter from Moscow which upset him greatly. He went to beg some sort of favour of my mother and, so they told me, actually broke down and wept—he, my father! On the morning of the very day on which he had the stroke, he had begun a letter to me, written in French. ‘My son,’ he wrote, ‘beware of the love of women; beware of that ecstasy—that slow poison.’

My mother, after his death, sent a considerable sum of money to Moscow.

那封信，无论是虚构的还是真实的，都预言了宝琳·维亚尔多给屠格涅夫带来的狂喜和慢性毒药。

That letter, whether fictive or real, prophesies the ecstasy and slow poison that Pauline Viardot brought to Turgenev.

迈达诺夫给了我齐娜伊达的地址。她住在德穆特酒店。往事涌上心头……我暗暗发誓第二天就去拜访我的“挚爱”。然而，各种事情接踵而至。一周过去了，又过了一周，当我终于来到德穆特酒店，询问多尔斯基夫人时，却被告知她四天前因难产猝然离世。

我记得，在得知齐奈达去世几天后，我出于一种无法抑制的冲动，去见了和我们住在同一屋檐下的一位贫穷老妇人。她衣衫褴褛，躺在光秃秃的木板上，枕着一个麻袋，离世的过程十分艰难痛苦。她一生都在与每日的匮乏作斗争，从未享受过快乐，从未尝过幸福的滋味——她难道不会欣然接受死亡吗？死亡是解脱，是安宁。然而，只要她虚弱的身体还在顽强抵抗，只要冰冷的手放在她胸口，她的胸膛就痛苦地起伏着，只要她体内还剩下一点力气，这位老妇人就不停地划着十字，不停地低声说着“主啊，请原谅我的罪过……”直到最后一丝意识消失，她眼中的恐惧，对死亡的恐惧才消失……我记得，就在那可怜的老妇人的床边，我感到害怕，为齐奈达感到害怕，我想为她，为我的父亲，也为我自己祈祷。

Maidanov gave me Zinaida’s address. She was staying in the Hotel Demuth. Old memories began to stir within me…I promised myself to pay a visit to my ‘flame’ on the very next day. But various things turned up. A week passed, and then another, and when I made my way to the Demuth, and asked for Madame Dolsky, I was told that she had died four days before, quite suddenly, in childbirth.

I remember how several days after that on which I had learnt of Zinaida’s death, I myself, obeying an irresistible impulse, was present at the death of a poor old woman who lived in the same house with us. Covered with rags, lying on bare boards, with a sack for a pillow, her end was hard and painful. Her whole life was spent in a bitter struggle with daily want, she had had no joy, had never tasted the sweets of happiness—surely she would welcome death with gladness—its deliverance—its peace? Yet so long as her frail body resisted obstinately, her breast rose and fell in agony under the icy hand that was laid upon it, so long as any strength was left within her, the little old woman kept crossing herself, kept whispering ‘Lord forgive me my sins…’ and not until the last spark of consciousness had gone, did the look of fear, of the terror of death, vanish from her eyes…and I remember that there, by the death-bed of that poor old woman, I grew afraid, afraid for Zinaida, and I wanted to say a prayer for her, for my father—and for myself.

彼得突发中风，很可能是因为收到齐娜伊达的来信后，他情绪失控，痛哭流涕。他们之间那种带有虐恋色彩、充满狂喜的关系，慢慢地毒害了彼得。而齐娜伊达，尽管饱受折磨，却顽强地活了下来，嫁给了一个经济条件优渥的男人，但不幸的是，她很快就死于难产。屠格涅夫的笔触含蓄，没有直白地描述彼得的死因，而是让读者自行判断究竟是什么摧毁了他。我的推测是，这位长期压抑着内心的父亲和丈夫，在面对自己崩溃痛哭的那一刻，无法承受失去既定身份的打击，最终精神崩溃，走向了生命的终点。

Pyotr suffers a fatal stroke, quite possibly augmented by his extraordinary outburst into tears on receipt of a letter from Zinaida. Their relationship, with its sadomasochistic aura and undoubted ecstasy, has slowly poisoned Pyotr, while Zinaida, however battered, survives long enough to make a financially favorable marriage that unfortunately soon slays her in childbirth. Turgenev, too subtle to be explicit, allows his readers to decide what has destroyed Pyotr. My surmise is that the fiercely repressed father and husband, confronted by his own collapse into weeping, could not sustain this loss of an assumed identity, and underwent a psychic fragmentation so intense that it ended him.

然而，这似乎不足以概括弗拉基米尔对怀旧之情的深入研究。我们不妨以叶芝的精神来探讨这个问题：

Yet that seems inadequate to Vladimir’s consuming study of the nostalgias. One wants to begin in the spirit of W. B. Yeats:

但这样下去，我们能找到一丝慰藉吗？

人爱上了会消逝的事物。

还有什么好说的呢？

But is there any comfort to be found?

Man is in love and loves what vanishes,

What more is there to say?

这是我经常默念的诗句之一，当我拄着助行器在家里走动，或者费力地爬上三楼的书房时，我都会想起它。想到屠格涅夫的《初恋》，我不禁感到有些伤感，因为我们大多数人都有过类似的经历。

That is one of the verse passages that I over-quote to myself as I move around my house on a walker or laboriously chug up the stairs to my third-floor study. Thinking about Turgenev’s First Love, I become rather sad, since most of us have some such memories.

传说中，垂死的屠格涅夫在剧痛中将墨水瓶砸向了试图安慰他的宝琳·维亚尔多。学者们有时认为这是一种转喻，即用一个词来指代前一个词，因此，转喻也可以被称作——虽然令人恼火但却很贴切——转喻的转喻。前例是臭名昭著的马丁·路德将墨水瓶砸向某个倒霉蛋的场景。屠格涅夫那虐待成性的母亲总是称宝琳为吉普赛人。长久的迷恋必然充满矛盾，随着年龄的增长，日益绝望的屠格涅夫开始相信宝琳有犹太血统。我们无从知晓他临终时究竟在想些什么。很可能是他对那份永远无法割舍的激情的怨恨。

There is a tradition that the dying Turgenev, in great pain, threw an inkwell at Pauline Viardot, who was attempting to comfort him. Scholars sometimes regard this as a metalepsis, a trope in which a word is substituted metonymically for a word in a previous trope, so that a metalepsis can be called, maddeningly but accurately, a metonymy of a metonymy. The precedent trope is a notorious heave of an inkwell by the horribly great Martin Luther at some poor devil or other. Turgenev’s sadistic mother always termed Pauline a Gypsy. Permanent infatuation necessarily has its ambivalences, and as he aged, the increasingly desperate Turgenev began to believe that Pauline was partly Jewish. We cannot know what dominated his consciousness in the act of dying. It may well have been a resentment of the passion he could never forsake.

第21章

CHAPTER 21

哥萨克（1863）

The Cossacks (1863)

利奥·托尔斯托伊​

LEO TOLSTOY

托尔斯泰最初想把这部短篇小说命名为《青年时代》，但在重读《伊利亚特》后，他修改了书名和内容。小说的主人公是奥列宁，一位沉溺于饮酒、赌博、风流韵事和上流社会的年轻贵族。年轻的托尔斯泰本人则远不止于此，他放荡不羁，经常与妓女和农妇厮混，赌博挥霍无度，饱受淋病折磨。我怀疑他于1862年9月与索菲娅·贝尔斯结婚并非出于爱情，而是为了改变自己的人生。当时他34岁，索菲娅18岁。在《安娜·卡列尼娜》中，列文——托尔斯泰的化身——在34岁时也娶了18岁的基蒂，但他对基蒂的爱却无比深沉。

TOLSTOY ORIGINALLY WISHED to call this short novel Young Manhood but revised both the book and the title after rereading the Iliad. The ostensible protagonist is Olenin, a young nobleman who had been wasting his life in drinking, gambling, love affairs, and aristocratic society. The young Tolstoy went considerably beyond that and was wildly promiscuous, frequently with whores and peasant women, gambled ruinously, struggled with gonorrhea, and I suspect married Sophia Behrs in September 1862 not because he fell in love with her but in the hope of changing his life. He was thirty-four; Sophia was eighteen. In Anna Karenina, Levin, Tolstoy’s surrogate, is also thirty-four when he marries Kitty, who is eighteen, but he loves her profoundly.

托尔斯泰塑造女性角色几乎堪比莎士比亚，但他本人却极度厌女，这本身就是一个悖论。经托尔斯泰本人同意，我引用大卫·贝西亚（显然是普希金研究领域的杰出学者）写给我的一封信：

It is a paradox that Tolstoy, almost Shakespearean in his creation of women, was viciously misogynistic. With his permission, I quote from a letter sent to me by David Bethea, clearly the outstanding scholar of Pushkin:

关于托尔斯泰和女性的关系，没错，他对女性的刻画精准得无人能及，但同时，她们对他的掌控力，尤其是性方面的掌控力，也令他怒不可遏。他始终无法释怀这一点：即使到了晚年，每当他看到一位容貌姣好的农妇站在梯子上，他都会想要把她拖进灌木丛，这让他怒火中烧，怨恨难消。为什么一个几乎没有任何理性思考能力的女人，会拥有如此原始的吸引力，让他想要与她交合？这一定是她或者“她们”的错。海伦娜·库拉金裸露的双肩和胸部。正因如此，他的愤怒最终走向了一个极端的逻辑结局（《克莱采奏鸣曲》）：通过禁欲来拒绝生物本能。

With regard to Tolstoy and women, yes, he portrayed them as accurately as anyone ever has but at the same time they could enrage him with their power over him, especially their sexual power. He never came to terms with this: even in later years he’d see a comely peasant woman on a ladder and he’d want to drag her into the bushes and this brought his anger and resentment to a boil. Why should she, with no reasoning power to speak of, possess this animal attraction to make him want to couple with her? Somehow that must be her or “their” fault. Hélène Kuragin’s bare shoulders and bust. That’s why the anger played out to an extreme logical conclusion (The Kreutzer Sonata): rejection of biology through abstinence.

我在一本名为《西方经典》 （1994）的书中写到了《克莱采奏鸣曲》，书中我基本上是说，我感到震惊，却又不得不一遍遍地读它。有时我觉得，我最敬佩的作家往往也是最能伤害我的人。我每年都教《威尼斯商人》，写过关于它的文章，永远无法放弃它，但它却让我感到沮丧和愤怒。我的朋友兼学生肯尼斯·格罗斯写了一本精辟的著作《夏洛克就是莎士比亚》（2006），他认为夏洛克是莎士比亚的突破之作，是他自身才华的展现，也是他试图更好地掌控观众的一次尝试。也许是这样。如果我是导演，我会把《威尼斯商人》拍成一出闹剧，类似于克里斯托弗·马洛的《马耳他岛的犹太人》。夏洛克会戴着红色假发和假鼻子，由一位伟大的喜剧演员来扮演。然而，我自己恐怕也无法忍受观看这样的演出。

I wrote about The Kreutzer Sonata in a book called The Western Canon (1994), essentially saying that I was appalled and yet sentenced to read it over and over again. Sometimes I think that the authors I most admire are the ones who can badly hurt me. I teach The Merchant of Venice every year, have written essays on it, cannot ever give it up, yet it depresses and infuriates me. My friend and former student Kenneth Gross wrote a strong brief book, Shylock Is Shakespeare (2006), arguing that Shylock was Shakespeare’s breakthrough, a revelation of his own powers and a reach toward surer control of his audience. That may be. If I were a director, I would have The Merchant of Venice played as a farce, akin to Christopher Marlowe’s The Jew of Malta. Shylock would have a red wig and a false nose and would be played by a great comedian. And yet I myself would not be able to bear watching it.

奥列宁性情温和、慷慨善良——正如我已故的朋友菲利普·罗斯所说，他是“怀揣梦想的泥土”——但他也缺乏个性，而且一心想成为一名哥萨克，娶美丽的玛丽安卡为妻，过着狩猎、骑马、军事劫掠的生活，欣赏山川河流的景色，在各方面都与自然亲近，这种想法简直荒谬至极：

Olenin is good-natured, generous, kind—“clay with aspirations,” as my late friend Philip Roth would say—but he is also colorless and hopelessly absurd in his desire to become a Cossack, marry the beautiful Maryánka, and live a life of hunting, horsemanship, military raiding, absorbing mountain and river scenery, staying close to the natural in every way:

“即便青草长出来又怎样呢？”他继续想着，“我还是必须活着，必须快乐，因为快乐是我唯一的渴望。无论我是什么——像其他动物一样，青草只能在我头顶生长，仅此而已；或者只是上帝赋予的一副躯壳——我都必须以最好的方式生活。那么，我该如何生活才能快乐？为什么我以前不快乐呢？”他开始回忆起过去的生活，对自己感到厌恶。他觉得自己以前是多么苛求自私，尽管现在他明白，其实他一直都不需要任何东西。他环顾四周，阳光透过树叶洒下斑驳的光影，夕阳西下，天空晴朗，他感到和以前一样快乐。“我为什么快乐？我以前活着是为了什么？”他想，“我曾经对自己索取了多少；我曾经算计了多少，结果却只得到了羞耻和悲伤！而现在，我什么都不需要，就能快乐。”突然间，仿佛一道新的光芒照耀在他面前。“这就是幸福！”他自言自语道，“幸福在于为他人而活。这是显而易见的。每个人天生都渴望幸福，因此这种渴望是正当的。如果试图自私地满足这种渴望——也就是追求财富、名誉、舒适或爱情——那么就可能出现一些情况，使这些欲望无法得到满足。由此可见，不正当的是这些欲望本身，而不是对幸福的需求。但是，究竟有哪些欲望能够不受外界环境的影响而始终得到满足呢？它们是什么？爱，自我牺牲。”当他发现这个在他看来是全新的真理时，他欣喜若狂，激动不已，他跳了起来，急切地寻找一个可以让他为之牺牲、为之行善、为之爱的人。“既然人什么都不为自己求，”他不断地想，“为什么不为他人而活呢？”他拿起枪，打算赶紧回家好好想想，找个机会行善。他走出了灌木丛。来到林间空地，他环顾四周；太阳已经不见了，落入了树梢。天气转凉，这地方在他看来十分陌生，与村子周围的景色截然不同。一切都变了——天气和森林的样貌；天空阴云密布，风吹过树梢沙沙作响，四周除了芦苇和枯死的断木，什么也看不见。他呼唤着跑开去追赶某种动物的狗，狗的声音却像在沙漠中一样狰狞。突然，一种可怕的怪异感袭来。他感到害怕。他想起了那些阿布雷克人和他听说的谋杀案，他时刻担心着会不会有阿布雷克人……他感觉随时都会有东西从灌木丛后窜出来，他要么奋力求生，要么就只能认命，否则就会沦为懦夫。他想起了上帝和来世，这种感觉他已经很久没有过了。周围依然是那阴郁而严酷的荒野。“为自己而活，”他想，“随时都可能死去，而且死前一无所获，无人知晓，这样的生活还有意义吗？”他朝着自己猜测的村庄方向走去。他不再想起刚才的射击；但他感到筋疲力尽，于是格外仔细地、近乎恐惧地环顾四周，仔细观察每一丛灌木和每一棵树木，生怕自己随时会被追究责任。他漫无目的地走了很久，来到一条沟渠边，泰雷克河的河水冰冷而沙质，他不想再迷路，决定沿着沟渠走下去。他继续前行，不知道这条沟渠会通向何方。突然，身后的芦苇发出噼啪声。他浑身一颤，抓起枪，然后感到羞愧：那只兴奋过头的狗，气喘吁吁地跳进沟渠的冰冷水中，正在舔舐水面！

‘But what though the grass does grow?’ he continued thinking. ‘Still I must live and be happy, because happiness is all I desire. Never mind what I am—an animal like all the rest, above whom the grass will grow and nothing more; or a frame in which a bit of the one God has been set,—still I must live in the very best way. How then must I live to be happy, and why was I not happy before?’ And he began to recall his former life and he felt disgusted with himself. He appeared to himself to have been terribly exacting and selfish, though he now saw that all the while he really needed nothing for himself. And he looked round at the foliage with the light shining through it, at the setting sun and the clear sky, and he felt just as happy as before. ‘Why am I happy, and what used I to live for?’ thought he. ‘How much I exacted for myself; how I schemed and did not manage to gain anything but shame and sorrow! and, there now, I require nothing to be happy;’ and suddenly, a new light seemed to reveal itself to him. ‘Happiness is this!’ he said to himself. ‘Happiness lies in living for others. That is evident. The desire for happiness is innate in every man; therefore it is legitimate. When trying to satisfy it selfishly—that is, by seeking for oneself riches, fame, comforts, or love—it may happen that circumstances arise which make it impossible to satisfy those desires. It follows that it is these desires that are illegitimate, but not the need for happiness. But what desires can always be satisfied despite external circumstances? What are they? Love, self-sacrifice.’ He was so glad and excited when he had discovered this, as it seemed to him, new truth, that he jumped up and began impatiently seeking some one to sacrifice himself for, to do good to and to love. ‘Since one wants nothing for oneself,’ he kept thinking, ‘why not live for others?’ He took up his gun with the intention of returning home quickly to think this out and to find an opportunity of doing good. He made his way out of the thicket. When he had come out into the glade he looked around him; the sun was no longer visible above the tree-tops. It had grown cooler and the place seemed to him quite strange and not like the country round the village. Everything seemed changed—the weather and the character of the forest; the sky was wrapped in clouds, the wind was rustling in the tree-tops, and all around nothing was visible but reeds and dying broken-down trees. He called to his dog who had run away to follow some animal, and his voice came back as in a desert. And suddenly he was seized with a terrible sense of weirdness. He grew frightened. He remembered the abreks and the murders he had been told about, and he expected every moment that an abrek would spring from behind every bush and he would have to defend his life and die, or be a coward. He thought of God and of the future life as for long he had not thought about them. And all around was that same gloomy stern wild nature. ‘And is it worth while living for oneself,’ thought he, ‘when at any moment you may die, and die without having done any good, and so that no one will know of it?’ He went in the direction where he fancied the village lay. Of his shooting he had no further thought; but he felt tired to death and peered round at every bush and tree with particular attention and almost with terror, expecting every moment to be called to account for his life. After having wandered about for a considerable time he came upon a ditch down which was flowing cold sandy water from the Térek, and, not to go astray any longer, he decided to follow it. He went on without knowing where the ditch would lead him. Suddenly the reeds behind him crackled. He shuddered and seized his gun, and then felt ashamed of himself: the over-excited dog, panting hard, had thrown itself into the cold water of the ditch and was lapping it!

这就是托尔斯泰式的精神世界。他对现实的把握，几乎超越了所有其他作家。我这里说的“现实感”并非指味道，而是指刀刃的形状，握柄可以牢牢握住。我很少读到托尔斯泰的幽默，而我之所以对下面这段文字感到愉悦，或许要归功于译者：“他拿起枪，打算尽快回家好好想想，并寻找行善的机会。”

That is the authentic Tolstoyan weather of the mind. It surpasses almost every other writer in its grasp of the tang of the actual. I mean “tang” not as flavor but the secondary meaning of a knife blade so shaped that it can be held securely by the handle. I do not often hear Tolstoy being humorous, and the delight I take in the following may be what I owe to the translators: “He took up his gun with the intention of returning home quickly to think this out and to find an opportunity of doing good.”

很难看出奥列宁能为哥萨克们——埃罗什卡、卢卡什卡和玛丽安卡——带来什么好处。他与埃罗什卡一起打猎喝酒，自欺欺人地以为自己爱上了玛丽安卡，并向她求婚。玛丽安卡已经与哥萨克中最胆大的“勇士”卢卡什卡订婚，只等父亲允许她出嫁。奥列宁慷慨过头，送给卢卡什卡一匹马，结果这位年轻的哥萨克又用它换了一匹更好的马，这让他开始怀疑奥列宁对玛丽安卡另有所图。

It is a little difficult to see what good Olenin can do for the Cossacks Daddy Eroshka, Lukáshka, and Maryánka. He hunts and drinks with Eroshka, deceives himself into believing he is in love with Maryánka, and makes her an offer of marriage. She is betrothed to Lukáshka, the most daring “brave” among the Cossacks, and waits only for her father’s permission to marry. Olenin, with excessive generosity, gives Lukáshka a horse, resulting in the young Cossack’s trading it for an even better horse, and rightly becoming suspicious of Olenin’s interest in Maryánka.

恐怕没有哪个作家能像托尔斯泰那样描绘暴力场面。当卢卡什卡身负重伤，甚至可能丧命时，他的笔触清晰得令人惊叹，毫无悲悯之情。

Probably no writer can match Tolstoy in depicting violent action. There is an amazing clarity, unmarked by pathos, when Lukáshka is severely, perhaps mortally wounded:

又过了一会儿，哥萨克们欢呼一声，从马车后方两侧冲了出来——卢卡什卡冲在最前面。奥列宁只听到几声枪响，然后是喊叫声和呻吟声。他似乎看到了烟雾和血迹，于是弃马而去，神情恍惚地朝哥萨克们跑去。恐惧仿佛蒙蔽了他的双眼。他什么也看不清，但他明白一切都结束了。卢卡什卡脸色苍白如死，正抓着一个受伤的车臣人的胳膊，喊道：“别杀他！我要活捉他！”那个车臣人就是那个红头发的男人，他哥哥被卢卡什卡杀死后，他把哥哥的尸体拖走了。卢卡什卡正扭着他的胳膊。突然，车臣人挣脱开枪。卢卡什卡倒下了，鲜血从他的腹部涌了出来。他跳了起来，但又倒了下去，用俄语和鞑靼语咒骂着。他的衣服上和身下都沾满了血迹。几个哥萨克走近他，开始解开他的腰带。其中一个名叫纳扎尔卡的哥萨克，在帮忙之前，笨手笨脚地摸索了一会儿，怎么也插不进剑鞘：剑柄怎么也插不进去。剑刃上沾满了鲜血。

那些红头发、留着修剪过的胡须的车臣人横七竖八地躺着，尸体被砍得稀烂。只有我们知道的那个，就是曾向卢卡什卡开枪的那个，虽然身负重伤，却还活着。他像一只浑身是血的受伤老鹰（鲜血正从他右眼下方的伤口汩汩流出），脸色苍白，神情阴郁，他紧紧咬牙切齿，双眼睁得大大的，惊恐地环顾四周，手里紧握着匕首，仍然准备自卫。号手走到他跟前，仿佛要从他身边经过，却突然猛地一枪，正中他的耳朵。车臣人猛地站了起来，但为时已晚，他倒下了。

Another moment passed and the Cossacks with a whoop rushed out on both sides from behind the cart—Lukáshka in front of them. Olenin heard only a few shots, then shouting and moans. He thought he saw smoke and blood, and abandoning his horse and quite beside himself he ran towards the Cossacks. Horror seemed to blind him. He could not make out anything, but understood that all was over. Lukáshka, pale as death, was holding a wounded Chéchen by the arms and shouting, ‘Don’t kill him. I’ll take him alive!’ The Chéchen was the red-haired man who had fetched his brother’s body away after Lukáshka had killed him. Lukáshka was twisting his arms. Suddenly the Chéchen wrenched himself free and fired his pistol. Lukáshka fell, and blood began to flow from his stomach. He jumped up, but fell again, swearing in Russian and in Tartar. More and more blood appeared on his clothes and under him. Some Cossacks approached him and began loosening his girdle. One of them, Nazárka, before beginning to help, fumbled for some time, unable to put his sword in its sheath: it would not go the right way. The blade of the sword was blood-stained.

The Chéchens with their red hair and clipped moustaches lay dead and hacked about. Only the one we know of, who had fired at Lukáshka, though wounded in many places was still alive. Like a wounded hawk all covered with blood (blood was flowing from a wound under his right eye), pale and gloomy, he looked about him with wide-open excited eyes and clenched teeth as he crouched, dagger in hand, still prepared to defend himself. The cornet went up to him as if intending to pass by, and with a quick movement shot him in the ear. The Chéchen started up, but it was too late, and he fell.

书中从未提及卢卡什卡是否幸存，尽管这似乎不太可能。托尔斯泰借此将奥列宁从他幻想自己成为哥萨克的梦境中唤醒出来。

We are never told whether Lukáshka survives, though it seems unlikely. Tolstoy employs the wounding to awaken Olenin from his reveries of transformation into a Cossack.

“玛丽安卡，”他说，“我说，玛丽安卡！我可以进来吗？”她突然转过身来。她的眼眶里噙着一丝不易察觉的泪水，悲伤的表情让她的脸庞显得格外美丽。她默默地、带着尊严地望着他。

奥列宁再次说道：

“玛丽安卡，我来了——”

“别管我！”她说。她的表情没有丝毫变化，但泪水却顺着脸颊流了下来。

你哭什么？到底发生了什么事？

“什么？”她用沙哑的声音重复道，“哥萨克人被杀了，就是因为这个。”

“卢卡什卡？”奥列宁问道。

“走开！你想要什么？”

“玛丽安卡！”奥列宁走近她，说道。

“你休想从我这里得到任何东西！”

“玛丽安卡，别那样说话，”奥列宁恳求道。

“滚开！我受够你了！”女孩跺着脚喊道，气势汹汹地朝他走来。她脸上满是厌恶、轻蔑和愤怒，奥列宁顿时明白自己毫无希望，之前对这个女人难以接近的印象完全正确。

奥列宁什么也没再说，就跑出了小屋。

‘Maryánka,’ said he, ‘I say, Maryánka! May I come in?’ She suddenly turned. There was a scarcely perceptible trace of tears in her eyes and her face was beautiful in its sadness. She looked at him in silent dignity.

Olenin again said:

‘Maryánka, I have come —’

‘Leave me alone!’ she said. Her face did not change but the tears ran down her cheeks.

‘What are you crying for? What is it?’

‘What?’ she repeated with a rough voice. ‘Cossacks have been killed, that’s what for.’

‘Lukáshka?’ said Olenin.

‘Go away! What do you want?’

‘Maryánka!’ said Olenin, approaching her.

‘You will never get anything from me!’

‘Maryánka, don’t speak like that,’ Olenin entreated.

‘Get away. I’m sick of you!’ shouted the girl, stamping her foot, and moved threateningly towards him. And her face expressed such abhorrence, such contempt, and such anger that Olenin suddenly understood that there was no hope for him, and that his first impression of this woman’s inaccessibility had been perfectly correct.

Olenin said nothing more, but ran out of the hut.

我们可以推测，玛丽安卡，一个真正的哥萨克，会给奥列宁重重一击。这在现实中会起到警示作用。托尔斯泰是一位伟大的艺术家，他不会在没有必要的时候就超越暗示。

We are to suppose that Maryánka, a true Cossack, would have given Olenin quite a severe blow. It would have been an instruction in reality. Tolstoy is too great an artist to go beyond implication when more seems unnecessary.

与《战争与和平》相比， 《哥萨克》不过是微缩版。尽管笔锋犀利，《哥萨克》却缺乏《哈吉·穆拉特》的那种奔放不羁。托尔斯泰式的完美需要大地本身的蓬勃生机，一种与托尔斯泰自身生命力相匹配的活力。尚未陷入预言家式自负的深渊，托尔斯泰得以用一种恰到好处的庄严告别自己的青春。可怜的奥列宁不过是他那神一般的创造者的影子，但这无关紧要。卢卡什卡的形象依然鲜活生动。玛丽安卡则是托尔斯泰欲望的另一个终极象征。重读《哥萨克》后，我想起了叶芝的《一九一九年》，这首诗是对爱尔兰共和军与英国之间爱尔兰革命战争时期的沉思：

On the scale of War and Peace the reader will find only a miniature in The Cossacks. Keen as it is, The Cossacks lacks the ebullience of Hadji Murat. Tolstoyan perfection demands the earth’s own exuberance, a vitalism matching Tolstoy’s own. Not yet fallen into the abyss of prophetic pretensions, Tolstoy can say farewell to his own youth with calibrated stateliness. It does not much matter that poor Olenin is only a shadow of his godlike creator. Lukáshka remains vivid as an image. Maryánka is another ultimate image of Tolstoy’s desires. I complete a rereading of The Cossacks and I think of Yeats’s “Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen,” a meditation on the time of the Irish Revolutionary War between the IRA and the British:

能读懂征兆而不沉没的人

陷入某种麻醉剂的半欺骗之中

出身浅薄之人；他们不懂任何作品都无法经受考验。

无论花费的是健康、财富还是内心的平静。

关于智力或手艺的杰作，

没有荣誉留在它雄伟的纪念碑上，

只剩下一个安慰：所有的胜利都将

但打破他幽灵般的孤独。

He who can read the signs nor sink unmanned

Into the half-deceit of some intoxicant

From shallow wits; who knows no work can stand,

Whether health, wealth or peace of mind were spent

On master-work of intellect or hand,

No honour leave its mighty monument,

Has but one comfort left: all triumph would

But break upon his ghostly solitude.

但这样下去，我们能找到一丝慰藉吗？

But is there any comfort to be found?

人爱上了会消逝的事物。

还有什么好说的呢？那片乡村

谁也不敢承认，如果他真的有过这样的想法。

煽动者或偏执狂可能会被发现

在卫城上烧掉那截树桩，

或者把著名的象牙制品打碎成碎片

或者蚱蜢或蜜蜂的迁徙。

Man is in love and loves what vanishes,

What more is there to say? That country round

None dared admit, if Such a thought were his,

Incendiary or bigot could be found

To burn that stump on the Acropolis,

Or break in bits the famous ivories

Or traffic in the grasshoppers or bees.

我从中听出了一种类似于叶芝最令人难忘的诗作《哥萨克人》的结尾悲伤：

I hear a final sadness akin to The Cossacks in Yeats at his most memorable:

人爱上了会消逝的事物。

还有什么好说的呢？

Man is in love and loves what vanishes,

What more is there to say?

第22章

CHAPTER 22

《战争与和平》（1869）

War and Peace (1869)

利奥·托尔斯托伊​

LEO TOLSTOY

它似乎只是断言，西方传统中最有影响力的两位古代叙事作家分别是《伊利亚特》的作者荷马和最早讲述亚伯拉罕、雅各、约瑟、摩西故事的耶和华主义者，也就是我们现在所说的《创世记》和《出埃及记》。

IT SEEMS JUST TO ASSERT that the two most powerful narrative ancient writers in Western tradition are the Homer of the Iliad, and the Yahwist, who first told the tales of Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, in what we now call Genesis and Exodus.

我发现《伊利亚特》和J的作者之间几乎没有共同之处。他们在道德和认知上都格格不入。阿喀琉斯是海仙女忒提斯和珀琉斯的儿子，珀琉斯是一位战士国王，曾与赫拉克勒斯和伊阿宋一起寻找金羊毛。忒提斯将幼小的阿喀琉斯浸入冥河斯堤克斯，使他获得永生，但由于她抓住他的一只脚后跟，这反而成了他的弱点。在《伊利亚特》中，他幸存了下来，但在后来的诗歌传说中，他被一支射中脚后跟的毒箭射杀。

I find little in common between the Iliad and the J writer. They are morally and cognitively incompatible. Achilles is the son of the sea nymph Thetis and of Peleus, a warrior king who accompanies Heracles and Jason in the quest for the Golden Fleece. Thetis dips the infant Achilles in the Styx so as to make him immortal, but since she holds him by one heel, that becomes his vulnerability. He survives the Iliad but in later poetic legends is slain by a poisoned arrow in that heel.

雅各与死神摔跤，赢得了新名字以色列，这个名字似乎意味着“神（El）挣扎”。但由于固执的雅各，甚至在母腹中就狡猾，紧紧抓住他孪生兄弟（以扫）的脚后跟，这个希伯来名字可能意味着“过度控制”、“脚后跟”或“跟随”。

Jacob wrestles with the Angel of Death and wins the new name Israel, which appears to mean “El (God) struggles.” But since the stubborn Jacob, wily even in the womb, held on tight to his twin brother’s (Esau’s) heel, the Hebrew name might mean “overreach” or “heel” or “to follow.”

除了“脚后跟”这个奇特的关联之外，文学人物中再也没有比阿喀琉斯和雅各/以色列更不相似的了。阿喀琉斯是亚该亚人中最杰出的，他拥有勇气、英俊的外表、强大的力量和高超的作战技巧。雅各则足智多谋、足智多谋、耐心、智慧过人，并且深知自己蒙受耶和华的祝福。

Except for this curious interplay on “heel,” no two literary characters share less than Achilles and Jacob/Israel. Achilles is the best of the Achaeans in courage, appearance, strength, skill in battle. Jacob is cunning, endlessly resourceful, patient, wise, and knows that he bears the blessing of Yahweh.

托尔斯泰，作为莎士比亚之后最精通写实艺术的作家，在其表现手法中融合了荷马史诗和圣经中看似矛盾的力量。众所周知，托尔斯泰厌恶威廉·莎士比亚。想必其他莎士比亚的读者都不会觉得《哈姆雷特》、 《麦克白》和《李尔王》枯燥乏味、令人反感。托尔斯泰为何能接受《伊利亚特》的道德观，却不能接受《哈姆雷特》的道德观，这令人费解，因为哈姆雷特与约瑟或《撒母耳记下》中的大卫的相似之处远多于与阿喀琉斯或赫克托耳的相似之处。我推测，托尔斯泰或许不自觉地深受莎士比亚表现手法的影响，却又不愿承认这种不可避免的借鉴。安德烈王子身上更多的是霍茨珀的影子，而非拜伦的风格；就连皮埃尔，在其喜剧形象中，也体现了莎士比亚式的自然主义，而非荷马式或圣经式的。如果你的角色变化与其说是源于经验，不如说是源于他们自己对自身与经验关系的反思，那么你也是莎士比亚模仿创新的又一继承者，即使你热情地坚持认为你的现实感是以道德为中心的，而莎士比亚的现实感并非如此。

Tolstoy, as befits the writer since Shakespeare who most has the art of the actual, combines in his representational praxis the incompatible powers of Homer and the Yahwist. Notoriously, Tolstoy loathed William Shakespeare. Surely no other reader of Shakespeare ever has found Hamlet, Macbeth, and King Lear tedious and offensive. Why Tolstoy could accept the Iliad’s morality, and not Hamlet’s, is a profound puzzle, since Hamlet has more in common with Joseph or with the David of 2 Samuel than he does with Achilles or Hector. I surmise that Tolstoy, despite himself, owed too much to Shakespearean representation, and could not bear to acknowledge the inevitable debt. Prince Andrei has more of Hotspur than of Lord Byron in him, and even Pierre, in his comic aspects, reflects the Shakespearean rather than Homeric or Biblical naturalism. If your characters change less because of experience than by listening to themselves reflect upon their relation to experience, then you are another heir of Shakespeare’s innovations in mimesis, even if you insist passionately that your sense of reality is morally centered whereas Shakespeare’s was not.

莎士比亚和托尔斯泰的共同点是《圣经》而非《伊利亚特》，而最令托尔斯泰反感的莎士比亚戏剧本应是《特洛伊罗斯与克瑞西达》。然而，令人遗憾的是， 《李尔王》却让他声名狼藉，只有《福斯塔夫》出人意料地打动了托尔斯泰。不过，伟大作家之间的相互影响往往十分奇特。亨利·詹姆斯在1908年写道，《战争与和平》与萨克雷的《纽科姆一家》和仲马的《三个火枪手》相提并论，因为这些作品都是“庞大而松散的怪物，其中……充满了偶然性和任意性的怪异元素”。二十年前，詹姆斯曾设想托尔斯泰是“一个被套上缰绳的怪物，他所描绘的伟大主题——整个人类生活！——就像大象为了拉车，不是套在马车上，而是套在马车房上一样。”

Shakespeare and Tolstoy had the Bible rather than the Iliad in common, and the Shakespearean drama that should have offended Tolstoy most was Troilus and Cressida. Alas, King Lear achieved that bad eminence, and only Falstaff, rather surprisingly, convinced Tolstoy. But, then, the effect of the greatest writers upon one another can be very odd. Writing in 1908, Henry James associated War and Peace with Thackeray’s The Newcomes and Dumas’s The Three Musketeers, since all these were “large loose baggy monsters, with…queer elements of the accidental and the arbitrary.” Twenty years earlier, James had a vision of Tolstoy as “a monster harnessed to his great subject—all human life!—as an elephant might be harnessed, for purposes of traction, not to a carriage, but to a coach-house.”

詹姆斯对“绝对预先构思的艺术”的要求似乎与托尔斯泰著名的论战著作《何谓艺术？》 （1897）相悖，但这只是一种错觉。托尔斯泰作为作家和艺术家显然超越了詹姆斯，正如荷马超越了维吉尔，莎士比亚远胜本·琼森一样。 《战争与和平》中人物的刻画具有权威性和掌控力，这种权威性和掌控力体现了我们不得不称之为“现实”的东西，而托尔斯泰与少数几位作家——荷马、圣经、但丁、乔叟、莎士比亚、塞万提斯，或许还有普鲁斯特——共享这种权威性和掌控力。菲利普·拉夫曾精辟地评论道：“评论家们在托尔斯泰式的氛围中欣喜若狂。”这里最贴切的词就是“氛围”。《战争与和平》如同我们的宇宙一样，拥有氛围，但没有人会认为托尔斯泰像那些浪漫主义盛行的作家或陀思妥耶夫斯基一样，创造了一个异质世界。在托尔斯泰笔下的现实世界中，你会经历苦难和死亡，也会享受快乐和生活，而不是在虚幻的国度里。

James’s demand for “an absolutely premeditated art” might seem to collide with Tolstoy’s notorious polemic, What Is Art? (1897), but that is an illusion. Tolstoy is clearly a writer who transcends James as an artist, even as Homer overgoes Virgil and Shakespeare dwarfs Ben Jonson. The representation of persons in War and Peace has the authority and the mastery of what we are compelled to call the real that Tolstoy shares with only a few: Homer, the Bible, Dante, Chaucer, Shakespeare, Cervantes, perhaps Proust. Philip Rahv remarked memorably upon “the critic’s euphoria in the Tolstoyan weather.” The best word there is “weather.” War and Peace, like our cosmos, has weather, but no one would want to say that Tolstoy, like the High Romantics or Dostoevsky, had created a heterocosm. You suffer and die, or joy and live, on our earth in Tolstoy, and not in a visionary realm.

马克思主义批评家卢卡奇勉强承认，托尔斯泰在某些时刻突破了“一个清晰区分、具体而真实的世界，如果这个世界能够扩展成一个整体，它将完全超出小说的范畴，需要一种新的艺术创作形式：一种复兴史诗的形式。”卢卡奇否认托尔斯泰能够实现这种整体性，但他的意识形态使他对托尔斯泰不够宽容。像《哈吉·穆拉德》这样的短篇小说当然可以算作这样一种整体性，但即使考虑到如此长篇的《战争与和平》不可能达到绝对的整体性，这部超过一千二百页的巨著也为我们呈现了一个“清晰区分、具体而真实的世界”。托尔斯泰做到了十九世纪小说家不应该做到的事：他揭示了我们日常现实中那些我们若非他先发现便永远无法察觉的层面。狄更斯和巴尔扎克描绘了非凡的奇幻景象，我们渴望将其融入现实，但托尔斯泰却比他自己更像莎士比亚，尽管他可能不愿承认这一点，他却说服我们，模仿看似本质的自然就足够了。

The Marxist critic Lukács reluctantly conceded that in certain moments Tolstoy broke through to “a clearly differentiated, concrete and existent world, which, if it could spread out into a totality, would be completely inaccessible to the categories of the novel and would require a new form of artistic creation: the form of the renewed epic.” Lukács denied that Tolstoy could accomplish this as a totality, but his ideology made him less than generous toward Tolstoy. A short novel like Hadji Murad certainly is such a totality, but the more than twelve hundred pages of War and Peace, granted the impossibility of an absolute totality at such a length, also gives us “a clearly differentiated, concrete and existent world.” Tolstoy does what a nineteenth-century novelist ought not to be able to do: he reveals aspects of our ordinary reality that we could never see if he had not seen them first. Dickens and Balzac render an extraordinary phantasmagoria that we are eager to absorb into reality, but Tolstoy, more like Shakespeare than he could bear to know, persuades us that the imitation of what seems to be essential nature is more than enough.

莎士比亚的作品值得分析，部分原因在于他的修辞艺术近乎无穷无尽。托尔斯泰的作品则几乎无法进行分析，因为他的修辞显然也营造了一种自然的效果。你必须仔细思考托尔斯泰笔下人物的决定论与自由意志之间的平衡，因为他坚持认为这才是你该做的。然而，你又会被他叙事的力量以及人物言行举止的必然性所深深吸引，以至于无暇质疑情节的结构或故事中人物的个体声音形象。如果詹姆斯、福楼拜和乔伊斯这三位作家可以被视为小说家的原型，那么托尔斯泰似乎又是另一种存在，一种更宏大、更鲜活的存在，我们或许无法为其命名。卢卡奇无疑是正确的，他坚持认为“伟大的史诗是一种与历史时刻紧密相连的形式”，而那个时刻既非托尔斯泰的，也非我们的。

Shakespeare is inexhaustible to analysis, partly because his rhetorical art is nearly infinite. Tolstoy scarcely yields to analysis at all, because his rhetoric evidently also gives the effect of the natural. You have to brood on the balance of determinism and free will in Tolstoy’s personages because he insists that this is your proper work, but you are too carried along by the force of his narrative and the inevitability of his characters’ modes of speaking and thinking to question either the structure of plot or the individual images of voice that inhabit the story. If James and Flaubert and Joyce, the three together, are to be considered archetypes of the novelist, then Tolstoy seems something else, larger and more vital, for which we may lack a name, since Lukács was doubtless correct when he insisted that “the great epic is a form bound to the historical moment,” and that moment was neither Tolstoy’s nor ours.

W·加雷斯·琼斯强调，《战争与和平》与其说是托尔斯泰讲述的单一叙事，不如说是众多叙事交织而成的网络，仿佛我们每个人都是安德烈公爵，以接纳和冷静的视角来审视这一切。或许，安德烈在小说中的主要作用就在于此：他作为托尔斯泰式读者的理想典范，而皮埃尔最终或许也成为了托尔斯泰式故事讲述者的理想化身。以赛亚·伯林和马丁·普莱斯都阐明了托尔斯泰笔下的主人公如何通过接受“事物永恒的关联和人类生活的普遍本质”（正如伯林所言）而最终获得内心的平静。那么，评论家该如何传达托尔斯泰在描写皮埃尔获释、从囚禁中解脱、经历疾病和康复后回到莫斯科，在玛丽亚公主府邸与娜塔莎相遇时所展现的认知智慧，以及其中蕴含的克制而又令人动容的悲怆呢？托尔斯泰在描写皮埃尔意识到陪伴玛丽亚公主哀悼的正是娜塔莎，并且自己爱上了娜塔莎的过程中所展现的艺术，其精妙程度难以想象：

W. Gareth Jones emphasizes that War and Peace is not so much a single narrative related by Tolstoy as a network of many narratives, addressed to us as though each of us were Prince Andrei, receptive and dispassionate. Perhaps that is Andrei’s prime function in the novel, to serve as an ideal model for the Tolstoyan reader, even as Pierre perhaps becomes at last the ideal Tolstoyan storyteller. Isaiah Berlin and Martin Price both have illuminated the way that Tolstoy’s heroes win through to serenity by coming to accept “the permanent relationships of things and the universal texture of human life,” as Berlin phrases it. How can a critic convey either the cognitive wisdom or the restrained yet overwhelming pathos that is manifested in Tolstoy’s account of the meeting between Pierre and Natasha at Princess Marya’s when Pierre returns to Moscow after his liberation and imprisonment, and subsequent illness and recovery? It is difficult to conceive of an art that is subtler than the one Tolstoy exercises in Pierre’s realization that Princess Marya’s mourning companion is Natasha, and that he is in love with Natasha:

房间里天花板很低，只有一根蜡烛照明，公主和一位身穿黑裙的女士坐在那里。皮埃尔记得公主身边总是有女伴，但这些女伴是谁，是什么类型的，他既不知道也想不起来了。“是她的一位女伴，”他想着，目光落在了那位黑裙女士身上。

公主连忙起身迎上去，向他伸出了手。

“是的，”她说着，目光专注地看着他吻过她的手后变化的脸，“原来我们就是这样认识的。在最后的日子里，他经常提起你，”她说着，羞涩地将目光从皮埃尔身上移开，看向他的同伴，这让皮埃尔愣了一下。

“得知你得救了，我真是太高兴了。这是我们很久以来收到的唯一好消息。”公主再次不安地瞥了一眼她的同伴，正要开口，皮埃尔却打断了她。

“你能想象吗？我对这个人一无所知，”他说。“我一直以为他死了。我所知道的一切都是从别人那里听来的，还是道听途说。我只知道他最后落入了罗斯托夫家……真是悲惨的命运！”

皮埃尔语速很快，语气也很激动。他瞥了一眼同伴的脸，看到那人正专注、温柔、好奇地看着他。就像谈话中经常发生的那样，不知为何，他觉得这位身穿黑裙的同伴是个温柔、善良、和蔼的人，不会妨碍他和玛丽亚公主的促膝长谈。

但当他最后提到罗斯托夫一家时，玛丽亚公主脸上的困惑更加明显了。她再次将目光从皮埃尔的脸上移到那位身穿黑裙的女士脸上，说道：

你不认识她吗？

皮埃尔又瞥了一眼同伴苍白而精致的脸庞，那双深邃的眼睛和奇特的嘴唇。从那双专注的眼睛里，他仿佛看到了某种珍贵、久违、却又无比甜蜜的东西。

“不，不可能，”他想。“这张严肃、瘦削、苍白、饱经风霜的脸？不可能是她。这只是对她的一种回忆。”就在这时，玛丽亚公主开口道：“娜塔莎。”那张脸，带着专注的眼神，艰难地、费力地，如同打开一扇锈迹斑斑的门——笑了。从那扇敞开的门里，突然涌出一股气息，倾泻而出，将皮埃尔心中那份早已被遗忘的幸福，尤其是此刻，他甚至都想不起来了。那气息吹出，将他包裹，将他彻底吞噬。当她微笑时，一切都毋庸置疑：那就是娜塔莎，他爱她。

（译者：Richard Pevear 和 Larissa Volokhonsky）

In a room with a low ceiling, lit by one candle, sat the princess and with her someone else in a black dress. Pierre recalled that the princess always had lady companions, but who and what sort these companions were, Pierre did not know and did not recall. “It’s one of her companions,” he thought, glancing at the lady in the black dress.

The princess rose quickly to meet him and gave him her hand.

“Yes,” she said, looking intently into his changed face after he had kissed her hand, “so this is how you and I meet. During the last days, he often spoke of you,” she said, shifting her gaze from Pierre to the companion with a shyness that struck him for a moment.

“I was so glad to learn that you had been saved. It was the only joyful news we had received for a long time.” Again, still more uneasily, the princess glanced at her companion and was about to say something, but Pierre interrupted her.

“Can you imagine, I knew nothing about him,” he said. “I counted him as killed. All I knew, I knew from other people, at third hand. I know only that he ended up with the Rostovs…What a fate!”

Pierre was speaking quickly, animatedly. He glanced once at the face of the companion, saw an attentively tender, curious gaze directed at him, and, as often happens during a conversation, felt for some reason that this companion in the black dress was a sweet, kind, nice being, who would not hinder his heart-to-heart talk with Princess Marya.

But when he said the last words about the Rostovs, the perplexity on Princess Marya’s face showed still more strongly. She again shifted her gaze from Pierre’s face to the face of the lady in the black dress and said:

“Don’t you recognize her?”

Pierre glanced once more at the pale, fine face of the companion, with its dark eyes and strange mouth. Something dear, long forgotten, and more than sweet looked at him from those attentive eyes.

“But no, it can’t be,” he thought. “This stern, thin, pale, aged face? It can’t be her. It’s only a reminiscence of that one.” But just then Princess Marya said: “Natasha.” And the face, with its attentive eyes, with difficulty, with effort, like a rusty door opening—smiled, and from that open door there suddenly breathed and poured out upon Pierre that long-forgotten happiness of which, especially now, he was not even thinking. It breathed out, enveloped, and swallowed him whole. When she smiled, there could no longer be any doubt: it was Natasha, and he loved her.

(trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky)

这部作品极其简洁、直接、写实，但放在其完整的语境中，依托于这部鸿篇巨著的强大力量，它又是一部经过精心构思的艺术。亨利·詹姆斯并非伟大的文学评论家，尽管他的崇拜者对他推崇备至。托尔斯泰、狄更斯和沃尔特·惠特曼与詹姆斯眼中的形象截然不同，尽管年老的詹姆斯后来对惠特曼的看法有所反思。如果说最高的艺术最终会让我们猝不及防，即便我们和皮埃尔一同在这一关键时刻领悟到他生命的秘密和意义，那么任何小说艺术，即使是普鲁斯特的作品，也无法超越托尔斯泰的这部作品。“伟大的艺术作品之所以伟大，正是因为它们能够被所有人理解和接受。”托尔斯泰式的严谨原则无疑在此得到了印证，但我们不能忘记，李尔王和格洛斯特——一个疯癫，一个盲目——之间的对话并非人人都能理解，它触及了艺术的极限，甚至连托尔斯泰本人也未曾触及。令人遗憾的是，托尔斯泰无法或不愿接纳《李尔王》、 《麦克白》和《哈姆雷特》中那些超凡脱俗的元素，却并未排斥约瑟和他的兄弟们的圣经故事，或是阿喀琉斯和赫克托耳的争斗。托尔斯泰对莎士比亚的否定，无论多么扭曲，或许正是莎士比亚的戏剧表现力所获得的最为崇高的赞誉。

Massively simple, direct, realistic, as this is, it is also, in its full context, with the strength of the vast novel behind it, an absolutely premeditated art. Henry James is not one of the great literary critics, despite the idolatry of his admirers. Tolstoy, Dickens, and Walt Whitman bear not the slightest resemblance to what James saw them as being, though the old James repented on the question of Whitman. If the highest art after all catches us unaware, even as we and Pierre together learn the secret and meaning of his life in this central moment, then no novelistic art, not even that of Proust, can surpass Tolstoy’s. “Great works of art are only great because they are accessible and comprehensible to everyone.” That rugged Tolstoyan principle is certainly supported by this moment, but we cannot forget that Lear and Gloucester’s conversing, one mad and the other blind, is not accessible and comprehensible to everyone, and touches the limits of art as even Tolstoy does not. It is a sadness that Tolstoy could not or would not accommodate the transcendental and extraordinary in King Lear, Macbeth, and Hamlet, and yet did not resist the Biblical story of Joseph and his brothers, or the strife of Achilles and Hector. The Tolstoyan rejection of Shakespeare may be, however twisted askew, the most formidable tribute that Shakespeare’s powers of representation have ever received.

托尔斯泰对莎士比亚务实地摆脱基督教信仰的做法感到愤怒。我完全不明白，即使是托尔斯泰理性化的基督教信仰，与《战争与和平》或《安娜·卡列尼娜》又有何关联。托尔斯泰作品中最重要的是他那莎士比亚式的天赋，即赋予哪怕是次要角色鲜明的个性。四个世纪过去了，莎士比亚依然是最伟大的心理学家，而托尔斯泰除了莎士比亚之外，还能从哪里获得他作为心理学家的深刻见解呢？《战争与和平》的最初草稿名为《终成眷属》，这真是一个奇妙的巧合。重读《战争与和平》，欣赏其中精彩绝伦、近乎戏剧化的场景交替，我不禁开始思考：除了莎士比亚之外，托尔斯泰究竟是从哪里习得了这种将场景转换作为人物性格冲突的进一步象征的技巧呢？

Tolstoy was furious at Shakespeare’s pragmatic freedom from Christianity. I am not at all clear as to just what even Tolstoy’s rationalized Christianity has to do with War and Peace, or with Anna Karenina. What matters most in Tolstoy is his altogether Shakespearean gift for individualizing even his minor characters. Shakespeare remains, after four centuries, the greatest of all psychologists, and where else but in Shakespeare could Tolstoy learn his own depth as a psychologist? It is weirdly appropriate that the first sketches of War and Peace were entitled All’s Well That Ends Well. Rereading War and Peace, with its effective, almost theatrical alternation of scenes, I also begin to ask: where, but from Shakespeare, did Tolstoy acquire his sense of scene-shifting as a further index to the clash of personalities?

托马斯·曼对托尔斯泰憎恨莎士比亚的解释可谓一针见血，他认为这是因为托尔斯泰“反对莎士比亚那种普世包容的本性：一个饱受道德折磨的人，面对一位才华横溢的创作天才那轻松诙谐的讽刺，必然会产生嫉妒之情。” 我不禁想到，曼的这番话是否也暗示了哲学家维特根斯坦——这位对托尔斯泰无比推崇的作家——为何也对莎士比亚抱有怀疑？维特根斯坦曾坚持认为：“的确，有些东西是无法用语言表达的。” 但我反复研读莎士比亚的作品，对维特根斯坦的观点表示怀疑，因为莎士比亚用他那三万五千多字的文字（其中一千七百字是他自己创造的）几乎囊括了一切。

Thomas Mann got it right when he ascribed Tolstoy’s hatred of Shakespeare to “antagonism against that universal and all-accepting nature: in the jealousy which a man enduring moral torment was bound to feel in face of the blithe irony of an absolutely creative genius.” I wonder if Mann does not give us another clue as to why the philosopher Wittgenstein, who was so fiercely devoted to Tolstoy, was also distrustful of Shakespeare. Wittgenstein insisted, “There are, indeed, things that cannot be put into words.” Incessantly rereading Shakespeare, I doubt Wittgenstein, as there is nothing that Shakespeare cannot get into his more than thirty-five thousand words, seventeen hundred of which he had coined for himself.

维克托·什克洛夫斯基曾指出托尔斯泰的艺术在于“使之陌生化”，在于“拒绝承认事物的本来面目，仿佛它是第一次被看到”。托尔斯泰在描绘事物方面追求并实现了独创性，但他塑造人物性格的最佳方式却令人想起莎士比亚，这一观察想必会让托尔斯泰恼火不已。《战争与和平》中皮埃尔的非凡转变，遵循了莎士比亚式的通过无意间听到自己内心独白而产生的惊喜范式。托尔斯泰惧怕自身的虚无主义，并且曾暗中将上帝与死亡等同起来，他敏锐地意识到莎士比亚摆脱了教条的束缚，《李尔王》和《麦克白》的悲剧反映了莎士比亚务实的虚无主义。莎士比亚或许是所有伟大作家中最不唯我论的，而托尔斯泰则是最唯我论的。托尔斯泰对莎士比亚的怨恨，是天才在对立的天才身上认出了自己的对手。

Viktor Shklovsky famously called attention to Tolstoy’s art of “making it strange,” of “refusing to recognize an object, of describing it as if it were seen for the first time.” Tolstoy sought and achieved originality in object representation, but his modes of portraying personality and character at their best recall Shakespeare’s, an observation that would have infuriated Tolstoy. The extraordinary changes in Pierre, in War and Peace, follow the Shakespearean paradigm of surprise through involuntary self-overhearing. Tolstoy, who feared his own nihilism, and who secretly had identified God with death, accurately saw that Shakespeare was free of dogmatic shadows, and that Lear’s tragedy, and Macbeth’s, reflected Shakespeare’s pragmatic nihilism. Shakespeare was perhaps the least solipsistic of all great writers; Tolstoy, the most. Tolstoy’s resentment of Shakespeare was genius recognizing its antagonist in an opposed genius.

在莎士比亚的所有角色中，托尔斯泰最厌恶李尔王，因为他敏锐地意识到，《李尔王》是一部面向基督教观众的异教戏剧。1910年，82岁的托尔斯泰抛弃了妻子和家人，最终死于火车站。李尔王的死状并非托尔斯泰的原作，但当我们思考托尔斯泰悲惨的结局时，却很难不联想到李尔王的死。

Of all Shakespearean roles, Tolstoy most resented Lear’s, as he accurately perceived that King Lear was a pagan play directed to a Christian audience. In 1910, at eighty-two, Tolstoy fled his wife and family, to die at a railway station. The image of Lear’s death was not in Tolstoy’s mind, but it is difficult to keep it away from ours as we contemplate Tolstoy’s desperate end.

我读过几本托尔斯泰的传记：艾尔默·莫德、A·N·威尔逊、安东尼·布里格斯和罗莎蒙德·巴特利特的。它们各有千秋，都很有价值。但我始终不明白，为什么一位既是伟大的作家又是德高望重的道德家，却不爱他那贤惠的妻子索菲娅·贝尔斯（后来的索菲娅·托尔斯泰伯爵夫人），她为他生了十三个孩子，其中八个活到了成年，她一生都奉献给了他和他的写作事业。除了女儿亚历山德拉，托尔斯泰与所有子女都争吵不断，如果可以，他甚至想剥夺他们的继承权。

I have read several of the biographies of Tolstoy: Aylmer Maude, A. N. Wilson, Anthony Briggs, Rosamund Bartlett. In different ways, they are all of considerable use. But I am left puzzled about why and how someone who was both a great writer and a towering moralist failed to love a marvelous wife, Sophia Behrs, who became Countess Sophia Tolstaya, and who gave him thirteen children, eight of whom survived childhood, and devoted her life to him, and to his work as a writer. Except for his daughter Alexandra, Tolstoy quarreled with all of his children, and would have disinherited them if he could.

托尔斯泰和比他小十六岁的索菲娅之间存在着真挚的性爱，但他对她的福祉却漠不关心，甚至迫使她断绝了与一位和蔼音乐家的纯真友谊。她的日记于2010年以英文出版，我的老相识迈克尔·迪尔达对此书的评论尖锐犀利，为她伸张了迟来的正义：

There was authentic sexual passion between Tolstoy and Sophia, who was sixteen years younger, yet he manifested only the slightest interest in her welfare, and compelled her to break off an innocent friendship with a benign musician. The publication of her diaries in English (2010) was reviewed by my old acquaintance Michael Dirda with a pungency that rendered her belated justice:

在丈夫日记的一页上，勤恳的抄写员索菲娅偶然发现了这样一句话：“世上根本没有爱情，只有性交的生理需求和对生活伴侣的实际需要。 ”她尖刻地评论道：“我真希望29年前就读到这句话，那样我就不会嫁给他了。”

1910年，就在82岁的托尔斯泰逃离亚斯纳亚·波利亚纳，踏上最终导致他死于远离家乡的火车站的旅程前一个月，年近七旬的索菲娅庆祝了她的“命名日”，而这一天也是托尔斯泰向她求婚的日子。她不禁自问：“他究竟对那个十八岁的索涅奇卡·贝尔斯做了什么？她把自己的一生、爱情和信任都给了他。”她总结了他们共同生活的48年：“他用他的冷酷、残忍和极端的自私折磨着我。”

On one page of her husband’s diaries, devoted copyist Sofia comes across this sentence: “There is no such thing as love, only the physical need for intercourse and the practical need for a life companion.” She acidly comments: “I only wish I had read that 29 years ago, then I would never have married him.”…

In 1910, just a month before the 82-year-old Tolstoy fled Yasnaya Polyana on the trip that would lead to his death in a railway station far from his home, Sofia—now in her late 60s—celebrates her “name day,” which is also the day that Tolstoy proposed to her. She asks herself: “What did he do to that eighteen-year-old Sonechka Behrs, who gave him her whole life, her love and her trust?” She sums up the 48 years of their life together: “He has tortured me with his coldness, his cruelty and his extreme egotism.”

托尔斯泰的忠实女性读者可以为他惊人的成就而感激不尽，但无论男女，我们都应该感谢索涅奇卡·贝尔斯，并相信她对托尔斯泰人性弱点的描述。一些最伟大的作家也曾是自私自利的怪物。除了托尔斯泰，我们还可以想到但丁、弥尔顿、歌德、华兹华斯、维克多·雨果、易卜生、叶芝、托马斯·曼，以及风格更为温和的普鲁斯特和乔伊斯。从我们对塞万提斯、蒙田、莫里哀、莎士比亚、塞缪尔·约翰逊博士、简·奥斯汀、乔治·艾略特，以及我们这个时代的弗朗茨·卡夫卡和塞缪尔·贝克特的了解来看，文学的伟大与人性的光辉是可以并存的。

Devoted women readers of Tolstoy can be grateful for his astonishing achievement, but, women and men alike, we owe something also to Sonechka Behrs, and we have to be convinced by her testimony as to his human flaws. Some of the greatest writers have been monsters of egoism. In addition to Tolstoy we can think of Dante, Milton, Goethe, Wordsworth, Victor Hugo, Ibsen, Yeats, Thomas Mann, and in a gentler way Proust and Joyce. From what we know of Cervantes, Montaigne, Molière, Shakespeare, Dr. Samuel Johnson, Jane Austen, George Eliot, and in our time Franz Kafka and Samuel Beckett, literary greatness and humane splendor can coexist.

最近，我开始阅读莉迪亚·金兹伯格的《论心理散文》（1971年出版；贾德森·罗森格兰特译，1991年），想了解她对托尔斯泰小说中人物性格的深刻见解。我对她的其他作品了解不多，但令我惊讶的是，她讨论了蒙田，却只字未提莎士比亚和塞万提斯——正是他们与蒙田共同开创了我们今天所知的文学人物性格表现形式。尽管如此，她对托尔斯泰的思考仍然令我受益匪浅。

Recently, I have taken to reading Lydia Ginzburg’s On Psychological Prose (1971; translated by Judson Rosengrant, 1991) for her insights into personality in Tolstoy’s novels. I do not know much of her other work, but I’m surprised that she discusses Montaigne yet does not mention Shakespeare and Cervantes, who with Montaigne invented the literary representation of personality as we know it.
