It is just to observe that this is not so much suicide as it is Gudrun’s assassination of her lover.

德国雕塑家勒克（其名字源于北欧神话中的洛基，一个爱恶作剧的神祇），既带有同性恋色彩又阴郁神秘，他与古德伦结为好友，这种明显的亲密关系激怒了杰拉尔德。勒克邀请她与他一同前往德累斯顿，建立一段艺术关系：

The German sculptor Loerke (the name alludes to the Old Norse god Loki, a mischief maker), homoerotic and deathly, has become friendly with Gudrun and infuriates Gerald by this apparent intimacy. Loerke asks her to join him in Dresden in an aesthetic relationship:

“你不肯告诉我你要去哪里吗？”他问道。

“说真的，”她说，“我不知道。这要看风向了。”

他疑惑地看着她，然后抿了抿嘴，像西风神泽费罗斯吹过雪地一样。

“它流向德国，”他说。

“我也这么认为，”她笑着说。

突然，他们察觉到附近有个模糊的白色身影。那是杰拉尔德。古德伦的心猛地一跳，恐惧袭来，无比强烈。她猛地站了起来。

“他们告诉我你在哪里，”杰拉德的声音传来，如同暮色中一片苍白空气中的审判。

“玛丽亚！你像幽灵一样来了！”洛尔克惊呼道。

杰拉德没有回答。在他们看来，他的出现既不自然，又像个幽灵。

勒克摇晃了一下烧瓶，然后把它倒扣在雪地上。只有几滴棕色的液体缓缓流了出来。

“全没了！”他说。

在杰拉尔德眼里，那个矮小怪异的德国人身影清晰而客观，就像透过望远镜看到的那样。他极其厌恶这个小身影，恨不得把它抹去。

然后，洛尔克摇晃了一下装饼干的盒子。

“那里还有饼干，”他说。

他坐在雪橇上，伸手把饼干递给古德伦。古德伦笨手笨脚地接过一块。他本想把饼干递给杰拉尔德，但杰拉尔德显然不想吃饼干，于是洛克含糊地把盒子放到一边。然后他拿起小瓶子，对着光看了看。

“还有一些烈酒，”他自言自语道。

然后，他突然潇洒地将瓶子高高举起，一个怪异滑稽的身影向古德伦倾斜，说道：

“Gnädiges Fräulein，”他说，“哇——”

一声脆响，瓶子飞了出去，洛尔克向后退去，三人站在那里，激动得浑身颤抖。

洛克转向杰拉尔德，他那白皙的脸上露出一丝邪恶的笑容。

“干得好！”他用一种讽刺而狂热的语气说道。“这就是运动，毫无疑问。”

下一刻，他滑稽地坐在雪地里，杰拉尔德的拳头狠狠地砸在他的后脑勺上。但洛尔克强作镇定，颤抖着站起身来，直直地盯着杰拉尔德，身体虚弱而鬼祟，但眼神中却充满了讽刺的魔鬼般的意味。

“英雄万岁，英雄万岁——”

但他却畏缩了一下，只见一道黑光闪过，杰拉德的拳头击中了他，狠狠地撞在他脑袋的另一侧，把他像一根断了的稻草一样打飞到一边。

但古德伦继续向前。她高高举起紧握的手，然后猛地向下挥去，狠狠地击打在杰拉尔德的脸上和胸口。

一股巨大的震惊袭来，仿佛空气都破碎了。他的灵魂豁然开朗，惊叹不已，同时感受到了痛苦。然后，它笑了，转身伸出强有力的双手，终于摘下了他梦寐以求的苹果。他终于可以实现他的愿望了。

他用那双坚硬而无比有力的双手扼住了古德伦的喉咙。她的喉咙柔软得令人心醉，然而，他却能感受到其中滑溜溜的生命之弦。他碾碎了它，他能碾碎它。多么极乐！哦，多么极乐，终于，多么满足，终于！纯粹的满足感充盈着他的灵魂。他看着她肿胀的脸庞渐渐失去知觉，看着她的双眼翻白。她多么丑陋！多么圆满，多么满足！这感觉多么美好，哦，多么美好，多么神圣的恩赐，终于！他没有察觉到她的挣扎和反抗。那挣扎是她在这拥抱中回应的欲望，越是激烈，快感就越是狂喜，直到达到顶峰，危机来临，挣扎被压制，她的动作变得柔和，平静下来。

勒克在雪地上挣扎着醒来，他晕头转向，浑身疼痛，无法起身。只有他的眼睛还清醒着。

“先生！”他用微弱而激动的声音说道：“Quand vous aurez fini——”

一股强烈的厌恶和鄙夷涌上杰拉德的心头。这厌恶感直达他的灵魂深处，让他感到一阵恶心。啊，他到底在做什么？他究竟堕落到了何种地步！仿佛他真的在乎她到要杀了她，要把她的性命掌握在自己手中！

一股虚弱感席卷了他的全身，一种可怕的放松，一种解冻，一种力量的衰弱。不知不觉中，他松开了手，古德伦跪倒在地。他必须看到吗？他必须知道吗？

他感到一阵可怕的虚弱，关节仿佛化作了水。他像被风吹动一样，飘忽不定，最终随波逐流。

“我真的不想这样，”这是他灵魂深处最后的厌恶告白。他虚弱地、筋疲力尽地沿着山坡向上飘去，下意识地避开一切进一步的接触。“我受够了——我想睡觉。我受够了。”一阵恶心涌上心头。

他很虚弱，却不愿休息，他想一直走下去，直到生命的尽头。他再也不停留，直到走到生命的尽头，这就是他仅存的愿望。于是，他就这样漫无目的地游荡着，昏昏沉沉，虚弱无力，什么也不想，只要还能继续行动。

暮色笼罩着头顶，一片诡异而诡异的蓝玫瑰色光芒，寒冷的夜色沉入雪地。山谷下方，在厚厚的积雪中，有两个小小的身影：古德伦跪倒在地，如同被处决一般，而洛尔克则在她身旁倚靠着。仅此而已。

杰拉尔德在昏暗的蓝色光线下，跌跌撞撞地沿着雪坡向上攀爬，尽管疲惫不堪，却依然不知不觉地向上攀登。他的左侧是陡峭的斜坡，遍布黑色的岩石和崩落的石块，雪脉在黑色的岩石间蜿蜒曲折，隐隐约约地划破夜空。然而，周围一片寂静，这一切都悄无声息。

“You won’t tell me where you will go?” he asked.

“Really and truly,” she said, “I don’t know. It depends which way the wind blows.”

He looked at her quizzically, then he pursed up his lips, like Zephyrus, blowing across the snow.

“It goes towards Germany,” he said.

“I believe so,” she laughed.

Suddenly, they were aware of a vague white figure near them. It was Gerald. Gudrun’s heart leapt in sudden terror, profound terror. She rose to her feet.

“They told me where you were,” came Gerald’s voice, like a judgment in the whitish air of twilight.

“Maria! You come like a ghost,” exclaimed Loerke.

Gerald did not answer. His presence was unnatural and ghostly to them.

Loerke shook the flask—then he held it inverted over the snow. Only a few brown drops trickled out.

“All gone!” he said.

To Gerald, the smallish, odd figure of the German was distinct and objective, as if seen through field glasses. And he disliked the small figure exceedingly, he wanted it removed.

Then Loerke rattled the box which held the biscuits.

“Biscuits there are still,” he said.

And reaching from his seated posture in the sledge, he handed them to Gudrun. She fumbled, and took one. He would have held them to Gerald, but Gerald so definitely did not want to be offered a biscuit, that Loerke, rather vaguely, put the box aside. Then he took up the small bottle, and held it to the light.

“Also there is some Schnapps,” he said to himself.

Then suddenly, he elevated the bottle gallantly in the air, a strange, grotesque figure leaning towards Gudrun, and said:

“Gnädiges Fräulein,” he said, “wohl—”

There was a crack, the bottle was flying, Loerke had started back, the three stood quivering in violent emotion.

Loerke turned to Gerald, a devilish leer on his bright-skinned face.

“Well done!” he said, in a satirical demoniac frenzy. “C’est le sport, sans doute.”

The next instant he was sitting ludicrously in the snow, Gerald’s fist having rung against the side of his head. But Loerke pulled himself together, rose, quivering, looking full at Gerald, his body weak and furtive, but his eyes demoniacal with satire.

“Vive le héros, vive—”

But he flinched, as, in a black flash, Gerald’s fist came upon him, banged into the other side of his head, and sent him aside like a broken straw.

But Gudrun moved forward. She raised her clenched hand high, and brought it down, with a great downward stroke on to the face and on to the breast of Gerald.

A great astonishment burst upon him, as if the air had broken. Wide, wide his soul opened, in wonder, feeling the pain. Then it laughed, turning, with strong hands outstretched, at last to take the apple of his desire. At last he could finish his desire.

He took the throat of Gudrun between his hands, that were hard and indomitably powerful. And her throat was beautifully, so beautifully soft, save that, within, he could feel the slippery chords of her life. And this he crushed, this he could crush. What bliss! Oh what bliss, at last, what satisfaction, at last! The pure zest of satisfaction filled his soul. He was watching the unconsciousness come unto her swollen face, watching the eyes roll back. How ugly she was! What a fulfilment, what a satisfaction! How good this was, oh how good it was, what a God-given gratification, at last! He was unconscious of her fighting and struggling. The struggling was her reciprocal lustful passion in this embrace, the more violent it became, the greater the frenzy of delight, till the zenith was reached, the crisis, the struggle was overborne, her movement became softer, appeased.

Loerke roused himself on the snow, too dazed and hurt to get up. Only his eyes were conscious.

“Monsieur!” he said, in his thin, roused voice: “Quand vous aurez fini—”

A revulsion of contempt and disgust came over Gerald’s soul. The disgust went to the very bottom of him, a nausea. Ah, what was he doing, to what depths was he letting himself go! As if he cared about her enough to kill her, to have her life on his hands!

A weakness ran over his body, a terrible relaxing, a thaw, a decay of strength. Without knowing, he had let go his grip, and Gudrun had fallen to her knees. Must he see, must he know?

A fearful weakness possessed him, his joints were turned to water. He drifted, as on a wind, veered, and went drifting away.

“I didn’t want it, really,” was the last confession of disgust in his soul, as he drifted up the slope, weak, finished, only sheering off unconsciously from any further contact. “I’ve had enough—I want to go to sleep. I’ve had enough.” He was sunk under a sense of nausea.

He was weak, but he did not want to rest, he wanted to go on and on, to the end. Never again to stay, till he came to the end, that was all the desire that remained to him. So he drifted on and on, unconscious and weak, not thinking of anything, so long as he could keep in action.

The twilight spread a weird, unearthly light overhead, bluish-rose in colour, the cold blue night sank on the snow. In the valley below, behind, in the great bed of snow, were two small figures; Gudrun dropped on her knees, like one executed, and Loerke sitting propped up near her. That was all.

Gerald stumbled on up the slope of snow, in the bluish darkness, always climbing, always unconsciously climbing, weary though he was. On his left was a steep slope with black rocks and fallen masses of rock and veins of snow slashing in and about the blackness of rock, veins of snow slashing vaguely in and about the blackness of rock. Yet there was no sound, all this made no noise.

小说前文中，古德伦在亲吻杰拉尔德后扇了他一巴掌，并发誓要给他最后一击。在这里，她使出了浑身解数：

Earlier in the novel, having slapped Gerald after a kiss, Gudrun had vowed that she would give the last blow. Here she uses all her strength:

她高高举起紧握的手，然后猛地向下挥去，狠狠地击打在杰拉德的脸上和胸口上。

She raised her clenched hand high, and brought it down, with a great downward stroke on to the face and on to the breast of Gerald.

或许她救了可怜的洛克，但她实现了自己最深的愿望：杀死杰拉尔德。而杰拉尔德也渴望被杀，因为他身上带有该隐的印记——年轻时，他因枪击事故杀死了自己的兄弟。在几乎勒死古德伦之后，杰拉尔德选择了对他而言唯一的出路：

Perhaps she has saved the wretched Loerke, but she has accomplished her deepest desire: to murder Gerald. And he wants to be murdered, since he bears the mark of Cain, having killed his own brother in a gun accident in their youth. After nearly strangling Gudrun, Gerald chooses what for him is the only alternative:

他来到一个被陡峭山坡和悬崖环绕的雪谷，一条小路从雪谷延伸到山顶。但他漫无目的地游荡，直到脚下一滑，跌落谷底。就在他跌倒的那一刻，他的灵魂仿佛被撕裂，随即沉沉睡去。

He had come to the hollow basin of snow, surrounded by sheer slopes and precipices, out of which rose a track that brought one to the top of the mountain. But he wandered unconsciously, till he slipped and fell down, and as he fell something broke in his soul, and immediately he went to sleep.

有时我觉得这就是《恋爱中的女人》的阴暗魅力所在。无论劳伦斯的意图如何，杰拉尔德几乎从头到尾都令人难以产生共鸣。古德伦令我恐惧，但我似乎无法拒绝她。她的活力是消极的，却又暗示着人类逝去的可能性，而杰拉尔德的空虚则是持久且不可逆转的。或许劳伦斯在结尾处过于严苛，剥夺了古德伦除一种拙劣的讽刺和一种迟迟不愿转向自身的轻蔑之外的任何情感。伯金来看望杰拉尔德的遗体，并问古德伦，如果当局需要解释，他该如何应对：

Sometimes I think that this is the dark glory of Women in Love. Whatever Lawrence’s intentions, Gerald remains unsympathetic, almost from start to finish. Gudrun frightens me, but it seems not possible to reject her. Her vitalism is negative yet remains suggestive of lost human possibilities, whereas Gerald’s vacuity is prolonged and irreversible. Perhaps Lawrence was too severe at the close in denying Gudrun any affect except a poor irony and a contempt she delays turning upon herself. Birkin has come to see Gerald’s body and asks Gudrun what he can say to the authorities, if they require explanation:

古德伦抬起头看着他，脸色苍白，像个孩子一样，一言不发，满脸愁容。

“他们甚至一句话都没说，”她说。“他把洛克打倒在地，把他打晕，然后掐住我的脖子，几乎把我掐死了，之后他就走了。”

她自言自语道：

“这不就是永恒三角关系的一个绝佳例子吗！”说完，她讽刺地转过身去，因为她知道这场争斗原本只是她和杰拉德之间的事，第三者的出现不过是个偶然因素——或许是不可避免的偶然因素，但终究只是个偶然因素。不过，就让他们把这当成永恒三角关系、仇恨三位一体的例子吧。这样对他们来说更容易理解。

伯金走了，神情冷漠而疏离。但她知道他终究会为她做些事，他会帮她渡过难关。她不屑地轻笑一声。就让他去做吧，反正他那么擅长照顾别人。

Gudrun looked up at him, white, childlike, mute with trouble.

“There weren’t even any words,” she said. “He knocked Loerke down and stunned him, he half strangled me, then he went away.”

To herself she was saying:

“A pretty little sample of the eternal triangle!” And she turned ironically away, because she knew that the fight had been between Gerald and herself and that the presence of the third party was a mere contingency—an inevitable contingency perhaps, but a contingency none the less. But let them have it as an example of the eternal triangle, the trinity of hate. It would be simpler for them.

Birkin went away, his manner cold and abstracted. But she knew he would do things for her, nevertheless, he would see her through. She smiled slightly to herself, with contempt. Let him do the work, since he was so extremely good at looking after other people.

我内心深处对古德伦遭受的这种贬低感到愤慨。我更愿意记住她像个女祭司一样在长角牛群前跳舞，把它们吓跑的场景。

Something in me rebels at this debasement of Gudrun. I prefer to remember her dancing like a maenad in front of the horned cattle and frightening them away.

第35章

CHAPTER 35

尤利西斯（1922）

Ulysses (1922)

詹姆斯·艾姆斯·奥伊斯

JAMES JOYCE

二十世纪最重要的两部小说分别是马塞尔·普鲁斯特的《追忆似水年华》（ 1913年至1927年分章节出版，普鲁斯特本人于1922年去世，享年五十一岁）和詹姆斯·乔伊斯的《尤利西斯》（1917年至1922年创作，乔伊斯于1941年去世，享年不到五十九岁）。我不认为普鲁斯特读过乔伊斯的作品，尽管他们曾在巴黎的一次晚宴上相遇，并互相抱怨彼此的身体状况不佳。乔伊斯读过《追忆似水年华》（1913），觉得它平平无奇，但还是参加了普鲁斯特的葬礼。

THE MAJOR NOVELS of the twentieth century are Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, which was published in sections from 1913 to 1927, Proust himself dying in 1922 at the age of fifty-one, and the Ulysses of James Joyce, composed between 1917 and 1922. Joyce died in 1941, not quite fifty-nine. I do not believe that Proust ever read Joyce, though they met at one Parisian dinner, and complained to each other about their mutual bad health. Joyce read Swann’s Way (1913) and thought it was quite ordinary, but nevertheless attended Proust’s funeral.

我能想到的能与普鲁斯特和《尤利西斯》相提并论的作品只有一部，那就是乔伊斯耗费十七年心血，于1939年出版的《芬尼根守灵夜》 。如果非要在《普鲁斯特》、 《尤利西斯》和《芬尼根守灵夜》之间做出选择，我会非常不舍。就情感而言， 《追忆似水年华》更能触动我的内心，但《芬尼根守灵夜》读过几遍之后，你会发现它妙趣横生；而《尤利西斯》的内涵之丰富，几乎可以与但丁和莎士比亚相媲美。读者更容易接受《普鲁斯特》和《尤利西斯》，而不是《芬尼根守灵夜》。我希望在离开之前至少再重读一遍《芬尼根守灵夜》 ，而《普鲁斯特》和《尤利西斯》我每年都会重读好几遍。

I can think of only one peer of Proust and Ulysses, and that has to be Finnegans Wake, published by Joyce in 1939 after seventeen years of extraordinary labor. If forced to choose between Proust, Ulysses, and the Wake, I would be very unhappy. Emotionally, I am more turned inside out by In Search of Lost Time, but the Wake is hilarious, once you have read it a few times, and Ulysses has a richness that all but rivals Dante and Shakespeare. Readers are likelier to absorb Proust and Ulysses than to accommodate the Wake. I hope to reread all of Finnegans Wake at least once more ere I depart, but I reread Proust and Ulysses several times a year.

解读乔伊斯《尤利西斯》的方式有很多种。这部小说以1904年6月16日为背景，主人公是38岁的利奥波德·布鲁姆。在世界文学史上，这一天被称为“布鲁姆日”，也是诺拉·巴纳克尔和詹姆斯·乔伊斯第一次约会的日子。他们一同离开都柏林前往欧洲大陆，在那里他们成为了伴侣，并育有两个孩子：乔治和露西娅。乔治曾尝试成为一名职业歌手，但他明智地爱上了一位美国女继承人，并将唱歌作为业余爱好。露西娅患有精神分裂症，不得不长期住院治疗。1931年，诺拉和乔伊斯勉强结为夫妻。

There are many ways to read through Joyce’s Ulysses. It depicts the day of June 16, 1904, with Leopold Bloom, aged thirty-eight, as its protagonist. In the world’s literary calendar this is known as Bloomsday, and was also the day of the first date between Nora Barnacle and James Joyce, who left Dublin together for the Continent, remained partners, and had two children, Giorgio and Lucia. Giorgio attempted a career as a professional singer but wisely fell in love with an American heiress and was able to treat singing as an avocation. Lucia was schizophrenic and had to be permanently institutionalized. Rather reluctantly, Nora and Joyce were formally married in 1931.

利奥波德·布鲁姆的父亲鲁道夫·维拉格是匈牙利犹太人，他改名为鲁道夫·布鲁姆，并在与艾伦·希金斯结婚后皈依基督教。利奥波德，或者我们不妨像乔伊斯一样称他为波尔迪，从小接受新教教育，因此没有接受割礼。波尔迪为了迎娶莫莉·特威迪——小说中那位令人惊艳的莫莉·布鲁姆——而改信罗马天主教。鲁道夫·布鲁姆最终自杀身亡。莫莉和波尔迪育有一女米莉，但他们的儿子鲁迪出生仅十一天便夭折了。

Leopold Bloom had a Hungarian Jewish father, Rudolf Virag, who changed his name to Rudolph Bloom and converted to Protestantism when he married Ellen Higgins. Leopold or Poldy, as we will join Joyce in calling him, was raised a Protestant and therefore was uncircumcised. Poldy converted to Roman Catholicism to marry Molly Tweedy, the astonishing Molly Bloom of the novel. Rudolph Bloom died by his own hand. Molly and Poldy have a daughter, Milly, but their son, Rudy, died only eleven days old.

由于波尔迪的母亲和祖母都是基督徒，根据《塔木德》，他并不被视为犹太人。这便成了一个相当复杂的问题。尽管他曾是一个不信教的新教徒，也曾是一个不虔诚的天主教徒，但波尔迪自认为是犹太人，整个都柏林也都这样认为。詹姆斯·乔伊斯为何要在他的《尤利西斯》中赋予人物某种犹太身份呢？

Poldy, since both his mother and grandmother were Christian, would not be considered Jewish by the Talmud. This becomes a rather complex matter. Though he has been both an unbelieving Protestant and a faithless Catholic, Poldy considers himself to be Jewish, and all of Dublin regards him as such. Why did James Joyce want some kind of Jewish identity for his Ulysses?

大多数评论家一致认为，可能的答案是，詹姆斯·乔伊斯于1904年与诺拉·巴纳克尔离开爱尔兰前往欧洲大陆，并一直生活在国外直至1941年去世。他一生的大部分时间都自愿远离都柏林。然而，他所有的作品都围绕着都柏林及其市民展开。乔伊斯经常自比为新但丁，但丁被迫离开佛罗伦萨的苦涩经历成为他生活和创作的典范，只是詹姆斯·乔伊斯拒绝屈服于苦涩。波尔迪·布卢姆在都柏林感到自在，但他的同胞却视他为异乡人，一个漂泊的犹太人。

The possible answer, as most critics agree, is that James Joyce left Ireland for the European continent in 1904 with Nora Barnacle, and lived abroad until his death in 1941. Most of his life was spent in voluntary exile from Dublin. Yet all of his writing centers on Dublin and its citizens. Joyce frequently thought of himself as the new Dante, and the bitterness of Dante’s forced exile from Florence became the model for his life and work, except that James Joyce refused to yield to bitterness. Poldy Bloom feels at home in Dublin, yet his fellow citizens consider him alien, a Wandering Jew.

乔伊斯放弃都柏林，也意味着他放弃了出生并受洗的罗马天主教信仰。他对新教更是毫无兴趣，无论从性情还是信仰上，都绝非虔诚之人。乔伊斯效仿威廉·布莱克，抛弃了神父和国王，但布莱克始终认为自己是基督徒，即便他只是个独行的教派成员。波尔迪几乎对他的犹太祖先传统一无所知。他与詹姆斯·乔伊斯和威廉·莎士比亚一样世俗。在《尤利西斯》的深层含义中，波尔迪既是莎士比亚，又是乔伊斯。这正是乔伊斯的用意。尽管他欣赏丹尼尔·笛福、古斯塔夫·福楼拜、威廉·华兹华斯和珀西·比希·雪莱等风格迥异的作家，乔伊斯却有意与但丁和莎士比亚展开一场较量。他的抱负的确堪比荷马史诗；他渴望与但丁和莎士比亚并肩，甚至超越他们。

By abandoning Dublin, Joyce also renounced the Roman Catholicism into which he had been born and baptized. He had even less use for Protestantism and in no way can be regarded as religious, either in temperament or in conviction. Joyce emulated William Blake in casting out both priest and king, but Blake always regarded himself as a Christian even if he was in a sect of one. Poldy knows almost nothing about his ancestral Jewish tradition. He is as secular as James Joyce and William Shakespeare. At the deepest level of Ulysses, Poldy is Shakespeare and Joyce. This is Joyce’s design. Though he admired writers as diverse as Daniel Defoe and Gustave Flaubert, William Wordsworth and Percy Bysshe Shelley, Joyce consciously staged an agon with Dante and with Shakespeare. His aspirations were indeed Homeric; he desired to make a third with Dante and Shakespeare or even to surpass them.

除了弥尔顿和托尔斯泰之外，我想不出还有哪位作家像他那样雄心勃勃。像歌德、普希金、维克多·雨果、巴尔扎克、曼佐尼、简·奥斯汀、狄更斯、梅尔维尔、乔治·艾略特、普鲁斯特、卡夫卡和叶芝这样伟大的作家，都明智地避免了直接模仿但丁或莎士比亚。

I cannot think of another writer that ambitious, with the likely exceptions of Milton and of Tolstoy. Figures as grand as Goethe, Pushkin, Victor Hugo, Balzac, Manzoni, Jane Austen, Dickens, Melville, George Eliot, Proust, Kafka, and Yeats judiciously held back from too direct an emulation of Dante or of Shakespeare.

要想与但丁和莎士比亚比肩，就必须重塑语言，改变表现方式。我实在无力评判詹姆斯·乔伊斯是否实现了他自己的创作目标，从而与但丁和莎士比亚并肩登上文学的巅峰。但如果不是乔伊斯，那又是谁呢？当你充分领略了《都柏林人》、 《青年艺术家画像》、《流亡者》、《尤利西斯》，甚至《芬尼根守灵夜》的精髓之后，你便可以开始思考乔伊斯文学追求的更广阔背景。

To rival Dante and Shakespeare, you have to remake language and change modes of representation. I am hardly competent to judge whether James Joyce so fulfilled his own project as to join Dante and Shakespeare on the final heights. But if not Joyce, then who? Once you have fully enjoyed the reading of Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Exiles, Ulysses, even Finnegans Wake, you can begin to consider the larger contexts of Joyce’s literary desires.

关于乔伊斯与但丁的​​关系，有三部非常优秀的论述。第一部是玛丽·T·雷诺兹（Mary T. Reynolds）的《乔伊斯与但丁：塑造想象力》 （Joyce and Dante: The Shaping Imagination ，1981）。我至今仍清晰地记得在耶鲁大学期间与玛丽·雷诺兹和玛丽·埃尔曼（Mary Ellmann）共饮茶点的美好时光。她们两位都是风趣、善良、才华横溢的女性，比我年长许多，我很高兴能与她们相伴，并从中学习。玛丽·雷诺兹对乔伊斯与但丁的​​研究，着重探讨了《神曲》中的父权形象及其在乔伊斯作品中的复兴。乔伊斯从但丁独立自主的思想和修辞手法中找到了反抗天主教的先例。另一部精彩的论著是露西亚·博尔德里尼（Lucia Boldrini）的《乔伊斯、但丁与文学关系诗学》（Joyce, Dante, and the Poetics of Literary Relations，2001），该书研究了但丁对《芬尼根守灵夜》的影响。最近，詹姆斯·罗宾逊的《乔伊斯的但丁》（2016 年）追溯了从雪莱和拜伦到但丁·加布里埃尔·罗塞蒂的十九世纪传统，该传统将非正统的但丁传承给了乔伊斯。

There are three very good discussions of Joyce’s relation to Dante. The first is Joyce and Dante: The Shaping Imagination by Mary T. Reynolds (1981). I have the happiest memories of many teas shared with Mary Reynolds and Mary Ellmann during the years they were at Yale. Both were witty, kind, brilliant women considerably older than I, and I was glad to sit in their company and learn. Mary Reynolds’s study of Joyce and Dante meditates upon the paternal figures of the Commedia and their resurrection in the panoply of Joycean works. Joyce found precedent for his own rebellion against Catholicism in Dante’s own independence of thought and of figuration. Another vivid treatise is Lucia Boldrini’s Joyce, Dante, and the Poetics of Literary Relations (2001), which studies Dante’s influence on Finnegans Wake. More recently, there is James Robinson’s Joyce’s Dante (2016), which traces the unorthodox Dante bequeathed to Joyce by the nineteenth-century tradition that moves from Shelley and Byron to Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

近几代英美学者对但丁的研究倾向于将但丁描绘成一位神学化的但丁，一位诗人，他更关注托马斯·阿奎那和奥古斯丁，而非他与布鲁内托·拉蒂尼、圭多·卡瓦尔坎蒂和圭多·圭尼泽利之间的文学较量。圭尼泽利是抒情诗“甜美新风格”的创始人，但丁承认这是他创作的起点之一。卡瓦尔坎蒂是但丁最好的朋友，对他影响深远；布鲁内托·拉蒂尼是但丁的老师，也是《宝藏集》（ Tesoretto或Tesoro）的作者，这部作品为但丁创作《神曲》提供了范例。

Anglo-American Dante scholarship of the last few generations tends to give us a theological Dante, a poet more intent on Aquinas and Augustine than on his own literary agon with Brunetto Latini, Guido Cavalcanti, and Guido Guinizelli. The latter was the inventor of the lyrical “sweet new style” that Dante acknowledged as one starting point. Cavalcanti was Dante’s best friend and a strong influence upon him; Brunetto Latini was his teacher and the author of the Tesoretto or Tesoro, which served Dante as an example for the Commedia.

恩斯特·罗伯特·库尔提乌斯（Ernst Robert Curtius）的《欧洲文学与拉丁中世纪》（European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages， 1953年英译本）是我解读但丁作为诗人而非神学家的起点。在天主教的救赎体系中，但丁赋予贝阿特丽切崇高的地位。她最终不仅激励但丁，也激励所有罗马天主教信徒走上正道。但丁的成就如此伟大，以至于教会最终欣然接纳了他。然而，正如库尔提乌斯所坚持的，对贝阿特丽切的颂扬要么是异端邪说，要么是神话。问题是：究竟是哪一种？库尔提乌斯认为，这种颂扬显然与诺斯替主义有关，或许并非源于诺斯替主义，但肯定是一种体系或建构。

Ernst Robert Curtius in his European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages, translated into English in 1953, was my own starting point in reading Dante as a poet and not as a theologian. Beatrice is granted by Dante a high place in the Catholic scheme of salvation. She will ultimately inspire not only Dante but all Roman Catholic believers to take the true path. So great was Dante’s achievement that in time the Church was glad to subsume him. Still, as Curtius insists, the glorification of Beatrice is either heresy or myth. The question is: of what kind? Curtius answers that this glorification is clearly related to Gnosticism, perhaps not in origin but certainly as a scheme or construction.

詹姆斯·乔伊斯对教会的反叛是永久性的，他显然在但丁身上找到了与正统教义的不同之处，这可以帮助这位年轻的爱尔兰作家在寻求与拉丁传统巅峰诗人认同的过程中找到自己的位置。

James Joyce, whose rebellion against the Church was permanent, evidently found in Dante a difference from orthodoxy that could aid the young Irish writer in his quest toward identity with the culminating poet of the Latin tradition.

但丁对维吉尔在伊壁鸠鲁传统中的地位必然有所扭曲。这位《神曲》的诗人从未听说过卢克莱修，而卢克莱修的伊壁鸠鲁主义杰作《物性论》对维吉尔的《埃涅阿斯纪》产生了深远的影响。直到1417年，卢克莱修的完整著作才在德国的一座修道院中被重新发现。作为这两部诗作的爱好者，我每次重读《埃涅阿斯纪》时，都会觉得维吉尔面前仿佛摆着一本卢克莱修的著作，这印证了他对人类苦难的伊壁鸠鲁式态度。但丁笔下的维吉尔被基督教化，成为了一个寻求恩典的人，但在但丁的构想中，历史上的维吉尔应该身处地狱，与伟大的法里纳塔并肩而立。法里纳塔笔下的维吉尔直立于燃烧的墓穴之中，仿佛对地狱充满了蔑视。

Dante had a necessarily distorted sense of Virgil’s place in that tradition. The poet of the Commedia had never heard of Lucretius, whose Epicurean masterpiece, De rerum natura, is an overwhelming influence upon Virgil’s Aeneid. It was not until 1417 that a complete Lucretius was rediscovered in a German monastery. As a lover of both poems, I cannot reread the Aeneid without the sensation that Virgil had a copy of Lucretius in front of him, confirming his Epicurean stance toward human suffering. Dante’s Virgil is Christianized into a seeker after grace, but in Dante’s scheme the historical Virgil belongs in the Inferno, side by side with the great Farinata, who stands upright in his flaming tomb, as if of hell he had a great disdain.

卢克莱修的影响似乎渗透到了后世作家之中，从马洛和莎士比亚，到雪莱和丁尼生，最终在《尤利西斯》和《芬尼根守灵夜》中达到顶峰。波尔迪并未读过卢克莱修，但他对苦难和死亡的态度带有伊壁鸠鲁主义色彩，似乎与詹姆斯·乔伊斯不谋而合。无论是《尤利西斯》还是《芬尼根守灵夜》，任何标签都难以准确定义。即使波尔迪的史诗结构带有荷马史诗的影子，你也无法将其描述为荷马史诗。或许唯一恰当的词是“完整”。利奥波德·布鲁姆如同奥德修斯，是一个完整的人；如同他笔下的都柏林，他更偏向喜剧而​​非悲剧，但他似乎是他所处世界中最有人情味的人。

Lucretius has a way of contaminating later writers, from Marlowe and Shakespeare on through Shelley and Tennyson and culminating in Ulysses and Finnegans Wake. Poldy has not read Lucretius, but his stance toward suffering and death is Epicurean and seems to be consonant with that of James Joyce. No labels will work, for either Ulysses or the Wake. You cannot even describe Poldy’s epic as Homeric despite its scaffolding. Perhaps the only word that will work is “completeness.” Leopold Bloom, like Odysseus, is the complete man and, like his Dublin, he is comic rather than tragic, except that he appears to be the most humane individual in his world.

我年少时读过奥尔德斯·赫胥黎的散文《悲剧与全部真相》（1931），并深受启发。虽然半个多世纪以来我都没再重读过这篇文章，但我仍然记得其中的要点：在《奥德赛》中，奥德修斯和其他幸存者在经历了各种灾难，失去了许多同伴之后，只是短暂地哀悼了一下，便继续享用美食美酒，然后酣然入睡。这种“全部真相”的模式在雅典悲剧和莎士比亚的悲剧中是行不通的。詹姆斯·乔伊斯在《尤利西斯》中试图为非同寻常的读者呈现一些普遍真理。他曾对弗兰克·巴德根说过，无论《尤利西斯》和《芬尼根守灵夜》的语言多么丰富，他想要表达的其实很简单。这话不无道理，尤其在《尤利西斯》中更是如此。但在《芬尼根守灵夜》中，华丽的语言与朴素的情节之间的不协调，或许会成为其吸引更广泛读者群的一大障碍。

When I was very young, I read and was impressed by Aldous Huxley’s essay “Tragedy and the Whole Truth” (1931). I have not reread it for more than half a century, but I remember the essential point: in the Odyssey, after losing a number of their shipmates to various hazards, Odysseus and the other survivors mourn briefly, and then turn to their meat and wine and subsequent sleep. In Athenian and Shakespearean tragedy, this wholeness would not work. James Joyce in Ulysses desires to give us common truths for uncommon readers. He remarked to Frank Budgen that, however rich the language of Ulysses and the Wake became, what he meant to convey was quite simple. There is some truth in that, particularly in Ulysses, but in the Wake the disproportion between the extraordinary language and the simple actions may be a permanent impediment to a wider readership.

我打算在本章后面谈谈《守灵夜》 ，或许会有一些帮助，但现在我先回到《尤利西斯》。许多喜爱这部小说的人最推崇的是“瑟茜”，即午夜时分夜城妓院的幻觉；或是“佩内洛普”，即莫莉·布卢姆在凌晨时的内心独白。我并不反对这样的评价，但我最钟情于开篇的“忒勒马科斯”，故事发生在早上八点的马泰罗塔，斯蒂芬·迪达勒斯支付了房租，而卑鄙的马拉基（巴克）·穆里根却拿到了钥匙，剥夺了斯蒂芬的住所。巴克·穆里根让奥利弗·圣约翰·戈加蒂获得了某种可疑的永生，如今人们记住他，仅仅是因为乔伊斯笔下这位昔日好友兼酒友的生动刻画。戈加蒂于1957年在纽约去世，享年七十九岁。当他因败诉和爱尔兰共和军烧毁他的房子而心怀怨恨地离开爱尔兰时，他去了伦敦，然后又去了美国，把家人留在了身后。

I intend to say something that may be helpful about the Wake later in this chapter, but here I return to Ulysses. Many who love the novel set highest the “Circe,” the midnight hallucinatory vision of the Nighttown whorehouse, or the “Penelope,” the internal monologue of Molly Bloom in the small hours. I would not quarrel with such judgments, but I care most for the opening “Telemachus,” set at 8:00 a.m. in the Martello Tower, for which Stephen Dedalus has paid the rent, while the egregious Malachi (Buck) Mulligan secures the key and so dispossesses Stephen. Buck Mulligan has given a dubious immortality to Oliver St. John Gogarty, who is now remembered only for Joyce’s exuberant portrait of his former friend and drinking companion. Gogarty died in New York City in 1957, aged seventy-nine. When he abandoned Ireland, embittered by lost lawsuits and the burning of his house by the IRA, he went to London, but then on to the United States, leaving his family behind him.

在遭遇种种挫折之前，戈加蒂在爱尔兰的职业生涯可谓辉煌，他是一位文学家、政治家、外科医生和运动员。他与叶芝、乔治·摩尔以及亚瑟·格里菲斯和迈克尔·柯林斯等爱尔兰反抗英国斗争中的重要人物关系密切。内战爆发后，戈加蒂成为爱尔兰自由邦的参议员，并亲历了格里菲斯的去世和柯林斯的遇刺。1922年，《尤利西斯》出版的那一年，爱尔兰共和军绑架了戈加蒂，意图谋杀他。凭借机智和毅力，他成功逃脱，纵身跃入利菲河，凭借游泳健将的身份，他轻松游回岸边。他曾许诺给利菲河两只天鹅，并最终兑现了诺言。

Until his various debacles, Gogarty enjoyed a remarkable career in Ireland, as a literary figure, a politician, a surgeon, and an athlete. He was close to W. B. Yeats and George Moore, as well as to Arthur Griffith and Michael Collins, important figures in the Irish struggle against England. When civil war ignited Ireland, Gogarty became an Irish Free State senator and had to endure the death of Griffith and the assassination of Michael Collins. In 1922, the year Ulysses was published, the IRA kidnapped Gogarty with the intent of murdering him. By wit and stamina, he escaped, leaped into the River Liffey, and, being a champion swimmer, had no trouble getting to safety. Famously, he promised the Liffey two swans and kept his word.

我只见过戈加蒂一次，大约是在1955年，在格林威治村的白马酒馆。在那里，我欣赏了他略带醉意的雄辩和朗诵。然而，即使他已年过七旬，我仍然能从他身上看到不朽的巴克·穆里根的影子。他热情奔放、粗俗不堪、油腔滑调，却又莫名地令人不安。我读过他的一些诗，都没什么令人印象深刻的，还有那本滑稽的《当我沿着萨克维尔街走下去》，这是一部虚构的回忆录，其中叶芝、乔伊斯和其他一些爱尔兰文学和政治名人被漫画化了。这本书最终让戈加蒂破产，因为他被辛克莱兄弟中的一位告上了法庭。辛克莱兄弟是都柏林的一位犹太人，也是艺术品经销商。这场官司对他不利，因为他显然在一些相当糟糕的反犹太主义诗句中诽谤了他们，这些诗句不值得在此引用。审判中一个引人入胜的片段是年轻的塞缪尔·贝克特的证词，他的一位姑姑嫁给了辛克莱兄弟中的一位。戈加蒂的律师称贝克特为“来自巴黎的放荡不羁的亵渎神明者”。我有幸在巴黎和纽约分别与贝克特有过两次短暂的会面，因此我不得不对这种描述感到震惊。贝克特温文尔雅、和蔼可亲，令人惋惜的是他高尚的品格，他曾是法国抵抗纳粹的英雄。

I met Gogarty only once, in about 1955, at the White Horse Tavern in Greenwich Village, where I enjoyed his somewhat intoxicated eloquence and recitations. And yet I could see in him, even in his seventies, the traits of the immortal Buck Mulligan. He was fierce, ribald, unctuous, yet somehow disquieting. I had read some of his poems, none of them impressive, and the rollicking As I Was Going Down Sackville Street, a fictionalized memoir in which Yeats, Joyce, and other Irish literary and political notables are caricatured. The book eventually ruined Gogarty financially, as he was sued by one of the Sinclair brothers, Dublin art dealers who were Jewish. The case was decided against him, since clearly he had slandered them in some rather bad anti-Semitic verses, not worth quoting here. A charming element in the trial was the testimony of the young Samuel Beckett, one of whose aunts had been married to a Sinclair brother. A lawyer for Gogarty referred to Beckett as “the bawd and blasphemer from Paris.” As someone privileged to have met Beckett, just twice and briefly, in Paris and in New York City, I have to be charmed by the description. Beckett was gentle, kind, sadly noble, and had been a hero of the French Resistance against the Nazis.

最后，我来到了《尤利西斯》优美的开篇，也就是“忒勒马科斯”部分的开头：

I come at last to the beautiful opening of Ulysses, leading off the “Telemachus” section:

身材魁梧、略显臃肿的巴克·穆里根从楼梯口走下来，手里端着一碗泡沫剃须膏，碗上交叉放着一面镜子和一把剃刀。一件未系腰带的黄色晨衣在他身后，被清晨的微风轻轻托起。他高举着碗，低声说道：

— Introibo ad altare Dei.

他停下脚步，向下望去，只见黑暗蜿蜒的楼梯通向楼上，粗声粗气地喊道：

—上来吧，金奇！上来吧，你这胆小的耶稣会士。

他庄严地走上前，登上圆形的炮架。他环顾四周，郑重地三次祝福了这座塔楼、周围的乡村和正在苏醒的群山。然后，他看到了斯蒂芬·迪达勒斯，便俯身朝他走去，快速地在空中划十字，喉咙里发出咕噜咕噜的声音，同时摇着头。斯蒂芬·迪达勒斯不悦且昏昏欲睡，双臂倚在楼梯顶端，冷冷地看着那张颤抖着、发出咕噜声的脸——那张脸修长如马，还有那浅色的、未经修剪的头发，纹理和颜色都像浅橡树。

巴克·穆里根从镜子底下瞥了一眼，然后迅速盖上了碗。

“回营房去！”他严厉地说。

他用传教士的语气补充道：

——亲爱的，这才是真正的克里斯汀：身、魂、血、父。请放慢音乐。先生们，闭上眼睛。稍等片刻。关于那些白细胞，有点小问题。所有人保持安静。

他侧过头，发出了一声悠长的哨声，然后停顿片刻，全神贯注地听着，洁白的牙齿间或闪着金光。“金口圣徒。”两声尖锐而响亮的哨声打破了寂静。

“谢谢，老兄，”他干脆利落地说道，“这样就行了。把电源关掉好吗？”

他从枪架上跳下来，神情严肃地看着他的观察者，拢了拢长袍松散的衣褶。那张饱满的、阴影笼罩的脸庞和阴郁的椭圆形下巴，让人想起中世纪的艺术赞助人，一位教士。他嘴角悄然浮现出一丝和蔼的微笑。

“真是滑稽，”他兴高采烈地说，“你这荒唐的名字，居然是个古希腊名字！”

他友好地指了指，然后笑着走到城垛边。斯蒂芬·迪达勒斯走上前，疲惫地跟着他走到一半，坐在炮架边缘，静静地看着他把镜子支在城垛上，把刷子蘸进碗里，往脸颊和脖子上抹泡沫。

（《尤利西斯》， Everyman's Library版）

Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed. A yellow dressinggown, ungirdled, was sustained gently behind him by the mild morning air. He held the bowl aloft and intoned:

—Introibo ad altare Dei.

Halted, he peered down the dark winding stairs and called up coarsely:

—Come up, Kinch! Come up, you fearful jesuit.

Solemnly he came forward and mounted the round gunrest. He faced about and blessed gravely thrice the tower, the surrounding country and the awaking mountains. Then, catching sight of Stephen Dedalus, he bent towards him and made rapid crosses in the air, gurgling in his throat and shaking his head. Stephen Dedalus, displeased and sleepy, leaned his arms on the top of the staircase and looked coldly at the shaking gurgling face that blessed him, equine in its length, and at the light untonsured hair, grained and hued like pale oak.

Buck Mulligan peeped an instant under the mirror and then covered the bowl smartly.

—Back to barracks! he said sternly.

He added in a preacher’s tone:

—For this, O dearly beloved, is the genuine Christine: body and soul and blood and ouns. Slow music, please. Shut your eyes, gents. One moment. A little trouble about those white corpuscles. Silence, all.

He peered sideways up and gave a long slow whistle of call, then paused awhile in rapt attention, his even white teeth glistening here and there with gold points. Chrysostomos. Two strong shrill whistles answered through the calm.

—Thanks, old chap, he cried briskly. That will do nicely. Switch off the current, will you?

He skipped off the gunrest and looked gravely at his watcher, gathering about his legs the loose folds of his gown. The plump shadowed face and sullen oval jowl recalled a prelate, patron of arts in the middle ages. A pleasant smile broke quietly over his lips.

—The mockery of it, he said gaily. Your absurd name, an ancient Greek!

He pointed his finger in friendly jest and went over to the parapet, laughing to himself. Stephen Dedalus stepped up, followed him wearily halfway and sat down on the edge of the gunrest, watching him still as he propped his mirror on the parapet, dipped the brush in the bowl and lathered cheeks and neck.

(Ulysses, Everyman’s Library Edition)

对我而言，要描述《忒勒马科斯》的辉煌绝妙，是一项艰巨的评论任务。1947年9月，我在康奈尔书店买到了我的第一本《尤利西斯》。我立刻就爱上了“高贵丰腴的巴克·穆里根”这几个字，一遍又一遍地在舌尖回味。它们当时感觉妙不可言，现在依然如此。即使在开篇这一段，乔伊斯也流露出对巴克的善意厌恶。然而，随着斯蒂芬和穆里根之间鲜明对比的刻画，整篇的语调流畅自然。从巴克身上，我们能感受到一种居高临下的喜爱，以及对代达罗斯的谨慎敬意。而从斯蒂芬的沉默中，我们则能感受到他最终将拥抱的流放和狡诈。

To describe the splendor of “Telemachus” is for me a difficult critical task. I purchased my first copy of Ulysses in the Cornell bookstore in September 1947. At once I fell in love with the words “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan,” rolling them over and over on my tongue. They felt and still feel delicious. Even in this opening passage, Joyce conveys an amiable distaste for the Buck. The tone, however, flows smoothly as the contrast between Stephen and Mulligan is vividly etched. One hears in the Buck a condescending affection mixed with a wary respect for Dedalus. In Stephen’s silence we hear the exile and cunning he will come to embrace.

“告诉我，穆里根，”斯蒂芬轻声说道。

-是的亲爱的？

—海恩斯将在这座塔里待多久？

巴克·穆里根露出右肩上方刮过的脸颊。

“天哪，他真是太可怕了！”他直言不讳地说，“一个笨拙的撒克逊人。他觉得你不是个绅士。天哪，这些该死的英国佬！满脑子都是钱，还消化不良。就因为他来自牛津。你知道吗，戴达勒斯，你才真正有牛津人的风度。他根本认不出你。哦，我给你起的名字最好听：金奇，刀锋。”

他小心翼翼地刮着下巴上的胡子。

“他整晚都在念叨黑豹，”斯蒂芬说，“他的枪盒在哪儿？”

“真是个疯子！”穆里根说，“你当时心情不好吗？”

“我当时确实在，”斯蒂芬语气激动，但恐惧却与日俱增。“我跟一个我不认识的男人待在这儿，在黑漆漆的外面，他一边胡言乱语一边呻吟着要射杀一只黑豹。你救过溺水的人。但我可不是什么英雄。如果他继续待在这儿，我就走了。”

—Tell me, Mulligan, Stephen said quietly.

—Yes, my love?

—How long is Haines going to stay in this tower?

Buck Mulligan showed a shaven cheek over his right shoulder.

—God, isn’t he dreadful? he said frankly. A ponderous Saxon. He thinks you’re not a gentleman. God, these bloody English! Bursting with money and indigestion. Because he comes from Oxford. You know, Dedalus, you have the real Oxford manner. He can’t make you out. O, my name for you is the best: Kinch, the knife-blade.

He shaved warily over his chin.

—He was raving all night about a black panther, Stephen said. Where is his guncase?

—A woful lunatic! Mulligan said. Were you in a funk?

—I was, Stephen said with energy and growing fear. Out here in the dark with a man I don’t know raving and moaning to himself about shooting a black panther. You saved men from drowning. I’m not a hero, however. If he stays on here I am off.

“Kinch”是苏格兰语，意为绳圈或绳索的套索。想必穆里根将“套索”与“刀刃”联系起来，再次暗示了他对斯蒂芬能力的某种恐惧。戈加蒂曾救起四名溺水者，但乔伊斯却像他的波尔迪一样平和，避免暴力。斯蒂芬无处可去，却仍然选择离开，他对穆里根所谓的友谊心存疑虑。

“Kinch” is a Scottish word for a loop or noose of a rope. Presumably, Mulligan associates “noose” and “knife-blade,” again intimating a certain fear of Stephen’s capacities. Gogarty had saved four men from drowning, but Joyce was as peaceful as his Poldy and avoided violence. Stephen has nowhere to go but chooses departure anyway, distrustful of Mulligan’s professed friendship:

“看看你自己，”他说，“你这个糟糕的吟游诗人！”

斯蒂芬俯身凝视着递到他面前的镜子，镜子上有一道歪斜的裂缝，头发都竖了起来。镜子上写着：他和其他人眼中的我。是谁为我选择了这张脸？这个用来除虫的杂役。它也在问我。

“我从女佣房间里偷来的，”巴克·穆里根说，“她戴着挺合适的。姑妈总是给马拉基雇相貌平平的仆人。别让他陷入诱惑。她的名字叫乌苏拉。”

他又笑了起来，把镜子从斯蒂芬窥视的目光中拿开。

他说，那就像卡利班因为在镜子里看不到自己的脸而愤怒一样。如果王尔德还活着，他一定会看到你。

斯蒂芬后退一步，指着前方，苦涩地说：

——它是爱尔兰艺术的象征。那是仆人的裂纹镜子。

—Look at yourself, he said, you dreadful bard!

Stephen bent forward and peered at the mirror held out to him, cleft by a crooked crack, hair on end. As he and others see me. Who chose this face for me? This dogsbody to rid of vermin. It asks me too.

—I pinched it out of the skivvy’s room, Buck Mulligan said. It does her all right. The aunt always keeps plain-looking servants for Malachi. Lead him not into temptation. And her name is Ursula.

Laughing again, he brought the mirror away from Stephen’s peering eyes.

—The rage of Caliban at not seeing his face in a mirror, he said. If Wilde were only alive to see you.

Drawing back and pointing, Stephen said with bitterness:

—It is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked lookingglass of a servant.

奥斯卡·王尔德在其著作《道林·格雷的画像》 （1891）的序言中写道：“十九世纪对现实主义的厌恶，如同卡利班在镜中看到自己的脸时的愤怒；十九世纪对浪漫主义的厌恶，如同卡利班在镜中看不到自己的脸时的愤怒。”乔伊斯和王尔德都钦佩沃尔特·佩特，佩特启发了乔伊斯“顿悟”的概念——即平凡事物迸发出富有远见的洞察力的瞬间。普鲁斯特的顿悟则源于约翰·罗斯金，而佩特出于竞争精神，对罗斯金心怀不满。乔伊斯甚至超越了王尔德，他那句精彩而辛辣的话语更是令人叹服：“这是爱尔兰艺术的象征。仆人破碎的镜子。”然而，詹姆斯·乔伊斯是一位杰出的竞争者，他甚至敢于与但丁和莎士比亚争夺艺术的巅峰地位。

Oscar Wilde, in the preface to his The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), had remarked: “The nineteenth century dislike of Realism is the rage of Caliban seeing his own face in a glass. The nineteenth century dislike of Romanticism is the rage of Caliban not seeing his own face in a glass.” Joyce and Wilde both admired Walter Pater, who gave Joyce the idea of “epiphanies,” sudden moments in which the commonplace flamed into visionary perception. Proust took his epiphanies from the example of John Ruskin, whom Pater, in an agonistic spirit, resented. Joyce surmounts even Oscar in his splendidly bitter: “It is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked lookingglass of a servant.” But, then, James Joyce was the master agonist, daring to contend even against Dante and Shakespeare for the foremost place.

“内斯特”这一部分以斯蒂芬温和而勉强的校长形象开篇，随后，更令人印象深刻的是，转而描写他与迪西先生的对话。迪西先生是这所位于都柏林附近达尔基学校的苏格兰校长。迪西先生是个可怕的老人，他憎恨女人、犹太人以及所有不交学费的人。

The “Nestor” section begins with Stephen as gentle and reluctant schoolmaster and then, more memorably, passes to his colloquy with Mr. Deasy, the Scottish headmaster of this Dalkey school, not far from Dublin. Mr. Deasy is a dreadful old man who loathes women, Jews, and all those who do not pay their way:

“记住我的话，德达勒斯先生，”他说，“英国现在落入了犹太人手中。他们掌控着所有最高层：财政、媒体。而这正是国家衰落的标志。他们聚集之处，便会吞噬国家的命脉。这些年来，我一直预见到这一切。就我们此刻站在这里，我可以肯定地说，犹太商人已经开始了他们的破坏活动。古老的英国正在走向灭亡。”

他迅速走下台阶，一束阳光掠过他的双眼，湛蓝的光芒瞬间映照出他的神采。他转过身，又转过身来。

“快死了，”他又说，“如果现在还没死的话。”

妓女的叫喊声从一条街传到另一条街

将会编织古老的英格兰裹尸布。

他睁大双眼，目光锐利地盯着他停下的那束阳光。

斯蒂芬说：“商人就是低买高卖的人，不管是犹太人还是非犹太人，不是吗？”

“他们违背了光明，”迪西先生严肃地说，“你看，他们的眼里全是黑暗。这就是为什么他们至今仍是世间的流浪者。”

在巴黎证券交易所的台阶上，那些皮肤黝黑的男人用镶满宝石的手指报着价。如同鹅群的鸣叫。他们粗鲁地、喧闹地聚集在交易所周围，笨拙的丝绸帽子下，他们笨拙的脑袋里盘算着什么。这些衣服、这些言谈、这些举止都不是他们的。他们深邃而迟钝的眼神与言语、热情而无害的举止形成鲜明对比，但他们知道周围聚集的怨恨，也知道他们的热情是徒劳的。徒劳地积攒和囤积。时间终将将它们全部冲散。路边堆积的财物：掠夺而来，正在消逝。他们的眼神诉说着多年的漂泊，也默默地承受着肉体的耻辱。

谁没有过呢？斯蒂芬说。

“你这话是什么意思？”迪西先生问道。

他上前一步，站在桌旁。他的下颚微微张开，一脸茫然。这就是古老的智慧吗？他等着我的回答。

斯蒂芬说：“历史是一场噩梦，我正努力从中醒来。”

球场上，男孩们齐声呐喊。一声哨响：进球了！如果那场噩梦给你来了个反踢呢？

迪西先生说：“造物主的道路并非我们的道路。所有历史都朝着同一个伟大的目标发展，那就是上帝的显现。”

斯蒂芬用拇指朝窗户猛地一指，说道：

——那就是上帝。

万岁！哎！呼！

“什么？”迪西先生问道。

“街上有人喊叫，”斯蒂芬耸了耸肩回答道。

迪西先生低头看了看，用手指捏着自己的鼻翼，扭动了一会儿。然后他抬起头，松开了手指。

“我比你快乐，”他说。“我们犯过许多错误，犯过许多罪孽。一个女人把罪恶带到了世上。就因为一个并不比她应有的更贤良的女人——海伦，墨涅拉俄斯的逃妻，希腊人发动了长达十年的特洛伊战争。一个不忠的妻子，首先把陌生人带到了我们这片海岸——麦克默罗的妻子和她的情人，布雷夫尼王子奥罗克。一个女人也让帕内尔陷入了困境。许多错误，许多失败，但并非只有这一个罪孽。如今我已走到生命的尽头，仍在苦苦挣扎。但我会为正义而战，直到最后一刻。”

阿尔斯特必将奋战

阿尔斯特是对的。

斯蒂芬举起了手中的床单。

“嗯，先生，”他开口说道。

“我预感，”迪西先生说，“你不会在这里待太久。我觉得你天生就不适合当老师。也许我错了。”

“他更像是一个学习者，”斯蒂芬说。

—Mark my words, Mr Dedalus, he said. England is in the hands of the jews. In all the highest places: her finance, her press. And they are the signs of a nation’s decay. Wherever they gather they eat up the nation’s vital strength. I have seen it coming these years. As sure as we are standing here the jew merchants are already at their work of destruction. Old England is dying.

He stepped swiftly off, his eyes coming to blue life as they passed a broad sunbeam. He faced about and back again.

—Dying, he said again, if not dead by now.

The harlot’s cry from street to street

Shall weave old England’s winding sheet.

His eyes open wide in vision stared sternly across the sunbeam in which he halted.

—A merchant, Stephen said, is one who buys cheap and sells dear, jew or gentile, is he not?

—They sinned against the light, Mr Deasy said gravely. And you can see the darkness in their eyes. And that is why they are wanderers on the earth to this day.

On the steps of the Paris Stock Exchange the gold-skinned men quoting prices on their gemmed fingers. Gabbles of geese. They swarmed loud, uncouth about the temple, their heads thickplotting under maladroit silk hats. Not theirs: these clothes, this speech, these gestures. Their full slow eyes belied the words, the gestures eager and unoffending, but knew the rancours massed about them and knew their zeal was vain. Vain patience to heap and hoard. Time surely would scatter all. A hoard heaped by the roadside: plundered and passing on. Their eyes knew the years of wandering and, patient, knew the dishonours of their flesh.

—Who has not? Stephen said.

—What do you mean? Mr Deasy asked.

He came forward a pace and stood by the table. His underjaw fell sideways open uncertainly. Is this old wisdom? He waits to hear from me.

—History, Stephen said, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.

From the playfield the boys raised a shout. A whirring whistle: goal. What if that nightmare gave you a back kick?

—The ways of the Creator are not our ways, Mr Deasy said. All history moves towards one great goal, the manifestation of God.

Stephen jerked his thumb towards the window, saying:

—That is God.

Hooray! Ay! Whrrwhee!

—What? Mr Deasy asked.

—A shout in the street, Stephen answered, shrugging his shoulders.

Mr Deasy looked down and held for a while the wings of his nose tweaked between his fingers. Looking up again he set them free.

—I am happier than you are, he said. We have committed many errors and many sins. A woman brought sin into the world. For a woman who was no better than she should be, Helen, the runaway wife of Menelaus, ten years the Greeks made war on Troy. A faithless wife first brought the strangers to our shore here, MacMurrough’s wife and her leman O’Rourke, prince of Breffni. A woman too brought Parnell low. Many errors, many failures but not the one sin. I am a struggler now at the end of my days. But I will fight for the right till the end.

For Ulster will fight

And Ulster will be right.

Stephen raised the sheets in his hand.

—Well, sir, he began.

—I foresee, Mr Deasy said, that you will not remain here very long at this work. You were not born to be a teacher, I think. Perhaps I am wrong.

—A learner rather, Stephen said.

乔伊斯对这一切的叙述节奏把握得如此沉稳均匀，令人钦佩。尽管迪西令人厌恶，但人们还是接受了他本来的样子，无论多么微不足道。这当然不是《青年艺术家画像》中的斯蒂芬，他曾受到成为耶稣会神父的诱惑，却最终放弃了，转而投身于如同新伊卡洛斯般充满危险的审美飞跃，仿佛父亲就是自己的儿子。威廉·布莱克的影子萦绕在斯蒂芬的脑海中，乔伊斯在《尤利西斯》和《守灵夜》中都回响着布莱克的思想。斯蒂芬痛苦地厌恶迪西的反犹主义，他想起了威廉·布莱克的诗集《天真之歌》中的一节诗句：

It is admirable how calmly and evenly Joyce paces this. Though he is dreadful, Deasy is accepted as what he is, however little. This is certainly not the Stephen of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, who experienced the temptation of becoming a Jesuit priest and rejected it for the hazardous aesthetic flight of a new Icarus, as though the father could be his own son. William Blake haunts Stephen, and Joyce echoes him throughout Ulysses and the Wake. Painfully wincing at Deasy’s anti-Semitism, Stephen remembers a couplet from William Blake’s Notebook poem “Auguries of Innocence”:

妓女的叫喊声从一条街传到另一条街

将会编织古老英格兰的裹尸布

The harlot’s cry from street to street

Shall weave old England’s winding sheet

对于迪西先生的“他们违背了光明”，斯蒂芬回答说：“谁没有呢？”突然，一种幻象，一种消极的顿悟，占据了斯蒂芬的心：

To Mr. Deasy’s “They sinned against the light,” Stephen replies, “Who has not?” A vision, a kind of negative epiphany, suddenly possesses Stephen:

在巴黎证券交易所的台阶上，那些皮肤黝黑的男人们用镶满宝石的手指报着价。如同鹅群的鸣叫。他们喧闹地、粗鲁地聚集在交易所周围，笨拙的丝绸帽子下，他们笨拙的脑袋里盘算着什么。这些衣服、这些言谈、这些举止都不是他们的。他们深邃而迟钝的眼神与言语、热情而无害的举止形成鲜明对比，但他们明白周围积聚的怨恨，也明白自己的热情是徒劳的。徒劳地积攒和囤积。时间终将将它们全部冲散。路边堆积的财物：掠夺而来，随风飘散。他们的眼神诉说着多年的漂泊，也默默地承受着肉体的耻辱。

On the steps of the Paris Stock Exchange the gold-skinned men quoting prices on their gemmed fingers. Gabbles of geese. They swarmed loud, uncouth about the temple, their heads thickplotting under maladroit silk hats. Not theirs: these clothes, this speech, these gestures. Their full slow eyes belied the words, the gestures eager and unoffending, but knew the rancours massed about them and knew their zeal was vain. Vain patience to heap and hoard. Time surely would scatter all. A hoard heaped by the roadside: plundered and passing on. Their eyes knew their years of wandering and, patient, knew the dishonours of their flesh.

流亡并非唯一影响此景的因素；即便在2018年，它依然具有现实意义。我的思绪飘向保罗·莱昂的悲剧故事。莱昂是乔伊斯的无薪秘书兼顾问，一位博学的律师，精通七种语言。他冒着生命危险重返纳粹占领下的巴黎，只为拯救并带走乔伊​​斯的文稿。最终，莱昂被纳粹抓获，送往集中营惨遭杀害。与莱昂关系密切的塞缪尔·贝克特曾暗示，正是因为这场暴行，他才加入了法国抵抗运动。

It is not just exile that informs this vista; even in 2018, this retains relevance. My mind wanders to the tragic story of Paul Léon, Joyce’s unpaid secretary and adviser, a learned lawyer who had mastered seven languages, and who risked his life by returning to Nazi-occupied Paris so as to save and bring away Joyce’s papers. Eventually, Léon was seized by the Nazis and sent off to perish in a death camp. Samuel Beckett, who was close to Léon, intimated that he joined the French Resistance because of this atrocity.

斯蒂芬带着讽刺的礼貌试图摆脱迪西，但最终还是遭受了不幸的折磨：

With ironic courtesy, Stephen attempts to rid himself of Deasy, but not without being afflicted by a final nastiness:

“早上好，先生，”斯蒂芬再次说道，同时向他弯曲的背鞠了一躬。

他走出敞开的门廊，沿着树下的碎石小路走去，听见操场上传来喊叫声和棍棒击打的噼啪声。他穿过大门时，狮子们正卧在柱子上；真是些没牙的恐怖家伙。但我仍会帮助他战斗。穆里根会给我起个新绰号：与牛为友的吟游诗人。

——戴达罗斯先生！

追着我跑。希望不会再有信了。

稍等片刻。

“是的，先生，”斯蒂芬说着，转身走向大门。

迪西先生停了下来，气喘吁吁，咽了口唾沫。

“我只是想说，”他说，“据说爱尔兰是唯一一个从未迫害过犹太人的国家，这是我的荣幸。你知道吗？” “不知道。” “那你知道为什么吗？”

他皱着眉头，神情严肃地看着明亮的空气。

“为什么，先生？”斯蒂芬问道，脸上露出了笑容。

“因为她从来不让他们进来，”迪西先生严肃地说。

一声咯咯的笑声从他喉咙里迸发而出，拖着一串咯咯作响的痰液。他迅速转过身，一边咳嗽，一边大笑，举起双臂在空中挥舞。

“她从来不让他们进来，”他一边笑着，一边跺着穿着绑腿的脚踩在碎石路上，再次喊道，“这就是原因。”

阳光透过树叶交错的缝隙，洒在他睿智的肩膀上，如同闪烁的金币。

—Good morning, sir, Stephen said again, bowing to his bent back.

He went out by the open porch and down the gravel path under the trees, hearing the cries of voices and crack of sticks from the playfield. The lions couchant on the pillars as he passed out through the gate; toothless terrors. Still I will help him in his fight. Mulligan will dub me a new name: the bullockbefriending bard.

—Mr Dedalus!

Running after me. No more letters, I hope.

—Just one moment.

—Yes, sir, Stephen said, turning back at the gate.

Mr Deasy halted, breathing hard and swallowing his breath.

—I just wanted to say, he said. Ireland, they say, has the honour of being the only country which never persecuted the jews. Do you know that? No. And do you know why?

He frowned sternly on the bright air.

—Why, sir? Stephen asked, beginning to smile.

—Because she never let them in, Mr Deasy said solemnly.

A coughball of laughter leaped from his throat dragging after it a rattling chain of phlegm. He turned back quickly, coughing, laughing, his lifted arms waving to the air.

—She never let them in, he cried again through his laughter as he stamped on gaitered feet over the gravel of the path. That’s why.

On his wise shoulders through the checkerwork of leaves the sun flung spangles, dancing coins.

舞动的硬币让我们回想起斯蒂芬对急需的金钱的蔑视，以及迪西对现金的崇拜。我记得克里斯托弗·斯马特曾将硬币描述为“带有人类虚荣印记的死物” （《欢呼吧，阿格诺》），尽管我不认为乔伊斯读过斯马特的《欢呼吧，阿格诺》，因为它首次出版于1939年。乔伊斯赋予斯蒂芬一种如刀锋般锋利的格言家气质：“——斯蒂芬说，历史是一场我正试图从中醒来的噩梦。”

The dancing coins return us to Stephen’s contempt for much-needed money, and Deasy’s worship of cash. I remember Christopher Smart’s description of coins as “dead matter with the stamp of human vanity” (Jubilate Agno), though I do not believe Joyce ever read Smart’s Jubilate, since it was first published in 1939. Joyce endows Stephen with a knifelike edge as a maker of apothegms: “—History, Stephen said, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.”

这固然名声在外，但紧接着却对人们的轻信程度进行了更深层次的抨击：

Justly famous, that is followed by an even deeper slash into credulity:

迪西先生说：“造物主的道路并非我们的道路。所有历史都朝着同一个伟大的目标发展，那就是上帝的显现。”

斯蒂芬用拇指朝窗户猛地一指，说道：

——那就是上帝。

万岁！哎！呼！

“什么？”迪西先生问道。

“街上有人喊叫，”斯蒂芬耸了耸肩回答道。

—The ways of the Creator are not our ways, Mr Deasy said. All history moves towards one great goal, the manifestation of God.

Stephen jerked his thumb towards the window, saying:

—That is God.

Hooray! Ay! Whrrwhee!

—What? Mr Deasy asked.

—A shout in the street, Stephen answered, shrugging his shoulders.

接下来是“普罗透斯”的故事，斯蒂芬上午11点在海滩上漫步，沉思着潮汐和自己的困境。在《奥德赛》第四卷中，墨涅拉俄斯讲述了他在法罗斯岛上俘虏海神普罗透斯的故事。墨涅拉俄斯和他的手下冲向普罗透斯，将他牢牢抓住，尽管普罗透斯能够随意变身成狮子、蛇、豹子、野猪、流水和开花的树木。狡猾的普罗透斯最终屈服，并预言墨涅拉俄斯不会死，而是会被带到极乐世界，那是为神之后裔准备的。

The “Proteus” episode follows, in which Stephen walks on the beach at 11:00 a.m., brooding on the tides and on his predicament. In the fourth book of the Odyssey, Menelaus tells the story of his capture of Proteus, the old man of the sea, on the island of Pharos. Menelaus and his men rush upon Proteus and hold him fast, despite his willed transformations into a lion, a snake, a panther, a boar, running water, a flowering tree. The wily Proteus yields and prophesies that Menelaus will not die but will be taken to the Elysian Fields, reserved for those descended from the gods.

斯蒂芬在海滩上的沉思始于对伟大神秘主义者雅各布·伯麦（1575-1624）的清晰召唤。伯麦创作了《万物之印》（1621），威廉·布莱克读过此书，部分吸收，部分摒弃；詹姆斯·乔伊斯显然也读过并赞赏此书。在斯蒂芬的海滩遐想中，伯麦的影响力远胜于贝克莱主教。

Stephen’s meditation on the strand begins with a clear summoning of the great mystic Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), who composed The Signature of All Things (1621), which William Blake read and partly absorbed, partly rejected, and which James Joyce evidently read and admired. In Stephen’s beach reverie it is Boehme, more than Bishop Berkeley, who is prevalent:

可见之物的必然模式：至少如此，即便不更多，也通过我的双眼得以感知。我在此解读万物的印记，海卵与海藻，逼近的潮水，那只生锈的靴子。鼻涕绿，蓝银，锈色：彩色的符号。透明的界限。但他补充道：在肉体之中。然后他意识到，在它们之前，肉体是有颜色的。如何？当然，用壁灯敲击它们。别着急。他秃顶，是个百万富翁，色彩大师。透明的界限在……之中。为什么在……之中？透明，非透明。如果你能把五根手指伸进去，那就是一扇门，如果不是，那就是一扇门。闭上眼睛看看。

Ineluctable modality of the visible: at least that if no more, thought through my eyes. Signatures of all things I am here to read, seaspawn and seawrack, the nearing tide, that rusty boot. Snotgreen, bluesilver, rust: coloured signs. Limits of the diaphane. But he adds: in bodies. Then he was aware of them bodies before of them coloured. How? By knocking his sconce against them, sure. Go easy. Bald he was and a millionaire, maestro di color che sanno. Limit of the diaphane in. Why in? Diaphane, adiaphane. If you can put your five fingers through it it is a gate, if not a door. Shut your eyes and see.

这段精彩的文字堪称斯蒂芬和乔伊斯思想的缩影。它巧妙地融合了雅各布·伯麦关于物质与精神对应关系的观点，以及亚里士多德的思想，并借鉴了塞缪尔·约翰逊博士用“踢石头”的方式驳斥贝克莱主教的唯心主义：“我这样反驳它。”后世传说将秃顶和巨额财富与亚里士多德联系起来，但丁称他为“知者之师”（maestro di color che sanno）。约翰逊博士的词典在“gate”（大门）和“door”（门）的实用区别中得到了戏仿。然而，这里最重要的还是透明性及其局限性，即亚里士多德式的用客观事物检验超越性的方法。

This rich passage is an epitome of Stephen’s and of Joyce’s minds. Intricately it mixes Jacob Boehme’s idea of correspondences between the physical and the spiritual with a good dose of Aristotle, adding a dash of Dr. Samuel Johnson’s kicking a stone to cast aside Bishop Berkeley’s Idealism: “I refute it thus.” Later legend attributed baldness and enormous wealth to Aristotle, described by Dante as the “master of those who know”: maestro di color che sanno. Dr. Johnson’s dictionary is parodied in the pragmatic difference between gate and door. And yet what matters most here is transparency and its limits, an Aristotelian testing of transcendence against objects.

斯蒂芬闭上眼睛，听着靴子碾碎噼啪作响的残骸和贝壳。你正在穿过它。我也是，一步一步地走着。极短的时间，穿过极短的空间。五，六：那无尽的交错。没错：这就是听觉不可避免的模式。睁开你的眼睛。不。天哪！如果我从悬崖上掉下去，那悬崖像甲虫一样覆盖着他的底部，我就会无可避免地穿过那无尽的交错。我在黑暗中走得很顺利。我的白蜡木剑挂在我的身侧。用它敲击：它们确实敲击着。我的两只脚在他的靴子里，位于他腿的末端，无尽的交错。听起来很结实：像是造物主的木槌敲出来的。我是否正沿着桑迪芒特海滩走向永恒？碾碎，咔嚓，嘎吱，嘎吱。狂野的海钱。多米尼·迪西都认识它们。

你愿意来桑迪芒特吗？

那匹名叫玛德琳的母马？

节奏开始了，你看。我听见了。抑扬格四音步行进。不，是疾驰：描绘出母马的轮廓。

现在睁开眼睛。我会的。稍等片刻。一切都消失了吗？如果我睁开眼，就永远身处那片漆黑的透明之中。够了！我看看能不能看见。

你看，它一直都在那里，没有你也一样；而且永远都会在那里，直到世界末日。

Stephen closed his eyes to hear his boots crush crackling wrack and shells. You are walking through it howsomever. I am, a stride at a time. A very short space of time through very short times of space. Five, six: the nacheinander. Exactly: and that is the ineluctable modality of the audible. Open your eyes. No. Jesus! If I fell over a cliff that beetles o’er his base, fell through the nebeneinander ineluctably. I am getting on nicely in the dark. My ash sword hangs at my side. Tap with it: they do. My two feet in his boots are at the ends of his legs, nebeneinander. Sounds solid: made by the mallet of Los Demiurgos. Am I walking into eternity along Sandymount strand? Crush, crack, crick, crick. Wild sea money. Dominie Deasy kens them a’.

Won’t you come to Sandymount,

Madeline the mare?

Rhythm begins, you see. I hear. A catalectic tetrameter of iambs marching. No, agallop: deline the mare.

Open your eyes now. I will. One moment. Has all vanished since? If I open and am for ever in the black adiaphane. Basta! I will see if I can see.

See now. There all the time without you: and ever shall be, world without end.

“黑色的半透明物”指的是不透明物。莱辛的《拉奥孔》（1766）为斯蒂芬提供了他的“纳切因安德”（ nacheinander），或者说“一件事接着一件事”，其中可听见的是时间性的，可见的是空间性的。这位未来的爱尔兰学者紧闭双眼，想起哈姆雷特被警告不要跟随鬼魂，以免被引向悬崖。穿着巴克·穆里根的鞋子和裤子，斯蒂芬玩味着“内贝内因安德”（nebeneinander），或者说并列的空间美学概念。我内心深处的布莱克式情怀总是为“洛斯”（Los）这位造物主的出现而激动不已，但布莱克或许并不乐见斯蒂芬将他笔下的“真实之人”——想象力——等同于诺斯替教的造物主，后者既创造又扭曲世界。然而，布莱克的精神始终与斯蒂芬同在，伴他沿着海滩走向永恒：

“The black adiaphane” is the opaque. Lessing’s Laocoön (1766) provides Stephen with his nacheinander, or one thing after another, the audible being temporal and the visible spatial. Eyes tight shut, the Irish magister-to-be thinks of Hamlet being warned not to follow the Ghost lest he be led to a sudden cliff. Wearing Buck Mulligan’s shoes and trousers, Stephen plays with the nebeneinander or side-by-side aesthetic idea of space. The old Blakean in me always thrills to the invocation of Los the artificer, but Blake might not have been happy with Stephen’s identification of his Real Man the Imagination with the Gnostic Demiurge, who at once makes and deforms the world. Still, Blake’s spirit is with Stephen as he walks into eternity along the strand:

亚当·卡德蒙的配偶和助手：希瓦，赤裸的夏娃。她没有肚脐。凝视。无瑕的腹部，隆起而丰满，如同紧绷的羊皮纸盾牌，不，是堆积如山的白色玉米，东方不朽，从亘古到永恒。罪恶的子宫。

我亦孕于罪恶的黑暗之中，非受生而为人。他们，一个拥有我声音和双眼的男人，和一个气息中带着灰烬的幽灵女子。他们紧紧相拥，又彼此分离，遵行了结合者的意志。自亘古以来，祂就拣选了我，如今却再也无法将我抛弃。永恒的法则环绕着他。那么，这便是圣父与圣子同质的神圣本质吗？可怜的阿里乌斯又在哪里去验证这些结论呢？他一生都在为超越一切的神圣本质而战。命运多舛的异端首领。他在希腊的厕所里咽下了最后一口气：安乐死。他头戴珠饰主教冠，手持牧杖，佝偻着身子，坐在他的宝座上，一个寡居主教的鳏夫，胸前竖起的肩带，以及凝固的后背。

微风在他周围轻拂，急促而渴望。它们来了，波浪。白鬃海马，嘶鸣着，明亮的风缰，玛拿南的骏马。

Spouse and helpmate of Adam Kadmon: Heva, naked Eve. She had no navel. Gaze. Belly without blemish, bulging big, a buckler of taut vellum, no, whiteheaped corn, orient and immortal, standing from everlasting to everlasting. Womb of sin.

Wombed in sin darkness I was too, made not begotten. By them, the man with my voice and my eyes and a ghostwoman with ashes on her breath. They clasped and sundered, did the coupler’s will. From before the ages He willed me and now may not will me away or ever. A lex eterna stays about him. Is that then the divine substance wherein Father and Son are consubstantial? Where is poor dear Arius to try conclusions? Warring his life long on the contransmagnificandjewbangtantiality. Illstarred heresiarch. In a Greek watercloset he breathed his last: euthanasia. With beaded mitre and with crozier, stalled upon his throne, widower of a widowed see, with upstiffed omophorion, with clotted hinderparts.

Airs romped round him, nipping and eager airs. They are coming, waves. The whitemaned seahorses, champing, brightwindbridled, the steeds of Mananaan.

乔伊斯对卡巴拉的了解对我来说仍然是个谜。无论是在《尤利西斯》还是《芬尼根守灵夜》中，他所暗示的犹太神秘主义概念都比十九世纪末二十世纪初各种神秘主义者的著作更为详尽准确。或许他的天才直觉地领悟了自己需要了解的一切。在上面引用的第一段中，亚当·卡德蒙是卡巴拉中的神圣之人，雌雄同体，正如威廉·布莱克所言，他包罗万象，天地万物皆在其中。“东方与不朽”显然是指托马斯·特拉赫恩《沉思录》中最著名的段落：

Joyce’s knowledge of Kabbalah remains a puzzle to me. Both in Ulysses and the Wake he intimates more detailed and accurate notions of Jewish mysticism than were available to him in the various esotericists of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Perhaps his genius intuited what it needed to know. In the first paragraph quoted above, the Adam Kadmon is the Divine Man of Kabbalah, androgynous and containing all things in heaven and on earth in himself, as William Blake remarked. “Orient and immortal” is a clear reference to the most famous passage in Thomas Traherne’s Centuries of Meditations:

那玉米是东方不朽的小麦，既不应收割，也不应播种。我以为它从亘古到永远都屹立不倒。

The corn was orient and immortal wheat, which never should be reaped, nor was ever sown. I thought it had stood from everlasting to everlasting.

斯蒂芬的沉思中，他以戏谑的口吻提及阿里乌斯（256-336）的不幸结局。阿里乌斯死于君士坦丁堡的一间希腊式厕所，肠子塌陷而亡。阿里乌斯认为圣父先于圣子，且本质高于圣子，这一观点最终被教会判定为异端。令我着迷的是，乔伊斯并不信奉上帝，但上帝创造了斯蒂芬，而非生下他，却又受永恒法则的约束，永远无法终结他，因此乔伊斯仿佛成了基督或弥赛亚。哈姆雷特的形象始终萦绕在斯蒂芬的意识中，贯穿于这段文字。马纳南的坐骑是波浪，因为他是凯尔特海神，一个普罗透斯式的人物。

Stephen’s meditation proceeds to mix profundity with jesting in regard to the unfortunate end of Arius (256–336), who died in Constantinople in a Greek watercloset, his bowels collapsing. Arius argued that the Father preceded and was of a higher substance than the Son, a view eventually ruled heretical by the Church. It fascinates me that God, in whom Joyce did not believe, having made and not begot Stephen, is bound by eternal law never to end him, so that Joyce becomes a Christ or Messiah. Hamlet, always near in Stephen’s consciousness, is echoed throughout this passage. The steeds of Mananaan are the waves, since he is the Celtic god of the sea, a Proteus figure.

在《斯库拉与卡律布狄斯》这一集中，故事发生在下午两点的都柏林图书馆，斯蒂芬阐述了他那套精彩绝伦、匪夷所思的《哈姆雷特》理论，而他自己却声称并不相信这套理论。然而，理查德·埃尔曼在其权威的乔伊斯传记中却坚持认为，乔伊斯本人从未放弃过这套理论。

In the episode “Scylla and Charybdis,” set in the Dublin library at two in the afternoon, Stephen expounds his splendidly outrageous theory of Hamlet, in which he himself says he does not believe. Richard Ellmann, in his definitive biography of Joyce, nevertheless insists that Joyce himself never abandoned the theory.

——“罗伯特·格林称他为灵魂的死神，”斯蒂芬说道。“他出身屠夫之家，挥舞着雪橇式战斧，往手掌里吐口水，这绝非偶然。九条命换他父亲的一条命。我们的天父在炼狱中。身穿卡其布制服的哈姆雷特们毫不犹豫地开枪。第五幕血腥的屠杀预示着斯温伯恩先生歌唱的集中营。”

克兰利，我，他沉默的使者，远远地关注着战斗。

凶残敌人的幼崽和母兽，无人知晓

但我们还是留了下来……

介于撒克逊人的微笑和美国佬的咆哮之间。魔鬼与深海。

“他会说《哈姆雷特》是个鬼故事，”约翰·埃格林顿替贝斯特先生说道，“就像《匹克威克外传》里的胖小子一样，他想让我们毛骨悚然。”

名单！名单！名单！

我的肉体听见了他的声音：悄悄地，听见了。

如果你曾经……

“什么是鬼魂？”斯蒂芬带着一丝兴奋问道。“就是因死亡、因缺席、因行为改变而消逝于无形之物。伊丽莎白时代的伦敦与斯特拉特福德之间隔着如同腐败的巴黎与纯洁的都柏林之隔。那来自冥界、重返世间却已被遗忘的鬼魂是谁？哈姆雷特国王又是谁？”

约翰·埃格林顿挪了挪身子，向后靠去，准备评判。

已升起。

“现在是六月中旬的这个时候，”斯蒂芬说着，迅速瞥了一眼他们的耳朵。河岸边的剧场上挂着旗帜。萨克森熊在附近的坑里咆哮，那是巴黎花园。那些曾跟随德雷克航行的帆布攀岩者们在底层观众中嚼着香肠。

融入地方特色。把你所知道的一切都运用进去。让他们成为你的同谋。

莎士比亚离开了银街胡格诺派教徒的住所，沿着河岸漫步，经过天鹅棚。但他没有留下来喂那群正赶着小天鹅飞向芦苇丛的母天鹅。埃文河的天鹅另有打算。

地点构成。伊格内修斯·罗耀拉，快来帮帮我！

——戏开始了。一个演员在阴影下走上台，他身着宫廷侍从的旧锁子甲，身材魁梧，嗓音低沉。他是鬼魂，是国王，既是国王又是非国王，而扮演鬼魂的正是莎士比亚本人，他毕生研读《哈姆雷特》，只为扮演这个幽灵。他对着站在他面前、隔着麻布架的年轻演员伯比奇念出一个名字：

哈姆雷特，我是你父亲的亡灵。

让他听着。他向他的儿子说话，他灵魂的儿子，王子，年轻的哈姆雷特；也向他肉体的儿子，哈姆内特·莎士比亚说话，他已在斯特拉特福德去世，愿他的同名者永垂不朽。

难道那个演员莎士比亚，因缺席而化作幽灵，身披丹麦埋葬的衣袍，因死亡而化作幽灵，用自己的话语呼唤着自己儿子的名字（如果哈姆内特·莎士比亚还活着，他本该是哈姆雷特王子的孪生兄弟）？我想知道，他是否有可能没有得出或预见到这些前提的逻辑结论：你是被剥夺了财产的儿子；我是被谋杀的父亲；你的母亲是罪孽深重的王后，安妮·莎士比亚，原名海瑟薇？

—A deathsman of the soul Robert Greene called him, Stephen said. Not for nothing was he a butcher’s son, wielding the sledded poleaxe and spitting in his palms. Nine lives are taken off for his father’s one. Our Father who art in purgatory. Khaki Hamlets don’t hesitate to shoot. The bloodboltered shambles in act five is a forecast of the concentration camp sung by Mr Swinburne.

Cranly, I his mute orderly, following battles from afar.

Whelps and dams of murderous foes whom none

But we had spared…

Between the Saxon smile and yankee yawp. The devil and the deep sea.

—He will have it that Hamlet is a ghoststory, John Eglinton said for Mr Best’s behoof. Like the fat boy in Pickwick he wants to make our flesh creep.

List! List! O List!

My flesh hears him: creeping, hears.

If thou didst ever…

—What is a ghost? Stephen said with tingling energy. One who has faded into impalpability through death, through absence, through change of manners. Elizabethan London lay as far from Stratford as corrupt Paris lies from virgin Dublin. Who is the ghost from limbo patrum, returning to the world that has forgotten him? Who is King Hamlet?

John Eglinton shifted his spare body, leaning back to judge.

Lifted.

—It is this hour of a day in mid June, Stephen said, begging with a swift glance their hearing. The flag is up on the playhouse by the bankside. The bear Sackerson growls in the pit near it, Paris garden. Canvasclimbers who sailed with Drake chew their sausages among the groundlings.

Local colour. Work in all you know. Make them accomplices.

—Shakespeare has left the huguenot’s house in Silver street and walks by the swanmews along the riverbank. But he does not stay to feed the pen chivying her game of cygnets towards the rushes. The swan of Avon has other thoughts.

Composition of place. Ignatius Loyola, make haste to help me!

—The play begins. A player comes on under the shadow, made up in the castoff mail of a court buck, a wellset man with a bass voice. It is the ghost, the king, a king and no king, and the player is Shakespeare who has studied Hamlet all the years of his life which were not vanity in order to play the part of the spectre. He speaks the words to Burbage, the young player who stands before him beyond the rack of cerecloth, calling him by a name:

Hamlet, I am thy father’s spirit,

bidding him list. To a son he speaks, the son of his soul, the prince, young Hamlet and to the son of his body, Hamnet Shakespeare, who has died in Stratford that his namesake may live for ever.

Is it possible that that player Shakespeare, a ghost by absence, and in the vesture of buried Denmark, a ghost by death, speaking his own words to his own son’s name (had Hamnet Shakespeare lived he would have been prince Hamlet’s twin), is it possible, I want to know, or probable that he did not draw or foresee the logical conclusion of those premises: you are the dispossessed son: I am the murdered father: your mother is the guilty queen, Ann Shakespeare, born Hathaway?

唐·吉福德和罗伯特·J·塞德曼合著的《乔伊斯注释》（1974）对这里所有的典故都有详尽的解读，这本书极具参考价值，但我只想强调几点。乔伊斯或许是故意数错了，或许他更喜欢九这个数字。哈姆雷特一共造成了八条人命，包括他自己：他隔着帷幔刺死了波洛涅斯；恶毒地拒绝了奥菲莉娅，导致她自杀；漫不经心地将罗森克兰茨和吉尔登斯顿送往英国处决；在最后的毒剑毒杯场景中，他刺死了莱尔特斯，强迫克劳狄斯喝下刚刚毒死格特鲁德的毒酒，然后又猛地刺死了克劳狄斯。

A detailed exegesis of all the allusions here can be found in the endlessly useful Notes for Joyce by Don Gifford and Robert J. Seidman (1974), but I wish to emphasize only a few points. Joyce may have deliberately lost count or may have preferred the number nine. Hamlet is responsible for eight deaths, including his own: he stabs Polonius through a curtain; viciously rejects Ophelia, thus driving her to suicide; insouciantly sends Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to certain execution in England; and in the final poisoned sword and poisoned cup scene stabs Laertes, forces Claudius to drink of the cup that has just slain Gertrude, and with a flourish stabs Claudius also.

—

每个人都有自己的哈姆雷特。莎士比亚创造了唯一一个能与乔伊斯笔下的耶和华、马可福音中的耶稣、但丁笔下的朝圣者以及堂吉诃德相媲美的文学人物。斯蒂芬·金的《哈姆雷特》，正如乔伊斯本人所肯定的那样，是对父权虚构之谜的探索。哈姆雷特的父亲是谁？由于我们不知道格特鲁德和克劳狄斯的性关系始于何时，那么他的父亲是如今已成鬼魂的哈姆雷特国王，还是篡位者和弑父者克劳狄斯？哈姆雷特自己也不知道，虽然他对此只字未提，但他很少直言不讳，而且他的话语中常常带有刻意的讽刺意味。为什么他不在这部鸿篇巨制结束之前就蓄意杀死克劳狄斯呢？弑父可能会使任何人变得顽固不化，阻碍行动。然而，我很难相信这才是哈姆雷特迟迟不行动的主要原因。他不想再成为复仇悲剧的主角。任何人都可以刺杀篡位者；西方文学中最博大的思想也容不下早期《泰特斯·安德洛尼克斯》中那种血腥暴力，那种暴力玷污并贬低了这部戏剧的本质。在我看来，这部戏剧只能被解读为对托马斯·基德、约翰·马斯顿等人的刻意戏仿。

Everybody has his own Hamlet. Shakespeare created the only literary character who can compete with the J writer’s Yahweh, the Gospel of Mark’s Jesus, Dante’s Pilgrim, and Don Quixote. Stephen’s Hamlet, always affirmed by Joyce himself, is a study in the mystery of the fiction of fatherhood. Who is Hamlet’s father? Since we do not know when the sexual relationship between Gertrude and Claudius commenced, is it King Hamlet, now a Ghost, or is it the usurper and murderer Claudius? Hamlet does not know, and though he says nothing about this question, he rarely says exactly what he thinks, and he does not often speak without intentional irony. Why does he not slay Claudius deliberately, long before the end of this enormous play? Patricide might render anyone recalcitrant and inhibit action. And yet I scarcely believe that is the principal cause of Hamlet’s delay. He does not want to be the protagonist of one more revenger’s tragedy. Anyone can stab a usurper; the most capacious consciousness in all of Western literature is too large for the bloodiness that mars and trivializes the early Titus Andronicus, a drama that I can interpret only as a deliberate parody of Thomas Kyd, John Marston, and others.

斯蒂芬虚构莎士比亚被他的三个兄弟都戴了绿帽子，还和安妮·海瑟薇有染，这种说法既离谱又荒谬。但将莎士比亚与鬼魂（我们知道他扮演过这个角色）以及哈姆雷特王子与11岁就夭折的哈姆内特·莎士比亚等同起来，则更令人费解。《哈姆雷特》可能早在1599年就已创作完成，也就是小哈姆内特去世三年之后。在此之前，1587年还上演过一部《哈姆雷特》，我们现在还能找到它的剧本。我一直同意彼得·亚历山大的观点，认为这部早期的《哈姆雷特》是威廉·莎士比亚而非托马斯·基德所作。这一点至关重要，因为1587年的《哈姆雷特》演出失败，并遭到观众的嘲笑。莎士比亚创作第二部《哈姆雷特》是为了寻求平反，而这部最终成为他篇幅最长、也最著名的戏剧作品，也让他赢得了认可。

Stephen’s fiction that Shakespeare was cuckolded by all three of his brothers with Anne Hathaway is extravagant and rather silly. But the identification of Shakespeare with the Ghost, a part we know he played, and of Prince Hamlet with Hamnet Shakespeare, who died at the age of eleven, is more troublesome. Hamlet may have been composed as early as 1599, three years after the death of young Hamnet. There was an earlier Hamlet, staged in 1587, of which we have the text. I have always agreed with Peter Alexander that this first Hamlet was by William Shakespeare and not Thomas Kyd. It makes a difference, because the 1587 Hamlet failed and was mocked by its audience. In writing his second Hamlet, Shakespeare sought vindication and earned it by what in time became his longest and most famous drama.

如果将第二四开本（1604年）和第一对开本（1623年）合并，完整的《哈姆雷特》大约有四千行。我从未见过如此完整的演出版本，尽管确实有过这样的演出。如果演出不设中场休息，时长可能长达五个小时，具体取决于导演的节奏。

The uncut Hamlet, if you combine the Second Quarto (1604) with the First Folio (1623), runs to about four thousand lines. I have never seen it performed at that length, though such performances have taken place. Played without intermission, it might take up to five hours, depending upon the pacing of the director.

描述詹姆斯·乔伊斯的胆识的一种方式是问：还有谁拥有如此权威和雄心去颠覆《哈姆雷特》乃至整个莎士比亚的创作？散文家兼诗人罗伯特·阿特万在我那部鸿篇巨著《莎士比亚：人的发明》（1998）的评论中，温和地批评我放弃了以往对弥尔顿笔下撒旦和布莱克《天堂与地狱的婚姻》的依赖： “他是否在莎士比亚身上找到了一个最终使颠覆变得不可想象的大师？”我想我的答案必须是“是的”。但我是一名教师，而非诗人或小说家。在所有莎士比亚之后的作家中，只有詹姆斯·乔伊斯能够像荷马、但丁、塞万提斯和莎士比亚那样重塑语言。普鲁斯特，这位擅长运用冗长句子的大师，却并未尝试去净化福楼拜的语言，这几乎是不可能完成的任务。

One way of describing James Joyce’s audacity is to ask: who else has had the authority and ambition to subvert Hamlet and all, indeed, of William Shakespeare’s creation? The essayist and poet Robert Atwan, in a generous review of my sprawling Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human (1998), gently chided me as forsaking my customary reliance on Milton’s Satan and Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell: “In Shakespeare has he found a master who finally makes subversion unthinkable?” I suppose my answer has to be “Yes.” But I am a teacher by profession and not a poet or a novelist. Of all post-Shakespearean writers, James Joyce alone was able to remake language as Homer, Dante, Cervantes, and Shakespeare had done before him. Proust, master of endless sentences, nevertheless does not attempt the impossible task of purifying the language of Flaubert.

乔伊斯与其说是试图颠覆莎士比亚，不如说是彻底吸收他，并将这一过程转化为某种丰富而奇特，但在认知上却远比莎士比亚简洁的东西。乔伊斯对莎士比亚抱有一种矛盾的态度，有时甚至接近荒谬。他认为易卜生比莎士比亚更优秀，并表示可以通过比较《当我们死而复生时》与莎士比亚的任何作品来证明这一点。此外，还有创作上的嫉妒问题。在创作《当我们死而复生时》时，乔伊斯反复思索，并将这部作品缺乏现成读者的情况与莎士比亚在环球剧院的处境进行了比较。

Joyce did not so much seek to subvert Shakespeare as totally to absorb him and transmute that process into something rich and strange, yet cognitively far simpler than Shakespeare. There is a Joycean ambivalence toward Shakespeare that sometimes risks absurdity. Joyce considered Ibsen a much better dramatist than Shakespeare and said this could be proved by comparing When We Dead Awaken to anything by the English Bard. There is also the question of creative envy. As he composed the Wake, Joyce brooded and compared that book’s lack of a ready audience to Shakespeare’s situation at the Globe Theatre.

1912年，乔伊斯在的里雅斯特为付费听众举办了十二场关于《哈姆雷特》的系列讲座。据我所知，我们没有他演讲的文本。但显然，他几乎完全关注语言，逐字逐句地阐释词源、双关语和句式。那时，乔伊斯将莎士比亚描述为一位意大利化的英国人，其笔下的主人公取材于欧洲大陆。这只是部分事实。然而，《尤利西斯》中图书馆场景里的斯蒂芬却提出了一系列引人入胜的推测：

In 1912, Joyce gave a series of a dozen lectures on Hamlet to a paying audience in Trieste. As far as I know, we do not have the texts of what he said. But evidently his concern was almost entirely with language, a kind of word-by-word explication of etymologies, puns, and turns of phrase. By then Joyce described Shakespeare as an Italianate Englishman, taking his protagonists from continental sources. That is a partial truth only. Yet Stephen in the library scene of Ulysses gives us a series of fascinating speculations:

——我从他的话语中感受到，某种肉体的冲动驱使他陷入新的激情，一种比之前更加黑暗的激情，甚至蒙蔽了他对自己认知的双眼。同样的命运正在等待着他，两种狂怒将在漩涡中交织融合。

他们列队。我把酒倾倒在他们耳畔。

——灵魂早已遭受致命打击，如同毒药倾倒在熟睡的耳畔。然而，那些在睡梦中死去的人，除非造物主在来世赋予他们的灵魂那份知识，否则他们无法知晓自己是如何消亡的。若非造物主赋予他知识，哈姆雷特国王的亡灵便无法知晓那中毒以及驱使它而来的那头双背怪兽。正因如此，他的言语（他那枯燥乏味的英语）总是转向别处，倒叙着。他渴望却又不愿面对的，那些他强暴又被强暴的事物，从卢克丽丝那镶着蓝圈的象牙球，到伊莫金裸露的胸膛，上面点缀着五颗痣。他返回，厌倦了自己为了逃避自我而堆积起来的一切，如同老狗舔舐着旧伤。但是，因为失去即是获得，他以未减损的个性走向永恒，既没有被他所书写的智慧所教诲，也没有被他所揭示的法则所束缚。他的海狸已经升起。他现在像个幽灵，一个影子，像埃尔西诺岩石边的风，或者随便你怎么称呼它，像大海的声音，一个只有在他影子的实体——与父亲同质的儿子——的心中才能听到的声音。

—There is, I feel in the words, some goad of the flesh driving him into a new passion, a darker shadow of the first, darkening even his own understanding of himself. A like fate awaits him and the two rages commingle in a whirlpool.

They list. And in the porches of their ears I pour.

—The soul has been before stricken mortally, a poison poured in the porch of a sleeping ear. But those who are done to death in sleep cannot know the manner of their quell unless their Creator endow their souls with that knowledge in the life to come. The poisoning and the beast with two backs that urged it King Hamlet’s ghost could not know of were he not endowed with knowledge by his creator. That is why the speech (his lean unlovely English) is always turned elsewhere, backward. Ravisher and ravished, what he would but would not, go with him from Lucrece’s bluecircled ivory globes to Imogen’s breast, bare, with its mole cinquespotted. He goes back, weary of the creation he has piled up to hide him from himself, an old dog licking an old sore. But, because loss is his gain, he passes on towards eternity in undiminished personality, untaught by the wisdom he has written or by the laws he has revealed. His beaver is up. He is a ghost, a shadow now, the wind by Elsinore’s rocks or what you will, the sea’s voice, a voice heard only in the heart of him who is the substance of his shadow, the son consubstantial with the father.

人们很难想象，就连詹姆斯·乔伊斯也能如此令人信服地展现莎士比亚的内心世界。由于这位诗人兼剧作家创作《哈姆雷特国王的鬼魂》是为了让自己扮演这个角色，斯蒂芬的经院哲学既引人入胜又令人卸下防备。莎士比亚，作为凡人和剧作家，尽管是凡人中的神，也承受着他自我肯定的代价。性欲的狂怒推动着他的悲剧在《奥赛罗》中达到顶峰，随后又转化为《李尔王》、 《麦克白》、 《安东尼与克莉奥佩特拉》中人性的彻底狂怒。此后，莎士比亚的创作如同人生的潮汐般起伏：《科利奥兰纳斯》、 《雅典的泰门》以及他参与创作的《两贵亲》都展现了与令人不安的《一报还一报》 、 《终成眷属》、 《特洛伊罗斯与克瑞西达》相同的厌恶和矛盾心理。影子与实体，父亲与儿子，只有莎士比亚心中怀揣着荒凉的内陆海洋，因为他是与父亲同质的儿子，所以他既是耶稣又是耶和华。

One could hardly have thought that even James Joyce might give us so persuasive a vision of the inward Shakespeare. Since the poet-dramatist composed the part of the Ghost of King Hamlet for himself to perform, Stephen’s scholasticism entertains and disarms. Shakespeare, man and playwright, though a mortal God, suffers the cost of his confirmation. Sexual fury drives the High Tragedies to one apotheosis in Othello and then transmutes into the total fury of the human in King Lear, Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra. After that, Shakespeare ebbs with an ebb of the ocean of life: Coriolanus, Timon of Athens, and his share of The Two Noble Kinsmen show the same revulsions and ambivalences as do the troublesome Measure for Measure, All’s Well That Ends Well, Troilus and Cressida. Shadow and substance, father and son, Shakespeare alone carries in his heart the inland ocean of desolation, and since he is the son consubstantial with the father, he is both Jesus and Yahweh.

面对持怀疑态度的听众的挑战，斯蒂芬需要证明威廉·莎士比亚是犹太人，这预示了肯尼斯·格罗斯的《夏洛克是莎士比亚》（2006）：

Challenged by his skeptical auditors to prove that William Shakespeare was a Jew, Stephen anticipates Kenneth Gross’s Shylock Is Shakespeare (2006):

“还有财产意识，”斯蒂芬说道。他从自己长长的口袋里掏出夏洛克。夏洛克是麦芽商兼放贷人的儿子，他自己也是个粮食商兼放贷人，在饥荒暴乱期间囤积了十托德的粮食。毫无疑问，他的借款人就是切特尔·福斯塔夫提到的那些虔诚的信徒，福斯塔夫曾报道过他为人正直。他曾起诉一个同行，追讨几袋麦芽的钱，并且每借出一笔钱，就向对方索要一磅的利息。奥布里的马夫兼男仆还能怎么这么快发财呢？所有的事情都为他提供了发财的机会。夏洛克与女王的走狗洛佩兹被处以绞刑和肢解后引发的反犹浪潮不谋而合，洛佩兹的犹太心脏在鲜血淋漓时就被挖了出来；夏洛克也与哈姆雷特和麦克白中一位热衷于猎巫的苏格兰哲学家登上王位的故事相呼应。在《爱的徒劳》中，他嘲讽的是那支失落的舰队。他的盛大场面和历史剧，乘着马弗京式的热情浪潮，气势磅礴地扬帆远航。沃里克郡的耶稣会士们受审，我们则有了一个门房式的模棱两可理论。“海上冒险号”从百慕大归来，雷南欣赏的那部戏剧是他和我们的美国表亲帕齐·卡利班共同创作的。甜腻的十四行诗紧随西德尼之后。至于那位仙气十足的伊丽莎白，也就是那位胡萝卜贝丝，那位启发了《温莎的风流娘儿们》的粗俗处女，就让某个来自德国的男爵用他毕生的渴望，在花篮深处探寻那些深奥的含义吧。

And the sense of property, Stephen said. He drew Shylock out of his own long pocket. The son of a maltjobber and moneylender he was himself a cornjobber and moneylender, with ten tods of corn hoarded in the famine riots. His borrowers are no doubt those divers of worship mentioned by Chettle Falstaff who reported his uprightness of dealing. He sued a fellowplayer for the price of a few bags of malt and exacted his pound of flesh in interest for every money lent. How else could Aubrey’s ostler and callboy get rich quick? All events brought grist to his mill. Shylock chimes with the jewbaiting that followed the hanging and quartering of the queen’s leech Lopez, his jew’s heart being plucked forth while the sheeny was yet alive: Hamlet and Macbeth with the coming to the throne of a Scotch philosophaster with a turn for witchroasting. The lost armada is his jeer in Love’s Labour Lost. His pageants, the histories, sail fullbellied on a tide of Mafeking enthusiasm. Warwickshire jesuits are tried and we have a porter’s theory of equivocation. The Sea Venture comes home from Bermudas and the play Renan admired is written with Patsy Caliban, our American cousin. The sugared sonnets follow Sidney’s. As for fay Elizabeth, otherwise carrotty Bess, the gross virgin who inspired the Merry Wives of Windsor, let some meinherr from Almany grope his life long for deephid meanings in the depths of the buckbasket.

这番话妙语连珠，令人叹服，无可辩驳。就让它保留吧。乔伊斯再次展现了他的才华，如同他那神圣的前辈一般，他是一位智慧与语言的化身。

This is too high-spirited to be refutable. Let it stand. Again Joyce dazzles, lord of wit and of language like his divine precursor.

“圣托马斯，”斯蒂芬笑着说，“我喜欢读他那些冗长乏味的作品，尤其是原文。他论述乱伦的角度与马吉先生提到的维也纳新学派截然不同。他以睿智而奇特的方式将其比作情感的贪婪。”他的意思是，给予血缘近亲的爱，却被贪婪地保留给那些可能渴望这种爱的陌生人。基督徒指责犹太人贪婪，而犹太人恰恰是所有种族中最热衷于通婚的。人们在愤怒中指责他们。基督教的法律不仅使犹太人积累了财富（对他们来说，就像对罗拉德派一样，暴风雨是避难所），也用钢铁般的枷锁束缚了他们的情感。

这些究竟是罪过还是美德，老家伙会在末日审判时告诉我们。但一个如此执着于他所谓的“权利”（即他所谓的债务）的人，也会如此执着于他所谓的“权利”（即他所谓的妻子）。任何邻居都不应该觊觎他的牛、妻子、男仆、女仆或驴。

Saint Thomas, Stephen smiling said, whose gorbellied works I enjoy reading in the original, writing of incest from a standpoint different from that of the new Viennese school Mr Magee spoke of, likens it in his wise and curious way to an avarice of the emotions. He means that the love so given to one near in blood is covetously withheld from some stranger who, it may be, hungers for it. Jews, whom christians tax with avarice, are of all races the most given to intermarriage. Accusations are made in anger. The christian laws which built up the hoards of the jews (for whom, as for the lollards, storm was shelter) bound their affections too with hoops of steel.

Whether these be sins or virtues old Nobodaddy will tell us at doomsday leet. But a man who holds so tightly to what he calls his rights over what he calls his debts will hold tightly also to what he calls his rights over her whom he calls his wife. No sir smile neighbour shall covet his ox or his wife or his manservant or his maidservant or his jackass.

安东尼·伯吉斯称之为“将爱留在家庭内部”，但他指的是厄威克对女儿伊莎贝尔的欲望。威廉·布莱克称耶和华为“老无名氏”，这让乔伊斯欣喜不已，他称基督教的上帝为“刽子手之神”。罪恶与美德交织在一起。

Anthony Burgess called this “keeping love in the family,” though he meant Earwicker’s lust for his daughter, Isobel. William Blake’s name for Yahweh, “old Nobodaddy,” delighted Joyce, who called the God of the Christians the “hangman god.” Sins and virtues meld.

——斯蒂芬说，父亲，在与绝望抗争的过程中，是一种必要的恶。他是在父亲去世后的几个月里写出了这部剧。如果你认为他，一个头发花白、有两个待嫁女儿、年过三十五年（人生中途，五十年阅历）的男人，是那个来自维滕贝格、没有胡须的本科生，那么你也必须认为他七十岁的母亲是那个好色的女王。不。约翰·莎士比亚的尸体不会在夜里游荡。它日复一日地腐烂。他安息了，卸下了为人父的重担，将那神秘的使命托付给了他的儿子。薄伽丘笔下的卡兰德里诺是第一个也是最后一个感受到自己怀有身孕的男人。父权，就其有意识的生育而言，对人类来说是未知的。它是一种神秘的使命，一种使徒般的传承，从唯一的生育者到唯一的被生育者。教会并非建立在狡猾的意大利知识分子抛给欧洲乌合之众的圣母像之上，而是建立在那神秘之中，并且牢不可破，因为它如同世界本身，无论宏观还是微观，都建立在虚无之上，建立在不确定性和不可能性之上。母爱，主观和客观的属格，或许是生命中唯一真实的东西。父权或许只是法律上的虚构。谁是任何一个儿子的父亲，以至于任何一个儿子都爱他，或者他爱任何一个儿子？

—A father, Stephen said, battling against hopelessness, is a necessary evil. He wrote the play in the months that followed his father’s death. If you hold that he, a greying man with two marriageable daughters, with thirtyfive years of life, nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita, with fifty of experience, is the beardless undergraduate from Wittenberg then you must hold that his seventyyear old mother is the lustful queen. No. The corpse of John Shakespeare does not walk the night. From hour to hour it rots and rots. He rests, disarmed of fatherhood, having devised that mystical estate upon his son. Boccaccio’s Calandrino was the first and last man who felt himself with child. Fatherhood, in the sense of conscious begetting, is unknown to man. It is a mystical estate, an apostolic succession, from only begetter to only begotten. On that mystery and not on the madonna which the cunning Italian intellect flung to the mob of Europe the church is founded and founded irremovably because founded, like the world, macro and microcosm, upon the void. Upon incertitude, upon unlikelihood. Amor matris, subjective and objective genitive, may be the only true thing in life. Paternity may be a legal fiction. Who is the father of any son that any son should love him or he any son?

如果亲子关系只是法律上的虚构，那么我们还可以更进一步，就像哈姆雷特在第五幕中所做的那样：父亲的幽灵形象逐渐消失，只在提及克劳狄斯时出现——“他杀死了我的国王，玷污了我的母亲”——或者只在提及父亲的印章戒指时出现。在奥菲莉亚的墓前与莱尔特斯对峙时，哈姆雷特高声喊道：“我就是丹麦王子哈姆雷特！” 因此，我赞同斯蒂芬的理论，一旦撇开安妮·海瑟薇与莎士比亚兄弟的所谓“戴绿帽”情节，这套理论本身就是一件精妙绝伦的作品。

If paternity is a legal fiction, then one can go further, as Hamlet does when the image of the ghostly father fades away in Act 5 and appears only in a reference to Claudius as he who killed my king and whored my mother, or in a single mention of my father’s signet ring. Confronting Laertes at the grave of Ophelia, Hamlet cries out, “It is I, Hamlet the Dane.” Here, then, I go with Stephen’s theory, which is a splendid artifact once you divest it of the supposed cuckolding of Shakespeare by Anne Hathaway with his brothers.

詹姆斯·乔伊斯与父亲约翰·斯坦尼斯劳斯·乔伊斯关系亲密，但与母亲玛丽·简·默里之间却有些愧疚，因为即便在母亲临终之际，他也不肯再次皈依罗马天主教以示安慰。乔伊斯曾接受耶稣会教育，但他始终对神职人员抱有强烈的抵触情绪：“我不会侍奉神职人员。”

James Joyce had a warm relationship with his father, John Stanislaus Joyce, and something of a guilty one with his mother, Mary Jane Murray, since he would not embrace Roman Catholicism again even to comfort her on her deathbed. Educated by the Jesuits, Joyce remained obdurate against priestcraft: “I will not serve.”

作为托马斯·阿奎那的忠实读者，乔伊斯在三世纪神学家萨贝利乌斯身上找到了先驱，可惜萨贝利乌斯的著作均已失传：

A deep reader of Thomas Aquinas, Joyce found a precursor in the third-century theologian Sabellius, none of whose writings survived:

萨贝利乌斯，这位非洲人，田野里最狡猾的异端首领，竟然认为圣父就是他自己的儿子。阿奎那的斗牛犬，对任何话都无所不谈，驳斥了他。那么，如果一个没有儿子的父亲就不是父亲，那么一个没有父亲的儿子又怎么能算是儿子呢？当拉特兰·巴肯斯南安普顿莎士比亚（或另一位同名诗人）在创作《哈姆雷特》这部喜剧时，他不仅是自己儿子的父亲，而且，由于他不再是儿子，他成为了他整个种族的父亲，他祖父的父亲，他未出生的孙子的父亲——而这个孙子，按同样的逻辑，也从未出生过，因为正如麦吉先生所理解的那样，自然厌恶完美。

Sabellius, the African, subtlest heresiarch of all the beasts of the field, held that the Father was Himself His Own Son. The bulldog of Aquin, with whom no word shall be impossible, refutes him. Well: if the father who has not a son be not a father can the son who has not a father be a son? When Rutlandbaconsouthamptonshakespeare or another poet of the same name in the comedy of errors wrote Hamlet he was not the father of his own son merely but, being no more a son, he was and felt himself the father of all his race, the father of his own grandfather, the father of his unborn grandson who, by the same token, never was born, for nature, as Mr Magee understands her, abhors perfection.

马吉先生（《尤利西斯》中的约翰·埃格林顿）的原型是威廉·柯克帕特里克·马吉，一位当代爱尔兰散文家。萨贝利乌斯化身为斯蒂芬，斯蒂芬又化身为莎士比亚，莎士比亚成为一个先于一切存在的存在，一种超脱于自然的完美。因此，莎士比亚回到了创世与堕落之前，如同诺斯替教中的异神一般。由于乔伊斯致力于将莎士比亚、利奥波德·布鲁姆和詹姆斯·乔伊斯三者融为一体，因此，他也将在此基础上达到审美上的完美：

Mr. Magee (John Eglinton in Ulysses) was William Kirkpatrick Magee, a contemporary Irish essayist. Sabellius becomes Stephen becomes Shakespeare, who becomes a pre-existent being, a perfection alien to nature. Shakespeare thus goes back before the Creation-Fall, like the Stranger God of the Gnostics.
