Shem’s pretentions nevertheless prevail. Joyce will not rewrite Shakespeare, though he cannot stop utilizing him.

凌驾于这一切之上的，是乔伊斯写过的最精彩的篇章，其中安娜·莉维娅·普鲁拉贝尔——伟大的母亲，河流之河，所有人的妻子——如同利菲河注入爱尔兰海一般，流淌回家：

What rises above all this are the strongest pages Joyce ever wrote, where Anna Livia Plurabelle—great mother, river-of-rivers, wife to Everyone—flows home as the Liffey empties into the Irish Sea:

它又老又老，它又悲伤又老，它又悲伤又疲惫。我回到你身边，我冷漠的父亲，我冷酷疯狂的父亲，我冷酷疯狂又可怕的父亲，直到近距离看到他那庞大的身躯，那密密麻麻的、呻吟的身影，让我感到恶心反胃，于是我冲进你的怀抱，我唯一的爱人。我看到它们升起！救我脱离那三个尖刺！还有两个。再来两个。就这样。阿韦拉瓦尔。我的叶子都飘走了。全都飘走了。但还有一片依附着。我会把它带在身上。为了提醒我。Lff！今天早上，我们的叶子真柔软。是的。带着我走吧，爸爸，就像你带我穿过玩具展一样！如果我看到他现在张开白色的翅膀向我俯冲下来，就像他来自方舟天使城一样，我会沉沦，我会死在他的脚下，谦卑地、哑巴地，直到被冲刷干净。是的，爸爸。就是那里。首先。我们穿过草丛，来到灌木丛旁。嗖！一只海鸥。海鸥。远处传来叫声。来了，远处！到此为止。然后是我们。芬恩，又是他！拿走。巴士，记住！直到你结束。LPS。钥匙。给予！一条路，孤独，最后，被爱，一路

And it’s old and old it’s sad and old it’s sad and weary I go back to you, my cold father, my cold mad father, my cold mad feary father, till the near sight of the mere size of him, the moyles and moyles of it, moananoaning, makes me seasilt saltsick and I rush, my only, into your arms. I see them rising! Save me from those therrble prongs! Two more. Onetwo moremens more. So. Avelaval. My leaves have drifted from me. All. But one clings still. I’ll bear it on me. To remind me of. Lff! So soft this morning, ours. Yes. Carry me along, taddy, like you done through the toy fair! If I seen him bearing down on me now under whitespread wings like he’d come from Arkangels, I sink I’d die down over his feet, humbly dumbly, only to washup. Yes, tid. There’s where. First. We pass through grass behush the bush to. Whish! A gull. Gulls. Far calls. Coming, far! End here. Us then. Finn, again! Take. Bussoftlhee, mememormee! Till thous-endsthee. Lps. The keys to. Given! A way a lone a last a loved a long the

这可能是复活的科迪莉亚回到李尔王（利里饰）的怀抱。众所周知，这与《守灵夜》的开篇遥相呼应：

It could be a resurrected Cordelia returning to the arms of King Lear (Leary). Famously, this returns to the opening of the Wake:

河流奔流，经过夏娃和亚当，从海岸的弯曲处到海湾的拐弯处，将我们带过一个便利的循环区，回到霍斯城堡及其周边地区。

riverrun, past Eve and Adam’s, from swerve of shore to bend of bay, brings us by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs.

第36章

CHAPTER 36

《魔山》（1924）

The Magic Mountain (1924)

托马斯·曼​

THOMAS MANN

随着年龄的增长，我越来越感受到伟大的语言学家恩斯特·罗伯特·库尔提乌斯（1886-1956）的影响。我曾希望在1955年于罗马与他见面，但时间安排不合适。我们通过电话交谈，或许也互通了信件。他那部杰出的著作《欧洲文学与拉丁中世纪》（1948年出版，威拉德·特拉斯克1953年译）我反复阅读，以至于三本都磨损了。

AS I AGE, I feel increasingly under the influence of the great philologist Ernst Robert Curtius (1886–1956). I had hoped to meet him in Rome in 1955, but the timing did not work. We talked on the phone and may have exchanged letters. His extraordinary book, European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages (1948, translated 1953 by Willard Trask), has been reread by me so often that I have worn out three copies.

库尔提乌斯论证了欧洲文学从荷马到歌德的连续传统，之后又演变成另一种形式。在库尔提乌斯看来，真正的试金石是但丁和莎士比亚。有人可能会说，华兹华斯终结了一种传统，却又开创了另一种传统，而这种传统至今仍然影响深远。托马斯·曼（1875-1955）尽管笔下充满了无休止的（有时甚至令人厌倦的）讽刺，却始终试图回归歌德。他对歌德的执着既充满爱意又饱含矛盾。从他1922年的论文《歌德与托尔斯泰》到20世纪30年代他那三篇杰出的歌德论文（分别论述这位文人、“资产阶级时代的代表”以及《浮士德》），再到20世纪50年代的《歌德幻想曲》，曼从未停止过对这位伟大原作的重新诠释。在这些改编作品中，最杰出的当属小说《魏玛的洛特》，它于1939年在斯德​​哥尔摩出版。英文版名为《爱人归来》，它无疑是曼恩主要小说中最被忽视的一部。曼恩以《魔山》、四部曲《约瑟夫与他的兄弟们》、小说 《浮士德博士》 《威尼斯之死》和《费利克斯·克鲁尔》而闻名，就连早期的《布登勃洛克一家》也广为流传。然而，《魏玛的洛特》在最初获得一些成功之后，似乎变成了一部只有专家才能理解的作品，至少在英语国家是如此。或许是因为歌德——这位在卡莱尔和爱默生时代曾将作品成功输出到英国和美国的作家——如今却似乎成了一位难以翻译的作家。又或许是因为歌德的精神未能经受住1933年至1945年间德国发生的种种变故。

Curtius demonstrates that European literature is a continuous tradition from Homer to Goethe, and then becomes something else. For Curtius, the true touchstones are Dante and Shakespeare. One could argue that Wordsworth ended a tradition and inaugurated another, which is still very much with us. Thomas Mann (1875–1955), despite his endless (and sometimes wearisome) ironies, attempted to get back to Goethe. His agon with Goethe was loving though ambivalent. From his essay “Goethe and Tolstoy” (1922) through his remarkable triad of Goethe essays in the 1930s (on the man of letters, the “representative of the Bourgeois Age,” and Faust) on to the “Fantasy on Goethe” of the 1950s, Mann never wearied of reimagining his great original. The finest of these reimaginings, the novel Lotte in Weimar, was published in Stockholm in 1939. We know it in English as The Beloved Returns, and it is surely the most neglected of Mann’s major fictions. Mann is renowned as the author of The Magic Mountain, the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers, Doctor Faustus, Death in Venice, and Felix Krull, while even the early Buddenbrooks remains widely read. But Lotte in Weimar, after some initial success, seems to have become a story for specialists, at least in English-speaking countries. Perhaps this is because Goethe, who exported splendidly to Britain and America in the time of Carlyle and Emerson, now seems an untranslatable author. Or it may be that Goethe’s spirit has not survived what happened in and through Germany from 1933 until 1945.

在曼恩关于《浮士德》的文章中，他指出这首诗将爱情描绘成魔鬼的节日。他对歌德作为文学家的生涯的思考，集中在一个引人注目的段落中，这个段落既是对曼恩的评论，也是对歌德的评论：

In his essay on Faust, Mann remarks that the poem depicts love as a devil’s holiday. The meditation upon Goethe’s career as a man of letters centers itself in a remarkable paragraph that is as much a commentary upon Mann as upon Goethe:

然而，这种通过内在世界再现外在世界——以自身形式和方式重塑外在世界——的做法，无论散发出多么迷人的魅力，都永远无法完全满足或取悦外在世界。原因在于，作者的真实态度中总是包含着某种对立，而这种对立与他的性格密不可分。正是这种知识分子对迟钝、固执、邪恶的人类的态度，总是将诗人作家置于这种特殊的境地，塑造着他们的性格和气质，从而决定着他们的命运。“从理性的高峰来看，”歌德写道，“一切生活都像某种恶性疾病，世界就像一座疯人院。” 这正是这类作家的典型言论：表达了他们对人类的强烈不满。歌德的作品中比人们预想的更能体现这种特质：他经常提及“人类群体”，尤其是他笔下的“亲爱的德国人”，这些话语体现了他特有的易怒和疏离。那么，究竟是什么因素塑造了作家的生活呢？答案是二：感知和对形式的感悟；二者同时存在。奇特的是，对诗人而言，二者浑然一体，彼此相互启发、挑战和激发。这种统一性对他来说，就是心灵、美、自由——一切的一切。若非如此，便是庸俗的人类愚昧，表现为缺乏感知和对形式之美的麻木——他也无法告诉你，究竟是哪一种更令他恼火。

But this business of reproducing the outer world through the inner, which it re-creates after its own form and in its own way, never does, however much charm and fascination may emanate from it, quite satisfy or please the outer world. The reason is that the author’s real attitude always has something of opposition in it, which is quite inseparable from his character. It is the attitude of the man of intellect towards the ponderous, stubborn, evil-minded human race, which always places the poet and writer in this particular position, moulding his character and temperament and so conditioning his destiny. “Viewed from the heights of reason,” Goethe wrote, “all life looks like some malignant disease and the world like a madhouse.” This is a characteristic utterance of the kind of man who writes: the expression of his smarting impatience with mankind. More of the same thing than one would suppose is to be found in Goethe’s works: phrases about the “human pack” in general and his “dear Germans” in particular, typical of the specific irritability and aloofness I mean. For what are the factors that condition the life of the writer? They are twofold: perception and a feeling for form; both of these simultaneously. The strange thing is that for the poet they are one organic unity, in which the one implies, challenges, and draws out the other. This unity is, for him, mind, beauty, freedom—everything. Where it is not, there is vulgar human stupidity, expressing itself in lack of perception and imperviousness to beauty of form—nor can he tell you which of the two he finds the more irritating.

我们几乎不会意识到，这种审美立场是歌德而非福楼拜，是托马斯·曼而非T·S·艾略特的。这正是曼在其巨著《歌德作为资产阶级时代的代表》中所探讨的主题，该文清晰地阐明了歌德（以及曼）为了获得并保持这种审美状态所付出的艰辛努力：

We would hardly know that this aesthetic stance is that of Goethe rather than Flaubert, of Mann rather than T. S. Eliot. That is the subject of the grand essay by Mann on “Goethe as Representative of the Bourgeois Age,” which nevertheless makes clear how heroically Goethe (and Mann) had to struggle in order to achieve and maintain such health:

至于歌德，我在此或许可以就反理想体质的某些人性化和个人影响及症状作个注；这一注注实际上将我引向了如此私密和个人化的心理层面，以至于我只能略作暗示。毫无疑问，理想的信仰，即便需要做好殉道的准备，也比那种崇高而完全讽刺的、缺乏价值和观点的诗歌成就感更能使人精神愉悦，后者完全客观，以同样的爱和同样的冷漠来映照一切。仔细观察歌德，一旦他过了青春期的纯真，便会发现他身上有严重的适应不良和坏脾气的迹象，一种令人沮丧的抑郁，这必然与他对理念的不信任以及他那孩童般的业余爱好有着某种深层的、难以言喻的联系。有一种奇特的冷漠、恶意、疏离、玩世不恭的态度，一种非人般的、精灵般的漠不关心——这种特质令人难以抗拒，但如果你爱他，就必须与他一同去爱。如果你深入探究他性格的这一层面，就会明白，幸福与和谐更多地属于精神之子，而非自然之子。清晰的思路、内心的和谐、坚定的意志、积极的信念和明确的目标——简而言之，灵魂的平静——所有这些，对于精神之子来说都比自然之子更容易获得。自然无法赋予人内心的平静、纯朴和专注；她是一个值得怀疑的因素，她是一个矛盾体、否定体、彻底的怀疑体。她不赋予人仁慈，因为她本身就不仁慈。她不允许做出任何明确的判断，因为她是中立的。她赋予她的孩子们冷漠；伴随着一系列复杂的问题，这些问题更多地与痛苦和恶意有关，而不是与快乐和欢乐有关。

As for Goethe, I may make an observation here having to do with certain human and personal effects and symptoms of the anti-ideal constitution; an observation which, indeed, leads me so far into intimate and individual psychology that only indications are possible. There can be no doubt that ideal faith, although it must be prepared for martyrdom, makes one happier in spirit than belief in a lofty and completely ironic sense of poetic achievement without values and opinions, entirely objective, mirroring everything with the same love and the same indifference. There are in Goethe, on closer examination, as soon as the innocence of the youthful period is past, signs of profound maladjustment and ill humour, a hampering depression, which must certainly have a deep-lying uncanny connection with his mistrust of ideas, his child-of-nature dilettantism. There is a peculiar coldness, ill will, médisance, a devil-may-care mood, an inhuman, elfish irresponsibility—which one cannot indulge enough, but must love along with him if one loves him. If one peers into this region of his character one understands that happiness and harmony are much more the affair of the children of spirit than of the children of nature. Clarity, harmony within oneself, strength of purpose, a positive believing and decided aim—in short, peace in the soul—all this is much more easily achieved by these than by the children of nature. Nature does not confer peace of mind, simplicity, single-mindedness; she is a questionable element, she is a contradiction, denial, thorough-going doubt. She endows with no benevolence, not being benevolent herself. She permits no decided judgments, for she is neutral. She endows her children with indifference; with a complex of problems, which have more to do with torment and ill will than with joy and mirth.

歌德、托马斯·曼和自然在本质上是一致的；他们的幸福与和谐是审美建构，而非既定事实。歌德和托马斯·曼充满矛盾、怀疑和否定精神，他们通过将“自由经济原则应用于知识生活”而获得成功；他们实践了歌德所谓的“观念与情感的自由交流”。歌德晚期的《幻想曲》中有一段精彩的文字，论述了歌德的情感自由交流：

Goethe, Mann, and nature are everywhere the same; their happiness and harmony are aesthetic constructs, and never part of the given. Contradictory, skeptical, and full of the spirit that denies, Goethe and Mann triumph by transferring “liberal economic principles to the intellectual life”; they practice what Goethe called a “free trade of conceptions and feelings.” The late “Fantasy on Goethe” has a delicious paragraph on the matter of Goethe’s free trade in feelings:

歌德的爱情生活是一段奇特的经历。他的风流韵事如今已成为教育的必修课；在体面的德国社会，人们必须能像念宙斯的情人一样，滔滔不绝地列举出他的情人。那些弗里德里克、洛特、米娜和玛丽安娜，如今已化作雕像，安放在人类的殿堂壁龛之中；或许，这能弥补她们曾经的失望。因为这位反复无常的天才，虽然曾短暂地臣服于她们的怀抱，却从未准备好承担后果，从未准备好承受这些迷人邂逅可能带来的对自身生活和自由的限制。或许，这些女士的名声，是对他反复的离去、漫无目的的追求、虚伪的真诚，以及他爱情不过是达到目的的手段——推进其创作——的一种补偿。当工作与生活融为一体时，就像他那样，那些只懂得严肃对待生活的人，最终只能独自承受所有的痛苦。但他总是告诫他们不要把生活看得太重。 “维特一定是——一定是？”他写信给洛特·布夫和她的未婚夫。“你们俩感受不到他，你们只感受到我和你们自己……如果你们能感受到维特对千百颗心意味着什么，你们就不会明白这给你们带来了多大的代价。”他所有的女人都承受了这代价，无论她们是否愿意。

Goethe’s love life is a strange chapter. The list of his love affairs has become a requirement of education; in respectable German society one has to be able to rattle off the ladies like the loves of Zeus. Those Friederikes, Lottes, Minnas, and Mariannes have become statues installed in niches in the cathedral of humanity; and perhaps this makes amends to them for their disappointments. For the fickle genius who for short whiles lay at their feet was never prepared to take the consequences, to bear the restriction upon his life and liberty that these charming adventures might have involved. Perhaps the fame of the ladies is compensation to them for his recurrent flights, for the aimlessness of his wooing, the faithlessness of his sincerity, and the fact that his loving was a means to an end, a means to further his work. Where work and life are one, as was the case with him, those who know only how to take life seriously are left with all the sorrows in their laps. But he always reproved them for taking life seriously. “Werther must—must be?” he wrote to Lotte Buff and her fiancé. “You two do not feel him, you feel only me and yourselves….If only you could feel the thousandth part of what Werther means to a thousand hearts, you would not reckon the cost to you.” All his women bore the cost, whether they liked it or not.

曼在《爱人归来》中回归了歌德“善变的天才”这一特质，这部作品既可以代表曼的讽刺艺术的优势，也可以代表其局限性。

It is to this aspect of Goethe as “fickle genius” that Mann returned in The Beloved Returns, which can serve here as representative both of the strength and the limitation of Mann’s art of irony.

四十四年后，歌德那部臭名昭著的《少年维特的烦恼》中女主人公的原型人物前往魏玛朝圣，并非为了与她六十一岁、六十七岁的情人重聚，而是为了徒劳地追寻着与他们共同的过去融为一体，以及他心中那个关于她曾经的模样，或者说她本可以成为的模样的永恒理想。在四百页的篇幅里，托马斯·曼细腻地描绘了可怜的洛特名声背后几乎无穷无尽的讽刺：这位寡居的、受人尊敬的女士，虽然有她的局限，但绝非愚钝之辈，她既享受着自己作为活生生的神话的地位和作用，又忍受着这一切。曼最极致的讽刺，以其令人难以忍受的平庸而显得怪诞，莫过于对四十四年后，老态龙钟的歌德为他曾经的挚爱举办的那场晚宴的描写。可怜的洛特，在被当作一种文化遗迹和因时间流逝而凋零的青春轻率的混合体之后，被这位伟人用明显不真诚的话语打发走了：“生活让我们分离太久了，我不得不祈求，在你逗留期间，我们能经常见面。”

After forty-four years, the model for the heroine of Goethe’s notorious The Sorrows of Young Werther goes to Weimar on pilgrimage, not to be reunited with her lover, now sixty-seven to her sixty-one, but, rather, in the hopeless quest to be made one both with their mutual past, and with his immortal idea of what she once had been, or could have been. For four hundred pages, Mann plays out the all-but-endless ironies of poor Lotte’s fame, as the widowed and respectable lady, who has her limitations but is nobody’s fool, both enjoys and endures her status and function as a living mythology. Mann’s supreme irony, grotesque in its excruciating banalities, is the account of the dinner that the stiff, old Goethe gives in honor of the object of his passion, some forty-four years after the event. Poor Lotte, after being treated as a kind of amalgam of cultural relic and youthful indiscretion shriven by temporal decay, is dismissed by the great man with a palpably insincere: “Life has held us sundered far too long a time for me not to ask of it that we may meet often during your sojourn.”

但曼恩太过狡猾，他不会就此结束这本书。歌德亲自安排了一场精彩的最终会面。他听到洛特温和地问道：“所以，再次相遇只是一个短篇，一个片段吗？”便以同样高雅的审美方式回答道：

But Mann was too cunning to conclude his book there. A marvelous final meeting is arranged by Goethe himself, who hears Lotte’s gentle question, “So meeting again is a short chapter, a fragment?” and replies in the same high aesthetic mode:

亲爱的灵魂，让我发自内心地回答你，以此作为赎罪和告别。你谈到牺牲。但牺牲是一个奥秘，不可分割，如同世间万物，如同我们自身、生命和工作。转化，即一切。他们向神献祭，最终祭品本身就是神。你用了一个我熟悉且珍爱的比喻；很久以前，它就占据了我的灵魂。我指的是飞蛾扑火的寓言。如果你愿意，就说我是火焰，可怜的飞蛾扑向我。然而，在世事变迁中，我也是蜡烛，献出我的身体，让光芒燃烧。最终，我是那醉醺醺的蝴蝶，坠入火焰——永恒牺牲的象征，肉体转化为灵魂，生命转化为精神。亲爱的灵魂，亲爱的孩子，亲爱的童真老灵魂，我，从始至终，都是祭品，也是献祭者。我曾将你燃烧，如今也依然将你燃烧，化作精神和光明。须知那蜕变是你朋友最珍视、最内在的渴望，是他最大的希望，最深切的期盼：蜕变的戏剧，面容的变换，从白发苍苍到青春，再到少年，却始终保持着人性的面容，带着其人生阶段的特征，青春如同奇迹般在年老中闪耀，年老又从青春中流露。如此，亲爱的，愿你心满意足地安息，如同我一样，已将这一切深思熟虑，来到我身边，用青春的印记装点你古老的身躯。在变化与流动中保持统一，不断地自我转化，万物皆在蜕变，生命时而展现其自然面貌，时而展现其文化面貌，过去转向现在，现在又指向过去，既预示着未来，又以其朦胧的预兆已然丰盈。过去的感受，未来的感受——感受即一切。让我们睁开双眼，看清世界的统一——睁大双眼，宁静而睿智。你想向我索取悔意吗？只需等待。我看见她身披灰色斗篷，骑马向我而来。然后，维特与塔索的时光再次降临。午夜已至，正午已至，死亡将至。愿上帝赐予我倾诉苦难的能力——那时，唯有这最初与最终的告别将伴我左右。那时，舍弃将只是离别，永别，情感的垂死挣扎，以及充满恐怖痛楚的时刻，这痛楚或许会在死亡来临前持续一段时间，即便尚未死亡，也已走向消亡。死亡，最终飞向火焰——万物一体——为何它只能是蜕变？亲爱的幻象，愿你们安息在我宁静的心中——当我们再次醒来，那将是多么美好的时刻啊！

“Dear soul, let me answer you from my heart, in expiation and farewell. You speak of sacrifice. But it is a mystery, indivisible, like all else in the world and one’s person, one’s life, and one’s work. Conversion, transformation, is all. They sacrificed to the god, and in the end the sacrifice was God. You used a figure dear and familiar to me; long since, it took possession of my soul. I mean the parable of the moth and the fatal, luring flame. Say, if you will, that I am the flame, and into me the poor moth flings itself. Yet in the chance and change of things I am the candle too, giving my body that the light may burn. And finally, I am the drunken butterfly that falls to the flame—figure of the eternal sacrifice, body transmuted into soul, and life to spirit. Dear soul, dear child, dear childlike old soul, I, first and last, am the sacrifice, and he that offers it. Once I burned you, ever I burn you, into spirit and light. Know that metamorphosis is the dearest and most inward of thy friend, his great hope, his deepest craving: the play of transformation, changing face, greybeard to youth, to youth the boy, yet ever the human countenance with traits of its proper stage, youth like a miracle shining out in age, age out of youth. Thus mayst thou rest content, beloved, as I am, with having thought it out and come to me, decking thine ancient form with signs of youth. Unity in change and flux, conversion constant out of and into oneself, transmutation of all things, life showing now its natural, now its cultural face, past turning to present, present pointing back to past, both preluding future and with her dim foreshadowings already full. Past feeling, future feeling—feeling is all. Let us open wide eyes upon the unity of the world—eyes wide, serene, and wise. Wouldst thou ask of me repentance? Only wait. I see her ride towards me, in a mantle grey. Then once more the hour of Werther and Tasso will strike, as at midnight already midday strikes, and God give me to say what I suffer—only this first and last will then remain to me. Then forsaking will be only leave-taking, leave-taking for ever, death-struggle of feeling and the hour full of frightful pangs, pangs such as probably for some time precede the hour of death, pangs which are dying if not yet death. Death, final flight into the flame—the All-in-One—why should it too be aught but transformation? In my quiet heart, dear visions, may you rest—and what a pleasant moment that will be, when we anon awake together!”

从某种复杂的意义上说，这其中的讽刺之处在于曼恩对他的前辈的一种“复仇”，因为正是曼恩将歌德的灵魂和光芒燃烧殆尽，最终化作《爱人归来》中那充满希望与渴望的蜕变。曼恩和歌德彼此死去，又彼此经历死亡，这正是叶芝痴迷的那种前苏格拉底式的表述。但对曼恩而言，与神秘主义的叶芝不同，这种通过死亡走向蜕变的过程，是对歌德与其二十世纪后继者之间相互影响关系的复杂隐喻。曼恩在其《歌德幻想曲》中对前辈的描述，用在他自己身上却出奇地准确：

In some complex sense, part of the irony here is Mann’s revenge upon his precursor, since it is Mann who burns Goethe into spirit and light, into the metamorphosis of hope and craving that is The Beloved Returns. Mann and Goethe die each other’s lives, live each other’s deaths, in the pre-Socratic formulation that so obsessed W. B. Yeats. But for Mann, unlike the occult Yeats, the movement through death into transformation is a complex metaphor for the influence relationship between Goethe and his twentieth-century descendant. What Mann, in his “Fantasy on Goethe,” delineated in his precursor is charmingly accurate when applied to Mann himself:

这里展现的是一种极致的自恋，一种对自我极度的满足，这种满足如此认真，如此执着于自我完善、提升和提炼，以至于“虚荣”这种狭隘的词汇都无法恰当地形容。正是这种对自我及其成长的深刻喜悦，成就了《诗与真理》——至少是世上最精彩、最迷人的自传——它本质上是一部第一人称小说，以最动人的笔触，讲述了天才如何形成，运气与才华如何被某种未知的恩典紧密相连，以及人格如何在更高境界的阳光下成长绽放。人格！歌德称之为“凡人至高无上的幸福”——但它究竟是什么，它的内在本质是什么，它的奥秘又在哪里——因为它的确充满奥秘——就连他自己也从未解释过。事实上，尽管他热爱言辞，热爱直击人生核心的文字，但他从未认为一切都必须解释。当然，这种被称为“人格”的现象，将我们带离了纯粹的智力、理性、可分析的领域，进入了自然界，那里栖息着那些“令世人惊叹”却无法进一步阐释的原始而神秘的事物。

We have here a kind of splendid narcissism, a contentment with self far too serious and far too concerned to the very end with self-perfection, heightening, and distillation of personal endowment, for a petty-minded word like “vanity” to be applicable. Here is that profound delight in that self and its growth to which we owe Poetry and Truth, the best, at any rate the most charming autobiography the world has seen—essentially a novel in the first person which informs us, in the most wonderfully winning tone, how a genius is formed, how luck and merit are indissolubly linked by an unknown decree of grace and how a personality grows and flourishes under the sun of a higher dispensation. Personality! Goethe called it “the supreme bliss of mortal man”—but what it really is, in what its inner nature consists, wherein its mystery lies—for there is a mystery about it—not even he ever explained. For that matter, for all his love for the telling word, for the word that strikes to the heart of life, he never thought that everything must be explained. Certainly this phenomenon known as “personality” takes us beyond the sphere of purely intellectual, rational, analyzable matters into the realm of nature, where dwell those elemental and daemonic things which “astound the world” without being amenable to further elucidation.

曼恩的自恋，在他最强烈的表现中，恰恰是魔鬼般的，是对自我的深刻喜悦，如果没有这种喜悦，像《魔山》和《浮士德博士》这样风格迥异的作品都会沦为讽刺的疲惫。

The splendid narcissism of Mann, at his strongest, is precisely daemonic, is that profound delight in the self without which works as various as The Magic Mountain and Doctor Faustus would collapse into the weariness of the irony of irony.

在曼恩1936年发表的杰出论文《弗洛伊德与未来》中，他为自己模仿歌德奠定了基础：

In his remarkable essay “Freud and the Future” (1936), Mann wrote the pattern for his own imitation of Goethe:

古代人的自我及其自我意识与我们截然不同，它不那么排他，也不那么泾渭分明。它仿佛向后敞开，从过去汲取养分，并通过重复赋予其新的当下性。西班牙学者奥尔特加·伊·加塞特指出，古代人在做任何事情之前，都会后退一步，就像斗牛士向后跃起，准备给予致命一击。他追溯过去，寻找一种可以融入其中的模式，如同钻进潜水钟一般，从而既能伪装又能得到保护，进而冲向眼前的难题。因此，从某种意义上说，他的生活是一种复兴，一种回归古老的态度。但正是这种复兴式的生活，构成了神话般的生活。亚历山大追随米尔提亚德的足迹；古代凯撒的传记作者们确信（无论对错），凯撒以亚历山大为原型。但这种“模仿”的含义远比我们今天所理解的要丰富得多。这是一种神话般的认同，在古代尤为常见；但它一直延续到近代，并且在任何时代都具有心理上的可能性。我们不是经常听到拿破仑的形象是按照古代的模式塑造的吗？他遗憾当时的观念不允许他效仿亚历山大，自称是朱庇特·阿蒙之子。但我们无需怀疑——至少在他东征时期——他确实在神话中将自己与亚历山大混淆；而当他转向西方之后，据说他宣称：“我就是查理曼大帝。”请注意：不是“我像查理曼大帝”或“我的处境像查理曼大帝”，而是简单地“我就是他”。这就是神话的表述。因此，在古代，生活——至少是有意义的生活——是神话的血肉重现；它参照神话，诉诸神话；只有通过神话，通过对过去的参照，它才能使自身获得真实性和意义。神话赋予生命以合法性；唯有通过神话，生命才能获得自我意识、认可和神圣性。克利奥帕特拉直至死亡都完美诠释了她阿芙洛狄忒的形象——还有什么比颂扬神话更有意义、更值得地活着和死去呢？我们只需想想耶稣和他的生活，他的一生都是为了实现圣经预言。区分他自身的意识和福音书作者的约定俗成并非易事。但他在十字架上，大约在第九个小时时所说的“以利，以利，拉马撒巴各大尼？”显然绝非绝望和幻灭的爆发；恰恰相反，这是一种崇高的弥赛亚式的自我认知。​​因为这句话并非原创，也并非自发的呼喊。它出自诗篇第二十二篇的开头，而整篇诗篇都在宣告弥赛亚的到来。耶稣是在引用，而这引用意味着：“是的，我就是弥赛亚！”克利奥帕特拉正是这样引用了这句话，当时她把毒蛇贴在胸口等死；而这句话的意思又是：“是的，是我！

The ego of antiquity and its consciousness of itself were different from our own, less exclusive, less sharply defined. It was, as it were, open behind; it received much from the past and by repeating it gave it presentness again. The Spanish scholar Ortega y Gasset puts it that the man of antiquity, before he did anything, took a step backwards, like the bull-fighter who leaps back to deliver the mortal thrust. He searched the past for a pattern into which he might slip as into a diving-bell, and being thus at once disguised and protected might rush upon his present problem. Thus his life was in a sense a reanimation, an archaizing attitude. But it is just this life as reanimation that is the life as myth. Alexander walked in the footsteps of Miltiades; the ancient biographers of Caesar were convinced, rightly or wrongly, that he took Alexander as his prototype. But such “imitation” meant far more than we mean by the word today. It was mythical identification, peculiarly familiar to antiquity; but it is operative far into modern times, and at all times is psychically possible. How often have we not been told that the figure of Napoleon was cast in the antique mould! He regretted that the mentality of the time forbade him to give himself out for the son of Jupiter Ammon, in imitation of Alexander. But we need not doubt that—at least at the period of his Eastern exploits—he mythically confounded himself with Alexander; while after he turned his face westwards he is said to have declared: “I am Charlemagne.” Note that: not “I am like Charlemagne” or “My situation is like Charlemagne’s,” but quite simply “I am he.” That is the formulation of the myth. Life, then—at any rate, significant life—was in ancient times the reconstitution of the myth in flesh and blood; it referred to and appealed to the myth; only through it, through reference to the past, could it approve itself as genuine and significant. The myth is the legitimization of life; only through and in it does life find self-awareness, sanction, consecration. Cleopatra fulfilled her Aphrodite character even unto death—and can one live and die more significantly or worthily than in the celebration of the myth? We have only to think of Jesus and His life, which was lived in order that that which was written might be fulfilled. It is not easy to distinguish between his own consciousness and the conventionizations of the Evangelists. But His word on the Cross, about the ninth hour, that “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” was evidently not in the least an outburst of despair and disillusionment; but on the contrary a lofty messianic sense of self. For the phrase is not original, not a spontaneous outcry. It stands at the beginning of the Twenty-second Psalm, which from one end to the other is an announcement of the Messiah. Jesus was quoting, and the quotation meant: “Yes, it is I!” Precisely thus did Cleopatra quote when she took the asp to her breast to die; and again the quotation meant: “Yes, it is I!”

实际上，曼引用了歌德的话，从而宣称：“是的，那就是我。”古代的自我不过是艺术家的自我，挪用先驱者以克服影响过程的滞后性。曼在两段之后便揭示了他关于弗洛伊德的文章的真正主题：

In effect, Mann quotes Goethe, and thus proclaims, “Yes, it is I.” The ego of antiquity is simply the artist’s ego, appropriating the precursor in order to overcome the belatedness of the influence process. Mann reveals the true subject of his essay on Freud just two paragraphs farther on:

幼稚——换句话说，退行到童年——这种真正具有精神分析意义的因素在我们所有人的生活中扮演着多么重要的角色！它在塑造一个人的生命中占据着多么重要的地位；事实上，它的作用方式正如我所描述的那样：作为一种神话般的认同，一种生存方式，一种对既有足迹的追随！与父亲的联结，以及对更高层次、更成熟的父亲替代形象的移情——这些幼稚的特征是如何作用于个体的生命，从而标记和塑造它的！我用“塑造”这个词，因为对我而言，我们称之为教育（Bildung）的、塑造人格的最幸福、最愉悦的因素，正是这种强大的崇拜和爱的影响，这种源于深刻亲近感而选择的、孩童般对父亲形象的认同。艺术家，尤其是那些充满童真、沉迷于游戏的艺术家，能够告诉我们，这种孩童般的模仿对其自身生活产生了神秘却又显而易见的影响，并最终成就了他们富有成效的艺术生涯。而他们的艺术生涯，归根结底，往往不过是在截然不同的时代和个人境遇下，以截然不同的方式（姑且称之为孩童般的方式）重现昔日英雄形象。歌德的模仿，从《维特》和《威廉·迈斯特》的阶段，到晚年创作的《浮士德》和《迪万》，至今仍能塑造并赋予艺术家生命以神话般的色彩——它源于艺术家的潜意识，却又像艺术家那样，反复演绎，最终化作一种微笑、孩童般纯真而又深刻的觉悟。

Infantilism—in other words, regression to childhood—what a role this genuinely psychoanalytic element plays in all our lives! What a large share it has in shaping the life of a human being; operating, indeed, in just the way I have described: as mythical identification, as survival, as a treading in footprints already made! The bond with the father, and the transference to father-substitute pictures of a higher and more developed type—how these infantile traits work upon the life of the individual to mark and shape it! I use the word “shape,” for to me in all seriousness the happiest, most pleasurable element of what we call education (Bildung), the shaping of the human being, is just this powerful influence of admiration and love, this childish identification with a father-image elected out of profound affinity. The artist in particular, a passionately childlike and play-possessed being, can tell us of the mysterious yet after all obvious effect of such infantile imitation upon his own life, his productive conduct of a career which after all is often nothing but a reanimation of the hero under very different temporal and personal conditions and with very different, shall we say childish means. The imitatio Goethe, with its Werther and Wilhelm Meister stages, its old-age period of Faust and Diwan, can still shape and mythically mould the life of an artist—rising out of his unconscious, yet playing over—as is the artist way—into a smiling, childlike, and profound awareness.

这种深刻的觉悟是曼恩独有的，关乎他自身对歌德模仿的实践。歌德在其《色彩理论》中的论述——“即使是完美的典范也会产生令人不安的影响，因为它们会让我们跳过成长过程中必要的阶段，其结果往往是，我们被引入歧途，陷入无尽的谬误之中”——在这里得到了巧妙的呼应和反转。歌德也正是这样一位歌德，他既推崇自身的独创性，也推崇从他人那里汲取灵感的能力。因此，他可以说：“只有将他人的财富据为己有，我们才能创造出伟大的事物”，但他同时也坚持认为：“除了能量、力量和意志之外，我们究竟还能称之为我们自己的什么呢？”曼恩敏锐地意识到自己落后于时代，他喜欢引用歌德的那个问题：“当其他人也活着的时候，一个人还能活着吗？”

The profound awareness is Mann’s own, and concerns his own enactment of the imitatio Goethe. Subtly echoed and reversed here is Goethe’s observation in his Theory of Colours to the effect that “even perfect models have a disturbing effect in that they lead us to skip necessary stages in our Bildung, with the result, for the most part, that we are carried wide of the mark into limitless error.” This is also the Goethe who celebrated his own originality as well as his power of appropriating from others. Thus he could say, “Only by making the riches of the others our own do we bring anything great into being,” but also insist, “What can we in fact call our own except the energy, the force, the will!” Mann, acutely sensing his own belatedness, liked to quote the old Goethe’s question: “Does a man live when others also live?”

《爱人归来》中的歌德并非歌德本人，而是托马斯·曼——尼采预言并赞颂的未来艺术家，一位世界戏仿者。E·R·库尔提乌斯无疑准确地将歌德视为文化传统的终结而非新的开端。如今，曼也显得古老，他并非现代主义者或后浪漫主义者，而是一位迟来的歌德，一位凭借自身人格的神秘性和艺术的讽刺性趣味而获得胜利的人文主义者。如同他对歌德的诠释，曼如今似乎更像自然之子而非精神之子，但他雄辩地努力穿透自然，将死亡转化为辩证的艺术。

The Goethe of The Beloved Returns is not Goethe, but Mann himself, the world parodist prophesied and celebrated by Nietzsche as the artist of the future. E. R. Curtius doubtless was accurate in seeing Goethe as an ending and not as a fresh beginning of the cultural tradition. Mann, too, now seems archaic, not a modernist or post-Romantic, but a belated Goethe, a humanist triumphing through the mystery of his own personality and the ironic playfulness of his art. Like his vision of Goethe, Mann now seems a child of nature rather than of the spirit, but laboring eloquently to burn through nature into the transformation that converts deathliness into a dialectical art.

曼恩为自己辩护，否认自己是喋喋不休的讽刺家，并最终请求我们把他看作是一位幽默作家：

Defending himself from many characterizations as an incessant ironist, Mann belatedly asked us to think of him as a humorist:

每当评论家如此明确、完全地将我的作品归类为讽刺作品，并认为我彻头彻尾是个讽刺家，却不考虑幽默的概念时，我总是感到有点无聊。

（托马斯·曼）

I always feel a bit bored when critics assign my own work so definitely and completely to the realm of irony and consider me an ironist through and through, without also taking account of the concept of humor.

(Thomas Mann)

《魔山》的作者坚持认为，他希望读者发自内心地开怀大笑，而不是仅仅露出知性的微笑。然而，他的诠释者们却引发了太多知性的微笑，以至于我们都感到有些厌倦。讽刺的讽刺之处在于，它最终破坏的并非意义（正如解构主义批评家所坚持的那样），而是兴趣，而没有兴趣，我们就无法继续阅读。托马斯·曼无疑如埃里希·海勒所言，是“讽刺的德国人”，但重读《魔山》远不止是一次讽刺体验。当然，这本书从未让我发笑。曼远非S·J·佩雷尔曼或菲利普·罗斯。然而，这部小说出版至今已逾九十年，其内涵显然已然成熟。一个时代的讽刺与另一个时代的讽刺截然不同，《魔山》如今看来是一部温和而严肃的作品——如同其令人敬佩的主人公汉斯·卡斯托普一样，真挚、深情而坚实。

The author of The Magic Mountain insisted that he wished to draw laughter from his reader’s heart, rather than an intellectual smile. He has provoked so many intellectual smiles in his exegetes that they have bored us all more than a bit. The irony of irony is that finally it defeats not meaning (as deconstructionist critics insist) but interest, without which we cannot go on reading. Thomas Mann doubtless was what Erich Heller called him, “the ironic German,” but rereading The Magic Mountain is much more than an experience in irony. Not that the book ever provokes me to laughter. Mann is hardly S. J. Perelman or Philip Roth. Yet it is now more than ninety years since the novel first was published, and the book clearly has mellowed. The irony of one age is never the irony of another, and The Magic Mountain seems now a work of gentle high seriousness—as earnest, affectionate, and solid as its admirable hero, Hans Castorp.

《魔山》对众多文学体裁和惯例的戏仿显而易见。尼采对托马斯·曼的影响非常强烈，而戏仿正是尼采应对影响焦虑的方式。曼显然也认为，艺术的最终目标在于成为自身的戏仿。或许，这可以弥补某种本质上可能只是优柔寡断的讽刺。如今，普通读者阅读这部小说，几乎不会察觉到其中对浪漫主义惯例的戏仿，也完全可以忽略曼晚期浪漫主义讽刺中那些无穷无尽的歧义。

That The Magic Mountain parodies a host of literary genres and conventions is finely obvious. The effect of Nietzsche upon Mann was very strong, and parody was Nietzsche’s answer to the anxieties of influence. Mann evidently did believe that what remained to be done was for art to become its own parody. Presumably, that would have redeemed an irony that at bottom may have been mere indecisiveness. Reading the novel now, the common reader scarcely will recognize the parody of Romantic convention, and can afford to bypass the endless ambiguities of Mann’s late version of romantic irony.

这并非赞同埃里希·海勒的讽刺性结论：“我们所处的世界就是如此，意义和价值不得不被伪装——伪装成讽刺，伪装成文学，或者两者兼而有之：例如在《魔山》中。 ”如今，曼恩的故事主要提供的既非“意义”，也非讽刺，而是对过往现实的深情描绘，是对一种已逝的欧洲文化——歌德和弗洛伊德的文化——的深情再现。2018年的读者必须将这本书视为一部历史小说，一座永远逝去、永远令人怀念的人文主义的纪念碑。曼恩精湛的技艺塑造了我们所能看到的纳粹恐怖浩劫之前欧洲最生动的版本。曼恩原本意在戏仿，但时间的推移和变迁带来的反讽却促成了另一种转变，使得《魔山》在今天成为一部极其感人的怀旧之作。

This is not to agree with Erich Heller’s ironic conclusion: “Such is our world that sense and meaning have to be disguised—as irony, or as literature, or as both come together: for instance in The Magic Mountain.” Mann’s story now primarily offers neither “meaning” nor irony but, rather, a loving representation of past realities, of a European culture forever gone, the culture of Goethe and Freud. A reader in 2018 must experience the book as a historical novel, the cairn of a humanism forever lost, forever longed for. Mann’s superb workmanship fashioned the most vivid version we have of a Europe before the catastrophe of the Nazi horror. Where Mann intended parody, the counter-ironies of time and change have produced instead a transformation that today makes The Magic Mountain into an immensely poignant study of the nostalgias.

如今，汉斯·卡斯托普这个人物在我看来比我近75年前初读这部小说时更加微妙，也更讨人喜欢。尽管曼恩认可这种观点，但卡斯托普并非一个求索者，他也不追求任何圣杯或理想。他是一个相当超脱的角色，无论面对开明的塞滕布里尼、恐怖分子纳夫塔，还是充满英雄气概的生命力的皮珀科恩，他都能以几乎相同的心境聆听他们的教诲。他对情欲的超脱更是非同寻常；七个月后，他只与克拉维迪娅有过一次性关系，之后在疗养院的七年间，他都避免了任何其他性体验。即便他对克拉维迪娅怀有强烈的爱意，这种爱意也鲜少带有传统爱情的痛苦痕迹。他的超脱是否源于他自七岁起便成为孤儿的经历尚不明确，但本质上，他满足于观察、学习和吸收。也可能是克拉维迪亚与普里比斯拉夫·希佩重燃了少年时代的恋情，这种同性恋情愫从未在普里比斯拉夫·希佩身上得到满足，因为普里比斯拉夫·希佩的名字在德语中是一种镰刀或镰刀，这种吸引力带有死亡的意味。

Hans Castorp himself now seems to me both a subtler and a more likable representation than he did when I first read the novel, nearly three-quarters of a century ago. Despite Mann’s endorsement of the notion, Castorp is no quester, and pursues no grail or ideal. He is a character of considerable detachment, who will listen with almost equal contentment to the enlightened Settembrini, the terroristic Naphta, or the heroically vitalistic Peeperkorn. His erotic detachment is extraordinary; after seven months, he makes love to Clavdia just once, and then avoids any other sexual experience for the rest of his seven-year stay at the sanatorium. If he has a high passion for Clavdia, it nevertheless carries few of the traditional signs of love’s torments. Whether his detachment has some root in his having been an orphan since the age of seven is unclear, but essentially he is content to see, to be taught, to absorb. It may also be that Clavdia renews his schoolboy relationship with Pribislav Hippe, a homoeroticism never fulfilled with someone whose name is a kind of scythe or sickle in German, an attraction with deathly overtones.

我们并不认为卡斯托普软弱，然而他的本性似乎几乎完全没有攻击性。仿佛他内心的死亡本能并非源于受伤的自恋。卡斯托普身上没有任何心理创伤，或许永远也不会有。无论他的创造者意图如何，他本身并不讽刺，也不再像是对任何事物或任何人的模仿。普通读者会非常喜欢卡斯托普，甚至开始把他视为某种意义上的“普通人”，而他显然并非如此。他真正的动力在于自我教育，一种纯粹为了教育本身而追求的教育。卡斯托普是大学总是宣称却永远找不到的那种理想学生。他对一切事物、所有可能的知识都充满浓厚的兴趣，然而知识本身对他而言就是目的。知识对他来说并非权力，无论是对自身还是对他人；它绝非浮士德式的权力。

We do not think of Castorp as weak, and yet his nature seems almost totally free of aggressivity. It is as though the death drive in him does not take its origin in a wounded narcissism. Castorp bears no psychic scars, and probably never will acquire any. Whatever his maker’s intentions, he is not in himself ironic, nor does he seem anymore to be a parody of anything or anyone whatsoever. The common reader becomes very fond of Castorp, and even begins to regard him as a kind of Everyman, which he most certainly is not. His true drive is toward self-education, education sought for its own sake alone. Castorp is that ideal student the universities always proclaim yet never find. He is intensely interested in everything, in all possible knowledge, and yet that knowledge is an end in itself. Knowledge is not power for him, whether over himself or over others; it is in no way Faustian.

尽管卡斯托普对神秘主义充满热情，但他并不追求成为一位神秘学大师，无论是像塞滕布里尼那样的理性主义者，还是像纳夫塔那样的反理性主义者。虽然他被皮珀科恩的伟大个性和生命力论的倡导者身份所吸引，但卡斯托普却对自己表面上的平庸感到十分满足，并乐于逃避自己唯一一次满足的对克拉维迪娅的渴望——克拉维迪娅象征着交织着性爱与死亡的黑暗情欲。卡斯托普是个幸存者，我不认为他会在第一次世界大战的战场上死去。纳夫塔因缺乏杀死塞滕布里尼的勇气而自杀；塞滕布里尼因思考纳夫塔绝望的行为而崩溃；皮珀科恩也选择了自杀，无法承受阳痿的折磨。只有卡斯托普会继续前进，变得更加坚强和坚定，或许会完成从工程师到艺术家的自我转变，从而写出一部类似《魔山》的小说。

Despite his passion for hermeticism, Castorp is not striving to become an esoteric adept, whether rationalist like Settembrini or antirationalist like Naphta. And though he is fascinated by Peeperkorn as a grand personality and an apostle of vitalism, Castorp is more than content with his own apparent colorlessness, and with his own evasions of his only once fulfilled desire for Clavdia, representative as she is of the dark eros that mingles sexual love and death. Castorp is a survivor, and I do not believe that we are to foresee him as dying upon the battlefields of World War I. Naphta kills himself, in frustration at lacking the courage to kill Settembrini; Settembrini is broken by his contemplation of Naphta’s desperate act; Peeperkorn, too, is a suicide, unable to bear the onset of impotence. Only Castorp will go on, strengthened and resolute, and possibly will complete his self-transformation from engineer to artist, so as to write a novel not unlike The Magic Mountain.

—

这究竟是怎样的魔法——这座山间疗养院究竟蕴藏着怎样的魔力？在某种极端情况下，书中承认了神秘主义的存在，卡斯托普已故的表兄约阿希姆出现在降灵会上：

What kind of magic is it—what enchantment does the mountain sanatorium possess? At one extreme limit, the book admits the occult, when Castorp’s dead cousin, Joachim, appears at the séance:

房间里比之前多了一个人。在远处，红色的光线隐没在昏暗之中，视线几乎无法触及，在书桌和屏风之间，医生的诊疗椅上，也就是中场休息时艾莉坐的地方，约阿希姆正坐在那里。那是他生命最后几天的样子，面颊凹陷，阴影笼罩，蓄着战士般的胡须，嘴唇丰满而微微卷曲。他向后靠着，一条腿搭在另一条腿上。他那消瘦的脸上，虽然被头巾遮挡，但依然清晰可见苦难的印记，以及曾经赋予他美感的庄重和肃穆。他眉间，两道皱纹，深深地嵌在骨质的眼窝里；但他那双深邃的黑眸中，温和的神情丝毫未变，平静而友善的目光只注视着汉斯·卡斯托普一人。那对招风耳的古老缺陷，在头巾下依然隐约可见——他那顶奇特的头巾，他们根本看不清是什么。约阿希姆表兄没穿便服。他的佩剑似乎倚靠在腿上，他握着剑柄，有人觉得他腰带上好像有个手枪套。但他穿的并非正规军服。没有颜色，没有装饰；领子像一件立陶宛军服，还有侧袋。胸前下方某个地方别着一个十字架。他的脚看起来很大，腿却很细，似乎缠着绷带，与其说是为了打仗，不如说是为了运动。那是什么？这顶帽子？看起来就像约阿希姆把一个军用炊具倒扣在头上，用一根带子绑在下巴上。然而，这看起来却很像个真正的战士，或许像个老式步兵。

There was one more person in the room than before. There in the background, where the red rays lost themselves in gloom, so that the eye scarcely reached thither, between writing-desk and screen, in the doctor’s consulting-chair, where in the intermission Elly had been sitting, Joachim sat. It was the Joachim of the last days, with hollow, shadowy cheeks, warrior’s beard and full, curling lips. He sat leaning back, one leg crossed over the other. On his wasted face, shaded though it was by his head-covering, was plainly seen the stamp of suffering, the expression of gravity and austerity which had beautified it. Two folds stood on his brow, between the eyes, that lay deep in their bony cavities; but there was no change in the mildness of the great dark orbs, whose quiet friendly gaze sought out Hans Castorp, and him alone. That ancient grievance of the outstanding ears was still to be seen under the head-covering, his extraordinary head-covering, which they could not make out. Cousin Joachim was not in mufti. His sabre seemed to be leaning against his leg, he held the handle, one thought to distinguish something like a pistol-case in his belt. But that was no proper uniform he wore. No colour, no decorations; it had a collar like a litewka jacket, and side pockets. Somewhere low down on the breast was a cross. His feet looked large, his legs very thin, they seemed to be bound or wound as for the business of sport more than war. And what was it, this headgear? It seemed as though Joachim had turned an army cook-pot upside-down on his head, and fastened it under his chin with a band. Yet it looked quite properly warlike, like an old-fashioned foot-soldier, perhaps.

通过这种方式，神秘主义预示着未来——制服和头盔都来自第一次世界大战——曼恩实际上选择了一种神秘的时间理论，撇开所有讽刺意味不谈。许多注释家都注意到这本书对数字七及其各种变体的痴迷。另一些人则指出，约阿希姆死后，小说中所有关于时间的指涉都消失了。卡斯托普忘记了自己的年龄，也忘记了自己在魔山上停留的时间。他进入了永恒。

By thus making the occult prophetic of what was to come—the uniform and helmet are of World War I—Mann essentially chose, all ironies aside, a mystical theory of time. Many exegetes have noted the book’s obsession with the number seven, in all its variants. Others have noted that after Joachim dies all temporal references disappear from the novel. Castorp forgets his own age, and the length of his own stay on the Magic Mountain. He passes into timelessness.

约阿希姆和他的表兄在这里住了多久，直到他那次不幸的离开，或者总共住了多久；他离开的日期是什么时候，他走了多久，什么时候回来的；汉斯·卡斯托普自己在他表兄回来告别时在这里待了多久；——撇开约阿希姆不谈——肖沙夫人离开了多久；她回来（因为她确实回来了）是什么时候，从哪一天开始；在她回来之前，汉斯·卡斯托普自己在贝格霍夫府邸待了多久；没有人问过他所有这些问题，他自己可能也不愿去问。如果有人问他这些问题，他会用指尖轻敲额头，肯定答不上来——这和很久以前的第一个晚上，塞滕布里尼先生问他年龄时，他无法回答一样令人不安。

How long Joachim had lived here with his cousin, up to the time of his fateful departure, or taken all in all; what had been the date of his going, how long he had been gone, when he had come back; how long Hans Castorp himself had been up here when his cousin returned and then bade time farewell; how long—dismissing Joachim from our calculations—Frau Chauchat had been absent; how long, since what date, she had been back again (for she did come back); how much mortal time Hans Castorp himself had spent in House Berghof by the time she returned; no one asked him all these questions, and he probably shrank from asking himself. If they had been put to him, he would have tapped his forehead with the tips of his fingers, and most certainly not have known—a phenomenon as disquieting as his incapacity to answer Herr Settembrini, that long-ago first evening, when the latter had asked him his age.

小说开篇便将卡斯托普描述为“一个谦逊的年轻人”，但这位看似平凡至极的人物，实际上却是一位隐士，一位拥有魔性的人，他自出生起便被赋予了对永恒的独特洞见。书中从歌德、施蒂夫特、凯勒等人那里继承的所谓“教化”（Bildung）主题模式，对卡斯托普而言几乎是不可能的，因为他不需要像几乎所有人那样，接受无休止的文化熏陶。他无需成长，他只是自然而然地展现自我。因为他是原始人，是曼在其《约瑟夫》四部曲的“序曲”中深情阐述的诺斯替神话中的始祖亚当。事实上，他已经是曼笔下的约瑟夫，是天国的宠儿。

The opening words of the novel describe Castorp as “an unassuming young man,” but this fellow who seems the apotheosis of the average is of course hermetic and daemonic, marked from birth for singular visions of eternity. Bildung, the supposed thematic pattern that the book inherits from Goethe, Stifter, Keller, and others, hardly is possible for Castorp, who does not require the endless cultural instruction nearly everyone else wishes to inflict upon him. He need not develop; he simply unfolds. For he is Primal Man, the Ur-Adam of the Gnostic myth that Mann lovingly expounds in the “Prelude” of his Joseph tetralogy. Indeed, he already is Mann’s Joseph, the favored of heaven.

—

曼恩在《魔山》中想要留下深刻印象的许多东西，矛盾地，却已湮没在时间长河中。社会讽刺、知识分子式的反讽以及文化危机感，如今都显得相当过时。塞滕布里尼、纳夫塔、皮珀科恩、克拉维迪娅和约阿希姆都散发着一种古老的魅力，一种褪色的审美尊严，他们是戏仿的戏仿，是时代剧，是既诡异又恰到好处的老照片。汉斯·卡斯托普，如今依然像1924年那样苍白无力，却依然保持着他的直接性、他的现实意义，以及他那令人不安的吸引力。他并非尼采笔下没有超我的“新人”，而是尼采式的诠释意志：他更倾向于接受而非贪婪，更倾向于多元而非单一，更倾向于情感而非冷漠，更倾向于与欲望保持距离而非沉溺其中。在某种意义上，卡斯托普明白自己本身就是一种诠释，他既不代表叔本华的求生意志，也不代表弗洛伊德爱与死的交织冲动，而是代表尼采对生命文本的掌控意志。卡斯托普在书中不断向其他人提出的隐含问题是：你究竟是谁，这个诠释者？你试图从我的生命中获得什么权力？因为他也向我们提出了这些问题，这些疑问逐渐累积，最终使卡斯托普成为一个我们无法回避的象征。曼在告别他的主人公时说，卡斯托普之所以重要，是因为他“爱的梦想”，这大概就是“雪”这一章节中的景象。幸运的是，曼这位技艺精湛的作家，创造出了一个比他自己意识到的还要精彩的人物。卡斯托普是那种罕见的虚构人物，他拥有足以让我们对现实认知产生质疑的权威。读者在解读卡斯托普的作品时，必须扪心自问：我的爱情梦想是什么？我的情欲幻想是什么？这种梦想或幻想如何影响我自身发展的可能性？

Much of what Mann intended as memorable value in The Magic Mountain has, paradoxically, been lost to time. The social satire, intellectual irony, and sense of cultural crisis are all now quite archaic. Settembrini, Naphta, Peeperkorn, Clavdia, and Joachim all possess an antique charm, a kind of faded aesthetic dignity, parodies of parodies, period pieces, old photographs uncannily right and yet altogether odd. Hans Castorp, as colorless now as he was in 1924, retains his immediacy, his relevance, his disturbing claim upon us. He is not the Nietzschean new man, without a superego, but the Nietzschean will to interpretation: receptive rather than rapacious, plural rather than unitary, affective rather than indifferent, distanced from rather than abandoned to desire. In some sense, Castorp knows that he himself is an interpretation, knows that he represents neither Schopenhauer’s will to live, nor Freud’s mingled drives of love and death, but Nietzsche’s will to power over the text of life. The implicit questions Castorp is always putting to everyone else in the book are: who exactly are you, the interpreter, and what power do you seek to gain over my life? Because he puts these questions to us also, with cumulative force, Castorp becomes a representation we cannot evade. Mann, taking leave of his hero, said that Castorp mattered because of his “dream of love,” presumably the vision of the chapter “Snow.” It was fortunate that Mann, a miraculous artisan, had wrought better than even he himself knew. Castorp is one of those rare fictions who acquire the authority to call our versions of reality into some doubt. The reader, interpreting Castorp, must come to ask herself or himself: what is my dream of love, my erotic illusion, and how does that dream or illusion qualify my own possibilities of unfolding?

从这个意义上讲，托马斯·曼与托尔斯泰一样，是一位糟糕的丈夫和灾难性的父亲。他和妻子卡蒂娅·普林斯海姆育有六个孩子，卡蒂娅出身于一个世俗化的犹太家庭。他内心深处的欲望是同性恋，这几乎成了公开的秘密，而他的双性恋倾向也体现在他的三个孩子埃里卡、克劳斯和戈洛身上。卡蒂娅·普林斯海姆为了迎合曼而皈依了路德教，她不仅要照顾曼和六个孩子，还要承担维持家庭运转的所有日常决策，因此总是疲惫不堪。她最终因精疲力竭而倒下，被送往达沃斯的一家疗养院休养。曼显然是在探望她时，萌生了创作《魔山》的想法。

Thomas Mann, in this sense only like Tolstoy, was a dreadful husband and a catastrophic father. He had six children with his wife, Katia Pringsheim, who came from a secularized Jewish family. His deepest desires were homosexual, which became a kind of open secret, and his bisexuality was repeated in his children Erika, Klaus, and Golo. Katia Pringsheim, who had obliged Mann by converting to Lutheranism, was perpetually overworked, not only in caring for him and the six children, but by having to make all the daily decisions that kept the household going. She collapsed from exhaustion, and was sent to a Davos sanatorium to rest and recover. Visiting her there, Mann evidently first conceived of The Magic Mountain.

曼恩的孩子们慢慢学会了如何应对他的自私，并学会独立生活，但其中两个孩子，克劳斯和迈克尔，最终都选择了自杀。艾丽卡无疑是最令人瞩目的，她逐渐成为一家之主，尽其所能地照顾着父母和兄弟姐妹。

Mann’s children slowly learned to weather his egoism and to make their way on their own, but two of them, Klaus and Michael, eventually committed suicide. Erika, surely the most remarkable, in time became the true head of the household and presided over her parents and her siblings, insofar as she could.

我小时候很喜欢读托马斯·曼的哥哥海因里希·曼写的两部历史小说，都是关于纳瓦拉的亨利的，他后来成为法国国王亨利四世，波旁王朝的第一位君主。在我看来，海因里希·曼比他才华横溢的弟弟托马斯·曼更令人敬佩。与托马斯·曼不同，他从一开始就反对纳粹，被迫流亡法国，最终先是逃往西班牙，然后是葡萄牙，最后到了美国，但在那里他并没有过上好日子。他的第二任妻子自杀了，而他本人则孤独地死在了加利福尼亚的贫困之中。

When I was very young, I greatly enjoyed reading two historical novels by Mann’s older brother, Heinrich, both on Henry of Navarre, who was to become King Henry IV of France, first of the Bourbon monarchs. Heinrich Mann seems to me a much more impressive human being than his more gifted brother. Unlike Thomas Mann, he opposed the Nazis from the start and had to go into exile in France, and eventually fled first to Spain, then to Portugal, and finally to the United States, where he did not prosper. His second wife killed herself, and he died in solitude and poor circumstances in California.

我又回到了汉斯·卡斯托普身上，托马斯·曼曾讽刺地贬低他，说他是个平庸的年轻人。但卡斯托普绝非如此。托马斯·曼试图让他表面上显得乏味无趣，但真正读懂这部小说的读者会对此不以为意。在汉斯·卡斯托普于魔法山度过的七年间，他经历了种种变故，却又仿佛什么都没发生。他爱上了神秘的克拉维迪娅·肖沙，而克拉维迪娅只与他有过一次幽会。他固执地保留着这份激情——如果用“激情”来形容这段从未续约的奇异关系还算贴切的话。后来，克拉维迪娅在阔别许久之后带着她的新情人——热情奔放、充满酒神气息的米恩赫尔·皮珀科恩——回来了。皮珀科恩是一位荷兰大亨，在爪哇岛拥有一座种植园。 《窥视者》明显是对德国剧作家兼小说家格哈特·豪普特曼（1862-1946）的戏仿，他与纳粹有关联，并比托马斯·曼早十七年获得诺贝尔文学奖。

I return to Hans Castorp, whom Thomas Mann ironically deprecated as a perfectly ordinary young man. Castorp is anything but that. Thomas Mann tried to make him superficially drab, but a good reader of the novel learns to shrug that off. Everything and nothing happens to Hans Castorp during his seven-year sojourn on the Enchanted Mountain. He falls in love with the enigmatic Clavdia Chauchat, who grants him only a single tryst. Stubbornly, he retains the passion, if that is the accurate word for a bizarre relationship that is never renewed. Instead, Clavdia returns after a long absence with her new lover, the boisterously Dionysiac Mynheer Peeperkorn, a large Dutch owner of a plantation in Java. Peeperkorn is a manifest parody of Gerhart Hauptmann (1862–1946), a German dramatist and novelist who was rather tainted by Nazi associations, and who preceded Thomas Mann by seventeen years as a winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.

我认为每个《魔山》的读者都会喜欢皮珀科恩这个角色，因为好辩的人文主义者卢多维科·塞滕布里尼和他的对手——犹太裔耶稣会士、尼采主义者利奥·纳夫塔——为了争夺汉斯·卡斯托普的灵魂而展开的斗争，一开始会让人感到厌烦，直到他们那场可怕的决斗：塞滕布里尼故意朝空中开枪，而愤怒的纳夫塔则饮弹自尽。托马斯·曼很大程度上是以匈牙利犹太裔文学评论家和哲学家乔治·卢卡奇（1885-1971）为原型塑造了纳夫塔这个角色，卢卡奇倡导一种浪漫主义马克思主义。

I think every reader of The Magic Mountain enjoys Peeperkorn, since the polemical humanist Ludovico Settembrini and his antagonist, the Jewish-Jesuit-Nietzschean Leo Naphta, who battle for Hans Castorp’s soul, begin to weary us until their ghastly duel, in which Settembrini deliberately fires in the air, and the infuriated Naphta then shoots himself in the head. Thomas Mann largely based Naphta on György Lukács (1885–1971), Hungarian Jewish literary critic and philosopher who propounded a kind of Romantic Marxism.

正如我之前所说，汉斯·卡斯托普在我看来是一位非凡的年轻人，也是一位性格深刻的人。尽管他极其腼腆，但他却在追求与众不同，并且似乎知道最终他会在自己身上找到这种与众不同。他被塞滕布里尼所感动，又以另一种方式被纳夫塔所感动，但他最终找到的化身并非克拉维迪亚，而是那个体格魁梧、明显正走向可怕结局的狄俄尼索斯式人物：

As I have indicated, Hans Castorp seems to me an extraordinary young man and a profoundly realized personality. For all his exquisite diffidence, he is a seeker after otherness, and seems to know that at last he will find it in himself. Moved as he is by Settembrini, and in another mode by Naphta, he finds a culminating figure not in Clavdia but in the burly Dionysiac who so palpably is approaching a terrible end:

一听到“刀”这个字，明赫·皮珀科恩就稍微改变了在床上的坐姿，突然挪开身子，转过脸去，寻找客人的眼睛。他坐直了身子，用手肘撑着，说道：“年轻人，我听到了，也明白了。基于你刚才所说，请允许我郑重声明一下。如果我的头发不是花白的，如果我没有被这该死的热病折磨得如此虚弱，你会看到我随时准备与你当面对质，手持利器，为你无意中造成的伤害，以及我的旅伴造成的额外伤害（对此我也负有责任）讨回公道。没错，先生。你会看到我做好了准备。但就目前的情况而言，请允许我提出另一个建议。事情是这样的：我记得我们相识之初的一个美好瞬间——尽管当时我已喝了不少酒，但我仍然记得——那一刻，我被你和蔼的性情所感动，本想用非正式的代词称呼你，但我意识到这样做会……太过草率了。好吧，我今天指的是那一刻，我现在回到那一刻，我宣布我们当时约定的延期到此为止。年轻人，我们是兄弟，我宣布我们是兄弟。你谈到要充分理解非正式代词的含义——而我们对它们的使用也将充分理解兄弟情谊的含义。年老体衰使我无法用武器来表达我的满足，现在我以这种形式来表达；我以兄弟情谊的形式来表达，这种情谊通常是用来对抗第三方、对抗世界、对抗他人的，但我们将用我们对彼此的感情来建立它。年轻人，拿起你的酒杯，我再去拿我的水杯——这不会对这杯淡雅的佳酿造成任何损害——”

他的船长手微微颤抖着，在汉斯·卡斯托普带着敬畏和困惑的帮助下，斟满了酒杯。

“拿着，”皮珀科恩重复道。“挽着我的胳膊！现在就这么喝。一饮而尽！——同意了，年轻人。就这么定了。来，我的手放在上面。你满意了吗，汉斯·卡斯托普？”

“当然，这话不足以形容我的心情，皮珀科恩先生，”汉斯·卡斯托普说道，他费了好大劲才一口气喝完杯中的酒，然后掏出手帕擦了擦洒在膝盖上的酒。“我的意思是，我真是太高兴了，至今仍难以置信这竟是如此突然降临到我身上——说实话，这简直像做梦一样。这对我来说是莫大的荣幸——我不知道自己是如何赢得这份殊荣的，充其量也只是某种间接的，绝非其他途径。所以，如果我一开始觉得用这种新的称呼有些生疏，甚至磕磕绊绊，也请不要感到惊讶——尤其是在克拉维迪娅面前，她毕竟是个女人，或许对这种新的称呼方式不太满意。”

At the mention of the word “knife,” Mynheer Peeperkorn had changed his sitting position in bed somewhat, suddenly edging away and turning his face to search his guest’s eyes. Now he sat up more comfortably, propping himself on his elbows, and said, “Young man, I have heard, and I have the picture. And on the basis of what you have just said, permit me to make an honorable declaration of my own. Were my hair not white and were I not so debilitated by this malign fever, you would see me prepared to give you satisfaction, man to man, weapon in hand, for the injury I have unwittingly inflicted upon you, and for the additional injury caused by my traveling companion, for which I likewise must take responsibility. Agreed, my good sir. You would see me prepared. But as things stand, you will permit me to make another suggestion in lieu of that. It is as follows: I recall a sublime moment, at the very beginning of our acquaintance—I recall it, though I had copiously partaken of wine—a moment when, touched by your pleasant temperament, I was about to offer you the brotherhood of informal pronouns, but could not avoid the realization that such a step would have been overhasty. Fine, I refer today to that moment, I return to it now, I declare the postponement we agreed upon then to be at an end. Young man, we are brothers, I declare us to be such. You spoke of the use of informal pronouns in their full meaning—and our use of them shall also be in the full meaning of a brotherhood of feeling. The satisfaction that old age and infirmity prevent me from offering you by means of weapons, I now offer you in this form; I offer it in the form of a bond of brotherhood, of the sort that is usually established against a third part, against the world, against someone else, but which we shall establish in our feelings for someone. Take up your wineglass, young man, while I reach yet again for my water tumbler—it will do this modest vintage no further harm—”

His captain’s hand trembling slightly, he filled the glasses, with the assistance, offered in respectful bewilderment, of Hans Castorp.

“Take it,” Peeperkorn repeated. “Link arms with me! And drink now thus. Drink it down!—Agreed, young man. Settled. Here, my hand on it. Are you satisfied, Hans Castorp?”

“That is, of course, no word for it, Mynheer Peeperkorn,” said Hans Castorp, who had some difficulty downing the whole glass in one draft, and now took out his handkerchief to wipe the wine he had spilled on his knee. “What I mean is, I am terribly happy and still cannot grasp how this has so suddenly been bestowed on me—it is, I must admit, like a dream. It is an overwhelming honor for me—I don’t know how I have earned it, at best in some passive way, certainly not in any other. And one should not be surprised if at first I shall find it rather daring to utter this new form of address and stumble in the attempt—particularly in the presence of Clavdia, who, being but a woman, may not be quite so pleased with this new arrangement.”

皮珀科恩身上究竟有什么特质吸引了汉斯·卡斯托普？与克拉维迪娅的联系是次要的，因为她不过是普里比斯瓦夫·希佩的另一种化身。皮珀科恩的生命力正在消退：阳痿正在逼近。面对这无法逃避的命运，他早已计划好如何无痛自杀：他自制了一根皮下注射针，并随身携带了一种来自爪哇的致命毒药。拥抱汉斯·卡斯托普，是否意味着他对生命做出了最终的忠诚？

What is it in Peeperkorn that has found Hans Castorp? The link with Clavdia is secondary, since she was just a later form of Pribislaw Hippe. Peeperkorn’s vitalism is ebbing: impotence beckons. Confronted with that inescapable contingency, he has already planned a painless suicide, with a hypodermic needle of his own invention, and a fatal poison from Java carried with him. By embracing Hans Castorp, is he asserting a final allegiance to life?

我读过的关于《魔山》的最佳文章出自奥斯卡·塞德林之手。塞德林原名萨洛·奥斯卡·科普洛维茨（1911-1984），是一位犹太学者，他离开纳粹德国，在美国度过了余生，从事教学和写作。他的文章《皮珀科恩先生与高深的数字游戏》（1971）被我收录在我编辑的文集《托马斯·曼的〈魔山〉：现代批判解读》（1986）中。他笔下的数字游戏带有卡巴拉色彩，源于曼对数字七的痴迷。皮珀科恩既是狄俄尼索斯又是基督，他对汉斯·卡斯托普的求助是雌雄同体、神秘莫测的，呼唤着一种双性恋的视角，这种视角对奥斯卡·塞德林和曼都至关重要。

The best essay I have ever read on The Magic Mountain is by Oskar Seidlin, born Salo Oskar Koplowitz (1911–84), a Jewish scholar who left Nazi Germany to spend his remaining lifetime teaching and writing in the United States. His essay “Mynheer Peeperkorn and the Lofty Game of Numbers” (1971) was reprinted by me in a volume I edited, Thomas Mann’s The Magic Mountain: Modern Critical Interpretations (1986). His game of numbers is Kabbalistic, turning upon Mann’s obsession with the number seven. Peeperkorn is both Dionysos and Christ, and his appeal to Hans Castorp is androgynous, hermetic, calling upon a bisexual vision central both to Oskar Seidlin and to Mann:

我们尚未触及最深层。尽管我们试图阐明本体的“奥秘”和道成肉身，但皮珀科恩“仅仅”是一个人，因此，他所肩负的体现神性的任务注定无法完成。无论他的精神多么强大、多么热情，肉体都会耍弄他。它无法承载皮珀科恩所感受到的、他视为自身使命的那份生命的活力与丰盈。简而言之，他是无能的，是这种最粗浅的、肉体意义上的无能：肉体拒绝接受他自知肩负的挑战。这解释了他所遭受的恐惧和痛苦；这是他苦难的最深渊。他不可能成为上帝，充其量只能是上帝在世间的代理人——也就是说，他不是基督，而是彼得——因此，我们并不惊讶于这是他的名字。我们现在也明白了，为什么关于基督在客西马尼园的沮丧的那段圣经经文如此深深地印在梅恩赫尔·皮珀科恩的脑海中，以至于他能一字不差地背诵出来。那是他自己的故事：基督责备彼得（基督主要针对的就是彼得），而彼得正是他自己，那个在羞愧和绝望中不得不承认自己无能的人，因为无论精神多么渴望，肉体终究是软弱的。

We have not reached the deepest layer yet. With all the noumenal “Mysterium” and incarnation which we tried to elucidate, Peeperkorn is “only” a human being, and thus the task to embody the divine is bound to be unfulfillable. No matter how strong and enthusiastic the spirit, the flesh plays it a nasty trick. It cannot live up to the exuberance and overflow of life which Peeperkorn feels to be his and whose emanation he considers his mission. In short, he is impotent, impotent in the crassest physical sense of the word: the flesh refuses to accept the challenge with which he knows himself entrusted. This explains the terror and anguish that overcome him; this is the deepest abyss of his Passion. He cannot be God, but at best God’s deputy on earth—i.e., not Christ but Peter—and we are not surprised that this is his first name. We now understand, too, why the biblical passage relating to Christ’s desolation in the Garden of Gethsemane is so firmly imbedded in Mynheer Peeperkorn’s mind that he can recite it verbatim. It is his own story: Christ chiding Peter (and it is Peter whom Christ mainly addresses), who is no one else but he himself, the one who in shame and despair must recognize his insufficiency, because the flesh is weak no matter how willing the spirit.

客西马尼园的苦难，当然也有其异教版本。这便是皮珀科恩先生自杀前最后一个下午发生的一件事，事实上，正是这件事导致了他的自杀：七人前往达沃斯附近的一处瀑布，分乘两辆马车，一辆三人，另一辆四人。我们顺便注意到，七人途经的森林病入膏肓：一种癌变的真菌肆虐，侵蚀着针叶树的枝干，威胁着树木的生存。在皮珀科恩的坚持下，野餐（准备了充足的面包和葡萄酒）不仅在瀑布的正对面举行，而且距离咆哮的瀑布如此之近，以至于任何交谈都变得不可能。餐后，一件怪事发生了。皮珀科恩起身，面对着轰鸣的瀑布（瀑布从大约七八米高的地方倾泻而下），开始对着它说话，仿佛试图召唤大自然狂野奔放的能量。然而，瀑布的喧嚣声淹没了老人说的每一句话。显然，他试图与这股肆意奔放的自然之力抗衡，试图将其束缚，但一切都是徒劳。他的声音淹没在宇宙的轰鸣声中，他的同伴们只能从他嘴唇的动作中读出那句奇怪咒语的最后两个词：perfekt und erledigt（安定下来，结束了）。erledigt ，结束，完成。这是我们在小说中听到的皮珀科恩说的最后一个词。在返回疗养院的路上，皮珀科恩的马车里几乎没有人说话。凌晨两点刚过，夜班护士应肖沙夫人的要求，叫汉斯·卡斯托普到荷兰人的房间。他死了。他注射了一些剧毒的异域毒药，也就是他从印度带来的“香料”，自杀了。

The anguish of the Garden of Gethsemane has, of course, its pagan counterpart. It is the event that takes place on the last afternoon before Mynheer Peeperkorn’s suicide, and is, in fact, the cause of his suicide: nothing more than an excursion to a waterfall near Davos, in which seven persons participate, driving out in two carriages, three in the one, four in the other. We notice, in passing, that the forest through which the seven travel on their way to their destination is sick: afflicted by a cancerous fungus, which overgrows the branches of the conifers and threatens to choke the trees. Upon Peeperkorn’s insistence, the picnic (with plenty of bread and wine) is being held not only in full view of the waterfall, but actually so close to the roaring cataract that any conversation becomes impossible. After the collation, something strange happens. Peeperkorn rises, faces the thundering waterfall (which bursts down from a height of approximately seven or eight meters), and starts talking to it as if trying to conjure the wild unleashed energy of nature, whose tumultuous uproar blots out every word the old man utters. Clearly, he tries to measure himself against the riotously unchained force of the elemental, tries to transfix it, but in vain. His voice is drowned in the cosmic noise, and his companions can read from the motions of his lips only the two last words of the strange invocation perfekt und erledigt [settled and finished]—erledigt, done with, finished. It is the last word that we hear Peeperkorn utter in the novel. On the way back to the sanatorium, hardly a word is spoken in Peeperkorn’s carriage. Shortly after two o’clock in the morning, the night nurse, at Madame Chauchat’s request, calls Hans Castorp to the Dutchman’s room. He is dead. He has killed himself by injecting into his veins some of the violent, exotic poison, the “spice” that he brought with him from India.

我们深信，在每一位伟大作家的作品中，哪怕最细微的细节都意义非凡。因此，随着荷兰人的死亡，皮珀科恩的故事远未结束。贝伦斯医生诊断出自杀后，将汉斯叫到客厅一角，用冗长的技术讲解向他演示了皮珀科恩用来结束自己生命的装置。这并非简单的注射器，而是一个极其复杂、奇特的装置，由锋利无比的牙齿组成，牙齿上嵌有细如发丝的导管，通向一个装有毒液的“橡胶腺”。施加压力后，安装在微型弹簧上的牙齿会挤压橡胶容器，然后将致命的液体通过导管喷出。牙齿——腺体：贝伦斯医生明确指出，这装置正是眼镜蛇咬合机制的精确机械复制品，我们几乎无需赘言。导致皮珀科恩死亡的是蛇的所作所为。归根结底，他并非新亚当，而是亚当本身，就是血肉之躯，带着软弱和罪性，这才是人，因为希伯来语“亚当”一词的真正含义就是如此。

Convinced that in the work of every great writer even the minutest detail is significant, we are, with the Dutchman’s death, not yet at the end of the Peeperkorn episode. After Hofrat Behrens has diagnosed the suicide, he beckons Hans into a corner of the drawing room and demonstrates to him in a long technical explanation the workings of the instrument with which Peeperkorn ended his life. It is not a simple syringe, but a highly complicated, outlandish mechanism, made up of teeth, honed to pinpoint sharpness, in which are embedded hair-thin cannulae leading to a “rubber-gland” that contains the poison. Upon pressure, the teeth, mounted on tiny springs, squeeze the rubber container, which then squirts the deadly fluid through the tubulae outward. Teeth—gland: we would hardly need Dr. Behrens’s explicit statement that this instrument is an exact mechanical replica of the Beißzeugs der Brillenschlange [mechanism of the cobra’s bite]. What caused Peeperkorn’s death was the work of the snake. In the last analysis, he is not the new Adam, but Adam plain and simple, flesh in its weakness and sinfulness, which is man, because this is what the Hebrew word “Adam” actually means.

然而——这正是他的伟大和尊严所在——他渴望超越亚当，并以超越亚当的形象出现在书页之中。正如汉斯·卡斯托普在皮珀科恩出现在魔山之后，立即仔细打量这位新来者，并评估他奇特的个性一样，如今，站在老人的床榻前，他念诵的墓志铭寥寥数语便概括了这位荷兰人的本质，并最终印证了我们提出的论点：“他视自己为上帝婚礼的工具，你们必须知道。”狄俄尼索斯和基督的形象再次交织在一起。其中蕴含的性暗示，唤起人们对阳具的联想——肉体丰饶的象征，以及狄俄尼索斯秘仪中凯旋的统治者——显而易见。但同样显而易见的是基督作为天上的新郎的角色，通过他，人的灵魂与上帝结合。托马斯·曼选择的这个词再贴切不过了。它指向圆满的行为，从生理层面来说，它通过身体的解剖部位体现出来；从精神层面来说，它通过器官（organon）体现出来，器官是人与神结合的媒介。正如我们试图阐明的，这正是梅恩赫尔·皮珀科恩想要活出的生命：三位一体与四位一体的完美结合。

Yet—and this is his greatness and dignity—he wanted to be and walked through the pages of the book as more than Adam. Just as Hans Castorp, immediately after Peeperkorn’s appearance on the Magic Mountain, took a good look at the new guest and assessed his strange individuality, so now, standing at the old man’s deathbed, he speaks the epitaph which compresses into a few words the Dutchman’s substance and serves as a last verification of the argument we have presented: “er betrachtete sich als Gottes Hochzeitsorgan, müssen Sie wissen [For you must know, he regarded himself as the instrument of God’s marriage].” Again the images of Dionysos and Christ appear united. The sexual implication, evoking the phallus, signal of carnal fertility and triumphant ruler over the Dionysian mysteries, is obvious. But equally obvious is Christ’s role as the heavenly bridegroom, through whom man’s soul is wedded to God. There could be no more fitting word than the one Thomas Mann has chosen. It points to the act of consummation, in its physical aspect by the anatomical part of the body, in its spiritual aspect by the organon, the medium through which the union of man and God is achieved. As we have tried to show, this was what Mynheer Peeperkorn wanted to live: the sum of three and four.

我觉得这非常有说服力。奥斯卡·塞德林深入剖析了这座山令人着迷的本质。而且，他的分析远不止于此：

I find this extremely persuasive. Oskar Seidlin penetrates the matrix of what makes the mountain enchanting. And then he goes beyond that:

但汉斯·卡斯托普带给我们的远不止是那位在魔山上临行前最后一刻造访者的“独特性”。他做出了评判，如果读者们当初肯认真聆听他的评判，许多困惑本可避免。皮珀科恩先生自认为肩负着神圣使命，却因自己只是彼得而非基督而无法完成。如今我们听到，这不过是“一场盛大的愚行”。或许这的确是愚行，但所有批评皮珀科恩的人，无论在书中还是书外，都应该注意到，这是一种高贵的愚行。汉斯·卡斯托普继续说道，他非常明确地指出，“愚蠢”一词并非贬义，而是表达最深切的情感和最庄严的敬意：“当一个人被感动时，他会说出一些听起来粗俗不敬的话，但这些话实际上比传统的宗教祷文更加庄严。”皮珀科恩的这种愚蠢是人类所能承受的最罕见、最高尚的愚蠢——或许也是最智慧的愚蠢：他将自己与创造神性的鲜活存在融为一体。

But Hans Castorp gives us more than just the pinpointing of the “Eigenart [particularity]” of the eleventh-hour visitor on the magic mountain. He pronounces judgment, and much confusion could have been avoided had the readers of the book taken the trouble to listen to him. This divine mission which Mynheer Peeperkorn considered his and which he could not fulfill because he was only Peter and not Christ, was, so we now hear, “eine königliche Narretei [a piece of majestic tomfoolery].” Foolishness it may have been, but all the detractors of Peeperkorn, inside and outside the book, should take notice that it was a regal foolishness. And Hans Castorp continues, making crystal clear that the word “foolishness” is not to be taken in a deprecatory sense, but as an expression of the deepest emotion and the most solemn respect: “Wenn man ergriffen ist, hat man den Mut zu Ausdrücken, die kraß und pietätlos klingen, aber feierlicher sind als konzessionierte Andachtsworte [when one is moved one can say things that sound crass and irreverent, but are after all more solemn than the conventional religious formulas].” Peeperkorn’s is the rarest and noblest sort of foolishness—perhaps even the wisest—with which man can be afflicted: the self-identification with the living presence of the creatively divine.

威廉·布莱克曾说，愚人若执迷于愚行，终将变得睿智。塞缪尔·约翰逊博士虽然被布莱克戏谑地轻视，却先于布莱克说过，爱是愚人的智慧，是智者的愚昧。汉斯·卡斯托普最终爱上了人格的奥秘。正如塞德林所指出的，卡斯托普抛弃了嫉妒和激情，与克拉维迪娅订立盟约，共同守护日渐衰落的皮珀科恩。对克拉维迪娅而言，性欲即死亡。汉斯·卡斯托普则肯定生命，不愿屈服于死亡及其诱惑。

William Blake said that if the fool would persist in his folly, he would become wise. Dr. Samuel Johnson, treated by Blake with jocular contempt, nevertheless preceded him by saying that love was the wisdom of fools and the folly of the wise. Hans Castorp ultimately is in love with the mystery of personality. As Seidlin notes, Castorp casts aside both jealousy and passion, so as to enter into a covenant with Clavdia to help preserve the waning Peeperkorn. For Clavdia, sexuality is death. Hans Castorp affirms life, and will not yield to death and its attractions.

在或许过于冗长的“雪”这一章中，托马斯·曼勾勒出了一个矫揉造作的肯定句：

In the perhaps too deliberated chapter “Snow,” Thomas Mann sketches an overwrought affirmation:

爱与死亡对立——唯有爱，且仅凭爱，才能战胜死亡。唯有爱，而非理性，才能孕育善念。形式亦唯有源于爱与善：形式，以及人类美好境界、理性友善的社群所展现的文明礼仪——皆源于对血腥盛宴的默默敬畏。啊，我做了一个多么清晰的梦，我扮演国王的角色多么出色！我将铭记于心。我将在心中坚守对死亡的忠诚，但我也会清楚地记住，如果对死亡和过往的忠诚支配着我们的思想和行为，那只会导致邪恶、黑暗的欲望和对人类的仇恨。为了善与爱，人不应让死亡主宰自己的思想。我将以此醒来。因为我已以此梦境抵达终点，抵达目标。我长久以来都在追寻那真理：在希佩显现的草地上，在我的阳台上，在任何地方。对它的追寻驱使我来到这雪山之中。现在我终于拥有了。我的梦如此清晰地赐予我这一切，我将永远铭记。是的，我欣喜若狂，心中充满温暖。我的心跳强劲有力，并且明白个中缘由。它跳动并非出于纯粹的生理原因，不像尸体上的指甲那样生长。它跳动是为了人类的本能，因为我的灵魂真正地感到快乐。梦境的真谛让我精神焕发——比波特酒或麦芽酒更令人神清气爽，它像爱与生命一样流淌在我的血管里，让我得以从沉睡中挣脱出来，我知道沉睡可能会危及我年轻的生命。醒来，醒来！睁开你的双眼。那是你的四肢，你的双腿就在雪地里。振作起来，站起来。看——天气真好！

Love stands opposed to death—it alone, and not enough, is stronger than death. Only love, and not reason, yields kind thoughts. And form, too, comes only from love and goodness: form and the cultivated manners of man’s fair state, of a reasonable, genial community—out of silent regard for the bloody banquet. Oh, what a clear dream I’ve dreamed, how well I’ve ‘played king’! I will remember it. I will keep faith with death in my heart, but I will clearly remember that if faithfulness to death and to what is past rules our thoughts and deeds, that leads only to wickedness, dark lust, and hatred of humankind. For the sake of goodness and love, man shall grant death no dominion over his thoughts. And with that I shall awaken. For with that I have dreamed my dream to its end, to its goal. I’ve long been searching for that truth: in the meadow where Hippe appeared to me, on my balcony, everywhere. The search for it drove me into these snowy mountains. And now I have it. My dream has granted it to me so clearly that I will always remember. Yes, I am overjoyed and filled with its warmth. My heart is beating strong and knows why. It beats not for purely physical reasons, the way fingernails grow on a corpse. It beats for human reasons and because my spirit is truly happy. The truth of my dream has refreshed me—better than port or ale, it courses through my veins like love and life, so that I may tear myself out of my dreaming sleep, which I know only too well can be fatal to my young life. Awake, awake! Open your eyes. Those are your limbs, your legs there in the snow. Pull yourself together and stand up. Look—good weather!

遗憾的是，从美学角度来看，这部分并不成功。其中最精彩的部分是对希佩的回忆，她比克拉维迪娅更能预示爱与死。托马斯·曼的四部曲《约瑟夫和他的兄弟们》（1943）的序言重述了一个赫尔墨斯神话：一位神圣的人/神在夜水中看到了自己的倒影，爱上了那个影像，然后从圣光中降临到我们世界的黑暗之中。那黑暗被称为“爱与死”，也被称为“睡眠”。

I regret that aesthetically this just does not work. The best thing in it is the recollection of Hippe, who more than Clavdia was the portent of love and death. The prologue to Thomas Mann’s tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1943) retells the Hermetic myth of a divine Man/God who beholds her/his reflection in the Waters of Night, falls in love with that image, and descends from the Holy Light into the Darkness of our world. That Darkness is named “Love and Death.” It is also called “Sleep.”

在我看来，托马斯·曼的全部作品都浓缩在那篇序言里，包括《魔山》 。在山上，睡眠、死亡、欲望，如同漂浮的花朵般环绕着汉斯·卡斯托普。

It seems to me that all of Thomas Mann is in that prologue. That includes The Magic Mountain. On the mountain; sleep, death, desire, close around Hans Castorp like a floating flower.

正如曼恩最后所说，“这是一个晦涩难懂的故事。” 我本人怀疑，这种层出不穷的讽刺是否符合赫尔墨斯主义的神话。作者那种长辈般的语气令我感到不安，尤其是在《魔山》的结尾。但我未免有些忘恩负义。托马斯·曼并非马塞尔·普鲁斯特、詹姆斯·乔伊斯、弗朗茨·卡夫卡和塞缪尔·贝克特那样的大师。但如今又有谁能与之比肩呢？《布登勃洛克一家》、 《威尼斯之死》、 《魔山》、 《约瑟夫和他的兄弟们》、 《浮士德博士》、 《费利克斯·克鲁尔的自白》：所有这些作品至今仍熠熠生辉。

As Mann ends by saying, “It was a hermetic story.” I myself doubt that irony after irony is consistent with Hermetic myth. The author’s avuncular tone distresses me, particularly at the close of The Magic Mountain. But I am being ungrateful. Thomas Mann is not of the order of Marcel Proust and James Joyce, of Franz Kafka and Samuel Beckett. But who now is? Buddenbrooks, Death in Venice, The Magic Mountain, Joseph and His Brothers, Doctor Faustus, Confessions of Felix Krull: all these are still alive.

第37章

CHAPTER 37

《到灯塔去》（1927）

To the Lighthouse (1927)

弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫​

VIRGINIA WOOLF

弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫的一生是一场漫长而绝望的精神折磨。十三岁时，母亲去世，她精神崩溃。二十二岁时，父亲莱斯利·斯蒂芬（哲学家兼历史学家）也去世了，她再次陷入绝望。八年后，她嫁给了伦纳德·伍尔夫。这段婚姻一直持续到她自杀，无疑支撑着她，但这段婚姻很可能从未圆房。她与才华横溢却不称职的诗人维塔·萨克维尔-韦斯特的同性恋情断断续续持续了十年，最终因维塔频繁与男女情人交往而告终。维塔的法西斯倾向也是导致两人关系破裂的原因之一。

THE LIFE OF Virginia Woolf was an extended and desperate agon with psychosis. When she was thirteen, her mother died and Virginia Stephen collapsed. At twenty-two, she lost her father, Leslie Stephen, philosopher and historian, and again broke down. Eight years later, she married Leonard Woolf. The union lasted until her suicide and undoubtedly sustained her, but it is unlikely the marriage was ever consummated. Her lesbian relationship with the bad poet but great gardener Vita Sackville-West continued on and off for a decade, but then ended because of Vita’s frequent escapades with both female and male lovers. Another cause of the rift was Vita’s fascist sympathies.

第三次危机持续了三年，从她三十岁到三十三岁。最终，在德国空袭的巨大压力下，伍尔夫在五十九岁时投水自尽。

A third crisis lasted for three years, from age thirty to thirty-three. Finally, under the terrible stress of German air bombardment, Woolf drowned herself at the age of fifty-nine.

伍尔夫的主要小说，公认是《达洛维夫人》（1925）和《到灯塔去》（1927）。《奥兰多》（1928）至今仍广受欢迎，但只能算是次要作品。她后期的小说都是杰作，显然会流传后世：《海浪》（1931）、《岁月》（1937）以及最后的杰作《幕间》（1941）。从形式上看，伍尔夫最优秀的小说是《到灯塔去》，这部作品堪称她各种才华的完美融合。

Woolf’s major novels, by common consent, are Mrs. Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Orlando (1928) remains popular, but is a secondary work. Her later novels are all extraordinary work, and clearly will survive: The Waves (1931), The Years (1937), and a final masterpiece, Between the Acts (1941). Formally speaking, Woolf’s finest novel is To the Lighthouse, which is a miraculous concentration of her varied gifts.

伍尔夫坚持认为女性的创造力“与男性的创造力截然不同”。艾瑞斯·默多克对此提出了令人耳目一新的异议：“我认为存在着人类经验；而且我不认为女性的思维本质上与男性不同。”一些重要的男性小说家——例如塞缪尔·理查森、托尔斯泰和亨利·詹姆斯——对女性意识的探索或许比简·奥斯汀和弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫更为深入。此外，我们还可以加上马塞尔·普鲁斯特和詹姆斯·乔伊斯，他们对内心世界的刻画同样深刻有力，无论描绘的是女性还是男性。

Woolf insists that the creative power of women “differs greatly from the creative power of men.” Iris Murdoch refreshingly disagreed: “I think there’s human experience; and I don’t think a woman’s mind differs essentially from a man’s.” There are major male novelists—Samuel Richardson, Tolstoy, Henry James—who have explored female consciousness perhaps more fully than did Jane Austen and Virginia Woolf. One can add Marcel Proust and James Joyce, whose depictions of inwardness are equally strong, whether women or men are being portrayed.

撇开她的唯美主义不谈， 《到灯塔去》的作者伍尔夫完全是个虚无主义者，这一点也适用于佩特、罗斯金和普鲁斯特。伍尔夫教导的是感知，而非政治。她的“雌雄同体”并非一种实用主义的纲领，而是感知与感觉的融合，以及她对死亡和虚无的接纳——这种接纳超越了艺术所能暗示的瞬间意义。

Except for her aestheticism, the author of To the Lighthouse would be wholly nihilistic, which is true also of Pater, Ruskin, and Proust. Woolf teaches perception, and not politics. Her “androgyny” is not a pragmatic program, but a fusion of perception and sensation with her acceptance of death and meaninglessness, apart from the flow of momentary meanings that art can suggest.

1940年5月，在她溺水身亡不到一年前，弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫在布莱顿的工人教育协会宣读了一篇论文。这篇论文就是我们熟知的《斜塔》，其中雪莱笔下那座孤塔的象征意义更多地体现为社会层面而非想象层面。它不再是诗人阿塔纳斯俯瞰人类悲惨境遇的视角，也不再是超脱尘世、超然沉思的智慧象征。相反，它成为了“中产阶级出身和昂贵教育的象征”。伍尔夫或许更偏爱雪莱而非W·H·奥登，尽管她深知自己也身处这座斜塔之中，这与叶芝截然不同——对叶芝而言，孤塔始终是诗歌创作中不可或缺的隐喻。

In May 1940, less than a year before she drowned herself, Virginia Woolf read a paper to the Workers’ Educational Association in Brighton. We know it as the essay entitled “The Leaning Tower,” in which the Shelleyan emblem of the lonely tower takes on more of a social than an imaginative meaning. It is no longer the point of survey from which the poet Athanase gazes down in pity at the dark estate of mankind, and so is not an image of contemplative wisdom isolated from the mundane. Instead, it is “the tower of middle-class birth and expensive education.” It would be accurate to suggest that Woolf preferred Shelley to W. H. Auden, though she knew she herself dwelt in the leaning tower, unlike Yeats, to whom the lonely tower remained an inevitable metaphor for poetic stance.

《比萨斜塔》作为对浪漫主义意象走向衰落的推测，理应也关注诗歌影响的特殊性：

It is proper that “The Leaning Tower,” as a speculation upon the decline of a Romantic image into belatedness, should concern itself also with the peculiarities of poetic influence:

因此，理论是危险的。尽管如此，既然我们今天下午要讨论现代文学的倾向，就必须冒险提出一个理论。我们直接谈论倾向或运动，就等于默认存在某种力量、影响或外部压力，它强大到足以影响一大批不同的作家，使他们的作品都具有某种共同的相似性。那么，我们就必须提出一个理论来解释这种影响是什么。但我们始终要记住——影响无穷无尽；作家们的感受力也无穷无尽；每个作家都有不同的感性。这就是为什么文学总是在变化，就像天气，就像天空中的云朵。读一页斯科特的作品；再读一页亨利·詹姆斯的作品；试着找出是什么影响使前一页变成了后一页。这超出了我们的能力范围。因此，我们只能希望找出那些将作家群体塑造成不同风格的最明显的因素。然而，群体确实存在。书籍像家族一样，从书籍中传承而来。有些作家源自简·奥斯汀；有些则源自狄更斯。它们像它们的父母一样，就像人类的孩子像它们的父母一样。然而，他们之间也像孩子之间一样存在差异，他们的反抗也像孩子一样。或许，如果我们快速了解一下他们的一些前辈，就能更容易地理解当代作家。

Theories then are dangerous things. All the same we must risk making one this afternoon since we are going to discuss modern tendencies. Directly we speak of tendencies or movements we commit ourselves to the belief that there is some force, influence, outer pressure which is strong enough to stamp itself upon a whole group of different writers so that all their writing has a certain common likeness. We must then have a theory as to what this influence is. But let us always remember—influences are infinitely numerous; writers are infinitely sensitive; each writer has a different sensibility. That is why literature is always changing, like the weather, like clouds in the sky. Read a page of Scott; then of Henry James; try to work out the influences that have transformed the one page into the other. It is beyond our skill. We can only hope therefore to single out the most obvious influences that have formed writers into groups. Yet there are groups. Books descend from books as families descend from families. Some descend from Jane Austen; others from Dickens. They resemble their parents, as human children resemble their parents; yet they differ as children differ, and revolt as children revolt. Perhaps it will be easier to understand living writers as we take a quick look at some of their forebears.

“一道突如其来的光芒改变了一件微不足道的事物，风向标、风车、扬谷的连枷、谷仓门上的尘埃；刹那间——事物便消失了，因为它纯粹是效果。”这是沃尔特·佩特的写照，也是弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫的写照。伍尔夫和佩特一样，致力于“捕捉这种情境，在冰冷空旷的氛围中，定义那焦点——光线本身苍白无力，却汇聚在一起，开始燃烧……”。与此形成鲜明对比的是莉莉·布里斯科的幻象，它为小说画上了句号：

“A sudden light transfigures a trivial thing, a weather-vane, a windmill, a winnowing flail, the dust in the barn door; a moment—and the thing has vanished, because it was pure effect.” That is Walter Pater, and also Virginia Woolf. Woolf, like Pater, sets herself “to realize this situation, to define, in a chill and empty atmosphere, the focus where rays, in themselves pale and impotent, unite and begin to burn….” Against this can be set Lily Briscoe’s vision, which concludes the novel:

仿佛被什么召唤，她迅速转向画布。就在那里——她的画。没错，满眼的绿色和蓝色，纵横交错的线条，以及她试图表达的东西。她想，它会被挂在阁楼里；它会被毁掉。但那又有什么关系呢？她自问，再次拿起画笔。她看了看台阶；空无一人；她又看了看画布；画面模糊不清。突然间，仿佛一瞬间清晰起来，她猛地在画布中央画了一条线。完成了；一切都结束了。是的，她想，极度疲惫地放下画笔，我的灵感已经涌现。

Quickly, as if she were recalled by something over there, she turned to her canvas. There it was—her picture. Yes, with all its greens and blues, its lines running up and across, its attempt at something. It would be hung in the attics, she thought; it would be destroyed. But what did that matter? she asked herself, taking up her brush again. She looked at the steps; they were empty; she looked at her canvas; it was blurred. With a sudden intensity, as if she saw it clear for a second, she drew a line there, in the centre. It was done; it was finished. Yes, she thought, laying down her brush in extreme fatigue, I have had my vision.

对伍尔夫而言，“尝试做某事”本身就是一个中心，无论它多么摇摆不定。伍尔夫对意义这一艰难可能性的肯定，在此达到了感知原则的巅峰，她以一种优美而沉稳的方式肯定了意义的可能。《海浪》（1931）堪称莉莉·布里斯科画作的宏大版本。小说六位第一人称叙述者中，伯纳德的叙述最为全面，他在书的结尾处表达了一种克制的喜悦：

An “attempt at something” is, for Woolf, a center, however wavering. The apotheosis of perceptive principle here is Woolf’s beautifully poised approach to an affirmation of the difficult possibility of meaning. The Waves (1931) is a large-scale equivalent of Lily Briscoe’s painting. Bernard, the most comprehensive of the novel’s six first-person narrators, ends the book with a restrained exultation:

我眼前再次浮现出那熟悉的街道。文明的华盖已然熄灭。天空漆黑如抛光的鲸骨。但天空中却闪烁着微光，不知是灯光还是黎明的曙光。某种骚动正在发生——某处悬铃木上的麻雀在鸣叫。黎明的气息涌动。我不会称之为黎明。对于一个站在街上，头晕目眩地仰望天空的老人来说，城市的黎明又意味着什么呢？黎明不过是天空泛白；某种新生。又是一天；又是星期五；又是三月、一月或九月的二十日。又是一次普遍的觉醒。星辰退却，最终熄灭。波涛间的暗礁越来越深。田野上的薄雾越来越浓。玫瑰花也泛起了红晕，就连挂在卧室窗边的那朵苍白的玫瑰也不例外。鸟儿鸣叫。农舍的居民点燃了清晨的蜡烛。是的，这就是永恒的更新，永无止境的起伏，起伏，再起伏。

“我的心中也涌起一股浪潮。它翻腾，它弓起背脊。我再次感受到一种新的渴望，它像一匹骄傲的骏马，骑手先是策马扬鞭，然后又勒住缰绳，在我身下升腾。此刻，我骑着你，站在这片石板路上刨着蹄子，我们究竟看到了什么敌人正向我们逼近？是死亡。死亡是敌人。我策马迎战死亡，长矛已备，头发像年轻人一样向后飞扬，就像珀西瓦尔在印度驰骋时那样。我鞭策我的战马。我将向你奋勇向前，永不屈服，永不屈服，哦，死亡！”

海浪拍打着海岸。

“Again I see before me the usual street. The canopy of civilisation is burnt out. The sky is dark as polished whale-bone. But there is a kindling in the sky whether of lamplight or of dawn. There is a stir of some sort—sparrows on plane trees somewhere chirping. There is a sense of the break of day. I will not call it dawn. What is dawn in the city to an elderly man standing in the street looking up rather dizzily at the sky? Dawn is some sort of whitening of the sky; some sort of renewal. Another day; another Friday; another twentieth of March, January, or September. Another general awakening. The stars draw back and are extinguished. The bars deepen themselves between the waves. The film of mist thickens on the fields. A redness gathers on the roses, even on the pale rose that hangs by the bedroom window. A bird chirps. Cottagers light their early candles. Yes, this is the eternal renewal, the incessant rise and fall and fall and rise again.

“And in me too the wave rises. It swells; it arches its back. I am aware once more of a new desire, something rising beneath me like the proud horse whose rider first spurs and then pulls him back. What enemy do we now perceive advancing against us, you whom I ride now, as we stand pawing this stretch of pavement? It is death. Death is the enemy. It is death against whom I ride with my spear couched and my hair flying back like a young man’s, like Percival’s, when he galloped in India. I strike spurs into my horse. Against you I will fling myself, unvanquished and unyielding, O Death!”

The waves broke on the shore.

“永无止境的起伏，跌宕，再起伏”，虽然出自伯纳德之口，却蕴含着一种对自然残酷本质的深刻感悟，而这种感悟在男性意识中并不常见。尽管充满了战争意象，但这场与死亡的搏斗超越了攻击性，无论这种攻击性是针对自身还是针对他人。佩特曾坚持认为，我们唯一的选择在于尽可能地将动脉的脉动，或者说布莱克式的诗人作品意象，塞进我们的间隙之中。伍尔夫巧妙地暗示，即使是佩特也屈服于男性对经验数量的错觉，而非女性对经验质量层次的认知。一位男性评论家或许会为了维护佩特而低声辩解：男性对经验中空洞的视而不见是难以克服的，而且无论佩特的性别如何，他那精妙的感性绝非男性特有。

“Incessant rise and fall and fall and rise again,” though ascribed to Bernard, has in it the fine pathos of a recognition of natural harshness that does not come often to a male consciousness. And, for all the warlike imagery, the ride against death transcends aggressivity, whether against the self or against others. Pater had insisted that our one choice lies in packing as many pulsations of the artery, or Blakean visions of the poet’s work, into our interval as possible.
