“你觉得我疯了，是因为我的英语说得不好吗？见鬼，那又不是我的母语，老兄，我是非洲人！你真的觉得我疯了？”

“是的，是的！”

“你信这话？”​​拉斯说，“他们对你做了什么，黑鬼？给你那些臭女人？”

克利夫顿再次扑了过来，我又一次抓住了他；拉斯再次站稳了脚跟，他的头涨得通红。

“女人？我的天哪，兄弟！这就是平等吗？这就是黑人的自由吗？拍拍背，再来一发毫无激情的骚货？蛆虫！他们用这么便宜的价格就能买到这些婊子，兄弟？他们怎么能这样对待我的同胞！你们的脑子呢？这些女人都是渣滓，兄弟！她们只会榨取人血！你知道那些上流的白人兄弟憎恨黑人兄弟，这很简单。所以现在他利用这些渣滓，想让你们这些黑人年轻人替他干脏活。他们背叛你们，你们也背叛黑人。他们在欺骗你们，兄弟。让他们自相残杀吧。我们组织起来——组织是好事——但我们要组织黑人。黑人！去他妈的那个狗娘养的！他找了个妓女，告诉黑人兄弟他的自由就在她那两腿之间——而那个混蛋，却攫取了所有的权力和资本，什么也不给黑人兄弟留下。”他告诉黑人，善良的白人女性是强奸犯，并将她们囚禁起来，使她们愚昧无知，同时把黑人变成一群混蛋。

“黑人何时才会厌倦这种幼稚的背信弃义？他让你如此不信任自己的黑人智慧？你还年轻，别自作聪明，兄弟。别否定自己！你可是倾注了亿万加仑黑人血液才造就的。认清你内心的自我，你就能成为人中之王！一个真正的男人，即使一无所有，赤身裸体，也知道自己是男人——这无需他人言说。你身高六英尺，兄弟。你年轻又聪明。你肤色黝黑，容貌俊美——别让他们动摇你的信念！如果你不是那样的人，你早就死了，兄弟。死了！我会杀了你，兄弟。劝诫者拉斯举起刀，想要动手，但他没能做到。你为什么不动手呢？我问自己。我现在就动手，我说；但总有什么东西告诉我，‘不，不！你可能会杀死你的黑人国王！’”我说，是啊，是啊！所以我接受你这屈辱的举动。拉斯看到了你作为黑人的潜力，兄弟。拉斯不会把他的黑人兄弟献祭给白人奴隶主。相反，他哭了。拉斯是个男人——不需要任何白人告诉他——拉斯哭了。所以，你为什么不认清你作为黑人的责任，兄弟，加入我们呢？

“Hell, no,” Ras cried, wiping his eyes with his fists. “I talk! Bust me with the pipe but, by God, you listen to the Exhorter! Come in with us, mahn. We build a glorious movement of black people. Black People! What they do, give you money? Who wahnt the dahm stuff? Their money bleed black blood, mahn. It’s unclean! Taking their money is shit, mahn. Money without dignity— That’s bahd shit!”

Clifton lunged toward him. I held him, shaking my head. “Come on, the man’s crazy,” I said, pulling on his arm.

Ras struck his thighs with his fists. “Me crazy, mahn? You call me crazy? Look at you two and look at me—is this sanity? Standing here in three shades of blackness! Three black men fighting in the street because of the white enslaver? Is that sanity? Is that consciousness, scientific understahnding? Is that the modern black mahn of the twentieth century? Hell, mahn! Is it self-respect—black against black? What they give you to betray—their women? You fall for that?”

“Let’s go,” I said, listening and remembering and suddenly alive in the dark with the horror of the battle royal, but Clifton looked at Ras with a tight, fascinated expression, pulling away from me.

“Let’s go,” I repeated. He stood there, looking.

“Sure, you go,” Ras said, “but not him. You contahminated but he the real black mahn. In Africa this mahn be a chief, a black king! Here they say he rape them godahm women with no blood in their veins. I bet this mahn can’t beat them off with a baseball bat—shit! What kind of foolishness is it? Kick him ass from cradle to grave then call him brother? Does it make mahthematics? Is it logic? Look at him, mahn; open your eyes,” he said to me. “I look like that I rock the blahsted world! They know about me in Japan, India—all the colored countries. Youth! Intelligence! The mahn’s [a] natural prince! Where is your eyes? Where your self-respect? Working for them dahm people? Their days is numbered, the time is almost here and you fooling ’round like this was the nineteenth century. I don’t understahnd you. Am I ignorant? Answer me, mahn!”

“Yes,” Clifton burst out. “Hell, yes!”

“You t’ink I’m crazy, is it c’ase I speak bahd English? Hell, it ain’t my mama tongue, mahn, I’m African! You really t’ink I’m crazy?”

“Yes, yes!”

“You believe that?” said Ras. “What they do to you, black mahn? Give you them stinking women?”

Clifton lunged again, and again I grabbed him; and again Ras held his ground, his head glowing red.

“Women? Godahm, mahn! Is that equality? Is that the black mahn’s freedom? A pat on the back and a piece of cunt without no passion? Maggots! They buy you that blahsted cheap, mahn? What they do to my people! Where is your brains? These women dregs, mahn! They bilge water! You know the high-class white mahn hates the black mahn, that’s simple. So now he use the dregs and wahnt you black young men to do his dirty work. They betray you and you betray the black people. They tricking you, mahn. Let them fight among themselves. Let ’em kill off one another. We organize—organization is good—but we organize black. BLACK! To hell with that son of a bitch! He take one them strumpets and tell the black mahn his freedom lie between her skinny legs—while that son of a gun, he take all the power and the capital and don’t leave the black mahn not’ing. The good white women he tell the black mahn is a rapist and keep them locked up and ignorant while he makes the black mahn a race of bahstards.

“When the black mahn going to tire of this childish perfidity? He got you so you don’t trust your black intelligence? You young, don’t play you’self cheap, mahn. Don’t deny you’self! It took a billion gallons of black blood to make you. Recognize you’self inside and you wan the kings among men! A mahn knows he’s a mahn when he got not’ing, when he’s naked—nobody have to tell him that. You six foot tall, mahn. You young and intelligent. You black and beautiful—don’t let ’em tell you different! You wasn’t them t’ings you be dead, mahn. Dead! I’d have killed you, mahn. Ras the Exhorter raised up his knife and tried to do it, but he could not do it. Why don’t you do it? I ask myself. I will do it now, I say; but somet’ing tell me, ‘No, no! You might be killing your black king!’ And I say, yas, yas! So I accept your humiliating ahction. Ras recognized your black possibilities, mahn. Ras would not sahcrifice his black brother to the white enslaver. Instead he cry. Ras is a mahn—no white mahn have to tell him that—and Ras cry. So why don’t you recognize your black duty, mahn, and come jine us?”

托德·克利夫顿告诉“隐形人”，拉斯的危险之处在于他的内心，某种程度上，他屈服于这种无可辩驳的雄辩。作为读者，我无法抗拒。可怜的克利夫顿意志消沉，开始在街头兜售小黑木偶，直到被一名白人警察杀害。只有这件事，以及后来意识到兄弟会希望哈莱姆区爆发大规模种族骚乱，才让叙述者重新找回了自我——无论那自我究竟是什么。

Tod Clifton, who tells Invisible Man that it is on the inside that Ras is dangerous, in some sense yields to this irrefutable eloquence. As a reader I cannot resist. Poor Clifton is demoralized and takes to selling little black puppets on the streets, until he is murdered by a white policeman. Only that, and the later realization that the Brotherhood wishes Harlem to explode in a vast race riot, restores the narrator to himself, whatever that self may be.

主人公戴上墨镜和宽边帽，扮演着奔跑者莱因哈特，直到他顿悟了莱因哈特的宗教真谛：

Putting on dark glasses and a wide hat, the protagonist plays at being Rinehart the Runner, until he encounters the epiphany of the religion of Rinehart:

走了几个街区后，我停了下来，气喘吁吁。我既高兴又生气。这些人怎么能这么愚蠢？难道所有人都疯了吗？我环顾四周。街道灯火通明，人行道上挤满了人。我站在路边，努力呼吸。街对面，人行道上方一个带有十字架的标志牌闪闪发光：

圣路站

看哪，永活的神！

那些字母发出暗绿色的光芒，我琢磨着这光芒是来自镜头还是霓虹灯管本身的颜色。几个醉汉踉跄着走过。我朝着汉布罗的方向走去，路过一个坐在路边、头埋在膝盖上的男人。汽车来来往往。我继续往前走。两个表情严肃的孩子走过来分发传单，我一开始拒绝了，但后来又回去拿了。毕竟，我得了解社区里发生了什么事。我拿着传单，走到路灯旁，开始阅读。

看哪，那看不见的

主啊，愿你的旨意成就！

我洞察一切，知晓一切。我诉说一切，治愈一切。

你将会看到未知的奇观。

——牧师BP​​·莱因哈特

精神技术专家。

旧事物总是新的。

新奥尔良的驿站，神秘之都

伯明翰、纽约、芝加哥、底特律和洛杉矶

没有上帝解决不了的问题。

来到驿站。

看哪，那看不见的！

请参加我们每周三次的礼拜和祷告会。

加入我们，一同领略古老宗教的全新启示！

看哪，可见的，不可见的

看哪，那看不见的东西

疲惫的人们，回家吧！

我会按你说的做！别等了！

我把传单扔进路边的排水沟，继续往前走。我走得很慢，呼吸依然急促。难道是真的？很快，我走到了那块牌子前。它挂在一家改建成教堂的商店上方，我走进浅浅的大厅，用手帕擦了擦脸。身后传来一阵古老的祷告声，自从离开校园后，我就再也没听过这种祷告了；即使在校园里，也只有在邀请乡村牧师来做祷告时才会听到。那声音起伏跌宕，如同梦呓般吟诵——一部分是列举会众所经历的尘世苦难，一部分是倾诉衷肠的歌唱技巧，一部分是向上帝祈求。我还在擦脸，眯着眼睛看着窗户上粗糙的圣经故事画，这时两位老太太走了过来。

“安息吧，莱因哈特牧师，”其中一人说道。“我们亲爱的牧师在这个温暖的夜晚感觉如何？”

哦，不，我想，但是也许同意比拒绝带来的麻烦要少，于是我说道：“晚上好，姐妹们。”我用手帕捂住声音，闻到了手上女孩的香水味。

“这位是哈里斯姐妹，牧师。她来加入我们的小乐队。” “愿上帝保佑你，哈里斯姐妹，”我说着，握住了她伸出的手。

“牧师，您知道吗，我多年前就听过您布道。那时您还是个十二岁的小男孩，在弗吉尼亚。如今我来到北方，感谢上帝，竟然发现您还在传福音，做主的工。还在这座罪恶的城市里宣扬古老的信仰——”

“呃，哈里斯姐妹，”另一位姐妹说，“我们最好进去找座位。再说，牧师还有事要办。不过，您来得有点早，是吧，牧师？”

“是的，”我一边说着，一边用手帕擦了擦嘴。她们是典型的南方慈祥老妇人，我突然感到一阵莫名的绝望。我想告诉她们莱因哈特是个骗子，但这时教堂里传来一声喊叫，接着是一阵音乐。

“听听吧，哈里斯姐姐。这就是我跟你说过莱因哈特牧师给我们带来的那种新型吉他音乐。是不是美妙极了？”

“赞美上帝！”哈里斯修女说。“赞美上帝！”

“牧师，请原谅，我得去见见朱德金斯修女，关于她为教堂建设基金募集的款项。还有，牧师，昨晚我卖出了十张您那场鼓舞人心的布道录音带。甚至还卖了一张给我老板的白人女士。”

“愿上帝保佑你，”我发现自己用充满绝望的声音说道，“愿上帝保佑你，愿上帝保佑你。”

这时门开了，我越过他们的头顶，看到一间拥挤的小房间，男男女女都坐在折叠椅上。房间前面，一位身穿锈黑色长袍的苗条女子正激情地弹奏着立式钢琴上的布吉伍吉，旁边一位戴着小圆帽的年轻人则用电吉他弹奏着激昂的乐段，电吉他连接着一个悬挂在天花板上的放大器，放大器下方是一个闪闪发光的金白色讲坛。一位身穿优雅红色主教长袍、领口饰有高蕾丝花边的男子倚靠在一本巨大的圣经旁，开始带领会众用一种陌生的语言高声唱着一首激昂的赞美诗。在他身后，高高的墙上，用金色的字母拱形排列着一行字：

Several blocks away I stopped, out of breath. And both pleased and angry. How stupid could people be? Was everyone suddenly nuts? I looked about me. It was a bright street, the walks full of people. I stood at the curb trying to breathe. Up the street a sign with a cross glowed above the walk:

HOLY WAY STATION

BEHOLD THE LIVING GOD

The letters glowed dark green and I wondered if it were from the lenses or the actual color of the neon tubes. A couple of drunks stumbled past. I headed for Hambro’s, passing a man sitting on the curb with his head bent over his knees. Cars passed. I went on. Two solemn-faced children came passing out handbills which first I refused, then went back and took. After all, I had to know what was going on in the community. I took the bill and stepped close to the street light, reading.

Behold the Invisible

Thy will be done O Lord!

I See all, Know all. Tell all, Cure all.

You shall see the unknown wonders.

—REV. B. P. RINEHART,

SPIRITUAL TECHNOLOGIST.

The old is ever new

Way Stations in New Orleans, the home of mystery,

Birmingham, New York, Chicago, Detroit and L.A.

No Problem too Hard for God.

Come to the Way Station.

BEHOLD THE INVISIBLE!

Attend our services, prayer meetings Thrice weekly

Join us in the NEW REVELATION of the OLD TIME RELIGION!

BEHOLD THE SEEN UNSEEN

BEHOLD THE INVISIBLE

YE WHO ARE WEARY COME HOME!

I DO WHAT YOU WANT DONE! DON’T WAIT!

I dropped the leaflet into the gutter and moved on. I walked slowly, my breath still coming hard. Could it be? Soon I reached the sign. It hung above a store that had been converted into a church, and I stepped into the shallow lobby and wiped my face with a handkerchief. Behind me I heard the rise and fall of an old-fashioned prayer such as I hadn’t heard since leaving the campus; and then only when visiting country preachers were asked to pray. The voice rose and fell in a rhythmical, dreamlike recital—part enumeration of earthly trials undergone by the congregation, part rapt display of vocal virtuosity, part appeal to God. I was still wiping my face and squinting at crude Biblical scenes painted on the windows when two old ladies came up to me.

“Even’, Rever’n Rinehart,” one of them said. “How’s our dear pastor this warm evening?”

Oh, no, I thought, but perhaps agreeing will cause less trouble than denying, and I said, “Good evening, sisters,” muffling my voice with my handkerchief and catching the odor of the girl’s perfume from my hand.

“This here’s Sister Harris, Rever’n. She come to join our little band.” “God bless you, Sister Harris,” I said, taking her extended hand.

“You know, Rever’n, I once heard you preach years ago. You was just a lil’ ole twelve-year-old boy, back in Virginia. And here I come North and find you, praise God, still preaching the gospel, doing the Lord’s work. Still preaching the ole time religion here in this wicked city—”

“Er, Sister Harris,” the other sister said, “we better get on in and find our seats. Besides, the pastor’s kind of got things to do. Though you are here a little early, aren’t you, Rever’n?”

“Yes,” I said, dabbing my mouth with my handkerchief. They were motherly old women of the southern type and I suddenly felt a nameless despair. I wanted to tell them that Rinehart was a fraud, but now there came a shout from inside the church and I heard a burst of music.

“Just lissen to it, Sister Harris. That’s the new kind of guitar music I told you Rever’n Rinehart got for us. Ain’t it heavenly?”

“Praise God,” Sister Harris said. “Praise God!”

“Excuse us, Rever’n, I have to see Sister Judkins about the money she collected for the building fund. And, Rever’n, last night I sold ten recordings of your inspiring sermon. Even sold one to the white lady I work for.”

“Bless you,” I found myself saying in a voice heavy with despair, “bless you, bless you.”

Then the door opened and I looked past their heads into a small crowded room of men and women sitting in folding chairs, to the front where a slender woman in a rusty black robe played passionate boogie-woogie on an upright piano along with a young man wearing a skull cap who struck righteous riffs from an electric guitar which was connected to an amplifier that hung from the ceiling above a gleaming white and gold pulpit. A man in an elegant red cardinal’s robe and a high lace collar stood resting against an enormous Bible and now began to lead a hard-driving hymn which the congregation shouted in the unknown tongue. And back and high on the wall above him there arched the words in letters of gold:

让光明照耀大地！

LET THERE BE LIGHT!

埃里森的小说充满了精彩绝伦的高潮，但这或许是我最喜欢的一个。这段文笔精湛的描写与变形的莱因哈特相得益彰，而莱因哈特正是《看不见的人》所能给予我们的答案之一：

Ellison’s novel is replete with eloquent climaxes, but this may be my favorite. The heightened prose is worthy of the metamorphic Rinehart, who is as much of an answer as Invisible Man can give us:

这对我来说太过沉重。我摘下眼镜，小心翼翼地把白帽子夹在腋下，转身离开。难道是真的？我心想。我知道这是真的。我以前听说过，但从未如此接近过。然而，他真的能同时扮演所有这些角色吗：奔跑者莱恩、赌徒莱恩、行贿者莱恩、情人莱恩，以及牧师莱恩哈特？他自己难道既是冷酷的外表，又是充满爱心的内心？究竟什么是真实？但我又怎能怀疑呢？他是个宽广的胸怀，一个多才多艺、四处游历的人。莱恩哈特，一个圆滑世故的人。这和我一样真实。他的世界充满无限可能，他深知这一点。他比我领先好几年，而我却是个傻瓜。我一定是疯了，一定是瞎了眼。我们生活的世界没有边界。一个广阔、沸腾、炽热、流动的世界，而莱恩，这个无赖，却如鱼得水。或许只有莱恩，这个无赖，才能在这个世界里找到归属感。这简直难以置信，但或许只有难以置信的事才值得相信。或许真相从来都是谎言。

It was too much for me. I removed my glasses and tucked the white hat carefully beneath my arm and walked away. Can it be, I thought, can it actually be? And I knew that it was. I had heard of it before but I’d never come so close. Still, could he be all of them: Rine the runner and Rine the gambler and Rine the briber and Rine the lover and Rinehart the Reverend? Could he himself be both rind and heart? What is real anyway? But how could I doubt it? He was a broad man, a man of parts who got around. Rinehart the rounder. It was true as I was true. His world was possibility and he knew it. He was years ahead of me and I was a fool. I must have been crazy and blind. The world in which we lived was without boundaries. A vast seething, hot world of fluidity, and Rine the rascal was at home. Perhaps only Rine the rascal was at home in it. It was unbelievable, but perhaps only the unbelievable could be believed. Perhaps the truth was always a lie.

我们是否被这种说法说服了？我以前认识的记者迈克尔·安德森（我们多年未见）曾与我争论过埃里森，他认为埃里森在美学上是个失败者。安德森本人是非裔美国人，他曾写过一篇短文，对埃里森做出了如下严厉的评价：

Are we persuaded by this? My former acquaintance the journalist Michael Anderson, whom I have not seen for many years, once argued with me about Ellison, whom he regarded as an aesthetic failure. Anderson himself is African American, and wrote a brief essay with this severe judgment:

……一个常常将悖论误认为深刻的人：一个不写作的作家，一个阐述“复杂性”的人，他的思想有时简单，有时却又简单；一个描绘“混乱”的人，他的评论却是一部自满的汇编；一个倡导社会流动性的人，他的视野却凝固在过去；一个倡导美学纪律的人，他的作品却以无形和缺乏控制为特征；一个“种族主义者”，他鄙视自己的种族；一个批评社会学的人，他自己的小说却被扭曲成社会学的陈词滥调；一个倡导个人主义的人，他的事业每一步都依靠着一群令人惊叹的无私支持者；一个作品越少越受人尊敬的艺术家；一个公众人物，却像个隐形人……

…a man for whom paradox too often has been mistaken for profundity: a writer who did not write, the expositor of “complexity” whose ideas were simple when not simplistic, the delineator of “chaos” whose commentary was a compendium of complacency, the advocate of social fluidity whose vision was frozen in times past, the proponent of aesthetic discipline whose work is marked by formlessness and lack of control, a “race man” who disdained his race, the critic of sociology whose own novel has been distorted into a sociological cliché, the proponent of individualism whose career was propelled at every step by an astonishing array of selfless supporters, an artist all the more honored the less he produced, a public presence as an invisible man…

我仍然很喜欢迈克尔·安德森，但这并非事实。埃里森留下了两千页手稿，后来被编辑成一部不幸的小说—— 《六月节》（1999），而他生前也从未打算出版这部小说。拉尔夫是个完美主义者，他最大的遗憾是无法再写出一部像《看不见的人》那样的作品。说埃里森鄙视自己的种族是极其不准确的。安德森总结道：“埃里森并不适合他声称欣赏的艺术，这正是他的悲哀之处。他想成为黑人版的T·S·艾略特，而他本可以成为黑人版的贝克特。”

I am still fond of Michael Anderson, but this is simply not so. Ellison left two thousand manuscript pages which were edited into an unfortunate novel he would never have published: Juneteenth (1999). Ralph was a perfectionist, and his sorrow was that he could not again write an Invisible Man. It is dreadfully inaccurate to say that Ellison disdained his race. Anderson concluded by saying: “That Ellison was not fitted for the art he professed to admire is his pathos. He sought to be the black T. S. Eliot when he could have been the black Beckett.”

更准确地说，埃里森试图成为黑人版的陀思妥耶夫斯基，他在《看不见的人》中复活了陀思妥耶夫斯基笔下的“地下室人”。至于安德森为何会引用塞缪尔·贝克特，我百思不得其解。我将以这部不朽小说的结尾来结束这篇致敬，在结尾处，我们被邀请进入其普世意义的殿堂：

It would be truer to say that Ellison sought to be the black Dostoevsky, whose Underground Man he resurrected in his Invisible Man. Why Anderson invokes Samuel Beckett is beyond my surmise. I will end this tribute to a permanent novel with its conclusion, in which we are invited into its universalism:

“啊，”我仿佛听到你在说，“原来这一切都是为了用他那套胡言乱语来烦我们。他只是想让我们听他胡扯！” 但这只是部分事实：我既隐形又没有实体，就像一个脱离肉体的声音，我还能做什么呢？除了试着告诉你，当你透过我的双眼看到这一切时，究竟发生了什么，我还能做什么呢？而这正是令我恐惧的地方：

谁知道呢，或许在低频层面上，我能代表你们说话？

“Ah,” I can hear you say, “so it was all a build-up to bore us with his buggy jiving. He only wanted us to listen to him rave!” But only partially true: Being invisible and without substance, a disembodied voice, as it were, what else could I do? What else but try to tell you what was really happening when your eyes were looking through? And it is this which frightens me:

Who knows but that, on the lower frequencies, I speak for you?

第四十三章

CHAPTER 43

黑暗的左手(1969)

The Left Hand of Darkness (1969)

乌尔苏拉· K ·莱金​​

URSULA K. LE GUIN

我从未见过厄休拉·勒奎恩，她于2018年1月22日在俄勒冈州波特兰市去世，享年88岁，那里是她生活多年的家。然而，在她生命的最后两个月里，我们通过电子邮件成为了好朋友。我于2017年11月21日开始了这段通信，她于11月24日回复。此后，我们互通了16封信件，直到她于2018年1月16日发出最后一封信，信的结尾是：

I NEVER MET Ursula K. Le Guin, who died on January 22, 2018, at the age of eighty-eight in Portland, Oregon, her home for many years. And yet we became good friends during the last two months of her life, entirely by way of e-mail. I inaugurated the correspondence on November 21, 2017, and she replied on November 24. After that we exchanged letters sixteen times, until her final letter of January 16, 2018, which concluded:

年纪大了，我最不喜欢的一点就是精力不稳定。今天精神抖擞，明天就萎靡不振，唉！写诗或写故事一直是我最想做的工作，它能让我保持稳定和满足。但很多时候，我就是没有足够的精力。我想你的工作对你的身心健康也至关重要，希望你不会经历这种被迫闲散的时期。

我珍惜我们的友谊。

乌苏拉

One of the things I like least about being very old is the unreliability of my energy. Up one day, down the next, bleh! Working at poetry or a story is, always has been, the job I want to be doing, the work that keeps me steady and content. But too often there just isn’t the wherewithal. I suspect your work is central to your wellbeing in much this way, and hope you aren’t suffering such periods of enforced idleness.

I value our friendship.

Ursula

我隔了一段时间才回复，期间我病得很重。2018年1月23日，我才回复，当时还不知道乌苏拉已于前一天去世。我希望，为了纪念她，我能活着为美国文库编辑她的诗集，我想她或许也希望我这样做。现在，我先来读读她最优秀的两部小说：《黑暗的左手》（1969）和《被剥夺者》（1974）。

I replied after an interval, during which I was very ill, on January 23, 2018, not yet knowing that Ursula had died the day before. I hope, in tribute to her, that I live to edit her poems for the Library of America, thinking she might have wanted me to do that. For now, I turn to her two strongest novels, The Left Hand of Darkness (1969) and The Dispossessed (1974).

虽然我曾在1987年和2000年写过关于《黑暗的左手》的文章，但我已经忘记了当时的内容，现在也不想再翻阅，而是想重新开始阅读这部精彩的爱情故事。乌苏拉在一封信中提到，创作《一无所有》让她感到自由，而且她似乎更喜欢这部作品而不是《黑暗的左手》。重读这两部作品后，我发现自己难以抉择。 《一无所有》中的主人公谢维克比前作中的任何人物都更有趣，然而他和他的故事也体现了勒古恩副标题所蕴含的某种矛盾：一个暧昧的乌托邦。

Though I have written about The Left Hand of Darkness before, in 1987 and again in 2000, I have forgotten what I said and do not want to consult it now, but, rather, make a fresh start on this marvelous romance. In one of her letters Ursula remarked that writing The Dispossessed was liberating for her, and she seemed to prefer it to The Left Hand of Darkness. Rereading both, I find myself torn between the two. The protagonist Shevek in The Dispossessed is far more interesting than anyone in the earlier book, and yet he and his story manifest something of the ambivalence of Le Guin’s subtitle: An Ambiguous Utopia.

在《黑暗的左手》的精彩引言中，勒古恩妙语连珠地说道：“小说家的职业就是撒谎。”她暗示道：

In a fierce introduction to The Left Hand of Darkness, Le Guin charmingly remarks, “A novelist’s business is lying.” She adumbrates:

我谈论神明；我是个无神论者。但我也是个艺术家，因此也是个说谎者。不要相信我说的一切。我说的都是实话。

我唯一能够理解或表达的真理，从逻辑上讲，是一个谎言；从心理学上讲，是一个象征；从美学上讲，是一个隐喻。

I talk about the gods; I am an atheist. But I am an artist too, and therefore a liar. Distrust everything I say. I am telling the truth.

The only truth I can understand or express is, logically defined, a lie. Psychologically defined, a symbol. Aesthetically defined, a metaphor.

在勒古恩的作品中，我们总能听到老子《道德经》的回响。她与J. P. Seaton合译了《道德经》，书名为《论道与道的力量》（1997）。我们曾就她对“道”的理解进行过交流，但我不得不承认，我始终难以理解这种“非道之道”。我自己也一直随身带着一本芭芭拉·斯托勒·米勒翻译的《薄伽梵歌》，那是我在1986年秋天——也就是它出版的那一年——买的。读过数百遍之后，我想我明白了克里希那所说的“黑暗晦涩”、“激情”和“清明”的含义，但读了十几遍勒古恩和西顿合译的《道德经》之后，我仍然喃喃自语，说我没能领悟“道”的水与石。难道是我对自身的女性特质不够开放吗？这似乎不对。我更像我已故的母亲，而不是我已故的父亲。乌苏拉身上最打动我的是她的宁静。我完全缺乏它。

Always in Le Guin we hear reverberations of Lao Tzu’s Tao Te Ching, which she translated, with J. P. Seaton, as A Book About the Way and the Power of the Way (1997). We corresponded about her understanding of the Tao, yet I had to confess my permanent difficulty in absorbing this way that is not a way. I myself always keep to hand a copy of The Bhagavad-Gita as rendered by Barbara Stoler Miller, which I purchased in the autumn of 1986, the year of its publication. After hundreds of readings, I think I know what Krishna means by “dark opacity,” “passion,” and “lucidity,” but a dozen readings of the Le Guin–Seaton Tao Te Ching have left me muttering that I do not apprehend the water and stone of the Way. Is it that I am not enough open to my own female component? That seems not right. I am more my late mother than my late father. What moves me most in Ursula is the serenity. I lack it utterly.

—

勒古恩在评论《左手》中对性爱的迷人见解时，继续兴致勃勃地说道：

Commenting upon the fascinating vision of sexuality in Left Hand, Le Guin continues in gusto:

这本书并非关于未来。没错，它开头就宣称故事背景设定在“普世教会历1490-1497年”，但你肯定不会相信吧？

没错，书中的人物的确是雌雄同体，但这并不意味着我预言一千年后我们都会变成雌雄同体，或者宣称我认为我们理应如此。我只是以科幻小说特有的那种奇特、迂回且带有思想实验性质的方式观察：如果你在一天中的某些特殊时间、某些天气条件下观察我们，你会发现我们其实已经是雌雄同体了。我既没有预言，也没有开导。我只是在描述。我以小说家的方式——即通过精心编造的谎言——来描述心理现实的某些方面。

This book is not about the future. Yes, it begins by announcing that it’s set in the “Ekumenical Year 1490–97,” but surely you don’t believe that?

Yes, indeed the people in it are androgynous, but that doesn’t mean that I’m predicting that in a millennium or so we will all be androgynous, or announcing that I think we damned well ought to be androgynous. I’m merely observing, in the peculiar, devious, and thought-experimental manner proper to science fiction, that if you look at us at certain odd times of day in certain weathers, we already are. I am not predicting, or prescribing. I am describing. I am describing certain aspects of psychological reality in the novelist’s way, which is by inventing elaborately circumstantial lies.

《左手》的重担在于根利·艾能否说服盖森星球（又称冬星）上的卡尔海德国王加入“普罗旺斯联盟”（Ekumen），即众多星球之间开展贸易和文化交流的联盟。根利·艾在书中占据了大部分篇幅，但勒古恩经常采用第三人称叙述。尽管艾心地善良且智力尚可，但他始终无法真正理解他试图争取的雌雄同体者的意识。勒古恩在此处理得极为巧妙。她倾向于不信任弗洛伊德，因为她的心和思想都倾向于道家思想，但她也展现了弗洛伊德的观点：对我们几乎所有人来说，思想都无法摆脱其性方面的过去。

The burden of Left Hand is whether Genly Ai can persuade the king of Karhide on the planet Gethen or Winter to join the Ekumen or union of many planets in exchanges of trade and culture. Genly Ai speaks much of the book, but frequently Le Guin moves into third-person narration. Though Ai is a man of goodwill and adequate intelligence, he can never quite understand the consciousness of the androgynes whom he seeks to win over. Here Le Guin is admirably subtle. She tended to distrust Freud, since her heart and mind were with the Tao, and yet she shows what he meant in observing that for almost all of us thought could not be liberated from its sexual past.

颇为讽刺的是，勒古恩在第七章专门介绍了翁托特·奥蓬（Ong Tot Oppong）的田野笔记。奥蓬是代表埃库门（Ekumen）组织的一名女调查员，她登陆格森/温特星球（Gethen/Winter）研究“性问题”。奥蓬推测，殖民这颗奇特星球的人可能进行了人类基因改造，以创造格森人的性生理特征：

Rather wickedly, Le Guin devotes Chapter 7 to the field notes of one Ong Tot Oppong, a woman investigator on behalf of the Ekumen who lands on Gethen/Winter to study “The Question of Sex.” Oppong speculates that whoever colonized this odd planet practiced human genetic manipulation in order to produce Gethenian sexual physiology:

性周期平均为26至28天（他们通常将其称为26天，以近似于月相周期）。在21或22天里，个体处于“索默”（somer）状态，性不活跃，处于潜伏期。大约在第18天，垂体控制激素变化，个体在第22或23天进入“凯默”（kemmer）状态，即发情期。在“凯默”（kemmer，卡尔赫语： secher）的第一阶段，个体完全保持雌雄同体状态。性别和性能力并非孤立地获得。处于“凯默”（kemmer）第一阶段的格森人，如果独处或与未处于“凯默”（kemmer）状态的人在一起，仍然无法进行性交。然而，在这个阶段，性冲动极其强烈，控制着整个人格，使所有其他欲望都服从于它。当个体在性交（kemmer）中找到伴侣时，激素分泌会进一步受到刺激（主要通过触摸——分泌物？气味？），直到一方伴侣体内建立起男性或女性的激素优势。生殖器会相应地充血或萎缩，前戏也会加剧，而伴侣则会在这种变化的触发下，扮演另一种性角色（？无一例外？如果存在例外，例如同性伴侣，则极其罕见，可以忽略不计）。性交（kemmer，卡哈尔语：thorharmen）的第二阶段，即双方建立性欲和性能力的过程，显然会在两到二十小时内完成。如果其中一方已经完全进入性交状态，那么新伴侣的这一阶段可能很短；如果两人同时进入性交状态，则可能需要更长时间。正常人在性交中没有扮演任何一种性角色的倾向；他们不知道自己会是男性还是女性，对此也无能为力。（奥蒂·尼姆写道，在奥尔戈雷恩地区，使用激素衍生物来确定性别非常普遍；我在卡尔海德农村地区没有见过这种情况。）一旦性别确定，在凯默尔期就无法改变。凯默尔期的高潮阶段（卡尔海德语：thokemmer）性欲旺盛期持续两到五天，在此期间性欲和性能力达到顶峰。该阶段结束得相当突然，如果未受孕，个体将在几小时内返回到性欲旺盛期（注：奥蒂·尼姆认为这“第四阶段”相当于月经周期），然后新一轮周期开始。如果个体处于女性角色并已怀孕，激素活动自然会继续，在8.4个月的妊娠期和6到8个月的哺乳期内，该个体保持女性身份。男性性器官保持内缩状态（如同在性欲旺盛期一样），乳房略微增大，骨盆带扩张。哺乳期结束后，女性重新进入性欲旺盛期，再次成为完全的雌雄同体。此时不会形成任何生理习惯，几个孩子的母亲也可能是更多孩子的父亲。

The sexual cycle averages 26 to 28 days (they tend to speak of it as 26 days, approximating it to the lunar cycle). For 21 or 22 days the individual is somer, sexually inactive, latent. On about the 18th day hormonal changes are initiated by the pituitary control and on the 22nd or 23rd day the individual enters kemmer, estrus. In this first phase of kemmer (Karh. secher) he remains completely androgynous. Gender, and potency, are not attained in isolation. A Gethenian in first-phase kemmer, if kept alone or with others not in kemmer, remains incapable of coitus. Yet the sexual impulse is tremendously strong in this phase, controlling the entire personality, subjecting all other drives to its imperative. When the individual finds a partner in kemmer, hormonal secretion is further stimulated (most importantly by touch—secretion? scent?) until in one partner either a male or female hormonal dominance is established. The genitals engorge or shrink accordingly, foreplay intensifies, and the partner, triggered by the change, takes on the other sexual role (? without exception? If there are exceptions, resulting in kemmer-partners of the same sex, they are so rare as to be ignored). This second phase of kemmer (Karh. thorharmen), the mutual process of establishing sexuality and potency, apparently occurs within a timespan of two to twenty hours. If one of the partners is already in full kemmer, the phase for the newer partner is liable to be quite short; if the two are entering kemmer together, it is likely to take longer. Normal individuals have no predisposition to either sexual role in kemmer; they do not know whether they will be the male or the female, and have no choice in the matter. (Otie Nim wrote that in the Orgoreyn region the use of hormone derivatives to establish a preferred sexuality is quite common; I haven’t seen this done in rural Karhide.) Once the sex is determined it cannot change during the kemmer-period. The culminant phase of kemmer (Karh. thokemmer) lasts from two to five days, during which sexual drive and capacity are at maximum. It ends fairly abruptly, and if conception has not taken place, the individual returns to the somer phase within a few hours (note: Otie Nim thinks this “fourth phase” is the equivalent of the menstrual cycle) and the cycle begins anew. If the individual was in the female role and was impregnated, hormonal activity of course continues, and for the 8.4-month gestation period and the 6- to 8-month lactation period this individual remains female. The male sexual organs remain retracted (as they are in somer), the breasts enlarge somewhat, and the pelvic girdle widens. With the cessation of lactation the female reenters somer and becomes once more a perfect adrogyne. No physiological habit is established, and the mother of several children may be the father of several more.

最后那句话想必会让厄休拉·勒奎恩欣喜不已，她那和蔼可亲的讽刺功力几乎无人能及。我当然也很喜欢！我快八十八岁了，对这些早已习以为常，但即便我只有二十八岁，恐怕也会因此跑去最近的酒吧寻欢作乐。由于卡尔海德国王阿尔加文既疯癫又身怀六甲，根利·艾的冒险看似愚蠢，但却是以本书主人公哈斯·雷姆·伊尔·埃斯特拉文的牺牲换来的。

That last sentence must have delighted Ursula K. Le Guin, whose capacity for amiable irony is almost unsurpassed. It certainly pleases me! Going on eighty-eight, I am beyond all this, but even if I were twenty-eight it might send me to the nearest bar. Since King Argaven of Karhide is both crazy and pregnant, Genly Ai’s quest seems foolish yet it is earned by a sacrifice of the book’s hero, Harth rem ir Estraven.

埃斯特拉文在第一章结尾才正式登场，但我们对他的了解和认识都只能通过根利·艾的误解来判断。这位高贵的埃斯特拉文即将卸任首相——这对他来说并不意外，因为他曾直言不讳地指出阿尔加文国王既疯狂又愚蠢。但他正面临着来自竞争对手的威胁，并且担心艾的安危。格森是一个绝对君主制国家，根利·艾对这个国家一无所知。在温特星球上，虽然没有战争，但暗杀、血仇和突发的暴力事件却屡见不鲜。

Estraven is introduced to us at the close of the first chapter, but we see and hear him only through the misconceptions of Genly Ai. The noble Estraven is a prime minister on the way out—no surprise to him, because he candidly remarks that King Argaven is both crazy and stupid. But he is in some danger from rivals and has concern that Ai may be in danger also. Gethen is an absolute monarchy, itself an entity totally unknown to Genly Ai. No wars are fought on the planet Winter, but assassinations, blood feuds, sudden outbursts of violence are common.

埃斯特拉文的爱国情怀逐渐转变为一种认知：卡尔海德已经过时，需要加入星际联盟。在阿尔加文国王及其阴险狡诈的仆从眼中，埃斯特拉文的这种想法是叛国行为，他终将为此付出生命的代价。他被迫流亡，并遭到了禁令的颁布。

The patriotism of Estraven has modulated into a realization that Karhide is outmoded and needs to join the interplanetary union of worlds. In the eyes of King Argaven and his more duplicitous servitors, Estraven’s desire is treasonable, and in time he will suffer death for it. He flees into exile and a ban is proclaimed:

“……让卡尔海德的所有同胞都知道并宣告，哈斯·雷姆·伊尔·埃斯特拉文被流放的罪名是叛国罪：他假借效忠国王之名，在议会和宫廷中私下和公开鼓吹卡尔海德民族放弃主权和权力，成为某个民族联盟中一个卑微的附属国。关于这个所谓的民族联盟，所有人都应该知道并宣告，根本不存在这样的联盟，这只是某些阴谋叛徒为了削弱卡尔海德国王的权威，为国家真正的敌人谋利而捏造的阴谋诡计。奥德古尔尼·图瓦，第八时辰，埃尔亨朗宫：阿尔加文·哈格。”

“…Let all countrymen of Karhide know and say that the crime for which Harth rem ir Estraven is exiled is the crime of Treason: he having urged privily and openly in Assembly and Palace, under pretense of loyal service to the king, that the Nation-Dominion of Karhide cast away its sovereignty and surrender up its power in order to become an inferior and subject nation in a certain Union of Peoples, concerning which let all men know and say that no such Union does exist, being a device and baseless fiction of certain conspiring traitors who seek to weaken the Authority of Karhide in the king, to the profit of the real and present enemies of the land. Odguyrny Tuwa, Eighth Hour, in the Palace in Erhenrang: ARGAVEN HARGE.”

在与国王进行了一次颇为惊险的会面后，根利·艾开始理解埃斯特拉文对他的关心，并发誓要离开卡海德，前往卡海德的宿敌兼邻国奥戈雷恩。他向东行进，向预言者们寻求情报。《左手》中我最喜欢的章节是第五章“驯服直觉”，也就是预言者们的故事。他们的领袖是法克塞，一位温和的“负面之道”信徒，最终将在卡海德获得权力。法克塞是一名织工，在人类历史上，织工这一职业一直与超自然力量联系在一起。我总是会想起莎士比亚《仲夏夜之梦》中那位可爱的织工波顿，他是唯一能够看到并理解仙境的人类，那里有提泰妮娅、帕克、奥伯龙、芥菜籽、蛛网、豌豆花和飞蛾。

After a rather frightening meeting with the king, Genly Ai begins to understand Estraven’s concern for him and vows to leave Karhide for Orgoreyn, Karhide’s rival and neighbor. He goes east to seek information from the Foretellers. My favorite chapter in Left Hand is 5, “The Domestication of Hunch,” the chapter of the Foretellers. Their leader is Faxe, a benign follower of the Negative Way, who eventually will attain power in Karhide. Faxe is a weaver, a craft associated with the preternatural throughout human history. I always think of the delightful Bottom the Weaver in Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, who is the only human who can see and apprehend the faerie world of Titania, Puck, Oberon, Mustardseed, Cobweb, Peaseblossom, Moth.

预言者法克塞在高耸的大厅中，周围环绕着八个预言者，其中两个近乎疯癫，一个则是个古怪的男性变态，构成了一幅令人惊叹的景象。为了换取两颗红宝石，根利·艾问道：卡尔海德会加入埃库门吗？何时加入？突然，一个与法克塞融为一体的女子出现，她沐浴在银光之中，身披银色铠甲，手持利剑。她痛苦而恐惧地尖叫着，齐声回答“是！”随后消失。答案是：五年后，格森将成为埃库门的一员。

Faxe the Foreteller centers an amazing scene, in a high hall surrounded by eight other proleptic figures, two of them being quite insane and one a curious male pervert. In return for two rubies, Genly Ai asks the question: will Karhide join the Ekumen and when? Suddenly a woman appears merged with Faxe, bathed in silver light, encased in silver armor, and bearing a sword. She screams aloud, in pain and terror, a triple yes! She vanishes. The answer is that five years hence Gethen will be a member of the Ekumen.

在我看来，预言家法克塞的最终智慧在于乌苏拉对弗洛伊德格言的巧妙回避，即我们必须接受死亡的必然性：

The ultimate wisdom of Faxe the Foreteller seems to me Ursula’s eloquent evasion of the Freudian maxim that we must make friends with the necessity of dying:

“未知，”法克塞在森林中轻声说道，“未曾预料、未经证实的事物，才是生命的基础。无知是思想的根基，未经证实是行动的根基。如果证明没有上帝，就不会有宗教。不会有汉达拉，不会有约梅什，不会有炉灶之神，什么都不会有。但如果证明有上帝，也不会有宗教……告诉我，詹瑞，什么是已知的？什么是确定的、可预测的、不可避免的——关于你我的未来，你唯一确定的事情是什么？”

“我们终将死去。”

“是的。其实只有一个问题可以回答，Genry，而且我们已经知道答案了……让生活成为可能的唯一因素就是永恒的、难以忍受的不确定性：不知道接下来会发生什么。”

“The unknown,” said Faxe’s soft voice in the forest, “the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action. If it were proven that there is no God there would be no religion. No Handdara, no Yomesh, no hearthgods, nothing. But also if it were proven that there is a God, there would be no religion….Tell me, Genry, what is known? What is sure, predictable, inevitable—the one certain thing you know concerning your future, and mine?”

“That we shall die.”

“Yes. There’s really only one question that can be answered, Genry, and we already know the answer….The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.”

在我看来，这似乎是一种美学表达：最优秀的小说之所以能够反复阅读，正是因为我们不知道接下来会发生什么，即便我们已经读过一遍。在勒古恩的作品中，她既是小说家又是诗人，正如维克多·雨果和艾米莉·勃朗特一样，诗意本身就成了预言。我们无需付出任何代价；我们只需反复阅读。在法克斯对死亡的不确定性发出不祥的预感之后，勒古恩将叙述者换成了埃斯特拉文，他必须逃往奥尔戈雷恩，这绝非易事。他必须偷一艘船，划船而行，尽管他已被声波枪击伤。最终，他被一艘巡逻船救起，并被带到了奥尔戈雷恩的一个安全港口。

To me that seems an aesthetic formulation: the only thing that makes it possible to read and reread the best novels is not knowing what comes next, even though we have read them before. In Le Guin, as much the novelist as poet as were Victor Hugo and Emily Brontë, the poetry itself becomes Foretelling. We don’t have to pay her two rubies; we need only read and reread. Directly after the foreboding by Faxe of the uncertainty of mortality, Le Guin changes the narrator into Estraven, who has to flee into Orgoreyn, scarcely an easy purpose. He has to steal a boat and row it, though wounded by a sonic gun. Picked up by a patrol ship, he is taken to a safe port in Orgoreyn.

小说的情节在埃斯特拉文前往奥戈雷恩寻找根利·艾并警告他不要被该国任何派系利用时，以一种全新的紧张感展开。之后，埃斯特拉文从一座监狱农场救出了根利，两人一起拉着雪橇，开始了穿越冰面的艰辛跋涉。在这段冒险旅程中，他们成为了无比亲密的朋友，彼此间产生了一种令人动容的默契，这种默契将他们带到了性爱的边缘，而他们也恰好停顿在了那里。就在那一刻，勒古恩巧妙地安排了一段精彩的插曲：

The novel’s plot begins with fresh intensity when Estraven seeks out Genly Ai in Orgoreyn and warns him not to be used by any faction in that country. Later, Estraven rescues Genly from a prison farm, and their escape takes them on a tremendous trek across the ice, pulling a sledge together. In that adventure they become overwhelmingly close friends and develop a poignance in their mutual understanding that takes them to the border of sexual love, where they pause. At that moment Le Guin creates a remarkable excursus:

自从我们从火山的迷雾中出来后，我们的精神并没有完全被工作和忧虑耗尽，晚饭后我们在帐篷里又聊了起来。我正处于“kemmer”（一种冥想状态）中，本想更容易忽略艾的存在，但在双人帐篷里这很难做到。问题在于，他以他那奇特的方式也处于“kemmer”状态：​​总是处于“kemmer”状态。这一定是一种奇怪的、低级的欲望，贯穿一年中的每一天，永远无法选择性别，但它就在那里；而我，就在这里。今晚，我对他的强烈生理感知很难忽视，我太累了，无法将这种感知转移到“untense”（一种冥想状态）或其他任何冥想技巧中。最后他问，他冒犯到我了吗？我有些尴尬地解释了我的沉默。我害怕他会嘲笑我。毕竟，他并不比我更怪异，更不像性变态：在这冰天雪地上，我们每个人都是独一无二的，彼此孤立，我与同类、与我的社会及其规则隔绝，正如他与他的社会及其规则隔绝一样。这里没有一个充满其他格森人的世界来解释和支持我的存在。我们最终是平等的，平等的，异类的，孤独的。他当然没有笑。相反，他说话时带着一种我从未察觉的温柔。过了一会儿，他也开始谈论孤立，谈论孤独。

“你们的种族在这个世界上孤身一人，令人震惊。没有其他哺乳动物，没有其他雌雄同体的物种，甚至没有足够聪明到可以驯养成宠物的动物。这种独特性必然会影响你们的思维方式。我指的不仅仅是科学思维，尽管你们是杰出的假设者——面对你们与低等动物之间那道无法逾越的鸿沟，你们竟然还能提出进化论的概念，这本身就令人惊叹。但从哲学和情感层面来说，身处如此孤寂、如此充满敌意的世界，必然会影响你们的整个世界观。”

“约梅什塔会说，人的独特性就是他的神性。”

“没错，是大地之主。其他世界的其他教派也得出了同样的结论。他们往往是那些充满活力、好斗、破坏生态的文明的教派。奥戈雷恩也遵循着这种模式，至少他们似乎一心想要改变现状。汉达拉塔人怎么说呢？”

“嗯，在汉达拉……你知道，那里没有理论，没有教条……也许他们不太在意人与兽之间的鸿沟，更关注相似之处、联系，以及所有生物都是整体的一部分。”托默的歌谣在我脑海里萦绕了一整天，我脱口而出：

光明是黑暗的左手

黑暗是光明的右手

二合为一，生与死，躺着

像凯默尔的恋人一样在一起，

就像双手合十一样，

就像终点和路径一样。

我念出这些话时声音颤抖，因为我一边念一边想起，在我哥哥去世前写给我的信中，他也引用了同样的话。

艾未未沉思片刻，过了一会儿说道：“你是孤立的，也是不分裂的。或许你和我们一样，都痴迷于整体性。”

“我们也是二元论者。二元性是本质的，不是吗？只要有‘我’和‘他者’存在。 ”

“我与你，”他说。“是的，归根结底，它的意义甚至超越了性……”

Since we came up out of the volcano-murk our spirit is not all spent in work and worry, and we talk again in the tent after our dinner. As I am in kemmer I would find it easier to ignore Ai’s presence, but this is difficult in a two-man tent. The trouble is of course that he is, in his curious fashion, also in kemmer: always in kemmer. A strange lowgrade sort of desire it must be, to be spread out over every day of the year and never to know the choice of sex, but there it is; and here am I. Tonight my extreme physical awareness of him was rather hard to ignore, and I was too tired to divert it into untrance or any other channel of the discipline. Finally he asked, had he offended me? I explained my silence, with some embarrassment. I was afraid he would laugh at me. After all he is no more an oddity, a sexual freak, than I am: up here on the Ice each of us is singular, isolate, I as cut off from those like me, from my society and its rules, as he from his. There is no world full of other Gethenians here to explain and support my existence. We are equals at last, equal, alien, alone. He did not laugh, of course. Rather he spoke with a gentleness that I did not know was in him. After a while he too came to speak of isolation, of loneliness.

“Your race is appallingly alone in its world. No other mammalian species. No other ambisexual species. No animal intelligent enough even to domesticate as pets. It must color your thinking, this uniqueness. I don’t mean scientific thinking only, though you are extraordinary hypothesizers—it’s extraordinary that you arrived at any concept of evolution, faced with that unbridgeable gap between yourselves and the lower animals. But philosophically, emotionally: to be so solitary, in so hostile a world: it must affect your entire outlook.”

“The Yomeshta would say that man’s singularity is his divinity.”

“Lords of the Earth, yes. Other cults on other worlds have come to the same conclusion. They tend to be the cults of dynamic, aggressive, ecology-breaking cultures. Orgoreyn is in the pattern, in its way; at least they seem bent on pushing things around. What do the Handdarata say?”

“Well, in the Handdara…you know, there’s no theory, no dogma….Maybe they are less aware of the gap between men and beasts, being more occupied with the likenesses, the links, the whole of which living things are a part.” Tormer’s Lay had been all day in my mind, and I said the words,

Light is the left hand of darkness

And darkness the right hand of light

Two are one, life and death, lying

together like lovers in kemmer,

like hands joined together,

like the end and the way.

My voice shook as I said the lines, for I remembered as I said them that in the letter my brother wrote me before his death he had quoted the same words.

Ai brooded, and after some time he said, “You’re isolated, and undivided. Perhaps you are as obsessed with wholeness as we are with dualism.”

“We are dualists too. Duality is an essential, isn’t it? So long as there is myself and the other.”

“I and Thou,” he said. “Yes, it does, after all, go even wider than sex….”

勒古恩的道家诗赋予她的远不止一个称号。我回忆起在写给她的最后一封信中，我向她致敬的，正是那本书、那个女人、那个桀骜不驯、漂泊不定的精神。那封信写于她去世的第二天，我当时并不知道。她让艾在表达对埃斯特拉文与他之间爱情的理解时，达到了他创作生涯中最辉煌的时刻：

Le Guin’s Taoist poem gives her more than a title. It is the book, the woman, the spirit unappeasable and peregrine that I recall saluting in the last letter I sent to her, unknowingly written the day after her death. She gives Ai his finest moment in expressing an understanding of the love between Estraven and himself:

在我看来，我想他也这么认为，正是我们之间那份如今已被承认、已被理解却并未消解的性张力，孕育了我们之间那份伟大而突如其来的友谊：这份友谊在我们流亡期间如此迫切需要，在我们苦苦旅途的日日夜夜里早已得到了充分的考验，以至于无论现在还是将来，它都完全可以被称为爱情。然而，这份爱并非源于相似之处，而是源于我们之间的差异，正是这份差异本身，成为了跨越我们之间鸿沟的桥梁，唯一的桥梁。如果我们再次发生性关系，就如同再次以陌生人的身份相遇。我们曾以我们唯一能做到的方式触碰过彼此。我们止步于此。我不知道我们当时的做法是否正确。

For it seemed to me, and I think to him, that it was from that sexual tension between us, admitted now and understood but not assuaged, that the great and sudden assurance of friendship between us rose: a friendship so much needed by us both in our exile, and already so well proved in the days and nights of our bitter journey, that it might as well be called, now as later, love. But it was from the difference between us, not from the affinities and likenesses, but from the difference, that that love came: and it was itself the bridge, the only bridge, across what divided us. For us to meet sexually would be for us to meet once more as aliens. We had touched, in the only way we could touch. We left it at that. I do not know if we were right.

这段话措辞如此精准，仿佛出自勒古恩之口。她自己也不确定他们是否正确，作为读者，我也同样感到疑惑。如果他们真的发展成恋人关系，这本书将会截然不同。勒古恩曾在某处提到，她真正关注的主题是婚姻，而在这里，她为我们呈现了一场莎士比亚式的心灵婚姻。勒古恩毕竟是勒古恩，她并未止步于此。她创造的“心灵感应”便是其中之一，通过这种方式，两个心意相通的人无需言语即可交流，艾将这种能力传授给了埃斯特拉文：

This is so precisely phrased that the voice is Le Guin’s. She also is unsure if they were right, and as her reader I, too, am uncertain. It would be a very different book if they had become lovers in the complete sense. Somewhere Le Guin remarks that her true subject is marriage, and here she gives us a Shakespearean marriage of true minds. Le Guin being Le Guin, she does not stop there. One of her inventions is mindspeech, by which two empathics can communicate without speech, a praxis that Ai teaches Estraven:

我们再次尝试了心灵感应。我以前从未反复向一个完全没有接收能力的人发送过信息。这种体验令人不快。我开始觉得自己像个无神论者在祈祷。过了一会儿，埃斯特拉文打了个哈欠，说道：“我聋了，聋得像块石头。我们最好睡觉。”我同意了。他关了灯，低声赞叹着黑暗；我们钻进睡袋，一两分钟后，他就如同游泳者滑入黑暗的水中一般沉入了梦乡。我感觉他的睡眠就像我自己的睡眠一样：那种共情的联系依然存在，我再次迷迷糊糊地叫了他的名字——“瑟雷姆！ ”

他猛地坐直，因为他的声音在黑暗中响亮地回荡在我头顶。“阿雷克！是你吗？”

“不：艾根利：我是在跟你说话。”

他屏住了呼吸。一片寂静。他笨拙地摆弄着炉灶，打开灯，用充满恐惧的黑眼睛盯着我。“我做了个梦，”他说，“我以为我在家——”

“你听到了我的心灵感应。”

“你给我打电话了——是我哥哥。我听到的是他的声音。他死了。你给我打电话了——你叫我特雷姆？我……这比我想象的还要可怕。”他摇了摇头，就像男人为了摆脱噩梦而做的那样，然后双手捂住了脸。

“哈斯，我很抱歉——”

“不，叫我的名字。如果你能用死人的声音在我脑子里说话，那你就能叫我的名字！他会叫我‘哈斯’吗？哦，我明白了，为什么这种心灵感应里没有谎言。这真是太可怕了……好吧，好吧，再跟我说话吧。”

“等待。”

“不，继续。”

他用充满恐惧和凶狠的目光盯着我，我向他说道：“特雷姆，我的朋友，我们之间没有什么好怕的。”

他一直盯着我看，我以为他没听懂；但他其实听懂了。“啊，可是有的，”他说。

过了一会儿，他控制住自己的情绪，平静地说：“你用我的语言跟我说话。”

“嗯，你又不了解我的情况。”

“你说过会有言语交流，我知道……但我想象的是一种——默契——”

“同理心是另一种游戏，虽然并非毫无关联。它让我们今晚建立了联系。但在真正的心灵感应中，大脑的语言中枢会被激活，以及——”

“不，不，不。待会儿再说。你为什么用我哥哥的声音说话？”他的声音很紧张。

“我无法回答这个问题。我不知道。跟我说说他吧。”

“努苏斯……我的同父同母的哥哥，阿雷克·哈斯·雷姆·伊尔·埃斯特拉文。他比我大一岁。他本该成为埃斯特雷的领主。我们……你知道，我为了他离开了家。他已经去世十四年了。”

We tried mindspeech again. I had never before sent repeatedly to a total non-receiver. The experience was disagreeable. I began to feel like an atheist praying. Presently Estraven yawned and said, “I am deaf, deaf as a rock. We’d better sleep.” I assented. He turned out the light, murmuring his brief praise of darkness; we burrowed down into our bags, and within a minute or two he was sliding into sleep as a swimmer slides into dark water. I felt his sleep as if it were my own: the empathic bond was there, and once more I bespoke him, sleepily, by his name—“Therem!”

He sat bolt upright, for his voice rang out above me in the blackness, loud. “Arek! is that you?”

“No: Genly Ai: I am bespeaking you.”

His breath caught. Silence. He fumbled with the Chabe stove, turned up the light, stared at me with his dark eyes full of fear. “I dreamed,” he said, “I thought I was at home—”

“You heard me mindspeak.”

“You called me—It was my brother. It was his voice I heard. He’s dead. You called me—you called me Therem? I…This is more terrible than I had thought.” He shook his head, as a man will do to shake off nightmare, and then put his face in his hands.

“Harth, I’m very sorry—”

“No, call me by my name. If you can speak inside my skull with a dead man’s voice then you can call me by my name! Would he have called me ‘Harth’? Oh, I see why there’s no lying in this mindspeech. It is a terrible thing….All right. All right, speak to me again.”

“Wait.”

“No. Go on.”

With his fierce, frightened gaze on me I bespoke him: “Therem, my friend, there’s nothing to fear between us.”

He kept on staring at me, so that I thought he had not understood; but he had. “Ah, but there is,” he said.

After a while, controlling himself, he said calmly, “You spoke in my language.”

“Well, you don’t know mine.”

“You said there would be words, I know….Yet I imagined it as—an understanding—”

“Empathy’s another game, though not unconnected. It gave us the connection tonight. But in mindspeech proper, the speech centers of the brain are activated, as well as—”

“No, no, no. Tell me that later. Why do you speak in my brother’s voice?” His voice was strained.

“That I can’t answer. I don’t know. Tell me about him.”

“Nusuth…My full brother, Arek Harth rem ir Estraven. He was a year older than I. He would have been Lord of Estre. We…I left home, you know, for his sake. He has been dead fourteen years.”

这两个埃斯特拉文人曾是恋人，乱伦在格森尼亚并非禁忌。他们彼此发誓忠贞，并育有一子。当阿雷克英勇地试图逃离卡尔海德时，瑟雷姆将与他一同赴死。

The two Estravens had been lovers, incest not being a Gethenian taboo. They had sworn faithfulness to one another and had a son. Therem will join Arek in death when he attempts valiantly to make his escape from Karhide:

但他已经滑走了，一路向下：他滑雪速度极快，而且这次没有为我保留任何实力。他沿着雪地上的阴影，快速地、急促地滑下，形成一道长长的弧线。他逃离了我，径直冲进了边防军的枪口。我想他们喊了些警告或命令，让他停下，某个地方亮起了灯，但我不太确定；总之，他没有停下，而是朝着栅栏飞驰而去，在他到达栅栏之前就被击毙了。他们没有使用声波震荡器，而是使用了突击枪，这种古老的武器会发射一连串的金属碎片。他们开枪是为了杀死他。当我赶到他身边时，他已经奄奄一息，四肢摊开，身体扭曲着，滑雪板从雪里伸出来，胸口中弹了一半。我抱住他的头，跟他说话，但他始终没有回应我；他以某种方式回应了我的爱，在意识消逝、意识混乱、一片寂静之际，他用无声的语言，清晰地喊了一声“阿雷克！”然后就再也没有声音了。我抱着他，蹲在雪地里，看着他死去。他们让我这么做。然后他们让我站起来，把我带走，把他带走，我进了监狱，他被送进了黑暗。

But he was off, downhill: a magnificent fast skier, and this time not holding back for me. He shot away on a long quick curving descent through the shadows over the snow. He ran from me, and straight into the guns of the border-guards. I think they shouted warnings or orders to halt, and a light sprang up somewhere, but I am not sure; in any case he did not stop, but flashed on towards the fence, and they shot him down before he reached it. They did not use the sonic stunners but the foray gun, the ancient weapon that fires a set of metal fragments in a burst. They shot to kill him. He was dying when I got to him, sprawled and twisted away from his skis that stuck up out of the snow, his chest half shot away. I took his head in my arms and spoke to him, but he never answered me; only in a way he answered my love for him, crying out through the silent wreck and tumult of his mind as consciousness lapsed, in the unspoken tongue, once, clearly, “Arek!” Then no more. I held him, crouching there in the snow, while he died. They let me do that. Then they made me get up, and took me off one way and him another, I going to prison and he into the dark.

勒古恩的艺术魅力在于，每次重读此文，我都会感到无比悲伤。在某种程度上，根利·艾如同霍拉旭之于特雷姆·埃斯特拉文，而特雷姆则如同哈姆雷特。莎士比亚笔下的哈姆雷特最终升华，走向神化，而特雷姆则坠入冰冷的黑暗，呼喊着他早已逝去的兄弟的名字，仿佛根利与阿雷克融为一体。

It is a tribute to Le Guin’s art that every time I reread this I become very sad. In some ways Genly Ai plays Horatio to Therem Estraven’s Hamlet, but Shakespeare’s Hamlet dies upward in an apotheosis, whereas Therem descends to icy darkness, crying out the name of his long-dead brother as though Genly has fused with Arek.

根利·艾很快奉王室之命获释，并在安排击落埃库门飞船后再次觐见了阿尔加文国王：

Genly Ai is soon liberated by royal orders and has another audience with King Argaven, after arranging to bring down the Ekumen spaceship:

沉默片刻后，他问道：“穿越冰面的感觉如何？”

“不容易。”

“在那样疯狂的旅途中，埃斯特拉文会是个很棒的伙伴。他意志坚强，从不发脾气。我很遗憾他去世了。”

我没有找到回复。

“我将于明天下午第二小时接见你们的同胞。现在还有什么要说的吗？”

“大人，您能否撤销对埃斯特拉文的流放令，以还他清白？”

“还没呢，艾先生。别着急。还有其他问题吗？”

“不再。”

“那就继续吧。”

连我都背叛了他。我曾说过，除非他的流放结束，名誉洗清，否则我绝不会让船沉没。我不能因为坚持这个条件而放弃他为之献身的一切。那样做也无法让他摆脱流放。

After some silence, he said, “How was it, that pull across the Ice?”

“Not easy.”

“Estraven would be a good man to pull with, on a crazy trek like that. He was tough as iron. And never lost his temper. I’m sorry he’s dead.”

I found no reply.

“I’ll receive your…countrymen in audience tomorrow afternoon at Second Hour. Is there more needs saying now?”

“My lord, will you revoke the Order of Exile on Estraven, to clear his name?”

“Not yet, Mr. Ai. Don’t rush it. Anything more?”

“No more.”

“Go on, then.”

Even I betrayed him. I had said I would not bring the ship down till his banishment was ended, his name cleared. I could not throw away what he had died for, by insisting on the condition. It would not bring him out of this exile.

《黑暗的左手》以根利·艾拜访埃斯特雷之主的炉火为结尾，埃斯特雷之主是阿雷克和瑟雷姆的生父。

The Left Hand of Darkness concludes with Genly Ai visiting the Hearth of the Lord of Estre, who had borne both Arek and Therem.

埃斯万斯·哈斯·雷姆·伊尔·埃斯特拉文是一位年迈的老人，七十多岁，患有严重的髋关节炎，行动不便。他笔直地坐在火炉旁的滚椅上。他的脸宽阔，饱经风霜，像激流中的一块岩石：一张平静的脸，平静得可怕。

“您就是使者艾将军吗？”

“我是。”

他看着我，我也看着他。特雷姆曾是这位老领主的亲生儿子，血肉之躯。特雷姆是幼子；阿雷克是长子，那个他曾在我耳边听到声音的哥哥；如今他们都已死去。在那张饱经风霜、平静而坚毅的老脸上，我找不到一丝朋友的影子。我看到的只有确凿无疑的事实：特雷姆已经死了。

老领主看了看男孩，又看了看我。

“这位是索尔夫·哈斯，”他说，“埃斯特雷的继承人，我儿子的儿子。”

那里并不禁止乱伦，我很清楚这一点。只是对我这个地球人来说，这太奇怪了，而且在这个阴郁、凶悍的乡下男孩身上看到我朋友的灵魂闪现，也让我一时语塞。我开口说话时，声音颤抖。“国王会收回他的命令。他不是叛徒。那些傻瓜怎么称呼他又有什么关系呢？”

老领主缓缓地点了点头，动作平静而流畅。“这很重要，”他说。

“你们一起穿越了戈布林冰原，”索尔夫质问道，“你和他？​​”

“我们做到了。”

“我很想听听这个故事，使节大人，”老埃斯凡斯平静地说。但瑟伦的儿子，那个男孩，结结巴巴地说：“您能告诉我们他是怎么死的吗？——您能告诉我们星际间的其他世界吗？其他种类的人类；其他的生活？”

Esvans Harth rem ir Estraven was an old man, past seventy, crippled by an arthritic disease of the hips. He sat erect in a rolling-chair by the fire. His face was broad, much blunted and worn down by time, like a rock in a torrent: a calm face, terribly calm.

“You are the Envoy, Genry Ai?”

“I am.”

He looked at me, and I at him. Therem had been the son, child of the flesh, of this old lord. Therem the younger son; Arek the elder, that brother whose voice he had heard in mine bespeaking him; both dead now. I could not see anything of my friend in that worn, calm, hard old face that met my gaze. I found nothing there but the certainty, the sure fact of Therem’s death:

The old lord looked at the boy, then at me.

“This is Sorve Harth,” he said, “heir of Estre, my sons’ son.”

There is no ban on incest there, I knew it well enough. Only the strangeness of it, to me a Terran, and the strangeness of seeing the flash of my friend’s spirit in this grim, fierce, provincial boy, made me dumb for a while. When I spoke my voice was unsteady. “The king will recant. Therem was no traitor. What does it matter what fools call him?”

The old lord nodded slowly, smoothly. “It matters,” he said.

“You crossed the Gobrin Ice together,” Sorve demanded, “you and he?”

“We did.”

“I should like to hear that tale, my Lord Envoy,” said old Esvans, very calm. But the boy, Therem’s son, said stammering, “Will you tell us how he died?—Will you tell us about the other worlds out among the stars—the other kinds of men; the other lives?”

勒古恩在结尾的处理上有着特殊的天赋。在男孩索尔夫的声音中，我们再次听到了特雷姆的灵魂在说话，我们也重新意识到他死亡的讽刺性必要性——这是一种牺牲，为了让封闭的社会向他者敞开大门，正如“他者”一词的三次重复所暗示的那样。

Le Guin had a special genius for endings. In the boy Sorve’s voice we hear Therem’s spirit speak again, and we realize freshly the ironic necessity of his dying, a sacrifice to open up his closed society to otherness, indicated by the triple repetition of the refrain “other.”

第四十四章

CHAPTER 44

《被剥夺者》（1974）

The Dispossessed (1974)

乌尔苏拉· K ·莱金​​

URSULA K. LE GUIN

在给我的一封信中，勒古恩回应了我对《一无所有》的赞扬，她说，创作这本书的过程对她来说尤为重要，因为她觉得这教会了她如何让自己的作品更加包容。小说的主人公谢维克无疑是她笔下最复杂的人物，他是一位天才物理学家，一位坚定的无政府主义者，也是一位游走于对立世界之间的朝圣者。

IN ONE OF HER LETTERS TO ME, in response to my praise for The Dispossessed, Le Guin said that the process of writing this book was particularly important for her, in that she felt it had taught her how to make her work more capacious. Certainly Shevek, the novel’s protagonist, is by far her most complex character, a physicist of genius, a dedicated anarchist, and a pilgrim who mediates between antithetical worlds.

这本书的开头和结尾都设定在无政府主义国家阿纳瑞斯的发射港。港口和陆地之间有一堵令人望而生畏的墙，这堵墙看起来如此普通，反而更显不祥之兆：

The book begins and ends at the launch port of the anarchist nation of Anarres. Between the port and the rest of the land there is a forbidding wall, more ominous for looking so commonplace:

那里有一堵墙。它看起来毫不起眼。墙是用未经雕琢的石头粗略砌成的。成年人可以轻易地越过它，甚至孩子也能爬上去。墙与道路交汇处，没有栅栏门，而是简化成一条简单的几何图形，一条线，一种边界的概念。但这种概念是真实的。它很重要。七代人以来，世界上没有任何东西比这堵墙更重要。

像所有墙壁一样，它模棱两可，具有两面性。墙内是什么，墙外是什么，取决于你站在墙的哪一边。

从一侧看去，这道墙围起了一片名为阿纳瑞斯港的荒芜之地，占地六十英亩。港内有几台大型龙门起重机、一个火箭发射台、三个仓库、一个卡车车库和一栋宿舍楼。宿舍楼看起来坚固、肮脏而又阴森；没有花园，没有孩子；显然没有人住在那里，甚至可能也没打算在那里久留。事实上，它是一处隔离区。这道墙不仅封锁了着陆场，还封锁了从太空降落的飞船、飞船上的人、他们来自的星球，以及宇宙的其他部分。它封闭了整个宇宙，只留下阿纳瑞斯城在外，自由自在。

从另一侧看去，这堵墙将阿纳瑞斯围了起来：整个星球都在里面，就像一个巨大的监狱营地，与其他世界和其他人隔绝，处于隔离状态。

There was a wall. It did not look important. It was built of uncut rocks roughly mortared. An adult could look right over it, and even a child could climb it. Where it crossed the roadway, instead of having a gate it degenerated into mere geometry, a line, an idea of boundary. But the idea was real. It was important. For seven generations there had been nothing in the world more important than that wall.

Like all walls it was ambiguous, two-faced. What was inside it and what was outside it depended upon which side of it you were on.

Looked at from one side, the wall enclosed a barren sixty-acre field called the Port of Anarres. On the field there were a couple of large gantry cranes, a rocket pad, three warehouses, a truck garage, and a dormitory. The dormitory looked durable, grimy, and mournful; it had no gardens, no children; plainly nobody lived there or was even meant to stay there long. It was in fact a quarantine. The wall shut in not only the landing field but also the ships that came down out of space, and the men that came on the ships, and the worlds they came from, and the rest of the universe. It enclosed the universe, leaving Anarres outside, free.

Looked at from the other side, the wall enclosed Anarres: the whole planet was inside it, a great prison camp, cut off from other worlds and other men, in quarantine.

在谢韦克和飞船之间，站着一群愤怒的民众，他们决心阻止他离开：

Between Shevek and the spaceship is an angry crowd determined to prevent his departure:

他们当中有些人来此是为了刺杀叛徒。另一些人则是为了阻止他离开，或是对他破口大骂，或是仅仅为了看他一眼；而所有这些人都阻碍了刺客们短暂的行动。他们中没有人携带枪支，尽管有几个人带了刀。对他们来说，袭击就意味着肉体上的攻击；他们想要亲手制服这个叛徒。他们预料他会乘车前来，而且会有护卫。当他们正试图检查一辆货车并与愤怒的司机争论时，他们要找的人独自一人沿着路走了过来。当他们认出他时，他已经走到田野中央，身后跟着五名“防御”组织的成员。那些想要杀他的人开始追赶，但为时已晚；他们开始投掷石块，但还不算太晚。就在他们要找的人走到船边时，他们勉强击中了他，但一块两磅重的燧石击中了一名“防御”组织成员的头部侧面，当场将其击毙。

Some of them had come there to kill a traitor. Others had come to prevent him from leaving, or to yell insults at him, or just to look at him; and all these others obstructed the sheer brief path of the assassins. None of them had firearms, though a couple had knives. Assault to them meant bodily assault; they wanted to take the traitor into their own hands. They expected him to come guarded, in a vehicle. While they were trying to inspect a goods truck and arguing with its outraged driver, the man they wanted came walking up the road, alone. When they recognized him he was already halfway across the field, with five Defense syndics following him. Those who had wanted to kill him resorted to pursuit, too late, and to rock throwing, not quite too late. They barely winged the man they wanted, just as he got to the ship, but a two-pound flint caught one of the Defense crew on the side of the head and killed him on the spot.

谢韦克安全登船后，由于难以理解那些与他生活经验完全不同的观点和信息，他感到十分迷茫。照顾他的医生发表的性别观点，对于从未接触过此类社会谬论的无政府主义者和物理学家来说，简直是莫名其妙。

Once safely on board, Shevek is disoriented as he tries to absorb attitudes and information totally alien to his life experience. The doctor tending to him expresses views on gender that are senseless to the anarchist and physicist never exposed to such societal nonsense:

谢维克转移了话题，但他仍在思考这个问题。这种优劣之分必定是乌拉斯蒂人社会生活的核心问题。如果基莫为了自尊就必须认为半数人类都比他低等，那么女性又是如何自尊的呢？她们是否也认为男性低等？这一切又如何影响她们的性生活？他从奥多的著作中得知，两百年前乌拉斯蒂人主要的性制度是“婚姻”，一种由法律和经济制裁授权和强制执行的伴侣关系；以及“卖淫”，这似乎只是一个更宽泛的概念，指以经济为目的的性行为。奥多谴责了这两种制度，然而他自己却“已婚”。无论如何，两百年间这些制度可能发生了巨大的变化。如果他要生活在乌拉斯，与乌拉斯蒂人一起生活，他最好弄清楚这一点。

Shevek turned the conversation, but he went on thinking about it. This matter of superiority and inferiority must be a central one in Urrasti social life. If to respect himself Kimoe had to consider half the human race as inferior to him, how then did women manage to respect themselves—did they consider men inferior? And how did all that affect their sex lives? He knew from Odo’s writings that two hundred years ago the main Urrasti sexual institutions had been “marriage,” a partnership authorized and enforced by legal and economic sanctions, and “prostitution,” which seemed merely to be a wider term, copulation in the economic mode. Odo had condemned them both, and yet Odo had been “married.” And anyhow the institutions might have changed greatly in two hundred years. If he was going to live on Urras and with the Urrasti, he had better find out.

奥多是无政府主义思想的英雄理论家，阿纳瑞斯城正是建立在无政府主义思想之上，而《无政府主义者》的故事发生在七代人之前。小说巧妙地描绘了谢维克在乌拉斯的经历，章节之间交替叙述着他在阿纳瑞斯的过往。作为一位杰出的理论物理学家，他曾因阿纳瑞斯相对原始的资源和制度而无法专心工作。他逃往乌拉斯的举动融合了对科学真理的追求、个人内心的不安，以及最终对无政府主义信仰的复兴。

Odo was the heroic theoretician of the anarchist idea on which Anarres was founded some seven generations before The Dispossessed opens. The novel subtly traces Shevek’s career on Urras, alternating it chapter by chapter with his past life on Anarres. A great theoretical physicist, he had had his work inhibited by the relatively primitive resources and institutions of Anarres. His flight to Urras fuses elements of scientific truth seeking, personal restlessness, and at last a revival of his anarchist beliefs.

起初，谢维克对自己在乌拉斯大学的教研工作相当满意。舒适的生活对他来说是全新的体验，他一度感到满足。然而，当他生病时，他的母亲鲁拉格前来探望。鲁拉格冷漠而才华横溢，在他出生后不久便抛弃了他。母子二人之间无法建立起任何关系，鲁拉格甚至开始反对他的使命。谢维克身体恢复后，离开了大学，加入了乌拉斯的无政府工团主义者，参与了他们反对政权的大规模抗议活动。起义遭到血腥镇压，谢维克最终与他的伴侣塔克维尔以及他们四岁的女儿萨迪克重聚，这是他第一次见到萨迪克。当他抱着熟睡的塔克维尔辗转难眠时，他的意识开始将自己的人生经历与他作为一名物理学家对时间作为同时性的新理论的探索融合在一起：

Initially, Shevek is happy enough with his teaching and research activities at the university on Urras. The creature comforts are new to him, and for a while he is content. When he falls ill, he is visited by his mother, Rulag, a cold and brilliant person who had abandoned him soon after his birth. No relationship can develop between them, and she comes to oppose his mission. When he is strong enough, Shevek abandons the university and finds his way to join the anarcho-syndicalists of Urras in their mass protest against the regime. The uprising is quelled bloodily, and Shevek finds his way to be reunited with his life partner, Takver, and their four-year-old daughter, Sadik, whom he meets for the first time. As he lies awake, with a sleeping Takver in his arms, his consciousness begins to fuse his life experience with his quest as a physicist for a new theory of time as simultaneity:

谢维克认为，满足感取决于时间。对快乐的追求是循环往复、永无止境的。旁观者、寻求刺激者、性滥交者所追求的新鲜感，最终总是殊途同归。它终有尽头，走到尽头后又不得不重新开始。这不是一段旅程，也不是一次回归，而是一个封闭的循环，一间紧闭的房间，一个牢笼。

紧闭的房间外是时间的风景，在那里，凭借运气和勇气，精神可以构建脆弱的、临时的、不可思议的忠诚之路和城市：一个人类可以居住的风景。

只有当一个行为发生在过去与未来的交汇点上时，它才能称之为人类行为。忠诚，它维系着过去与未来的连续性，将时间牢牢束缚，是人类力量的根源；没有忠诚，一切都无从谈起。

所以，回首过去的四年，谢维克并不觉得虚度光阴，而是觉得那是他和塔克维尔用生命共同构建的丰碑的一部分。他想，顺应时间而不是与时间对抗，关键在于时间不会白白流逝。即使是痛苦也弥足珍贵。

Fulfillment, Shevek thought, is a function of time. The search for pleasure is circular, repetitive, atemporal. The variety seeking of the spectator, the thrill hunter, the sexually promiscuous, always ends in the same place. It has an end. It comes to the end and has to start over. It is not a journey and return, but a closed cycle, a locked room, a cell.

Outside the locked room is the landscape of time, in which the spirit may, with luck and courage, construct the fragile, makeshift, improbable roads and cities of fidelity: a landscape inhabitable by human beings.

It is not until an act occurs within the landscape of the past and the future that it is a human act. Loyalty, which asserts the continuity of past and future, binding time into a hole, is the root of human strength; there is no good to be done without it.

So, looking back on the last four years, Shevek saw them not as wasted, but as part of the edifice that he and Takver were building with their lives. The thing about working with time, instead of against it, he thought, is that it is not wasted. Even pain counts.

这种沉思中蕴含着一种静谧的热忱，其中既有勒古恩对道家思想的信奉，也有她从雪莱、克鲁泡特金和保罗·古德曼那里汲取的无政府主义思想，更重要的是，还有她毕生对婚姻意义的思考。在《无家者》接近尾声时，塔克维尔生下了第二个孩子，又是个女儿。谢维克不顾与他疏远的母亲鲁拉格的反对，协助组织了一个“倡议辛迪加”，旨在强制所有已知世界的科学和美学著作自由出版。

The quiet fervor of this contemplation has elements in it of Le Guin’s adherence to Taoism, of her anarchism, which she derives from Shelley, Kropotkin, and Paul Goodman, and most of all her lifelong meditation upon the meaning of marriage. As The Dispossessed approaches its end, Takver has a second baby, again a girl, and Shevek, against the opposition of his estranged mother, Rulag, helps organize a Syndicate of Initiative, which will force the free publication of scientific and aesthetic works on all the known worlds.

从乌拉斯返回后，谢维克与一名地球飞船大副会合，这名大副决定和他一起穿过那堵墙：

On returning from Urras, Shevek is joined by a Terran first mate of the spaceship who decides to go through the wall with him:

“那么，这是你自己的意愿——你自己的主动性？”

“完全。”

“你明白这可能会很危险吗？”

“是的。”

“阿纳瑞斯那边……有点乱。我的电台朋友们都是这么跟我说的。我们——我们这个组织，我这次的旅程——一直以来的目的就是为了搅动风云，搅动局势，打破一些旧习，让人们开始质疑。要像无政府主义者那样行事！这一切在我离开的这段时间里一直在发生。所以，你看，没人能确定接下来会发生什么。如果你跟我一起登陆，那将会引发更大的混乱。我不能走得太远。我不能把你当成某个外国政府的官方代表。在阿纳瑞斯，这行不通。”

我明白。

“一旦你到了那里，一旦你和我一起穿过那堵墙，在我看来，你就是我们的一员了。我们对你负责，你也对我们负责；你成为了一名阿纳雷斯蒂，拥有和其他人一样的选择。但这些选择并不安全。自由从来都不是安全的。”他环顾四周，这间宁静有序的房间，摆放着简洁的控制台和精密的仪器，高高的天花板和没有窗户的墙壁，然后他又看向凯索。“你会发现自己非常孤独，”他说。

“我的种族非常古老，”凯索说道，“我们已经文明了上千年。我们拥有数百千年的历史。我们尝试过一切，包括无政府主义等等。但我没有尝试过。人们常说太阳底下无新鲜事。但如果每个生命都不是全新的，那么我们为何还要出生呢？”

“我们是时间的孩子，”谢韦克用普拉维克语说道。年轻人看了他一会儿，然后用约提亚语重复了这句话：“我们是时间的孩子。”

“It is your own wish, then—your own initiative?”

“Entirely.”

“And you understand that it might be dangerous?”

“Yes.”

“Things are…a little broken loose, on Anarres. That’s what my friends on the radio have been telling me about. It was our purpose all along—our Syndicate, this journey of mine—to shake up things, to stir up, to break some habits, to make people ask questions. To behave like anarchists! All this has been going on while I was gone. So, you see, nobody is quite sure what happens next. And if you land with me, even more gets broken loose. I cannot push too far. I cannot take you as an official representative of some foreign government. That will not do, on Anarres.”

“I understand that.”

“Once you are there, once you walk through the wall with me, then as I see it you are one of us. We are responsible to you and you to us; you become an Anarresti, with the same options as all the others. But they are not safe options. Freedom is never very safe.” He looked around the tranquil, orderly room, with its simple consoles and delicate instruments, its high ceiling and windowless walls, and back at Ketho. “You would find yourself very much alone,” he said.

“My race is very old,” Ketho said. “We have been civilized for a thousand millennia. We have histories of hundreds of those millennia. We have tried everything. Anarchism, with the rest. But I have not tried it. They say there is nothing new under the sun. But if each life is not new, each single life, then why are we born?”

“We are the children of time,” Shevek said, in Pravic. The younger man looked at him a moment, and then repeated the words in Iotic: “We are the children of time.”

勒古恩的文风在其巅峰时期，如本文所示，有一种光辉灿烂的特质。正如我曾在我们书信往来中告诉她的那样，她拥有《薄伽梵歌》中克里希那对阿朱那的那种清醒洞察力。身为时间的儿女，就如同泰坦尼克号一般，从土星或克洛诺斯之手降临。

There is a quality of the luminous in Le Guin’s style at its best, as it is here. As I told her once in our exchange of letters, she is capable of the lucidity urged upon Arjuna by Krishna in the Gita. To be the children of time is to be Titanic, to descend from Saturn or Cronos.

“凯索，你确定要跟我一起穿过这堵墙吗？你知道，对我来说很容易。无论发生什么，我都会回家。但你却要离开家。‘真正的旅程在于回归……’”

“我希望有一天能回来，”凯索轻声说道，“总有一天。”

“我们什么时候进入登陆艇？”

“大约二十分钟后。”

“我准备好了，没什么要收拾的。”谢维克笑了，笑声清澈而纯粹，充满了喜悦。另一个人神情严肃地看着他，仿佛不太确定幸福究竟是什么，却又隐约感受到，或许是从远处记起了这种感觉。他站在谢维克身边，似乎有什么话想问，但最终什么也没说。“到阿纳瑞斯港时，天还没亮呢。”他最后说道，然后告辞离开，去收拾行李，到码头和谢维克会合。

谢韦克独自一人转身回到观察哨，看到耀眼的日出弧线正从特马埃河上缓缓升起。

“今晚我要躺在阿纳瑞斯岛上睡觉，”他想。“我要躺在塔克维尔旁边。我真希望我带了那幅画，那只小羊，去送给皮伦。”

但他什么也没带。他的双手空空如也，一如既往。

“You’re sure you want to walk through this wall with me, Ketho? You know, for me, it’s easy. Whatever happens, I am coming home. But you are leaving home. ‘True journey is return…’ ”

“I hope to return,” Ketho said in his quiet voice. “In time.”

“When are we to enter the landing craft?”

“In about twenty minutes.”

“I’m ready. I have nothing to pack.” Shevek laughed, a laugh of clear, unmixed happiness. The other man looked at him gravely, as if he was not sure what happiness was, and yet recognized or perhaps remembered it from afar. He stood beside Shevek as if there was something he wanted to ask him. But he did not ask it. “It will be early morning at Anarres Port,” he said at last, and took his leave, to get his things and meet Shevek at the launch port.

Alone, Shevek turned back to the observation port, and saw the blinding curve of sunrise over the Temae, just coming into sight.

“I will lie down to sleep on Anarres tonight,” he thought. “I will lie down beside Takver. I wish I’d brought the picture, the baby sheep, to give Pilun.”

But he had not brought anything. His hands were empty, as they had always been.

“真正的旅程即是回归”是奥多的一句格言，她将无政府工团主义带入乌拉斯，并最终建立了阿纳瑞斯。谢韦克的双手看似空洞，实则充满矛盾。勒古恩的道家思想是她的根基，而她的作品则是对这一根基的拓展。她的作品最打动我的，是其中蕴含的权威之声，既是审美的，也是道德的：

“True journey is return” is an adage of Odo, the woman who brought anarcho-syndicalism into Urras and thus ultimately founded Anarres. The perpetual emptiness of Shevek’s hands is paradoxically their fullness. Le Guin’s Taoism is her foundation, and her work was augmentation of the foundations. What moves me most in her books is the voice of authentic authority, at once aesthetic and moral:

文字是我的专长。我凿了一块石头。

三十年了，这件事还没完成。

那幅我无法看到的景象。

我无法完成它，也无法让它自由。

转化为能量。

Words are my matter. I have chipped one stone

for thirty years and still it is not done,

that image of the thing I cannot see.

I cannot finish it and set it free,

transformed to energy.

第四十五章

CHAPTER 45

失败者(1983)

The Loser (1983)

托马斯·伯恩哈德​

THOMAS BERNHARD

我读过托马斯·伯恩哈德的大部分作品，都是德语原版。这或许加剧了我对他作品的不安感。如今，我已八十八岁高龄，开始重读他的译本。这省时省力，却也让我有更多闲暇去感受他作品带来的不安。伯恩哈德的确乐于触动他最忠实的读者，这一点毋庸置疑。杰克·道森翻译的《失败者》在我看来忠于原著，尽管我尚未将其与德语原文进行比较。以我的年纪，每天只能勉强爬一次楼梯到三楼的书房兼图书馆。我听说，马克·安德森——一位令人敬佩的现代德国文学学者——也用杰克·道森的名字翻译了他自己的《失败者》。这其中似乎蕴含着某种伯恩哈德式的意味。

I HAVE READ MOST OF Thomas Bernhard in German. That may have augmented how disconcerting I found him. Now, at the age of eighty-eight, I have started to reread him in translation. That takes less effort but gives me more leisure to be upset by him. It is accurate to observe that Bernhard delighted in rattling even his most sympathetic readers. Jack Dawson’s version of The Loser seems faithful to me, though I have not compared it to the German text. At my age, climbing up the steps to my third-floor study and library is something I can manage only once a day. I gather that Mark Anderson, an admirable scholar of modern German literature, took the name of Jack Dawson for his own translation of The Loser. There is something Bernhardian about that.

伟大的加拿大钢琴家格伦·古尔德（1932-1982）的一生几乎处处都体现着伯恩哈德的风格，尽管两人从未谋面。伯恩哈德很可能在1958年和1959年两次在萨尔茨堡聆听过古尔德的演奏。古尔德人生中最不像伯恩哈德的，是他与指挥家兼作曲家卢卡斯·福斯的妻子科妮莉亚·福斯长达五年的恋情。当古尔德开始出现妄想症的症状，并有服用过量非必要药物的怪异行为时，科妮莉亚·福斯带着两个孩子回到了卢卡斯·福斯身边，这无疑令古尔德痛苦不堪。

There was everything (or almost everything) about the life of the great Canadian pianist Glenn Gould (1932–82) that was Bernhardian, though the two men never met. Probably Bernhard heard Gould play twice in Salzburg, in 1958 and 1959. The least Bernhardian aspect of Glenn Gould’s life was his five-year love affair with Cornelia Foss, wife of the conductor and composer Lukas Foss. When Gould began to show signs of paranoia and of weird overdosings with unnecessary medications, Cornelia Foss and her two children returned to Lukas Foss, doubtless to Gould’s sorrow.

伯恩哈德对此一无所知，这倒也好，因为知道了这件事会严重影响他的小说。他可以自由地发挥他那奇特的创造力。因此，弗拉基米尔·霍洛维茨从未教过人，尤其不可能教过格伦·古尔德，因为古尔德憎恨霍洛维茨。在《失败者》中，霍洛维茨似乎教导了叙述者古尔德和韦特海默——在古尔德这位执着的叙述者和不幸的韦特海默（他在五十一岁时自杀身亡）之间的斗争中，格伦·古尔德首先称韦特海默为“失败者”。格伦·古尔德五十岁去世，但伯恩哈德为了强化小说中令人不安的对称性，给古尔德多活了一年。伯恩哈德本人在五十八岁时接受了安乐死。

Bernhard could have known nothing about that, which is just as well, since it would have crippled his novel. He was free to indulge his bizarre inventiveness. Thus, Vladimir Horowitz never taught, and particularly could not have taught Glenn Gould, who loathed Horowitz. In The Loser, Horowitz supposedly teaches the narrator, Gould, and Wertheimer, whom Glenn Gould first labels “the loser” in the agon between Gould, the obsessive narrator, and the unfortunate Wertheimer, who commits suicide at the age of fifty-one. Glenn Gould died at fifty, but Bernhard adds a year to Gould’s life to abet the fearful symmetry of his novel. Bernhard himself was an assisted suicide at the age of fifty-eight.

伯恩哈德出生于荷兰，母亲未婚。他先是和祖父母一起生活，后来被带到巴伐利亚，被迫加入希特勒青年团，这让他十分不适应。他从未见过自己的父亲，父亲是个不正经的木匠，似乎在1940年自杀身亡。幸运的是，伯恩哈德的一位祖父安排他在奥地利接受音乐和艺术教育。更幸运的是，伯恩哈德与一位年长许多的女性建立了深厚的感情，这种感情是出于孝顺而非性欲。她成为了他的精神支柱，如同母亲一般。她去世后，伯恩哈德几乎孤身一人，过着苦行僧般的生活。由于患有肺结核，他无法成为一名歌手，于是转行从事新闻工作，之后又开始创作小说和戏剧。

Bernhard was born in Holland, the son of an unmarried mother. After living with his grandparents, he was taken to Bavaria, where he was required to serve in the Hitler Youth, not at all congenial to him. His father, whom he never met, was a crooked carpenter who seems to have committed suicide in 1940. Fortunately for Bernhard, one of his grandfathers arranged for him a musical and artistic education, in Austria. Again fortunately, Bernhard became attached to a much older woman, in a filial rather than sexual way. She became an emotional support or true mother to him. After she died, he was essentially alone, and always lived as an ascetic. Because he had tuberculosis, he could not become a singer, turned to journalism, and then to composing novels and plays.

伯恩哈德喜欢写一段没完没了的叙述者自言自语。我试着用德语或英语朗读他的作品时，很快就会气喘吁吁。他就像一位濒临死亡的内心演说家。你不能称他为讽刺作家、戏仿作家或反讽作家。他对一切都抱有矛盾的态度，尤其对奥地利更是如此。他想让我们相信，死亡的必然性使我们所有人都显得荒谬可笑。我想这对他来说是一种审美立场，但我并不认同。西格蒙德·弗洛伊德，这位最伟大的奥地利流亡者，曾敦促我们与死亡的必然性和解。这既严肃又成熟，而且是一种精神慰藉：它拓展了生命。伯恩哈德的艺术造诣令人叹服。他的观点自有其尊严。但我无法相信，我那不远的死亡会使我们中的任何人显得荒谬可笑。当然，这并不会贬低伯恩哈德的成就。

Bernhard tends to write an endless paragraph of his narrator’s dialogue with himself. When I try to read him out loud, in German or English, I quickly become breathless. He is a kind of interior orator on the verge of dying. One cannot call him a satirist, a parodist, or an ironist. Ambivalent about everything, Austria most of all, he wants us to believe that the inevitability of dying makes all of us ridiculous. I suppose that is in him an aesthetic stance, but I am unhappy with it. Sigmund Freud, the greatest of all Austrian exiles, urged us to make friends with the necessity of dying. That is somber, mature, and a tonic: it enlarges life. Bernhard’s artistry is compelling. His views have their own dignity. But I cannot believe that my own dying, which cannot be far away, makes any of us ridiculous. That of course does not vitiate Bernhard’s achievement.

如何定义伯恩哈德作品中的新颖之处和价值所在？他的确展现出一种与卡夫卡和卡内蒂相似的怪诞感，但又偏离了他们的路线，转而真正地颂扬矛盾心理，仿佛矛盾才是爱的真谛：

How can one define what is new and valuable in Bernhard? He does give a strangeness allied to Kafka and Canetti, but swerving from them into an actual celebration of ambivalence, as though it were the true form of love:

我心想，我自己也并非没有对格伦的恨意，我每时每刻都恨他，同时又无比坚定地爱着他。因为没有什么比看到一个如此杰出的人，他的杰出最终会摧毁我们，而我们却不得不眼睁睁地看着这一切发生，忍受这一切，最终不得不接受这一切更可怕的了。我们其实根本不相信这样的过程正在发生，恰恰相反，直到它成为无可辩驳的事实，我心想，那时一切都太迟了。我和韦特海默对格伦的成长至关重要，就像他生命中的其他一切一样，格伦利用了我们，我在旅店里这样想着。格伦做事时的傲慢，韦特海默的畏缩，以及我对一切事物的保留，我心想。突然之间，格伦变成了格伦·古尔德，在格伦·古尔德蜕变的那一刻，所有人都被忽略了，就连我和韦特海默也不例外，我不得不这样称呼它。

And I myself wasn’t free of Glenn hatred, I thought, I hated Glenn every moment, loved him at the same time with the utmost consistency. For there’s nothing more terrible than to see a person so magnificent that his magnificence destroys us and we must observe this process and put up with it and finally and ultimately also accept it, whereas we actually don’t believe such a process is happening, far from it, until it becomes an irrefutable fact, I thought, when it’s too late. Wertheimer and I had been necessary for Glenn’s development, like everything else in his life, Glenn misused us, I thought in the inn. The arrogance with which Glenn set about everything, Wertheimer’s fearful hesitation on the other hand, my reservations about everything and anything, I thought. Suddenly Glenn was Glenn Gould, everybody overlooked at the moment of the Glenn Gould transformation, as I have to call it, even Wertheimer and I.

被辉煌所毁灭，是软弱艺术家的宿命。接受辉煌与毁灭，方能走向萌芽的力量。马克·M·安德森在他为《失败者》所作的精彩后记中指出，正是叙述者对格伦·古尔德和韦特海默的热爱，才使这部小说免于自我嘲讽。“爱”无法定义：它意味着一切，也意味着虚无。对约翰·塞巴斯蒂安·巴赫的崇拜，几乎是一种普世的爱。每当我情绪低落时，我都会聆听内维尔·马里纳指挥的《音乐的奉献》（圣马丁室内乐团演奏）。在我这双缺乏音乐鉴赏力的耳朵听来，这便是至高无上的音乐，远超我应得的聆听。

To be destroyed by magnificence is the destiny of weak artists. To accept both magnificence and destruction is to move toward incipient strength. Mark M. Anderson, in his admirable afterword to The Loser, suggests that what saves the novel from its own self-mockery is the narrator’s love of Glenn Gould and Wertheimer. “Love” is beyond definition: it means everything and nothing. The worship of Johann Sebastian Bach is an all-but-universal form of love. Whenever I become too depressed, I listen to Neville Marriner’s recording of The Musical Offering (Academy of St Martin in the Fields). To my uneducated ear it is the ultimate music, more than I deserve to hear.

真正的格伦·古尔德和伯恩哈德鄙视他们认为带有自恋色彩的审美形式，例如海顿或莫扎特的奏鸣曲，以及司汤达、巴尔扎克和维克多·雨果的小说。这些作品达到了某种转折点或认知，最终促成了某种解决。古尔德和伯恩哈德崇拜巴赫，欣赏韦伯恩和勋伯格，并通过勋伯格及其学派（包括韦伯恩、阿尔班·贝尔格、恩斯特·克雷内克等人）的十二音序列主义来提炼巴赫的精髓。

The actual Glenn Gould and Bernhard disdained what they considered to be narcissistic aesthetic forms, like sonatas by Haydn or Mozart, novels by Stendhal, Balzac, and Victor Hugo. These achieved turning points or recognitions leading to resolution. Gould and Bernhard worshipped Bach, admired Webern and Schoenberg, and distilled Bach through the twelve-tone serialism of Schoenberg and his school: Webern, Alban Berg, Ernst Krenek, and others.

我认为阅读伯恩哈德小说的最佳准备是先阅读他的回忆录《收集证据》（1973-1982），由大卫·麦克林托克翻译。这五卷德文作品似乎小说成分至少与自传成分相当。《收集证据》以“我的奖项”一章结尾。书中对获奖经历的描述、三次获奖感言以及伯恩哈德从达姆施塔特语言与诗歌学院辞职的事件，同样融合了辛辣的虚构与真实的叙述，尽管伯恩哈德认为只有谎言才能被说出口并被人相信。在他看来，希特勒的国家社会主义和罗马天主教都不过是谎言。

I think the best preparation for reading Bernhard’s novels is to absorb first Gathering Evidence: A Memoir (1973–82), translated by David McLintock. The five German volumes seem at least as much fiction as autobiography. Gathering Evidence concludes with a section on “My Prizes.” The accounts of the prizes, three speeches on receiving awards, and Bernhard’s resignation from the Darmstadt Academy for Language and Poetry, also mix fierce fiction and truth telling, though Bernhard felt that only lies could be uttered and believed. For him the National Socialism of Hitler and the Roman Catholic Church alike were nothing but lies.

在《收集证据》一书接近尾声时，伯恩哈德给我们留下了一段非同寻常的文字：

Near the close of Gathering Evidence, Bernhard gives us an extraordinary passage:

与家乡的一切联系都断了。我没有收到家人的任何消息，而且据我所知，我对家里的情况也丝毫没有兴趣。他们没有给我写信，尽管他们完全可以不写；在埋葬了亲人之后，他们再也没有任何借口了。他们有他们的理由。我没有收到任何邮件，也不指望会收到。我沉浸在魏尔伦和特拉克尔的作品中，还读了陀思妥耶夫斯基的小说《群魔》。我一生中从未读过如此引人入胜、直击人心的作品，而且当时我也从未读过如此长篇的作品。它就像一种强效的毒品，让我一度完全沉浸其中。回家后的一段时间里，我拒绝阅读任何其他书籍，害怕再次陷入深深的失望之中。有好几个星期，我什么书都不读。《群魔》的震撼力让我变得坚强；它为我指明了一条可以遵循的道路，并告诉我我走在正确的道路上，这条路通往光明。我感受到了一部既狂野又伟大的作品所带来的冲击，从中我仿佛化身为英雄。文学作品很少能对我产生如此巨大的影响。我用在村里买的纸条，试图记录下一些对我来说重要的日期，一些我生命中的关键时刻，我害怕现在如此清晰的记忆会变得模糊，突然间从我脑海中消失，害怕它们会突然消失，害怕我再也没有力量将所有这些决定性的事件、骇人听闻的事件和荒诞的瞬间从遗忘的深渊中拯救出来。在这些纸条上，我试图保存所有可以保存的东西，所有我认为值得保存的东西，无一例外。我终于找到了自己的创作方法，我独有的恶名，我独特的残暴，我独特的品味，这些几乎与任何其他人的创作方法、恶名、残暴或品味都截然不同。什么是重要的？什么是有意义的？我当时觉得，我必须把脑子里的一切转移到这些纸片上，才能避免它们被遗忘。最后，纸片的数量达到了数百张，因为我不再信任我的大脑。我对我的大脑失去了信心——我对一切都失去了信心，因此也包括我的大脑。写诗的羞耻感比我想象的还要强烈，所以我一首诗也没写。我试着读祖父的书，却发现根本读不下去：这些年来，我经历了太多，见识了太多，所以我把它们搁置一边。我在《群魔》这本书里找到了我需要的东西。我在疗养院的图书馆里寻找其他类似的经典之作，却一无所获。我翻开那些书，又立刻合上，因为它们的庸俗和肤浅让我感到厌恶，所以一一列举那些作者的书是多余的。除了《群魔》之外……我当时根本没时间看文学作品，但我确信肯定还有其他类似的书。不过，在疗养院的图书馆里找是徒劳的，那里充斥着庸俗不堪、庸俗不堪的书籍，还有天主教和国家社会主义的书籍。

All contact with home had ceased. I got no news from my family, and as far as I remember I had no interest whatever in how things were at home. They did not write to me, though there was nothing to stop them; they no longer had any excuse after they had buried their dead. They had their reasons. I got no mail and I expected none. I immersed myself in Verlaine and Trakl, and I also read Dostoyevsky’s novel The Demons. Never in my whole life have I read a more engrossing and elemental work, and at the time I had never read such a long one. It had the effect of a powerful drug, and for a time I was totally absorbed by it. For some time after my return home I refused to read another book, fearing that I might be plunged headlong into the deepest disappointment. For weeks I refused to read anything at all. The monstrous quality of The Demons had made me strong; it had shown me a path that I could follow and told me that I was on the right one, the one that led out. I had felt the impact of a work that was both wild and great, and I emerged from the experience like a hero. Seldom has literature produced such an overwhelming effect on me. Using slips of paper which I had bought in the village, I tried to keep a record of certain dates which seemed important to me, certain crucial points in my existence, fearing that what was now so clear might blur and suddenly be lost on me, that it might suddenly vanish, and that I might no longer have the strength to save all these decisive occurrences, enormities, and absurdities from the obscurity of oblivion. On these slips of paper I tried to preserve everything that could be preserved, everything without exception which seemed to me to be worth preserving. I had now discovered my method of working, my own brand of infamy, my particular form of brutality, my own idiosyncratic taste, which had virtually nothing in common with anyone else’s method of working, anyone else’s infamy, anyone else’s brutality, or anyone else’s taste. What is important? What is significant? I believed that I must save everything from oblivion by transferring it from my brain onto these slips of paper, of which in the end there were hundreds, for I did not trust my brain. I had lost faith in my brain—I had lost faith in everything, hence even in my brain. The shame I felt at writing poetry was greater than I expected, and so I did not write a single poem. I tried to read my grandfather’s books, but found it impossible: I had experienced too much in the meantime, I had seen too much, and so I put them aside. What I needed I had found in The Demons. I searched the sanatorium library for other such elemental works, but there were none. It would be superfluous to enumerate the authors whose books I opened and immediately shut again, repelled by their cheapness and triviality. Apart from The Demons I had no time for literature, but I felt sure that there must be other books like it. But there was no point in looking for them in the sanatorium library, which was chock-full of tastelessness and banality, of Catholicism and National Socialism.

陀思妥耶夫斯基的《群魔》（1871-72）是他最狂野的作品，重读此书令我感到恐惧。这部作品是对俄国虚无主义的猛烈抨击，其化身尼古拉·斯塔夫罗金，其隐秘的野蛮和恶意甚至超过了《罪与罚》（1866）中的阿尔卡季·斯维德里盖洛夫。斯塔夫罗金强奸并逼死了一名十一岁的女孩。他甚至懒得救自己无力反抗的妻子。相比之下，斯维德里盖洛夫最终展现出一丝怜悯，表现得和善，并在自杀前留下了一句精彩的遗言：“我要去美国了。”

Dostoevsky’s The Demons (1871–72) is his wildest work, and rereading it frightens me. It is an assault on Russian nihilism, incarnated in Nikolai Stavrogin, a figure who exceeds Arkady Svidrigailov of Crime and Punishment (1866) in veiled savagery and malevolence. Stavrogin rapes and brings about the suicide of an eleven-year-old girl. He does not bother to save his own incapacitated wife from being murdered. Svidrigailov, in contrast, finally shows some compassion and behaves benignly, and then commits suicide with the splendid remark: “Going to America.”
